1 | # Walrus Code of Conduct
2 | 
3 | Walrus follows the same code of conduct as [Sui](https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui).
4 | 
5 | As an open-source project, we encourage free discussion rooted in respect. We endeavor to always be
6 | mindful of others' perspectives and ask all fellow contributors to do the same. We welcome you to
7 | the Walrus platform and ask you to help us grow it with relevant, on-point contributions.
8 | 
9 | ## Our pledge
10 | 
11 | We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a
12 | harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible
13 | disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience,
14 | education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, color, religion, or
15 | sexual identity and orientation.
16 | 
17 | We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and
18 | healthy community.
19 | 
20 | ## More information
21 | 
22 | See the central [Sui Code of Conduct](https://docs.sui.io/code-of-conduct) for full details.
23 | 
24 | Our Code of Conduct is adapted from the [Contributor Covenant version
25 | 2.1](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html).
```

walrus-docs/TRANSLATING.md
```
1 | # Translation Guidelines
2 | 
3 | The Walrus documentation uses [mdbook-i18n-helpers] as a translation framework.
4 | 
5 | ## Preparation
6 | 
7 | The following tools are required:
8 | 
9 | - GNU gettext utilities (`msgmerge` and `msgcat`)
10 | - mdbook-i18n-helpers (`cargo install mdbook-i18n-helpers`)
11 | 
12 | ## Creating and updating translations
13 | 
14 | Please see the [mdbook-i18n-helpers USAGE] file for the detailed usage of mdbook-i18n-helpers.
15 | We summarize the most important commands below.
16 | 
17 | ### Generating a message template
18 | 
19 | The generated message template `po/messages.pot` is required to create or update translations.
20 | 
21 | ```bash
22 | MDBOOK_OUTPUT='{"xgettext": {"pot-file": "messages.pot"}}' mdbook build -d po
23 | ```
24 | 
25 | ### Creating a new translation resource
26 | 
27 | In the following, replace `xx` by the [ISO 639][iso_639] language code.
28 | 
29 | ```bash
30 | msginit -i po/messages.pot -l xx -o po/xx.po
31 | ```
32 | 
33 | ### Updating an existing translation resource
34 | 
35 | ```bash
36 | msgmerge --update po/xx.po po/messages.pot
37 | ```
38 | 
39 | ## Editing translation resources
40 | 
41 | After generating a translation resource `po/xx.po`, you can write translation messages
42 | in `msgstr` entry of `po/xx.po`.
43 | To build a translated book, the following command can be used.
44 | 
45 | ```bash
46 | MDBOOK_BOOK__LANGUAGE=xx mdbook build
47 | MDBOOK_BOOK__LANGUAGE=xx mdbook serve
48 | ```
49 | 
50 | [mdbook-i18n-helpers]: https://github.com/google/mdbook-i18n-helpers
51 | [mdbook-i18n-helpers USAGE]: https://github.com/google/mdbook-i18n-helpers/blob/main/i18n-helpers
52 | [iso_639]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ISO_639-1_codes
```

move-book/book/foreword.md
```
1 | # Foreword
2 | 
3 | This book is dedicated to Move, a smart contract language that captures the essence of safe
4 | programming with digital assets. Move is designed around the following values:
5 | 
6 | 1. **Secure by default:** Insecure languages are a serious barrier both to accessible smart contract
7 |    development and to mainstream adoption of digital assets. The first duty of a smart contract
8 |    language is to prevent as many potential safety issues as possible (e.g. re-entrancy, missing
9 |    access control checks, arithmetic overflow, ...) by construction. Any changes to Move should
10 |    preserve or enhance its existing security guarantees.
11 | 
12 | 2. **Expressive by nature:** Move must enable programmers to write any smart contract they can
13 |    imagine. But we care as much about the way it _feels_ to write Move as we do about what Move
14 |    allows you to do - the language should be rich enough that the features needed for a task are
15 |    available, and minimal enough that the choice is obvious. The Move toolchain should be a
16 |    productivity enhancer and a thought partner.
17 | 
18 | 3. **Intuitive for all:** Smart contracts are only one part of a useful application. Move should
19 |    understand the broader context of its usage and design with both the smart contract developer and
20 |    the application developer in mind. It should be easy for developers to learn how to read
21 |    Move-managed state, build Move powered transactions, and write new Move code.
22 | 
23 | The core technical elements of Move are:
24 | 
25 | - Safe, familiar, and flexible abstractions for digital assets via programmable _objects_.
26 | - A rich _ability_ system (inspired by linear types) that gives programmers extreme control of how
27 |   values are created, destroyed, stored, copied, and transferred.
28 | - A _module_ system with strong encapsulation features to enable code reuse while maintaining this
29 |   control.
30 | - _Dynamic fields_ for creating hierarchical relationships between objects.
31 | - _Programmable transaction blocks_ (PTBs) to enable atomic client-side composition of Move-powered
32 |   APIs.
33 | 
34 | Move was born in 2018 as part of Facebook's Libra project. It was publicly revealed in 2019, the
35 | first Move-powered network launched in 2020. As of April 2024, there are numerous Move-powered
36 | chains in production with several more in the works. Move is an embedded language with a
37 | platform-agnostic core, which means it takes on a slightly different personality in each chain that
38 | uses it.
39 | 
40 | Creating a new programming language and bootstrapping a community around it is an ambitious, long
41 | term project. A language has to be an order of magnitude better than alternatives in relevant ways
42 | to have a chance, but even then the quality of the community matters more than the technical
43 | fundamentals. Move is a young language, but it's off to a good start in terms of both
44 | differentiation and community. A small, but fanatical group of smart contract programmers and core
45 | contributors united by the Move values are pushing the boundaries of what smart contracts can do,
46 | the applications they can enable, and who can (safely) write them. If that inspires you, read on!
47 | 
48 | — Sam Blackshear, creator of Move
```

move-book/reference/abilities.md
```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Abilities | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Abilities
7 | 
8 | Abilities are a typing feature in Move that control what actions are permissible for values of a
9 | given type. This system grants fine grained control over the "linear" typing behavior of values, as
10 | well as if and how values are used in storage (as defined by the specific deployment of Move, e.g.
11 | the notion of storage for the blockchain). This is implemented by gating access to certain bytecode
12 | instructions so that for a value to be used with the bytecode instruction, it must have the ability
13 | required (if one is required at all—not every instruction is gated by an ability).
14 | 
15 | For Sui, `key` is used to signify an [object](./abilities/object). Objects are the basic unit of
16 | storage where each object has a unique, 32-byte ID. `store` is then used to both indicate what data
17 | can be stored inside of an object, and is also used to indicate what types can be transferred
18 | outside of their defining module.
19 | 
20 | <!-- TODO future section on detailed walk through maybe. We have some examples at the end but it might be helpful to explain why we have precisely this set of abilities
21 | 
22 | If you are already somewhat familiar with abilities from writing Move programs, but are still confused as to what is going on, it might be helpful to skip to the [motivating walkthrough](#motivating-walkthrough) section to get an idea of what the system is setup in the way that it is. -->
23 | 
24 | ## The Four Abilities
25 | 
26 | The four abilities are:
27 | 
28 | - [`copy`](#copy)
29 |   - Allows values of types with this ability to be copied.
30 | - [`drop`](#drop)
31 |   - Allows values of types with this ability to be popped/dropped.
32 | - [`store`](#store)
33 |   - Allows values of types with this ability to exist inside a value in storage.
34 |   - For Sui, `store` controls what data can be stored inside of an [object](./abilities/object).
35 |     `store` also controls what types can be transferred outside of their defining module.
36 | - [`key`](#key)
37 |   - Allows the type to serve as a "key" for storage. Ostensibly this means the value can be a
38 |     top-level value in storage; in other words, it does not need to be contained in another value to
39 |     be in storage.
40 |   - For Sui, `key` is used to signify an [object](./abilities/object).
41 | 
42 | ### `copy`
43 | 
44 | The `copy` ability allows values of types with that ability to be copied. It gates the ability to
45 | copy values out of local variables with the [`copy`](./variables#move-and-copy) operator and to copy
46 | values via references with
47 | [dereference `*e`](./primitive-types/references#reading-and-writing-through-references).
48 | 
49 | If a value has `copy`, all values contained inside of that value have `copy`.
50 | 
51 | ### `drop`
52 | 
53 | The `drop` ability allows values of types with that ability to be dropped. By dropped, we mean that
54 | value is not transferred and is effectively destroyed as the Move program executes. As such, this
55 | ability gates the ability to ignore values in a multitude of locations, including:
56 | 
57 | - not using the value in a local variable or parameter
58 | - not using the value in a [sequence via `;`](./variables#expression-blocks)
59 | - overwriting values in variables in [assignments](./variables#assignments)
60 | - overwriting values via references when
61 |   [writing `*e1 = e2`](./primitive-types/references#reading-and-writing-through-references).
62 | 
63 | If a value has `drop`, all values contained inside of that value have `drop`.
64 | 
65 | ### `store`
66 | 
67 | The `store` ability allows values of types with this ability to exist inside of a value in storage,
68 | _but_ not necessarily as a top-level value in storage. This is the only ability that does not
69 | directly gate an operation. Instead it gates the existence in storage when used in tandem with
70 | `key`.
71 | 
72 | If a value has `store`, all values contained inside of that value have `store`.
73 | 
74 | For Sui, `store` serves double duty. It controls what values can appear inside of an
75 | [object](/storage/store-ability), and what objects can be
76 | [transferred](./abilities/object#transfer-rules) outside of their defining module.
77 | 
78 | ### `key`
79 | 
80 | The `key` ability allows the type to serve as a key for storage operations as defined by the
81 | deployment of Move. While it is specific per Move instance, it serves to gates all storage
82 | operations, so in order for a type to be used with storage primitives, the type must have the `key`
83 | ability.
84 | 
85 | If a value has `key`, all values contained inside of that value have `store`. This is the only
86 | ability with this sort of asymmetry.
87 | 
88 | For Sui, `key` is used to signify an [object](./abilities/object).
89 | 
90 | ## Builtin Types
91 | 
92 | All primitive, builtin types have `copy`, `drop`, and `store`.
93 | 
94 | - `bool`, `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `u128`, `u256`, and `address` all have `copy`, `drop`, and
95 |   `store`.
96 | - `vector<T>` may have `copy`, `drop`, and `store` depending on the abilities of `T`.
97 |   - See [Conditional Abilities and Generic Types](#conditional-abilities-and-generic-types) for more
98 |     details.
99 | - Immutable references `&` and mutable references `&mut` both have `copy` and `drop`.
100 |   - This refers to copying and dropping the reference itself, not what they refer to.
101 |   - References cannot appear in global storage, hence they do not have `store`.
102 | 
103 | Note that none of the primitive types have `key`, meaning none of them can be used directly with
104 | storage operations.
105 | 
106 | ## Annotating Structs and Enums
107 | 
108 | To declare that a `struct` or `enum` has an ability, it is declared with `has <ability>` after the
109 | datatype name and either before or after the fields/variants. For example:
110 | 
111 | ```move file=packages/reference/sources/abilities.move anchor=annotating_datatypes
112 | 
113 | ```
114 | 
115 | In this case: `Ignorable*` has the `drop` ability. `Pair*` and `MyVec*` both have `copy`, `drop`,
116 | and `store`.
117 | 
118 | All of these abilities have strong guarantees over these gated operations. The operation can be
119 | performed on the value only if it has that ability; even if the value is deeply nested inside of
120 | some other collection!
121 | 
122 | As such: when declaring a struct’s abilities, certain requirements are placed on the fields. All
123 | fields must satisfy these constraints. These rules are necessary so that structs satisfy the
124 | reachability rules for the abilities given above. If a struct is declared with the ability...
125 | 
126 | - `copy`, all fields must have `copy`.
127 | - `drop`, all fields must have `drop`.
128 | - `store`, all fields must have `store`.
129 | - `key`, all fields must have `store`.
130 |   - `key` is the only ability currently that doesn’t require itself.
131 | 
132 | An enum can have any of these abilities with the exception of `key`, which enums cannot have because
133 | they cannot be top-level values (objects) in storage. The same rules apply to fields of enum
134 | variants as they do for struct fields though. In particular, if an enum is declared with the
135 | ability...
136 | 
137 | - `copy`, all fields of all variants must have `copy`.
138 | - `drop`, all fields of all variants must have `drop`.
139 | - `store`, all fields of all variants must have `store`.
140 | - `key`, is not allowed on enums as previously mentioned.
141 | 
142 | For example:
143 | 
144 | ```move
145 | // A struct without any abilities
146 | public struct NoAbilities {}
147 | 
148 | public struct WantsCopy has copy {
149 |     f: NoAbilities, // ERROR 'NoAbilities' does not have 'copy'
150 | }
151 | 
152 | public enum WantsCopyEnum has copy {
153 |     Variant1
154 |     Variant2(NoAbilities), // ERROR 'NoAbilities' does not have 'copy'
155 | }
156 | ```
157 | 
158 | and similarly:
159 | 
160 | ```move
161 | // A struct without any abilities
162 | public struct NoAbilities {}
163 | 
164 | public struct MyData has key {
165 |     f: NoAbilities, // Error 'NoAbilities' does not have 'store'
166 | }
167 | 
168 | public struct MyDataEnum has store {
169 |     Variant1,
170 |     Variant2(NoAbilities), // Error 'NoAbilities' does not have 'store'
171 | }
172 | ```
173 | 
174 | ## Conditional Abilities and Generic Types
175 | 
176 | When abilities are annotated on a generic type, not all instances of that type are guaranteed to
177 | have that ability. Consider this struct declaration:
178 | 
179 | <!-- file=packages/reference/sources/abilities.move anchor=conditional_abilities -->
180 | 
181 | ```move
182 | public struct Cup<T> has copy, drop, store, key { item: T }
183 | ```
184 | 
185 | It might be very helpful if `Cup` could hold any type, regardless of its abilities. The type system
186 | can _see_ the type parameter, so it should be able to remove abilities from `Cup` if it _sees_ a
187 | type parameter that would violate the guarantees for that ability.
188 | 
189 | This behavior might sound a bit confusing at first, but it might be more understandable if we think
190 | about collection types. We could consider the builtin type `vector` to have the following type
191 | declaration:
192 | 
193 | ```move
194 | vector<T> has copy, drop, store;
195 | ```
196 | 
197 | We want `vector`s to work with any type. We don't want separate `vector` types for different
198 | abilities. So what are the rules we would want? Precisely the same that we would want with the field
199 | rules above. So, it would be safe to copy a `vector` value only if the inner elements can be copied.
200 | It would be safe to ignore a `vector` value only if the inner elements can be ignored/dropped. And,
[TRUNCATED]
```

move-book/reference/abort-and-assert.md
```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Abort and Assert | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Abort and Assert
7 | 
8 | [`return`](./functions) and `abort` are two control flow constructs that end execution, one for
9 | the current function and one for the entire transaction.
10 | 
11 | More information on [`return` can be found in the linked section](./functions#return-expression)
12 | 
13 | ## `abort`
14 | 
15 | `abort` is an expression that takes either takes no arguments, or just one - an **abort code** of
16 | type `u64`. For example:
17 | 
18 | ```move
19 | abort
20 | abort 42
21 | ```
22 | 
23 | The `abort` expression halts execution the current function and reverts all changes made to state by
24 | the current transaction (note though that this guarantee must be upheld by the adapter of the
25 | specific deployment of Move). There is no mechanism for "catching" or otherwise handling an `abort`.
26 | 
27 | Luckily, in Move transactions are all or nothing, meaning any changes to storage are made all at
28 | once only if the transaction succeeds. For Sui, this means no objects are modified.
29 | 
30 | Because of this transactional commitment of changes, after an abort there is no need to worry about
31 | backing out changes. While this approach is lacking in flexibility, it is incredibly simple and
32 | predictable.
33 | 
34 | Similar to [`return`](./functions), `abort` is useful for exiting control flow when some
35 | condition cannot be met.
36 | 
37 | In this example, the function will pop two items off of the vector, but will abort early if the
38 | vector does not have two items
39 | 
40 | <!-- {{#include ../../packages/reference/sources/abort-and-assert.move}} -->
41 | 
42 | ```move
43 | use std::vector;
44 | 
45 | fun pop_twice<T>(v: &mut vector<T>): (T, T) {
46 |     if (v.length() < 2) abort 42;
47 |     (v.pop_back(), v.pop_back())
48 | }
49 | ```
50 | 
51 | This is even more useful deep inside a control-flow construct. For example, this function checks
52 | that all numbers in the vector are less than the specified `bound`. And aborts otherwise
53 | 
54 | ```move
55 | use std::vector;
56 | fun check_vec(v: &vector<u64>, bound: u64) {
57 |     let mut i = 0;
58 |     let n = v.length();
59 |     while (i < n) {
60 |         let cur = v[i];
61 |         if (cur > bound) abort 42;
62 |         i = i + 1;
63 |     }
64 | }
65 | ```
66 | 
67 | ### `assert`
68 | 
69 | `assert` is a builtin, macro operation provided by the Move compiler. It takes two arguments, a
70 | condition of type `bool` and a code of type `u64`
71 | 
72 | ```move
73 | assert!(condition: bool, code: u64)
74 | ```
75 | 
76 | Since the operation is a macro, it must be invoked with the `!`. This is to convey that the
77 | arguments to `assert` are call-by-expression. In other words, `assert` is not a normal function and
78 | does not exist at the bytecode level. It is replaced inside the compiler with
79 | 
80 | ```move
81 | if (condition) () else abort code
82 | ```
83 | 
84 | `assert` is more commonly used than just `abort` by itself. The `abort` examples above can be
85 | rewritten using `assert`
86 | 
87 | ```move
88 | use std::vector;
89 | fun pop_twice<T>(v: &mut vector<T>): (T, T) {
90 |     assert!(v.length() >= 2, 42); // Now uses 'assert'
91 |     (v.pop_back(), v.pop_back())
92 | }
93 | ```
94 | 
95 | and
96 | 
97 | ```move
98 | use std::vector;
99 | fun check_vec(v: &vector<u64>, bound: u64) {
100 |     let mut i = 0;
101 |     let n = v.length();
102 |     while (i < n) {
103 |         let cur = v[i];
104 |         assert!(cur <= bound, 42); // Now uses 'assert'
105 |         i = i + 1;
106 |     }
107 | }
108 | ```
109 | 
110 | Note that because the operation is replaced with this `if-else`, the argument for the `code` is not
111 | always evaluated. For example:
112 | 
113 | ```move
114 | assert!(true, 1 / 0)
115 | ```
116 | 
117 | Will not result in an arithmetic error, it is equivalent to
118 | 
119 | ```move
120 | if (true) () else abort (1 / 0)
121 | ```
122 | 
123 | So the arithmetic expression is never evaluated!
124 | 
125 | ### Abort codes in the Move VM
126 | 
127 | When using `abort`, it is important to understand how the `u64` code will be used by the VM.
128 | 
129 | Normally, after successful execution, the Move VM, and the adapter for the specific deployment,
130 | determine the changes made to storage.
131 | 
132 | If an `abort` is reached, the VM will instead indicate an error. Included in that error will be two
133 | pieces of information:
134 | 
135 | - The module that produced the abort (package/address value and module name)
136 | - The abort code.
137 | 
138 | For example
139 | 
140 | ```move
141 | module 0x2::example {
142 |     public fun aborts() {
143 |         abort 42
144 |     }
145 | }
146 | 
147 | module 0x3::invoker {
148 |     public fun always_aborts() {
149 |         0x2::example::aborts()
150 |     }
151 | }
152 | ```
153 | 
154 | If a transaction, such as the function `always_aborts` above, calls `0x2::example::aborts`, the VM
155 | would produce an error that indicated the module `0x2::example` and the code `42`.
156 | 
157 | This can be useful for having multiple aborts being grouped together inside a module.
158 | 
159 | In this example, the module has two separate error codes used in multiple functions
160 | 
161 | ```move
162 | module 0::example;
163 | 
164 | use std::vector;
165 | 
166 | const EEmptyVector: u64 = 0;
167 | const EIndexOutOfBounds: u64 = 1;
168 | 
169 | // move i to j, move j to k, move k to i
170 | public fun rotate_three<T>(v: &mut vector<T>, i: u64, j: u64, k: u64) {
171 |     let n = v.length();
172 |     assert!(n > 0, EEmptyVector);
173 |     assert!(i < n, EIndexOutOfBounds);
174 |     assert!(j < n, EIndexOutOfBounds);
175 |     assert!(k < n, EIndexOutOfBounds);
176 | 
177 |     v.swap(i, k);
178 |     v.swap(j, k);
179 | }
180 | 
181 | public fun remove_twice<T>(v: &mut vector<T>, i: u64, j: u64): (T, T) {
182 |     let n = v.length();
183 |     assert!(n > 0, EEmptyVector);
184 |     assert!(i < n, EIndexOutOfBounds);
185 |     assert!(j < n, EIndexOutOfBounds);
186 |     assert!(i > j, EIndexOutOfBounds);
187 | 
188 |     (v.remove(i), v.remove(j))
189 | }
190 | ```
191 | 
192 | ## The type of `abort`
193 | 
194 | The `abort i` expression can have any type! This is because both constructs break from the normal
195 | control flow, so they never need to evaluate to the value of that type.
196 | 
197 | The following are not useful, but they will type check
198 | 
199 | ```move
200 | let y: address = abort 0;
201 | ```
202 | 
203 | This behavior can be helpful in situations where you have a branching instruction that produces a
204 | value on some branches, but not all. For example:
205 | 
206 | ```move
207 | let b =
208 |     if (x == 0) false
209 |     else if (x == 1) true
210 |     else abort 42;
211 | //       ^^^^^^^^ `abort 42` has type `bool`
212 | ```
```

move-book/reference/constants.md
```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Constants | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Constants
7 | 
8 | Constants are a way of giving a name to shared, static values inside of a `module`.
9 | 
10 | The constant's value must be known at compilation. The constant's value is stored in the compiled
11 | module. And each time the constant is used, a new copy of that value is made.
12 | 
13 | ## Declaration
14 | 
15 | Constant declarations begin with the `const` keyword, followed by a name, a type, and a value.
16 | 
17 | ```text
18 | const <name>: <type> = <expression>;
19 | ```
20 | 
21 | For example
22 | 
23 | ```move
24 | module a::example;
25 | 
26 | const MY_ADDRESS: address = @a;
27 | 
28 | public fun permissioned(addr: address) {
29 |     assert!(addr == MY_ADDRESS, 0);
30 | }
31 | ```
32 | 
33 | ## Naming
34 | 
35 | Constants must start with a capital letter `A` to `Z`. After the first letter, constant names can
36 | contain underscores `_`, letters `a` to `z`, letters `A` to `Z`, or digits `0` to `9`.
37 | 
38 | ```move
39 | const FLAG: bool = false;
40 | const EMyErrorCode: u64 = 0;
41 | const ADDRESS_42: address = @0x42;
42 | ```
43 | 
44 | Even though you can use letters `a` to `z` in a constant. The
45 | [general style guidelines](./coding-conventions) are to use just uppercase letters `A` to `Z`, with
46 | underscores `_` between each word. For error codes, we use `E` as a prefix and then upper camel case
47 | (also known as Pascal case) for the rest of the name, as seen in `EMyErrorCode`.
48 | 
49 | The current naming restriction of starting with `A` to `Z` is in place to give room for future
50 | language features.
51 | 
52 | ## Visibility
53 | 
54 | `public` or `public(package)` constants are not currently supported. `const` values can be used only
55 | in the declaring module. However, as a convenience, they can be used across modules in
56 | [unit tests attributes](./unit-testing).
57 | 
58 | ## Valid Expressions
59 | 
60 | Currently, constants are limited to the primitive types `bool`, `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `u128`,
61 | `u256`, `address`, and `vector<T>`, where `T` is the valid type for a constant.
62 | 
63 | ### Values
64 | 
65 | Commonly, `const`s are assigned a simple value, or literal, of their type. For example
66 | 
67 | ```move
68 | const MY_BOOL: bool = false;
69 | const MY_ADDRESS: address = @0x70DD;
70 | const BYTES: vector<u8> = b"hello world";
71 | const HEX_BYTES: vector<u8> = x"DEADBEEF";
72 | ```
73 | 
74 | ### Complex Expressions
75 | 
76 | In addition to literals, constants can include more complex expressions, as long as the compiler is
77 | able to reduce the expression to a value at compile time.
78 | 
79 | Currently, equality operations, all boolean operations, all bitwise operations, and all arithmetic
80 | operations can be used.
81 | 
82 | ```move
83 | const RULE: bool = true && false;
84 | const CAP: u64 = 10 * 100 + 1;
85 | const SHIFTY: u8 = {
86 |     (1 << 1) * (1 << 2) * (1 << 3) * (1 << 4)
87 | };
88 | const HALF_MAX: u128 = 340282366920938463463374607431768211455 / 2;
89 | const REM: u256 =
90 |     57896044618658097711785492504343953926634992332820282019728792003956564819968 % 654321;
91 | const EQUAL: bool = 1 == 1;
92 | ```
93 | 
94 | If the operation would result in a runtime exception, the compiler will give an error that it is
95 | unable to generate the constant's value
96 | 
97 | ```move
98 | const DIV_BY_ZERO: u64 = 1 / 0; // ERROR!
99 | const SHIFT_BY_A_LOT: u64 = 1 << 100; // ERROR!
100 | const NEGATIVE_U64: u64 = 0 - 1; // ERROR!
101 | ```
102 | 
103 | Additionally, constants can refer to other constants within the same module.
104 | 
105 | ```move
106 | const BASE: u8 = 4;
107 | const SQUARE: u8 = BASE * BASE;
108 | ```
109 | 
110 | Note though, that any cycle in the constant definitions results in an error.
111 | 
112 | ```move
113 | const A: u16 = B + 1;
114 | const B: u16 = A + 1; // ERROR!
115 | ```
```

5 | 
6 | # Control Flow
7 | 
8 | Move offers multiple constructs for control flow based on
9 | [boolean expressions](./primitive-types/bool), including common programming constructs such as `if`
10 | expressions and `while` and `for` loops, along with advanced control flow structures including
11 | labels for loops and escapable named blocks. It also supports more complex constructs based on
12 | structural pattern matching.
13 | 
14 | - [Conditional Expressions](./control-flow/conditionals)
15 | - [Pattern Matching](./control-flow/pattern-matching)
16 | - [Loops](./control-flow/loops)
17 | - [Labeled Control FLow](./control-flow/labeled-control-flow)
```

move-book/reference/enums.md
```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Enumerations | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Enumerations
7 | 
8 | An _enum_ is a user-defined data structure containing one or more _variants_. Each variant can
9 | optionally contain typed fields. The number, and types of these fields can differ for each variant
10 | in the enumeration. Fields in enums can store any non-reference, non-tuple type, including other
11 | structs or enums.
12 | 
13 | As a simple example, consider the following enum definition in Move:
14 | 
15 | ```move
16 | public enum Action {
17 |     Stop,
18 |     Pause { duration: u32 },
19 |     MoveTo { x: u64, y: u64 },
20 |     Jump(u64),
21 | }
22 | ```
23 | 
24 | This declares an enum `Action` that represents different actions that can be taken by a game -- you
25 | can `Stop`, `Pause` for a given duration, `MoveTo` a specific location, or `Jump` to a specific
26 | height.
27 | 
28 | Similar to structs, enums can have [abilities](./abilities) that control what operations can be
29 | performed on them. It is important to note however that enums cannot have the `key` ability since
30 | they cannot be top-level objects.
31 | 
32 | ## Defining Enums
33 | 
34 | Enums must be defined in a module, an enum must contain at least one variant, and each variant of an
35 | enum can either have no fields, positional fields, or named fields. Here are some examples of each:
36 | 
37 | ```move
38 | module a::m;
39 | 
40 | public enum Foo has drop {
41 |     VariantWithNoFields,
42 |     //                 ^ note: it is fine to have a trailing comma after variant declarations
43 | }
44 | public enum Bar has copy, drop {
45 |     VariantWithPositionalFields(u64, bool),
46 | }
47 | public enum Baz has drop {
48 |     VariantWithNamedFields { x: u64, y: bool, z: Bar },
49 | }
50 | ```
51 | 
52 | Enums cannot be recursive in any of their variants, so the following definitions of an enum are not
53 | allowed because they would be recursive in at least one variant.
54 | 
55 | Incorrect:
56 | 
57 | ```move
58 | module a::m;
59 | 
60 | public enum Foo {
61 |     Recursive(Foo),
62 |     //        ^ error: recursive enum variant
63 | }
64 | public enum List {
65 |     Nil,
66 |     Cons { head: u64, tail: List },
67 |     //                      ^ error: recursive enum variant
68 | }
69 | public enum BTree<T> {
70 |     Leaf(T),
71 |     Node { left: BTree<T>, right: BTree<T> },
72 |     //           ^ error: recursive enum variant
73 | }
74 | 
75 | // Mutually recursive enums are also not allowed
76 | public enum MutuallyRecursiveA {
77 |     Base,
78 |     Other(MutuallyRecursiveB),
79 |     //    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ error: recursive enum variant
80 | }
81 | 
82 | public enum MutuallyRecursiveB {
83 |     Base,
84 |     Other(MutuallyRecursiveA),
85 |     //    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ error: recursive enum variant
86 | }
87 | ```
88 | 
89 | ## Visibility
90 | 
91 | All enums are declared as `public`. This means that the type of the enum can be referred to from any
92 | other module. However, the variants of the enum, the fields within each variant, and the ability to
93 | create or destroy variants of the enum are internal to the module that defines the enum.
94 | 
95 | ### Abilities
96 | 
97 | Just like with structs, by default an enum declaration is linear and ephemeral. To use an enum value
98 | in a non-linear or non-ephemeral way -- i.e., copied, dropped, or stored in an
99 | [object](./abilities/object) -- you need to grant it additional [abilities](./abilities) by
100 | annotating them with `has <ability>`:
101 | 
102 | ```move
103 | module a::m;
104 | 
105 | public enum Foo has copy, drop {
106 |     VariantWithNoFields,
107 | }
108 | ```
109 | 
110 | The ability declaration can occur either before or after the enum's variants, however only one or
111 | the other can be used, and not both. If declared after the variants, the ability declaration must be
112 | terminated with a semicolon:
113 | 
114 | ```move
115 | module a::m;
116 | 
117 | public enum PreNamedAbilities has copy, drop { Variant }
118 | public enum PostNamedAbilities { Variant } has copy, drop;
119 | public enum PostNamedAbilitiesInvalid { Variant } has copy, drop
120 | //                                                              ^ ERROR! missing semicolon
121 | 
122 | public enum NamedInvalidAbilities has copy { Variant } has drop;
123 | //                                                     ^ ERROR! duplicate ability declaration
124 | ```
125 | 
126 | For more details, see the section on
127 | [annotating abilities](./abilities#annotating-structs-and-enums).
128 | 
129 | ## Naming
130 | 
131 | Enums and variants within enums must start with a capital letter `A` to `Z`. After the first letter,
132 | enum names can contain underscores `_`, lowercase letters `a` to `z`, uppercase letters `A` to `Z`,
133 | or digits `0` to `9`.
134 | 
135 | ```move
136 | public enum Foo { Variant }
137 | public enum BAR { Variant }
138 | public enum B_a_z_4_2 { V_a_riant_0 }
139 | ```
140 | 
141 | This naming restriction of starting with `A` to `Z` is in place to give room for future language
142 | features.
143 | 
144 | ## Using Enums
145 | 
146 | ### Creating Enum Variants
147 | 
148 | Values of an enum type can be created (or "packed") by indicating a variant of the enum, followed by
149 | a value for each field in the variant. The variant name must always be qualified by the enum's name.
150 | 
151 | Similarly to structs, for a variant with named fields, the order of the fields does not matter but
152 | the field names need to be provided. For a variant with positional fields, the order of the fields
153 | matters and the order of the fields must match the order in the variant declaration. It must also be
154 | created using `()` instead of `{}`. If the variant has no fields, the variant name is sufficient and
155 | no `()` or `{}` needs to be used.
156 | 
157 | ```move
158 | module a::m;
159 | 
160 | public enum Action has drop {
161 |     Stop,
162 |     Pause { duration: u32 },
163 |     MoveTo { x: u64, y: u64 },
164 |     Jump(u64),
165 | }
166 | public enum Other has drop {
167 |     Stop(u64),
168 | }
169 | 
170 | fun example() {
171 |     // Note: The `Stop` variant of `Action` doesn't have fields so no parentheses or curlies are needed.
172 |     let stop = Action::Stop;
173 |     let pause = Action::Pause { duration: 10 };
174 |     let move_to = Action::MoveTo { x: 10, y: 20 };
175 |     let jump = Action::Jump(10);
176 |     // Note: The `Stop` variant of `Other` does have positional fields so we need to supply them.
177 |     let other_stop = Other::Stop(10);
178 | }
179 | ```
180 | 
181 | For variants with named fields you can also use the shorthand syntax that you might be familiar with
182 | from structs to create the variant:
183 | 
184 | ```move
185 | let duration = 10;
186 | 
187 | let pause = Action::Pause { duration: duration };
188 | // is equivalent to
189 | let pause = Action::Pause { duration };
190 | ```
191 | 
192 | ### Pattern Matching Enum Variants and Destructuring
193 | 
194 | Since enum values can take on different shapes, dot access to fields of variants is not allowed like
195 | it is for struct fields. Instead, to access fields within a variant -- either by value, or immutable
196 | or mutable reference -- you must use pattern matching.
197 | 
198 | You can pattern match on Move values by value, immutable reference, and mutable reference. When
199 | pattern matching by value, the value is moved into the match arm. When pattern matching by
200 | reference, the value is borrowed into the match arm (either immutably or mutably). We'll go through
201 | a brief description of pattern matching using `match` here, but for more information on pattern
202 | matching using `match` in Move see the [Pattern Matching](./control-flow/pattern-matching) section.
203 | 
204 | A `match` statement is used to pattern match on a Move value and consists of a number of _match
205 | arms_. Each match arm consists of a pattern, an arrow `=>`, and an expression, followed by a comma
206 | `,`. The pattern can be a struct, enum variant, binding (`x`, `y`), wildcard (`_` or `..`), constant
207 | (`ConstValue`), or literal value (`true`, `42`, and so on). The value is matched against each
208 | pattern from the top-down, and will match the first pattern that structurally matches the value.
209 | Once the value is matched, the expression on the right hand side of the `=>` is executed.
210 | 
211 | Additionally, match arms can have optional _guards_ that are checked after the pattern matches but
212 | _before_ the expression is executed. Guards are specified by the `if` keyword followed by an
213 | expression that must evaluate to a boolean value before the `=>`.
214 | 
215 | ```move
216 | module a::m;
217 | 
218 | public enum Action has drop {
219 |     Stop,
220 |     Pause { duration: u32 },
221 |     MoveTo { x: u64, y: u64 },
222 |     Jump(u64),
223 | }
224 | 
225 | public struct GameState {
226 |     // Fields containing a game state
227 |     character_x: u64,
228 |     character_y: u64,
229 |     character_height: u64,
230 |     // ...
231 | }
232 | 
233 | fun perform_action(stat: &mut GameState, action: Action) {
234 |     match (action) {
235 |         // Handle the `Stop` variant
236 |         Action::Stop => state.stop(),
237 |         // Handle the `Pause` variant
238 |         // If the duration is 0, do nothing
239 |         Action::Pause { duration: 0 } => (),
240 |         Action::Pause { duration } => state.pause(duration),
241 |         // Handle the `MoveTo` variant
242 |         Action::MoveTo { x, y } => state.move_to(x, y),
243 |         // Handle the `Jump` variant
244 |         // if the game disallows jumps then do nothing
245 |         Action::Jump(_) if (state.jumps_not_allowed()) => (),
246 |         // otherwise, jump to the specified height
247 |         Action::Jump(height) => state.jump(height),
248 |     }
249 | }
250 | ```
251 | 
252 | To see how to pattern match on an enum to update values within it mutably, let's take the following
[TRUNCATED]
```

move-book/reference/equality.md
```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Equality | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Equality
7 | 
8 | Move supports two equality operations `==` and `!=`
9 | 
10 | ## Operations
11 | 
12 | | Syntax | Operation | Description                                                                 |
13 | | ------ | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
14 | | `==`   | equal     | Returns `true` if the two operands have the same value, `false` otherwise   |
15 | | `!=`   | not equal | Returns `true` if the two operands have different values, `false` otherwise |
16 | 
17 | ### Typing
18 | 
19 | Both the equal (`==`) and not-equal (`!=`) operations only work if both operands are the same type
20 | 
21 | ```move
22 | 0 == 0; // `true`
23 | 1u128 == 2u128; // `false`
24 | b"hello" != x"00"; // `true`
25 | ```
26 | 
27 | Equality and non-equality also work over _all_ user defined types!
28 | 
29 | ```move
30 | module 0::example;
31 | 
32 | public struct S has copy, drop { f: u64, s: vector<u8> }
33 | 
34 | fun always_true(): bool {
35 |     let s = S { f: 0, s: b"" };
36 |     s == s
37 | }
38 | 
39 | fun always_false(): bool {
40 |     let s = S { f: 0, s: b"" };
41 |     s != s
42 | }
43 | ```
44 | 
45 | If the operands have different types, there is a type checking error
46 | 
47 | ```move
48 | 1u8 == 1u128; // ERROR!
49 | //     ^^^^^ expected an argument of type 'u8'
50 | b"" != 0; // ERROR!
51 | //     ^ expected an argument of type 'vector<u8>'
52 | ```
53 | 
54 | ### Typing with references
55 | 
56 | When comparing [references](./primitive-types/references), the type of the reference (immutable or
57 | mutable) does not matter. This means that you can compare an immutable `&` reference with a mutable
58 | one `&mut` of the same underlying type.
59 | 
60 | ```move
61 | let i = &0;
62 | let m = &mut 1;
63 | 
64 | i == m; // `false`
65 | m == i; // `false`
66 | m == m; // `true`
67 | i == i; // `true`
68 | ```
69 | 
70 | The above is equivalent to applying an explicit freeze to each mutable reference where needed
71 | 
72 | ```move
73 | let i = &0;
74 | let m = &mut 1;
75 | 
76 | i == freeze(m); // `false`
77 | freeze(m) == i; // `false`
78 | m == m; // `true`
79 | i == i; // `true`
80 | ```
81 | 
82 | But again, the underlying type must be the same type
83 | 
84 | ```move
85 | let i = &0;
86 | let s = &b"";
87 | 
88 | i == s; // ERROR!
89 | //   ^ expected an argument of type '&u64'
90 | ```
91 | 
92 | ### Automatic Borrowing
93 | 
94 | Starting in Move 2024 edition, the `==` and `!=` operators automatically borrow their operands if
95 | one of the operands is a reference and the other is not. This means that the following code works
96 | without any errors:
97 | 
98 | ```move
99 | let r = &0;
100 | 
101 | // In all cases, `0` is automatically borrowed as `&0`
102 | r == 0; // `true`
103 | 0 == r; // `true`
104 | r != 0; // `false`
105 | 0 != r; // `false`
106 | ```
107 | 
108 | This automatic borrow is always an immutable borrow.
109 | 
110 | ## Restrictions
111 | 
112 | Both `==` and `!=` consume the value when comparing them. As a result, the type system enforces that
113 | the type must have [`drop`](./abilities). Recall that without the [`drop` ability](./abilities),
114 | ownership must be transferred by the end of the function, and such values can only be explicitly
115 | destroyed within their declaring module. If these were used directly with either equality `==` or
116 | non-equality `!=`, the value would be destroyed which would break [`drop` ability](./abilities)
117 | safety guarantees!
118 | 
119 | ```move
120 | module 0::example;
121 | 
122 | public struct Coin has store { value: u64 }
123 | fun invalid(c1: Coin, c2: Coin) {
124 |     c1 == c2 // ERROR!
125 | //  ^^    ^^ These assets would be destroyed!
126 | }
127 | ```
128 | 
129 | But, a programmer can _always_ borrow the value first instead of directly comparing the value, and
130 | reference types have the [`drop` ability](./abilities). For example
131 | 
132 | ```move
133 | module 0::example;
134 | 
135 | public struct Coin has store { value: u64 }
136 | fun swap_if_equal(c1: Coin, c2: Coin): (Coin, Coin) {
137 |     let are_equal = &c1 == c2; // valid, note `c2` is automatically borrowed
138 |     if (are_equal) (c2, c1) else (c1, c2)
139 | }
140 | ```
141 | 
142 | ## Avoid Extra Copies
143 | 
144 | While a programmer _can_ compare any value whose type has [`drop`](./abilities), a programmer should
145 | often compare by reference to avoid expensive copies.
146 | 
147 | ```move
148 | let v1: vector<u8> = function_that_returns_vector();
149 | let v2: vector<u8> = function_that_returns_vector();
150 | assert!(copy v1 == copy v2, 42);
151 | //      ^^^^       ^^^^
152 | use_two_vectors(v1, v2);
153 | 
154 | let s1: Foo = function_that_returns_large_struct();
155 | let s2: Foo = function_that_returns_large_struct();
156 | assert!(copy s1 == copy s2, 42);
157 | //      ^^^^       ^^^^
158 | use_two_foos(s1, s2);
159 | ```
160 | 
161 | This code is perfectly acceptable (assuming `Foo` has [`drop`](./abilities)), just not efficient.
162 | The highlighted copies can be removed and replaced with borrows
163 | 
164 | ```move
165 | let v1: vector<u8> = function_that_returns_vector();
166 | let v2: vector<u8> = function_that_returns_vector();
167 | assert!(&v1 == &v2, 42);
168 | //      ^      ^
169 | use_two_vectors(v1, v2);
170 | 
171 | let s1: Foo = function_that_returns_large_struct();
172 | let s2: Foo = function_that_returns_large_struct();
173 | assert!(&s1 == &s2, 42);
174 | //      ^      ^
175 | use_two_foos(s1, s2);
176 | ```
177 | 
178 | The efficiency of the `==` itself remains the same, but the `copy`s are removed and thus the program
179 | is more efficient.
```

```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Friends | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # DEPRECATED: Friends
7 | 
8 | NOTE: this feature has been superseded by [`public(package)`](./functions#visibility).
9 | 
10 | The `friend` syntax was used to declare modules that are trusted by the current module. A trusted
11 | module is allowed to call any function defined in the current module that have the `public(friend)`
12 | visibility. For details on function visibilities, refer to the _Visibility_ section in
13 | [Functions](./functions).
14 | 
15 | ## Friend declaration
16 | 
17 | A module can declare other modules as friends via friend declaration statements, in the format of
18 | 
19 | - `friend <address::name>` — friend declaration using fully qualified module name like the example
20 |   below, or
21 | 
22 |   ```move
23 |   module 0x42::a {
24 |       friend 0x42::b;
25 |   }
26 |   ```
27 | 
28 | - `friend <module-name-alias>` — friend declaration using a module name alias, where the module
29 |   alias is introduced via the `use` statement.
30 | 
31 |   ```move
32 |   module 0x42::a {
33 |       use 0x42::b;
34 |       friend b;
35 |   }
36 |   ```
37 | 
38 | A module may have multiple friend declarations, and the union of all the friend modules forms the
39 | friend list. In the example below, both `0x42::B` and `0x42::C` are considered as friends of
40 | `0x42::A`.
41 | 
42 | ```move
43 | module 0x42::a;
44 | 
45 | friend 0x42::b;
46 | friend 0x42::c;
47 | ```
48 | 
49 | Unlike `use` statements, `friend` can only be declared in the module scope and not in the expression
50 | block scope. `friend` declarations may be located anywhere a top-level construct (e.g., `use`,
51 | `function`, `struct`, etc.) is allowed. However, for readability, it is advised to place friend
52 | declarations near the beginning of the module definition.
53 | 
54 | ### Friend declaration rules
55 | 
56 | Friend declarations are subject to the following rules:
57 | 
58 | - A module cannot declare itself as a friend.
59 | 
60 |   ```move
61 |   module 0x42::m { friend Self; // ERROR! }
62 |   //                      ^^^^ Cannot declare the module itself as a friend
63 | 
64 |   module 0x43::m { friend 0x43::M; // ERROR! }
65 |   //                      ^^^^^^^ Cannot declare the module itself as a friend
66 |   ```
67 | 
68 | - Friend modules must be known by the compiler
69 | 
70 |   ```move
71 |   module 0x42::m { friend 0x42::nonexistent; // ERROR! }
72 |   //                      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ Unbound module '0x42::nonexistent'
73 |   ```
74 | 
75 | - Friend modules must be within the same account address.
76 | 
77 |   ```move
78 |   module 0x42::m {}
79 | 
80 |   module 0x42::n { friend 0x42::m; // ERROR! }
81 |   //                      ^^^^^^^ Cannot declare modules out of the current address as a friend
82 |   ```
83 | 
84 | - Friends relationships cannot create cyclic module dependencies.
85 | 
86 |   Cycles are not allowed in the friend relationships, e.g., the relation `0x2::a` friends `0x2::b`
87 |   friends `0x2::c` friends `0x2::a` is not allowed. More generally, declaring a friend module adds a
88 |   dependency upon the current module to the friend module (because the purpose is for the friend to
89 |   call functions in the current module). If that friend module is already used, either directly or
90 |   transitively, a cycle of dependencies would be created.
91 | 
92 |   ```move
93 |   module 0x2::a {
94 |       use 0x2::c;
95 |       friend 0x2::b;
96 | 
97 |       public fun a() {
98 |           c::c()
99 |       }
100 |   }
101 | 
102 |   module 0x2::b {
103 |       friend 0x2::c; // ERROR!
104 |   //         ^^^^^^ This friend relationship creates a dependency cycle: '0x2::b' is a friend of '0x2::a' uses '0x2::c' is a friend of '0x2::b'
105 |   }
106 | 
107 |   module 0x2::c {
108 |       public fun c() {}
109 |   }
110 |   ```
111 | 
112 | - The friend list for a module cannot contain duplicates.
113 | 
114 |   ```move
115 |   module 0x42::a {}
116 | 
117 |   module 0x42::m {
118 |       use 0x42::a as aliased_a;
119 |       friend 0x42::A;
120 |       friend aliased_a; // ERROR!
121 |   //         ^^^^^^^^^ Duplicate friend declaration '0x42::a'. Friend declarations in a module must be unique
122 |   }
123 |   ```
```

```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Functions | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Functions
7 | 
8 | Functions are declared inside of modules and define the logic and behavior of the module. Functions
9 | can be reused, either being called from other functions or as entry points for execution.
10 | 
11 | ## Declaration
12 | 
13 | Functions are declared with the `fun` keyword followed by the function name, type parameters,
14 | parameters, a return type, and finally the function body.
15 | 
16 | ```text
17 | <visibility>? <entry>? <macro>? fun <identifier><[type_parameters: constraint],*>([identifier: type],*): <return_type> <function_body>
18 | ```
19 | 
20 | For example
21 | 
22 | ```move
23 | fun foo<T1, T2>(x: u64, y: T1, z: T2): (T2, T1, u64) { (z, y, x) }
24 | ```
25 | 
26 | ### Visibility
27 | 
28 | Module functions, by default, can only be called within the same module. These internal (sometimes
29 | called private) functions cannot be called from other modules or as entry points.
30 | 
31 | ```move
32 | module a::m {
33 |     fun foo(): u64 { 0 }
34 |     fun calls_foo(): u64 { foo() } // valid
35 | }
36 | 
37 | module b::other {
38 |     fun calls_m_foo(): u64 {
39 |         a::m::foo() // ERROR!
40 | //      ^^^^^^^^^^^ 'foo' is internal to 'a::m'
41 |     }
42 | }
43 | ```
44 | 
45 | To allow access from other modules, the function must be declared `public` or `public(package)`.
46 | Tangential to visibility, an [`entry`](#entry-modifier) function can be called as an entry point for
47 | execution.
48 | 
49 | #### `public` visibility
50 | 
51 | A `public` function can be called by _any_ function defined in _any_ module. As shown in the
52 | following example, a `public` function can be called by:
53 | 
54 | - other functions defined in the same module,
55 | - functions defined in another module, or
56 | - as an entry point for execution.
57 | 
58 | ```move
59 | module a::m {
60 |     public fun foo(): u64 { 0 }
61 |     fun calls_foo(): u64 { foo() } // valid
62 | }
63 | 
64 | module b::other {
65 |     fun calls_m_foo(): u64 {
66 |         a::m::foo() // valid
67 |     }
68 | }
69 | ```
70 | 
71 | Fore more details on the entry point to execution see [the section below](#entry-modifier).
72 | 
73 | #### `public(package)` visibility
74 | 
75 | The `public(package)` visibility modifier is a more restricted form of the `public` modifier to give
76 | more control about where a function can be used. A `public(package)` function can be called by:
77 | 
78 | - other functions defined in the same module, or
79 | - other functions defined in the same package (the same address)
80 | 
81 | ```move
82 | module a::m {
83 |     public(package) fun foo(): u64 { 0 }
84 |     fun calls_foo(): u64 { foo() } // valid
85 | }
86 | 
87 | module a::n {
88 |     fun calls_m_foo(): u64 {
89 |         a::m::foo() // valid, also in `a`
90 |     }
91 | }
92 | 
93 | module b::other {
94 |     fun calls_m_foo(): u64 {
95 |         a::m::foo() // ERROR!
96 | //      ^^^^^^^^^^^ 'foo' can only be called from a module in `a`
97 |     }
98 | }
99 | ```
100 | 
101 | #### DEPRECATED `public(friend)` visibility
102 | 
103 | Before the addition of `public(package)`, `public(friend)` was used to allow limited public access
104 | to functions in the same package, but where the list of allowed modules had to be explicitly
105 | enumerated by the callee's module. see [Friends](./friends) for more details.
106 | 
107 | ### `entry` modifier
108 | 
109 | In addition to `public` functions, you might have some functions in your modules that you want to
110 | use as the entry point to execution. The `entry` modifier is designed to allow module functions to
111 | initiate execution, without having to expose the functionality to other modules.
112 | 
113 | Essentially, the combination of `public` and `entry` functions define the "main" functions of a
114 | module, and they specify where Move programs can start executing.
115 | 
116 | Keep in mind though, an `entry` function _can_ still be called by other Move functions. So while
117 | they _can_ serve as the start of a Move program, they aren't restricted to that case.
118 | 
119 | For example:
120 | 
121 | ```move
122 | module a::m {
123 |     entry fun foo(): u64 { 0 }
124 |     fun calls_foo(): u64 { foo() } // valid!
125 | }
126 | 
127 | module a::n {
128 |     fun calls_m_foo(): u64 {
129 |         a::m::foo() // ERROR!
130 | //      ^^^^^^^^^^^ 'foo' is internal to 'a::m'
131 |     }
132 | }
133 | ```
134 | 
135 | `entry` functions may have restrictions on their parameters and return types. Although, these
136 | restrictions are specific to each individual deployment of Move.
137 | 
138 | [The documentation for `entry` functions on Sui can be found here.](https://docs.sui.io/concepts/sui-move-concepts/entry-functions)
139 | 
140 | To enable easier testing, `entry` functions can be called from
141 | [`#[test]` and `#[test_only]`](./unit-testing) contexts.
142 | 
143 | ```move
144 | module a::m {
145 |     entry fun foo(): u64 { 0 }
146 | }
147 | module a::m_test {
148 |     #[test]
149 |     fun my_test(): u64 { a::m::foo() } // valid!
150 |     #[test_only]
151 |     fun my_test_helper(): u64 { a::m::foo() } // valid!
152 | }
153 | ```
154 | 
155 | ### `macro` modifier
156 | 
157 | Unlike normal functions, `macro` functions do not exist at runtime. Instead, these functions are
158 | substituted inline at each call site during compilation. These `macro` functions leverage this
159 | compilation process to provide functionality beyond standard functions, such as accepting
160 | higher-order _lambda_-style functions as arguments. These lambda arguments, also expanded during
161 | compilation, allow you to pass parts of the function body to the macro as arguments. For instance,
162 | consider the following simple loop macro, where the loop body is supplied as a lambda:
163 | 
164 | ```move
165 | macro fun n_times($n: u64, $body: |u64| -> ()) {
166 |     let n = $n;
167 |     let mut i = 0;
168 |     while (i < n) {
169 |         $body(i);
170 |         i = i + 1;
171 |     }
172 | }
173 | 
174 | fun example() {
175 |     let mut sum = 0;
176 |     n_times!(10, |x| sum = sum + x );
177 | }
178 | ```
179 | 
180 | See the chapter on [macros](./functions/macros) for more information.
181 | 
182 | ### Name
183 | 
184 | Function names can start with letters `a` to `z`. After the first character, function names can
185 | contain underscores `_`, letters `a` to `z`, letters `A` to `Z`, or digits `0` to `9`.
186 | 
187 | ```move
188 | fun fOO() {}
189 | fun bar_42() {}
190 | fun bAZ_19() {}
191 | ```
192 | 
193 | ### Type Parameters
194 | 
195 | After the name, functions can have type parameters
196 | 
197 | ```move
198 | fun id<T>(x: T): T { x }
199 | fun example<T1: copy, T2>(x: T1, y: T2): (T1, T1, T2) { (copy x, x, y) }
200 | ```
201 | 
202 | For more details, see [Move generics](./generics).
203 | 
204 | ### Parameters
205 | 
206 | Functions parameters are declared with a local variable name followed by a type annotation
207 | 
208 | ```move
209 | fun add(x: u64, y: u64): u64 { x + y }
210 | ```
211 | 
212 | We read this as `x` has type `u64`
213 | 
214 | A function does not have to have any parameters at all.
215 | 
216 | ```move
217 | fun useless() { }
218 | ```
219 | 
220 | This is very common for functions that create new or empty data structures
221 | 
222 | ```move
223 | module a::example;
224 | 
225 | public struct Counter { count: u64 }
226 | 
227 | fun new_counter(): Counter {
228 |     Counter { count: 0 }
229 | }
230 | ```
231 | 
232 | ### Return type
233 | 
234 | After the parameters, a function specifies its return type.
235 | 
236 | ```move
237 | fun zero(): u64 { 0 }
238 | ```
239 | 
240 | Here `: u64` indicates that the function's return type is `u64`.
241 | 
242 | Using [tuples](./primitive-types/tuples), a function can return multiple values:
243 | 
244 | ```move
245 | fun one_two_three(): (u64, u64, u64) { (0, 1, 2) }
246 | ```
247 | 
248 | If no return type is specified, the function has an implicit return type of unit `()`. These
249 | functions are equivalent:
250 | 
251 | ```move
252 | fun just_unit(): () { () }
253 | fun just_unit() { () }
254 | fun just_unit() { }
255 | ```
256 | 
257 | As mentioned in the [tuples section](./primitive-types/tuples), these tuple "values" do not exist as
258 | runtime values. This means that a function that returns unit `()` does not return any value during
259 | execution.
260 | 
261 | ### Function body
262 | 
263 | A function's body is an expression block. The return value of the function is the last value in the
264 | sequence
265 | 
266 | ```move
267 | fun example(): u64 {
268 |     let mut x = 0;
269 |     x = x + 1;
270 |     x // returns 'x'
271 | }
272 | ```
273 | 
274 | See [the section below for more information on returns](#returning-values)
275 | 
276 | For more information on expression blocks, see [Move variables](./variables).
277 | 
278 | ### Native Functions
279 | 
280 | Some functions do not have a body specified, and instead have the body provided by the VM. These
281 | functions are marked `native`.
282 | 
283 | Without modifying the VM source code, a programmer cannot add new native functions. Furthermore, it
284 | is the intent that `native` functions are used for either standard library code or for functionality
285 | needed for the given Move environment.
286 | 
287 | Most `native` functions you will likely see are in standard library code, such as `vector`
288 | 
289 | ```move
290 | module std::vector {
[TRUNCATED]
```

```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Generics | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Generics
7 | 
8 | Generics can be used to define functions and structs over different input data types. This language
9 | feature is sometimes referred to as parametric polymorphism. In Move, we will often use the term
10 | generics interchangeably with _type parameters_ and _type arguments_.
11 | 
12 | Generics are commonly used in library code, such as in [vector](./primitive-types/vector), to
13 | declare code that works over any possible type (that satisfies the specified constraints). This sort
14 | of parameterization allows you to reuse the same implementation across multiple types and
15 | situations.
16 | 
17 | ## Declaring Type Parameters
18 | 
19 | Both functions and structs can take a list of type parameters in their signatures, enclosed by a
20 | pair of angle brackets `<...>`.
21 | 
22 | ### Generic Functions
23 | 
24 | Type parameters for functions are placed after the function name and before the (value) parameter
25 | list. The following code defines a generic identity function that takes a value of any type and
26 | returns that value unchanged.
27 | 
28 | ```move
29 | fun id<T>(x: T): T {
30 |     // this type annotation is unnecessary but valid
31 |     (x: T)
32 | }
33 | ```
34 | 
35 | Once defined, the type parameter `T` can be used in parameter types, return types, and inside the
36 | function body.
37 | 
38 | ### Generic Structs
39 | 
40 | Type parameters for structs are placed after the struct name, and can be used to name the types of
41 | the fields.
42 | 
43 | ```move
44 | public struct Foo<T> has copy, drop { x: T }
45 | 
46 | public struct Bar<T1, T2> has copy, drop {
47 |     x: T1,
48 |     y: vector<T2>,
49 | }
50 | ```
51 | 
52 | Note that [type parameters do not have to be used](#unused-type-parameters)
53 | 
54 | ## Type Arguments
55 | 
56 | ### Calling Generic Functions
57 | 
58 | When calling a generic function, one can specify the type arguments for the function's type
59 | parameters in a list enclosed by a pair of angle brackets.
60 | 
61 | ```move
62 | fun foo() {
63 |     let x = id<bool>(true);
64 | }
65 | ```
66 | 
67 | If you do not specify the type arguments, Move's [type inference](#type-inference) will supply them
68 | for you.
69 | 
70 | ### Using Generic Structs
71 | 
72 | Similarly, one can attach a list of type arguments for the struct's type parameters when
73 | constructing or destructing values of generic types.
74 | 
75 | ```move
76 | fun foo() {
77 |     // type arguments on construction
78 |     let foo = Foo<bool> { x: true };
79 |     let bar = Bar<u64, u8> { x: 0, y: vector<u8>[] };
80 | 
81 |     // type arguments on destruction
82 |     let Foo<bool> { x } = foo;
83 |     let Bar<u64, u8> { x, y } = bar;
84 | }
85 | ```
86 | 
87 | In any case if you do not specify the type arguments, Move's [type inference](#type-inference) will
88 | supply them for you.
89 | 
90 | ### Type Argument Mismatch
91 | 
92 | If you specify the type arguments and they conflict with the actual values supplied, an error will
93 | be given:
94 | 
95 | ```move
96 | fun foo() {
97 |     let x = id<u64>(true); // ERROR! true is not a u64
98 | }
99 | ```
100 | 
101 | and similarly:
102 | 
103 | ```move
104 | fun foo() {
105 |     let foo = Foo<bool> { x: 0 }; // ERROR! 0 is not a bool
106 |     let Foo<address> { x } = foo; // ERROR! bool is incompatible with address
107 | }
108 | ```
109 | 
110 | ## Type Inference
111 | 
112 | In most cases, the Move compiler will be able to infer the type arguments so you don't have to write
113 | them down explicitly. Here's what the examples above would look like if we omit the type arguments:
114 | 
115 | ```move
116 | fun foo() {
117 |     let x = id(true);
118 |     //        ^ <bool> is inferred
119 | 
120 |     let foo = Foo { x: true };
121 |     //           ^ <bool> is inferred
122 | 
123 |     let Foo { x } = foo;
124 |     //     ^ <bool> is inferred
125 | }
126 | ```
127 | 
128 | Note: when the compiler is unable to infer the types, you'll need annotate them manually. A common
129 | scenario is to call a function with type parameters appearing only at return positions.
130 | 
131 | ```move
132 | module a::m;
133 | 
134 | fun foo() {
135 |     let v = vector[]; // ERROR!
136 |     //            ^ The compiler cannot figure out the element type, since it is never used
137 | 
138 |     let v = vector<u64>[];
139 |     //            ^~~~~ Must annotate manually in this case.
140 | }
141 | ```
142 | 
143 | Note that these cases are a bit contrived since the `vector[]` is never used, ad as such, Move's
144 | type inference cannot infer the type.
145 | 
146 | However, the compiler will be able to infer the type if that value is used later in that function:
147 | 
148 | ```move
149 | module a::m;
150 | 
151 | fun foo() {
152 |     let v = vector[];
153 |     //            ^ <u64> is inferred
154 |     vector::push_back(&mut v, 42);
155 |     //               ^ <u64> is inferred
156 | }
157 | ```
158 | 
159 | ### `_` Type
160 | 
161 | In some cases, you might want to explicitly annotate some of the type arguments, but let the
162 | compiler infer the others. The `_` type serves as such a placeholder for the compiler to infer the
163 | type.
164 | 
165 | ```move
166 | let bar = Bar<u64, _> { x: 0, y: vector[b"hello"] };
167 | //                 ^ vector<u8> is inferred
168 | ```
169 | 
170 | The placeholder `_` may only appear in expressions and macro function definitions, not signatures.
171 | This means you cannot use `_` as part of the definition of a function parameter, function return
172 | type, constant definition type, and datatype field.
173 | 
174 | ## Integers
175 | 
176 | In Move, the integer types `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `u128`, and `u256` are all distinct types.
177 | However, each one of these types can be created with the same numerical value syntax. In other
178 | words, if a type suffix is not provided, the compiler will infer the integer type based on the usage
179 | of the value.
180 | 
181 | ```move
182 | let x8: u8 = 0;
183 | let x16: u16 = 0;
184 | let x32: u32 = 0;
185 | let x64: u64 = 0;
186 | let x128: u128 = 0;
187 | let x256: u256 = 0;
188 | ```
189 | 
190 | If the value is not used in a context that requires a specific integer type, `u64` is taken as a
191 | default.
192 | 
193 | ```move
194 | let x = 0;
195 | //      ^ u64 is used by default
196 | ```
197 | 
198 | If the value however is too large for the inferred type, an error will be given
199 | 
200 | ```move
201 | let i: u8 = 256; // ERROR!
202 | //          ^^^ too large for u8
203 | let x = 340282366920938463463374607431768211454;
204 | //      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ too large for u64
205 | ```
206 | 
207 | In cases where the number is too large, you might need to annotate it explicitly
208 | 
209 | ```move
210 | let x = 340282366920938463463374607431768211454u128;
211 | //                                             ^^^^ valid!
212 | ```
213 | 
214 | ## Unused Type Parameters
215 | 
216 | For a struct definition, an unused type parameter is one that does not appear in any field defined
217 | in the struct, but is checked statically at compile time. Move allows unused type parameters so the
218 | following struct definition is valid:
219 | 
220 | ```move
221 | public struct Foo<T> {
222 |     foo: u64
223 | }
224 | ```
225 | 
226 | This can be convenient when modeling certain concepts. Here is an example:
227 | 
228 | ```move
229 | module a::m;
230 | 
231 | // Currency Specifiers
232 | public struct A {}
233 | public struct B {}
234 | 
235 | // A generic coin type that can be instantiated using a currency
236 | // specifier type.
237 | //   e.g. Coin<A>, Coin<B> etc.
238 | public struct Coin<Currency> has store {
239 |     value: u64
240 | }
241 | 
242 | // Write code generically about all currencies
243 | public fun mint_generic<Currency>(value: u64): Coin<Currency> {
244 |     Coin { value }
245 | }
246 | 
247 | // Write code concretely about one currency
248 | public fun mint_a(value: u64): Coin<A> {
249 |     mint_generic(value)
250 | }
251 | public fun mint_b(value: u64): Coin<B> {
252 |     mint_generic(value)
253 | }
254 | ```
255 | 
256 | In this example, `Coin<Currency>` is generic on the `Currency` type parameter, which specifies the
257 | currency of the coin and allows code to be written either generically on any currency or concretely
258 | on a specific currency. This generality applies even when the `Currency` type parameter does not
259 | appear in any of the fields defined in `Coin`.
260 | 
261 | ### Phantom Type Parameters
262 | 
263 | In the example above, although `struct Coin` asks for the `store` ability, neither `Coin<A>` nor
264 | `Coin<B>` will have the `store` ability. This is because of the rules for
265 | [Conditional Abilities and Generic Types](./abilities#conditional-abilities-and-generic-types) and
266 | the fact that `A` and `B` don't have the `store` ability, despite the fact that they are not even
267 | used in the body of `struct Coin`. This might cause some unpleasant consequences. For example, we
268 | are unable to put `Coin<A>` into a wallet in storage.
269 | 
270 | One possible solution would be to add spurious ability annotations to `A` and `B` (i.e.,
271 | `public struct Currency1 has store {}`). But, this might lead to bugs or security vulnerabilities
272 | because it weakens the types with unnecessary ability declarations. For example, we would never
[TRUNCATED]
```

1 | ---
2 | title: 'Index Syntax | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Index Syntax
7 | 
8 | Move provides syntax attributes to allow you to define operations that look and feel like native
9 | Move code, lowering these operations into your user-provided definitions.
10 | 
11 | Our first syntax method, `index`, allows you to define a group of operations that can be used as
12 | custom index accessors for your datatypes, such as accessing a matrix element as `m[i,j]`, by
13 | annotating functions that should be used for these index operations. Moreover, these definitions are
14 | bespoke per-type and available implicitly for any programmer using your type.
15 | 
16 | ## Overview and Summary
17 | 
18 | To start, consider a `Matrix` type that uses a vector of vectors to represent its values. You can
19 | write a small library using `index` syntax annotations on the `borrow` and `borrow_mut` functions as
20 | follows:
21 | 
22 | ```move
23 | module matrix::matrix;
24 | 
25 | public struct Matrix<T> { v: vector<vector<T>> }
26 | 
27 | #[syntax(index)]
28 | public fun borrow<T>(s: &Matrix<T>, i: u64, j: u64): &T {
29 |     vector::borrow(vector::borrow(&s.v, i), j)
30 | }
31 | 
32 | #[syntax(index)]
33 | public fun borrow_mut<T>(s: &mut Matrix<T>, i: u64, j: u64): &mut T {
34 |     vector::borrow_mut(vector::borrow_mut(&mut s.v, i), j)
35 | }
36 | 
37 | public fun make_matrix<T>(v: vector<vector<T>>):  Matrix<T> {
38 |     Matrix { v }
39 | }
40 | ```
41 | 
42 | Now anyone using this `Matrix` type has access to index syntax for it:
43 | 
44 | ```move
45 | let mut m = matrix::make_matrix(vector[
46 |     vector[1, 0, 0],
47 |     vector[0, 1, 0],
48 |     vector[0, 0, 1],
49 | ]);x
50 | 
51 | let mut i = 0;
52 | while (i < 3) {
53 |     let mut j = 0;
54 |     while (j < 3) {
55 |         if (i == j) {
56 |             assert!(m[i, j] == 1, 1);
57 |         } else {
58 |             assert!(m[i, j] == 0, 0);
59 |         };
60 |         *(&mut m[i,j]) = 2;
61 |         j = j + 1;
62 |     };
63 |     i = i + 1;
64 | }
65 | ```
66 | 
67 | ## Usage
68 | 
69 | As the example indicates, if you define a datatype and an associated index syntax method, anyone can
70 | invoke that method by writing index syntax on a value of that type:
71 | 
72 | ```move
73 | let mat = matrix::make_matrix(...);
74 | let m_0_0 = mat[0, 0];
75 | ```
76 | 
77 | During compilation, the compiler translates these into the appropriate function invocations based on
78 | the position and mutable usage of the expression:
79 | 
80 | ```move
81 | let mut mat = matrix::make_matrix(...);
82 | 
83 | let m_0_0 = mat[0, 0];
84 | // translates to `copy matrix::borrow(&mat, 0, 0)`
85 | 
86 | let m_0_0 = &mat[0, 0];
87 | // translates to `matrix::borrow(&mat, 0, 0)`
88 | 
89 | let m_0_0 = &mut mat[0, 0];
90 | // translates to `matrix::borrow_mut(&mut mat, 0, 0)`
91 | ```
92 | 
93 | You can also intermix index expressions with field accesses:
94 | 
95 | ```move
96 | public struct V { v: vector<u64> }
97 | 
98 | public struct Vs { vs: vector<V> }
99 | 
100 | fun borrow_first(input: &Vs): &u64 {
101 |     &input.vs[0].v[0]
102 |     // translates to `vector::borrow(&vector::borrow(&input.vs, 0).v, 0)`
103 | }
104 | ````
105 | 
106 | ### Index Functions Take Flexible Arguments
107 | 
108 | Note that, aside from the definition and type limitations described in the rest of this chapter,
109 | Move places no restrictions on the values your index syntax method takes as parameters. This allows
110 | you to implement intricate programmatic behavior when defining index syntax, such as a data
111 | structure that takes a default value if the index is out of bounds:
112 | 
113 | ```move
114 | #[syntax(index)]
115 | public fun borrow_or_set<Key: copy, Value: drop>(
116 |     input: &mut MTable<Key, Value>,
117 |     key: Key,
118 |     default: Value
119 | ): &mut Value {
120 |     if (contains(input, key)) {
121 |         borrow(input, key)
122 |     } else {
123 |         insert(input, key, default);
124 |         borrow(input, key)
125 |     }
126 | }
127 | ```
128 | 
129 | Now, when you index into `MTable`, you must also provide a default value:
130 | 
131 | ```move
132 | let string_key: String = ...;
133 | let mut table: MTable<String, u64> = m_table::make_table();
134 | let entry: &mut u64 = &mut table[string_key, 0];
135 | ```
136 | 
137 | This sort of extensible power allows you to write precise index interfaces for your types,
138 | concretely enforcing bespoke behavior.
139 | 
140 | ## Defining Index Syntax Functions
141 | 
142 | This powerful syntax form allows all of your user-defined datatypes to behave in this way, assuming
143 | your definitions adhere to the following rules:
144 | 
145 | 1. The `#[syntax(index)]` attribute is added to the designated functions defined in the same module
146 |    as the subject type.
147 | 1. The designated functions have `public` visibility.
148 | 1. The functions take a reference type as its subject type (its first argument) and returns a
149 |    matching references type (`mut` if the subject was `mut`).
150 | 1. Each type has only a single mutable and single immutable definition.
151 | 1. Immutable and mutable versions have type agreement:
152 |    - The subject types match, differing only in mutability.
153 |    - The return types match the mutability of their subject types.
154 |    - Type parameters, if present, have identical constraints between both versions.
155 |    - All parameters beyond the subject type are identical.
156 | 
157 | The following content and additional examples describe these rules in greater detail.
158 | 
159 | ### Declaration
160 | 
161 | To declare an index syntax method, add the `#[syntax(index)]` attribute above the relevant function
162 | definition in the same module as the subject type's definition. This signals to the compiler that
163 | the function is an index accessor for the specified type.
164 | 
165 | #### Immutable Accessor
166 | 
167 | The immutable index syntax method is defined for read-only access. It takes an immutable reference
168 | of the subject type and returns an immutable reference to the element type. The `borrow` function
169 | defined in `std::vector` is an example of this:
170 | 
171 | ```move
172 | #[syntax(index)]
173 | public native fun borrow<Element>(v: &vector<Element>, i: u64): &Element;
174 | ```
175 | 
176 | #### Mutable Accessor
177 | 
178 | The mutable index syntax method is the dual of the immutable one, allowing for both read and write
179 | operations. It takes a mutable reference of the subject type and returns a mutable reference to the
180 | element type. The `borrow_mut` function defined in `std::vector` is an example of this:
181 | 
182 | ```move
183 | #[syntax(index)]
184 | public native fun borrow_mut<Element>(v: &mut vector<Element>, i: u64): &mut Element;
185 | ```
186 | 
187 | #### Visibility
188 | 
189 | To ensure that indexing functions are available anywhere the type is used, all index syntax methods
190 | must have public visibility. This ensures ergonomic usage of indexing across modules and packages in
191 | Move.
192 | 
193 | #### No Duplicates
194 | 
195 | In addition to the above requirements, we restrict each subject base type to defining a single index
196 | syntax method for immutable references and a single index syntax method for mutable references. For
197 | example, you cannot define a specialized version for a polymorphic type:
198 | 
199 | ```move
200 | #[syntax(index)]
201 | public fun borrow_matrix_u64(s: &Matrix<u64>, i: u64, j: u64): &u64 { ... }
202 | 
203 | #[syntax(index)]
204 | public fun borrow_matrix<T>(s: &Matrix<T>, i: u64, j: u64): &T { ... }
205 |     // ERROR! Matrix already has a definition
206 |     // for its immutable index syntax method
207 | ```
208 | 
209 | This ensures that you can always tell which method is being invoked, without the need to inspect
210 | type instantiation.
211 | 
212 | ### Type Constraints
213 | 
214 | By default, an index syntax method has the following type constraints:
215 | 
216 | **Its subject type (first argument) must be a reference to a single type defined in the same module
217 | as the marked function.** This means that you cannot define index syntax methods for tuples, type
218 | parameters, or values:
219 | 
220 | ```move
221 | #[syntax(index)]
222 | public fun borrow_fst(x: &(u64, u64), ...): &u64 { ... }
223 |     // ERROR because the subject type is a tuple
224 | 
225 | #[syntax(index)]
226 | public fun borrow_tyarg<T>(x: &T, ...): &T { ... }
227 |     // ERROR because the subject type is a type parameter
228 | 
229 | #[syntax(index)]
230 | public fun borrow_value(x: Matrix<u64>, ...): &u64 { ... }
231 |     // ERROR because x is not a reference
232 | ```
233 | 
234 | **The subject type must match mutability with the return type.** This restriction allows you to
235 | clarify the expected behavior when borrowing an indexed expression as `&vec[i]` versus
236 | `&mut vec[i]`. The Move compiler uses the mutability marker to determine which borrow form to call
237 | to produce a reference of the appropriate mutability. As a result, we disallow index syntax methods
238 | whose subject and return mutability differ:
239 | 
240 | ```move
241 | #[syntax(index)]
242 | public fun borrow_imm(x: &mut Matrix<u64>, ...): &u64 { ... }
243 |     // ERROR! incompatible mutability
244 |     // expected a mutable reference '&mut' return type
245 | ```
246 | 
247 | ### Type Compatibility
248 | 
249 | When defining an immutable and mutable index syntax method pair, they are subject to a number of
250 | compatibility constraints:
251 | 
252 | 1. They must take the same number of type parameters, those type parameters must have the same
253 |    constraints.
[TRUNCATED]
```

1 | # The Move Reference
2 | 
3 | Welcome to Move, a next generation language for secure asset programming. Its primary use case is in
4 | blockchain environments, where Move programs are used to construct state changes. Move allows
5 | developers to write programs that flexibly manage and transfer assets, while providing the security
6 | and protections against attacks on those assets. However, Move has been developed with use cases in
7 | mind outside a blockchain context as well.
8 | 
9 | Move takes its cue from [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/) by using resource types with move (hence
10 | the name) semantics as an explicit representation of digital assets, such as currency.
11 |
