move-book/reference/method-syntax.md
```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Method Syntax | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Methods
7 | 
8 | As a syntactic convenience, some functions in Move can be called as "methods" on a value. This is done
9 | by using the `.` operator to call the function, where the value on the left-hand side of the `.` is
10 | the first argument to the function (sometimes called the receiver). The type of that value
11 | statically determines which function is called. This is an important difference from some other
12 | languages, where this syntax might indicate a dynamic call, where the function to be called is
13 | determined at runtime. In Move, all function calls are statically determined.
14 | 
15 | In short, this syntax exists to make it easier to call functions without having to create an alias
16 | with `use`, and without having to explicitly borrow the first argument to the function.
17 | Additionally, this can make code more readable, as it reduces the amount of boilerplate needed to
18 | call a function and makes it easier to chain function calls.
19 | 
20 | ## Syntax
21 | 
22 | The syntax for calling a method is as follows:
23 | 
24 | ```text
25 | <expression> . <identifier> <[type_arguments],*> ( <arguments> )
26 | ```
27 | 
28 | For example
29 | 
30 | ```move
31 | coin.value();
32 | *nums.borrow_mut(i) = 5;
33 | ```
34 | 
35 | ## Method Resolution
36 | 
37 | When a method is called, the compiler will statically determine which function is called based on
38 | the type of the receiver (the argument on the left-hand side of the `.`). The compiler maintains a
39 | mapping from type and method name to the module and function name that should be called. This
40 | mapping is created form the `use fun` aliases that are currently in scope, and from the appropriate
41 | functions in the receiver type's defining module. In all cases, the receiver type is the first
42 | argument to the function, whether by-value or by-reference.
43 | 
44 | In this section, when we say a method "resolves" to a function, we mean that the compiler will
45 | statically replace the method with a normal [function](./functions) call. For example if we have
46 | `x.foo(e)` with `foo` resolving to `a::m::foo`, the compiler will replace `x.foo(e)` with
47 | `a::m::foo(x, e)`, potentially [automatically borrowing](#automatic-borrowing) `x`.
48 | 
49 | ### Functions in the Defining Module
50 | 
51 | In a type’s defining module, the compiler will automatically create a method alias for any function
52 | declaration for its types when the type is the first argument in the function. For example,
53 | 
54 | ```move
55 | module a::m;
56 | 
57 | public struct X() has copy, drop, store;
58 | public fun foo(x: &X) { ... }
59 | public fun bar(flag: bool, x: &X) { ... }
60 | ```
61 | 
62 | The function `foo` can be called as a method on a value of type `X`. However, not the first argument
63 | (and one is not created for `bool` since `bool` is not defined in that module). For example,
64 | 
65 | ```move
66 | fun example(x: a::m::X) {
67 |     x.foo(); // valid
68 |     // x.bar(true); ERROR!
69 | }
70 | ```
71 | 
72 | ### `use fun` Aliases
73 | 
74 | Like a traditional [`use`](uses), a `use fun` statement creates an alias local to its current
75 | scope. This could be for the current module or the current expression block. However, the alias is
76 | associated to a type.
77 | 
78 | The syntax for a `use fun` statement is as follows:
79 | 
80 | ```move
81 | use fun <function> as <type>.<method alias>;
82 | ```
83 | 
84 | This creates an alias for the `<function>`, which the `<type>` can receive as `<method alias>`.
85 | 
86 | For example
87 | 
88 | ```move
89 | module a::cup;
90 | 
91 | public struct Cup<T>(T) has copy, drop, store;
92 | 
93 | public fun cup_borrow<T>(c: &Cup<T>): &T {
94 |     &c.0
95 | }
96 | 
97 | public fun cup_value<T>(c: Cup<T>): T {
98 |     let Cup(t) = c;
99 |     t
100 | }
101 | 
102 | public fun cup_swap<T: drop>(c: &mut Cup<T>, t: T) {
103 |     c.0 = t;
104 | }
105 | ```
106 | 
107 | We can now create `use fun` aliases to these functions
108 | 
109 | ```move
110 | module b::example;
111 | 
112 | use fun a::cup::cup_borrow as Cup.borrow;
113 | use fun a::cup::cup_value as Cup.value;
114 | use fun a::cup::cup_swap as Cup.set;
115 | 
116 | fun example(c: &mut Cup<u64>) {
117 |     let _ = c.borrow(); // resolves to a::cup::cup_borrow
118 |     let v = c.value(); // resolves to a::cup::cup_value
119 |     c.set(v * 2); // resolves to a::cup::cup_swap
120 | }
121 | ```
122 | 
123 | Note that the `<function>` in the `use fun` does not have to be a fully resolved path, and an alias
124 | can be used instead, so the declarations in the above example could equivalently be written as
125 | 
126 | ```move
127 | use a::cup::{Self, cup_swap};
128 | 
129 | use fun cup::cup_borrow as Cup.borrow;
130 | use fun cup::cup_value as Cup.value;
131 | use fun cup_swap as Cup.set;
132 | ```
133 | 
134 | While these examples are cute for renaming the functions in the current module, the feature is
135 | perhaps more useful for declaring methods on types from other modules. For example, if we wanted to
136 | add a new utility to `Cup`, we could do so with a `use fun` alias and still use method syntax
137 | 
138 | ```move
139 | module b::example;
140 | 
141 | fun double(c: &Cup<u64>): Cup<u64> {
142 |     let v = c.value();
143 |     Cup::new(v * 2)
144 | }
145 | ```
146 | 
147 | Normally, we would be stuck having to call it as `double(&c)` because `b::example` did not define
148 | `Cup`, but instead we can use a `use fun` alias
149 | 
150 | ```move
151 | fun double_double(c: Cup<u64>): (Cup<u64>, Cup<u64>) {
152 |     use fun b::example::double as Cup.dub;
153 |     (c.dub(), c.dub()) // resolves to b::example::double in both calls
154 | }
155 | ```
156 | 
157 | While `use fun` can be made in any scope, the target `<function>` of the `use fun` must have a first
158 | argument that is the same as the `<type>`.
159 | 
160 | ```move
161 | public struct X() has copy, drop, store;
162 | 
163 | fun new(): X { X() }
164 | fun flag(flag: bool): u8 { if (flag) 1 else 0 }
165 | 
166 | use fun new as X.new; // ERROR!
167 | use fun flag as X.flag; // ERROR!
168 | // Neither `new` nor `flag` has first argument of type `X`
169 | ```
170 | 
171 | But any first argument of the `<type>` can be used, including references and mutable references
172 | 
173 | ```move
174 | public struct X() has copy, drop, store;
175 | 
176 | public fun by_val(_: X) {}
177 | public fun by_ref(_: &X) {}
178 | public fun by_mut(_: &mut X) {}
179 | 
180 | // All 3 valid, in any scope
181 | use fun by_val as X.v;
182 | use fun by_ref as X.r;
183 | use fun by_mut as X.m;
184 | ```
185 | 
186 | Note for generics, the methods are associated for _all_ instances of the generic type. You cannot
187 | overload the method to resolve to different functions depending on the instantiation.
188 | 
189 | ```move
190 | public struct Cup<T>(T) has copy, drop, store;
191 | 
192 | public fun value<T: copy>(c: &Cup<T>): T {
193 |     c.0
194 | }
195 | 
196 | use fun value as Cup<bool>.flag; // ERROR!
197 | use fun value as Cup<u64>.num; // ERROR!
198 | // In both cases, `use fun` aliases cannot be generic, they must work for all instances of the type
199 | ```
200 | 
201 | ### `public use fun` Aliases
202 | 
203 | Unlike a traditional [`use`](uses), the `use fun` statement can be made `public`, which allows it
204 | to be used outside of its declared scope. A `use fun` can be made `public` if it is declared in the
205 | module that defines the receivers type, much like the method aliases that are
206 | [automatically created](#functions-in-the-defining-module) for functions in the defining module. Or
207 | conversely, one can think that an implicit `public use fun` is created automatically for every
208 | function in the defining module that has a first argument of the receiver type (if it is defined in
209 | that module). Both of these views are equivalent.
210 | 
211 | ```move
212 | module a::cup;
213 | 
214 | public struct Cup<T>(T) has copy, drop, store;
215 | 
216 | public use fun cup_borrow as Cup.borrow;
217 | public fun cup_borrow<T>(c: &Cup<T>): &T {
218 |     &c.0
219 | }
220 | ```
221 | 
222 | In this example, a public method alias is created for `a::cup::Cup.borrow` and
223 | `a::cup::Cup.cup_borrow`. Both resolve to `a::cup::cup_borrow`. And both are "public" in the sense
224 | that they can be used outside of `a::cup`, without an additional `use` or `use fun`.
225 | 
226 | ```move
227 | module b::example;
228 | 
229 | fun example<T: drop>(c: a::cup::Cup<u64>) {
230 |     c.borrow(); // resolves to a::cup::cup_borrow
231 |     c.cup_borrow(); // resolves to a::cup::cup_borrow
232 | }
233 | ```
234 | 
235 | The `public use fun` declarations thus serve as a way of renaming a function if you want to give it
236 | a cleaner name for use with method syntax. This is especially helpful if you have a module with
237 | multiple types, and similarly named functions for each type.
[TRUNCATED]
```

move-book/reference/modules.md
```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Modules | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Modules
7 | 
8 | **Modules** are the core program unit that define types along with functions that operate on these
9 | types. Struct types define the schema of Move's [storage](./abilities#key), and module functions
10 | define the rules interacting with values of those types. While modules themselves are also stored in
11 | storage, they are not accessible from within a Move program. In a blockchain environment, the
12 | modules are stored on chain in a process typically referred to as "publishing". After being
13 | published, [`entry`](./functions#entry-modifier) and [`public`](./functions#visibility)
14 | functions can be invoked according to the rules of that particular Move instance.
15 | 
16 | ## Syntax
17 | 
18 | A module has the following syntax:
19 | 
20 | ```text
21 | module <address>::<identifier> {
22 |     (<use> | <type> | <function> | <constant>)*
23 | }
24 | ```
25 | 
26 | where `<address>` is a valid [address](./primitive-types/address) specifying the module's
27 | package.
28 | 
29 | For example:
30 | 
31 | ```move
32 | module 0::test;
33 | 
34 | use std::debug;
35 | 
36 | const ONE: u64 = 1;
37 | 
38 | public struct Example has copy, drop { i: u64 }
39 | 
40 | public fun print(x: u64) {
41 |     let sum = x + ONE;
42 |     let example = Example { i: sum };
43 |     debug::print(&sum)
44 | }
45 | ```
46 | 
47 | ## Names
48 | 
49 | The `module test_addr::test` part specifies that the module `test` will be published under the
50 | numerical [address](./primitive-types/address) value assigned for the name `test_addr` in the
51 | [package settings](./packages).
52 | 
53 | Modules should normally be declared using [named addresses](./primitive-types/address) (as
54 | opposed to using the numerical value directly). For example:
55 | 
56 | ```move
57 | module test_addr::test;
58 | 
59 | use std::debug;
60 | use test_addr::another_test;
61 | 
62 | public struct Example has copy, drop { a: address }
63 | 
64 | public fun print() {
65 |     let example = Example { a: @test_addr };
66 |     debug::print(&example)
67 | }
68 | ```
69 | 
70 | These named addresses commonly match the name of the [package](./packages).
71 | 
72 | Because named addresses only exist at the source language level and during compilation, named
73 | addresses will be fully substituted for their value at the bytecode level. For example if we had the
74 | following code:
75 | 
76 | ```move
77 | fun example() {
78 |     my_addr::m::foo(@my_addr);
79 | }
80 | ```
81 | 
82 | and we compiled it with `my_addr` set to `0xC0FFEE`, then it would be operationally equivalent to
83 | the following:
84 | 
85 | ```move
86 | fun example() {
87 |     0xC0FFEE::m::foo(@0xC0FFEE);
88 | }
89 | ```
90 | 
91 | While at the source level these two different accesses are equivalent, it is a best practice to
92 | always use the named address and not the numerical value assigned to that address.
93 | 
94 | Module names can start with a lowercase letter from `a` to `z` or an uppercase letter from `A` to
95 | `Z`. After the first character, module names can contain underscores `_`, letters `a` to `z`,
96 | letters `A` to `Z`, or digits `0` to `9`.
97 | 
98 | ```move
99 | module a::my_module {}
100 | module a::foo_bar_42 {}
101 | ```
102 | 
103 | Typically, module names start with a lowercase letter. A module named `my_module` should be stored
104 | in a source file named `my_module.move`.
105 | 
106 | ## Members
107 | 
108 | All members inside a `module` block can appear in any order. Fundamentally, a module is a collection
109 | of [`types`](./structs) and [`functions`](./functions). The [`use`](./uses) keyword refers
110 | to members from other modules. The [`const`](./constants) keyword defines constants that can be
111 | used in the functions of a module.
112 | 
113 | The [`friend`](./friends) syntax is a deprecated concept for specifying a list of trusted
114 | modules. The concept has been superseded by [`public(package)`](./functions#visibility)
115 | 
116 | <!-- TODO member access rules -->
```

move-book/reference/packages.md
```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Packages | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Packages
7 | 
8 | Packages allow Move programmers to more easily re-use code and share it across projects. The Move
9 | package system allows programmers to easily:
10 | 
11 | - Define a package containing Move code;
12 | - Parameterize a package by [named addresses](./primitive-types/address);
13 | - Import and use packages in other Move code and instantiate named addresses;
14 | - Build packages and generate associated compilation artifacts from packages; and
15 | - Work with a common interface around compiled Move artifacts.
16 | 
17 | ## Package Layout and Manifest Syntax
18 | 
19 | A Move package source directory contains a `Move.toml` package manifest file, a generated
20 | `Move.lock` file, and a set of subdirectories:
21 | 
22 | ```plaintext
23 | a_move_package
24 | ├── Move.toml      (required)
25 | ├── Move.lock      (generated)
26 | ├── sources        (required)
27 | ├── doc_templates  (optional)
28 | ├── examples       (optional, test & dev mode)
29 | └── tests          (optional, test mode)
30 | ```
31 | 
32 | The directories and files labeled "required" must be present for a directory to be considered a Move
33 | package and built. Optional directories may be present, and if so, they will be included in the
34 | compilation process depending on the mode used to build the package. For instance, when built in
35 | "dev" or "test" modes, the `tests` and `examples` directories will also be included.
36 | 
37 | Going through each of these in turn:
38 | 
39 | 1. The [`Move.toml`](#movetoml) file is the package manifest and is required for a directory to be
40 |    considered a Move package. This file contains metadata about the package, such as name,
41 |    dependencies, and so on.
42 | 1. The [`Move.lock`](#movelock) file is generated by the Move CLI and contains the fixed build
43 |    versions of the package and its dependencies. It is used to ensure consistent versions are used
44 |    across different builds and that changes in dependencies are apparent as a change in this file.
45 | 1. The `sources` directory is required and contains the Move modules that make up the package.
46 |    Modules in this directory will always be included in the compilation process.
47 | 1. The `doc_templates` directory can contain documentation templates that will be used when
48 |    generating documentation for the package.
49 | 1. The `examples` directory can hold additional code to be used only for development and/or
50 |    tutorials, this will not be included when compiled outside of `test` or `dev` modes.
51 | 1. The `tests` directory can contain Move modules that are only included when compiled in `test`
52 |    mode or when [Move unit tests](./unit-testing) are run.
53 | 
54 | ### Move.toml
55 | 
56 | The Move package manifest is defined within the `Move.toml` file and has the following syntax.
57 | Optional fields are marked with `*`, `+` denotes one or more elements:
58 | 
59 | ```toml
60 | [package]
61 | name = <string>
62 | edition* = <string>      # e.g., "2024.alpha" to use the Move 2024 edition,
63 |                          # currently in alpha. Will default to the latest stable edition if not specified.
64 | license* = <string>              # e.g., "MIT", "GPL", "Apache 2.0"
65 | authors* = [<string>,+]  # e.g., ["Joe Smith (joesmith@noemail.com)", "John Snow (johnsnow@noemail.com)"]
66 | 
67 | # Additional fields may be added to this section by external tools. E.g., on Sui the following sections are added:
68 | published-at* = "<hex-address>" # The address that the package is published at. Should be set after the first publication.
69 | 
70 | [dependencies] # (Optional section) Paths to dependencies
71 | # One or more lines declaring dependencies in the following format
72 | 
73 | # ##### Local Dependencies #####
74 | # For local dependencies use `local = path`. Path is relative to the package root
75 | # Local = { local = "../path/to" }
76 | # To resolve a version conflict and force a specific version for dependency
77 | # override you can use `override = true`
78 | # Override = { local = "../conflicting/version", override = true }
79 | # To instantiate address values in a dependency, use `addr_subst`
80 | <string> = {
81 |     local = <string>,
82 |     override* = <bool>,
83 |     addr_subst* = { (<string> = (<string> | "<hex_address>"))+ }
84 | }
85 | 
86 | # ##### Git Dependencies #####
87 | # For remote import, use the `{ git = "...", subdir = "...", rev = "..." }`.
88 | # Revision must be supplied, it can be a branch, a tag, or a commit hash.
89 | # If no `subdir` is specified, the root of the repository is used.
90 | # MyRemotePackage = { git = "https://some.remote/host.git", subdir = "remote/path", rev = "main" }
91 | <string> = {
92 |     git = <URL ending in .git>,
93 |     subdir=<path to dir containing Move.toml inside git repo>,
94 |     rev=<git commit hash>,
95 |     override* = <bool>,
96 |     addr_subst* = { (<string> = (<string> | "<hex_address>"))+ }
97 | }
98 | 
99 | [addresses]  # (Optional section) Declares named addresses in this package
100 | # One or more lines declaring named addresses in the following format
101 | # Addresses that match the name of the package must be set to `"0x0"` or they will be unable to be published.
102 | <addr_name> = "_" | "<hex_address>" # e.g., std = "_" or my_addr = "0xC0FFEECAFE"
103 | 
104 | # Named addresses will be accessible in Move as `@name`. They're also exported:
105 | # for example, `std = "0x1"` is exported by the Standard Library.
106 | # alice = "0xA11CE"
107 | 
108 | [dev-dependencies] # (Optional section) Same as [dependencies] section, but only included in "dev" and "test" modes
109 | # The dev-dependencies section allows overriding dependencies for `--test` and
110 | # `--dev` modes. You can e.g., introduce test-only dependencies here.
111 | # Local = { local = "../path/to/dev-build" }
112 | <string> = {
113 |     local = <string>,
114 |     override* = <bool>,
115 |     addr_subst* = { (<string> = (<string> | "<hex_address>"))+ }
116 | }
117 | <string> = {
118 |     git = <URL ending in .git>,
119 |     subdir=<path to dir containing Move.toml inside git repo>,
120 |     rev=<git commit hash>,
121 |     override* = <bool>,
122 |     addr_subst* = { (<string> = (<string> | "<hex_address>"))+ }
123 | }
124 | 
125 | [dev-addresses] # (Optional section) Same as [addresses] section, but only included in "dev" and "test" modes
126 | # The dev-addresses section allows overwriting named addresses for the `--test`
127 | # and `--dev` modes.
128 | <addr_name> = "<hex_address>" # e.g., alice = "0xB0B"
129 | ```
130 | 
131 | An example of a minimal package manifest:
132 | 
133 | ```toml
134 | [package]
135 | name = "AName"
136 | ```
137 | 
138 | An example of a more standard package manifest that also includes the Move standard library and
139 | instantiates the named address `std` from the `LocalDep` package with the address value `0x1`:
140 | 
141 | ```toml
142 | [package]
143 | name = "AName"
144 | license = "Apache 2.0"
145 | 
146 | [addresses]
147 | address_to_be_filled_in = "_"
148 | specified_address = "0xB0B"
149 | 
150 | [dependencies]
151 | # Local dependency
152 | LocalDep = { local = "projects/move-awesomeness", addr_subst = { "std" = "0x1" } }
153 | # Git dependency
154 | MoveStdlib = { git = "https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui.git", subdir = "crates/sui-framework/packages/move-stdlib", rev = "framework/mainnet" }
155 | 
156 | [dev-addresses] # For use when developing this module
157 | address_to_be_filled_in = "0x101010101"
158 | ```
159 | 
160 | Most of the sections in the package manifest are self explanatory, but named addresses can be a bit
161 | difficult to understand so we examine them in more detail in
162 | [Named Addresses During Compilation](#named-addresses-during-compilation).
163 | 
164 | ## Named Addresses During Compilation
165 | 
166 | Recall that Move has [named addresses](./primitive-types/address) and that named addresses cannot be
167 | declared in Move. Instead they are declared at the package level: in the manifest file (`Move.toml`)
168 | for a Move package you declare named addresses in the package, instantiate other named addresses,
169 | and rename named addresses from other packages within the Move package system.
170 | 
171 | Let's go through each of these actions, and how they are performed in the package's manifest
172 | one-by-one:
173 | 
174 | ### Declaring Named Addresses
175 | 
176 | Let's say we have a Move module in `example_pkg/sources/A.move` as follows:
177 | 
178 | ```move
179 | module named_addr::a {
180 |     public fun x(): address { @named_addr }
181 | }
182 | ```
183 | 
184 | We could in `example_pkg/Move.toml` declare the named address `named_addr` in two different ways.
185 | The first:
186 | 
187 | ```toml
188 | [package]
189 | name = "example_pkg"
190 | ...
191 | [addresses]
192 | named_addr = "_"
193 | ```
194 | 
195 | Declares `named_addr` as a named address in the package `example_pkg` and that _this address can be
196 | any valid address value_. In particular, an importing package can pick the value of the named
197 | address `named_addr` to be any address it wishes. Intuitively you can think of this as
198 | parameterizing the package `example_pkg` by the named address `named_addr`, and the package can then
199 | be instantiated later on by an importing package.
200 | 
201 | `named_addr` can also be declared as:
202 | 
203 | ```toml
204 | [package]
205 | name = "example_pkg"
206 | ...
207 | [addresses]
208 | named_addr = "0xCAFE"
209 | ```
210 | 
211 | which states that the named address `named_addr` is exactly `0xCAFE` and cannot be changed. This is
212 | useful so other importing packages can use this named address without needing to worry about the
213 | exact value assigned to it.
214 | 
215 | With these two different declaration methods, there are two ways that information about named
216 | addresses can flow in the package graph:
217 | 
[TRUNCATED]
```

5 | 
6 | # Primitive Types
7 | 
8 | The primitive types are the basic building blocks of the language.
9 | 
10 | These primitive types can be used on their own or can be used to build more complex,
11 | user-defined types, e.g. in a [`struct`](./structs).
12 | 
13 | - [Integers](./primitive-types/integers)
14 | - [Bool](./primitive-types/bool)
15 | - [Address](./primitive-types/address)
16 | - [Vector](./primitive-types/vector)
17 | 
18 | These primitive types are used in conjunction with other types
19 | 
20 | - [References](./primitive-types/references)
21 | - [Tuples and Unit](./primitive-types/tuples)
```

move-book/reference/structs.md
```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Structs | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Structs and Resources
7 | 
8 | A _struct_ is a user-defined data structure containing typed fields. Structs can store any
9 | non-reference, non-tuple type, including other structs.
10 | 
11 | Structs can be used to define all "asset" values or unrestricted values, where the operations
12 | performed on those values can be controlled by the struct's [abilities](./abilities). By default,
13 | structs are linear and ephemeral. By this we mean that they: cannot be copied, cannot be dropped,
14 | and cannot be stored in storage. This means that all values have to have ownership transferred
15 | (linear) and the values must be dealt with by the end of the program's execution (ephemeral). We can
16 | relax this behavior by giving the struct [abilities](./abilities) which allow values to be copied
17 | or dropped and also to be stored in storage or to define storage schemas.
18 | 
19 | ## Defining Structs
20 | 
21 | Structs must be defined inside a module, and the struct's fields can either be named or positional:
22 | 
23 | ```move
24 | module a::m;
25 | 
26 | public struct Foo { x: u64, y: bool }
27 | public struct Bar {}
28 | public struct Baz { foo: Foo, }
29 | //                          ^ note: it is fine to have a trailing comma
30 | 
31 | public struct PosFoo(u64, bool)
32 | public struct PosBar()
33 | public struct PosBaz(Foo)
34 | ```
35 | 
36 | Structs cannot be recursive, so the following definitions are invalid:
37 | 
38 | ```move
39 | public struct Foo { x: Foo }
40 | //                     ^ ERROR! recursive definition
41 | 
42 | public struct A { b: B }
43 | public struct B { a: A }
44 | //                   ^ ERROR! recursive definition
45 | 
46 | public struct D(D)
47 | //              ^ ERROR! recursive definition
48 | ```
49 | 
50 | ### Visibility
51 | 
52 | As you may have noticed, all structs are declared as `public`. This means that the type of the
53 | struct can be referred to from any other module. However, the fields of the struct, and the ability
54 | to create or destroy the struct, are still internal to the module that defines the struct.
55 | 
56 | In the future, we plan on adding to declare structs as `public(package)` or as internal, much like
57 | [functions](./functions#visibility).
58 | 
59 | ### Abilities
60 | 
61 | As mentioned above: by default, a struct declaration is linear and ephemeral. So to allow the value
62 | to be used in these ways (e.g., copied, dropped, stored in an [object](./abilities/object), or
63 | used to define a storable [object](./abilities/object)), structs can be granted
64 | [abilities](./abilities) by annotating them with `has <ability>`:
65 | 
66 | ```move
67 | module a::m {
68 |     public struct Foo has copy, drop { x: u64, y: bool }
69 | }
70 | ```
71 | 
72 | The ability declaration can occur either before or after the struct's fields. However, only one or
73 | the other can be used, and not both. If declared after the struct's fields, the ability declaration
74 | must be terminated with a semicolon:
75 | 
76 | ```move
77 | module a::m;
78 | 
79 | public struct PreNamedAbilities has copy, drop { x: u64, y: bool }
80 | public struct PostNamedAbilities { x: u64, y: bool } has copy, drop;
81 | public struct PostNamedAbilitiesInvalid { x: u64, y: bool } has copy, drop
82 | //                                                                        ^ ERROR! missing semicolon
83 | 
84 | public struct NamedInvalidAbilities has copy { x: u64, y: bool } has drop;
85 | //                                                               ^ ERROR! duplicate ability declaration
86 | 
87 | public struct PrePositionalAbilities has copy, drop (u64, bool)
88 | public struct PostPositionalAbilities (u64, bool) has copy, drop;
89 | public struct PostPositionalAbilitiesInvalid (u64, bool) has copy, drop
90 | //                                                                     ^ ERROR! missing semicolon
91 | public struct InvalidAbilities has copy (u64, bool) has drop;
92 | //                                                  ^ ERROR! duplicate ability declaration
93 | ```
94 | 
95 | For more details, see the section on
96 | [annotating a struct's abilities](./abilities#annotating-structs-and-enums).
97 | 
98 | ### Naming
99 | 
100 | Structs must start with a capital letter `A` to `Z`. After the first letter, struct names can
101 | contain underscores `_`, letters `a` to `z`, letters `A` to `Z`, or digits `0` to `9`.
102 | 
103 | ```move
104 | public struct Foo {}
105 | public struct BAR {}
106 | public struct B_a_z_4_2 {}
107 | public struct P_o_s_Foo()
108 | ```
109 | 
110 | This naming restriction of starting with `A` to `Z` is in place to give room for future language
111 | features. It may or may not be removed later.
112 | 
113 | ## Using Structs
114 | 
115 | ### Creating Structs
116 | 
117 | Values of a struct type can be created (or "packed") by indicating the struct name, followed by
118 | value for each field.
119 | 
120 | For a struct with named fields, the order of the fields does not matter, but the field name needs to
121 | be provided. For a struct with positional fields, the order of the fields must match the order of
122 | the fields in the struct definition, and it must be created using `()` instead of `{}` to enclose
123 | the parameters.
124 | 
125 | ```move
126 | module a::m;
127 | 
128 | public struct Foo has drop { x: u64, y: bool }
129 | public struct Baz has drop { foo: Foo }
130 | public struct Positional(u64, bool) has drop;
131 | 
132 | fun example() {
133 |     let foo = Foo { x: 0, y: false };
134 |     let baz = Baz { foo: foo };
135 |     // Note: positional struct values are created using parentheses and
136 |     // based on position instead of name.
137 |     let pos = Positional(0, false);
138 |     let pos_invalid = Positional(false, 0);
139 |     //                           ^ ERROR! Fields are out of order and the types don't match.
140 | }
141 | ```
142 | 
143 | For structs with named fields, you can use the following shorthand if you have a local variable with
144 | the same name as the field:
145 | 
146 | ```move
147 | let baz = Baz { foo: foo };
148 | // is equivalent to
149 | let baz = Baz { foo };
150 | ```
151 | 
152 | This is sometimes called "field name punning".
153 | 
154 | ### Destroying Structs via Pattern Matching
155 | 
156 | Struct values can be destroyed by binding or assigning them in patterns using similar syntax to
157 | constructing them.
158 | 
159 | ```move
160 | module a::m;
161 | 
162 | public struct Foo { x: u64, y: bool }
163 | public struct Bar(Foo)
164 | public struct Baz {}
165 | public struct Qux()
166 | 
167 | fun example_destroy_foo() {
168 |     let foo = Foo { x: 3, y: false };
169 |     let Foo { x, y: foo_y } = foo;
170 |     //        ^ shorthand for `x: x`
171 | 
172 |     // two new bindings
173 |     //   x: u64 = 3
174 |     //   foo_y: bool = false
175 | }
176 | 
177 | fun example_destroy_foo_wildcard() {
178 |     let foo = Foo { x: 3, y: false };
179 |     let Foo { x, y: _ } = foo;
180 | 
181 |     // only one new binding since y was bound to a wildcard
182 |     //   x: u64 = 3
183 | }
184 | 
185 | fun example_destroy_foo_assignment() {
186 |     let x: u64;
187 |     let y: bool;
188 |     Foo { x, y } = Foo { x: 3, y: false };
189 | 
190 |     // mutating existing variables x and y
191 |     //   x = 3, y = false
192 | }
193 | 
194 | fun example_foo_ref() {
195 |     let foo = Foo { x: 3, y: false };
196 |     let Foo { x, y } = &foo;
197 | 
198 |     // two new bindings
199 |     //   x: &u64
200 |     //   y: &bool
201 | }
202 | 
203 | fun example_foo_ref_mut() {
204 |     let foo = Foo { x: 3, y: false };
205 |     let Foo { x, y } = &mut foo;
206 | 
207 |     // two new bindings
208 |     //   x: &mut u64
209 |     //   y: &mut bool
210 | }
211 | 
212 | fun example_destroy_bar() {
213 |     let bar = Bar(Foo { x: 3, y: false });
214 |     let Bar(Foo { x, y }) = bar;
215 |     //            ^ nested pattern
216 | 
217 |     // two new bindings
218 |     //   x: u64 = 3
219 |     //   y: bool = false
220 | }
221 | 
222 | fun example_destroy_baz() {
223 |     let baz = Baz {};
224 |     let Baz {} = baz;
225 | }
226 | 
227 | fun example_destroy_qux() {
228 |     let qux = Qux();
229 |     let Qux() = qux;
230 | }
231 | ```
232 | 
233 | ### Accessing Struct Fields
234 | 
235 | Fields of a struct can be accessed using the dot operator `.`.
236 | 
237 | For structs with named fields, the fields can be accessed by their name:
238 | 
239 | ```move
240 | public struct Foo { x: u64, y: bool }
241 | let foo = Foo { x: 3, y: true };
242 | let x = foo.x;  // x == 3
243 | let y = foo.y;  // y == true
244 | ```
245 | 
246 | For positional structs, fields can be accessed by their position in the struct definition:
247 | 
248 | ```move
249 | public struct PosFoo(u64, bool)
250 | let pos_foo = PosFoo(3, true);
251 | let x = pos_foo.0;  // x == 3
252 | let y = pos_foo.1;  // y == true
253 | ```
254 | 
255 | Accessing struct fields without borrowing or copying them is subject to the field's ability
256 | constraints. For more details see the sections on
257 | [borrowing structs and fields](#borrowing-structs-and-fields) and
258 | [reading and writing fields](#reading-and-writing-fields) for more information.
259 | 
260 | ### Borrowing Structs and Fields
261 | 
262 | The `&` and `&mut` operator can be used to create references to structs or fields. These examples
263 | include some optional type annotations (e.g., `: &Foo`) to demonstrate the type of operations.
264 | 
265 | ```move
[TRUNCATED]
```

1 | ---
2 | title: 'Unit Tests | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Unit Tests
7 | 
8 | Unit testing for Move uses three annotations in the Move source language:
9 | 
10 | - `#[test]` marks a function as a test;
11 | - `#[expected_failure]` marks that a test is expected to fail;
12 | - `#[test_only]` marks a module or module member ([`use`](./uses), [function](./functions),
13 |   [struct](./structs), or [constant](./constants)) as code to be included for testing only.
14 | 
15 | These annotations can be placed on any appropriate form with any visibility. Whenever a module or
16 | module member is annotated as `#[test_only]` or `#[test]`, it will not be included in the compiled
17 | bytecode unless it is compiled for testing.
18 | 
19 | ## Test Annotations
20 | 
21 | The `#[test]` annotation can only be placed on a function with no parameters. This annotation marks
22 | the function as a test to be run by the unit testing harness.
23 | 
24 | ```move
25 | #[test] // OK
26 | fun this_is_a_test() { ... }
27 | 
28 | #[test] // Will fail to compile since the test takes an argument
29 | fun this_is_not_correct(arg: u64) { ... }
30 | ```
31 | 
32 | A test can also be annotated as an `#[expected_failure]`. This annotation marks that the test is
33 | expected to raise an error. There are a number of options that can be used with the
34 | `#[expected_failure]` annotation to ensure only a failure with the specified condition is marked as
35 | passing, these options are detailed in [Expected Failures](#expected-failures). Only functions that
36 | have the `#[test]` annotation can also be annotated as an #`[expected_failure]`.
37 | 
38 | Some simple examples of using the `#[expected_failure]` annotation are shown below:
39 | 
40 | ```move
41 | #[test, expected_failure]
42 | public fun this_test_will_abort_and_pass() { abort 1 }
43 | 
44 | #[test, expected_failure]
45 | public fun test_will_error_and_pass() { 1/0; }
46 | 
47 | // Will pass since test fails with the expected abort code constant.
48 | // ENotFound is a constant defined in the module.
49 | #[test, expected_failure(abort_code = ENotFound)]
50 | public fun test_will_error_and_pass_abort_code() { abort ENotFound }
51 | 
52 | // Will fail since test fails with a different error than expected.
53 | #[test, expected_failure(abort_code = my_module::ENotFound)]
54 | public fun test_will_error_and_fail() { 1/0; }
55 | 
56 | #[test, expected_failure] // Can have multiple in one attribute. This test will pass.
57 | public fun this_other_test_will_abort_and_pass() { abort 1 }
58 | ```
59 | 
60 | > **Note**: `#[test]` and `#[test_only]` functions can also call
61 | > [`entry`](./functions#entry-modifier) functions, regardless of their visibility.
62 | 
63 | ## Expected Failures
64 | 
65 | There are a number of different ways that you can use the `#[expected_failure]` annotation to
66 | specify different types of error conditions. These are:
67 | 
68 | ### 1. `#[expected_failure(abort_code = <constant>)]`
69 | 
70 | This will pass if the test aborts with the specified constant value in the module that defines the
71 | constant and fail otherwise. This is the recommended way of testing for expected test failures.
72 | 
73 | > **Note**: You can reference constants outside of the current module or package in
74 | > `expected_failure` annotations.
75 | 
76 | ```move
77 | module pkg_addr::other_module {
78 |     const ENotFound: u64 = 1;
79 |     public fun will_abort() {
80 |         abort ENotFound
81 |     }
82 | }
83 | 
84 | module pkg_addr::my_module {
85 |     use pkg_addr::other_module;
86 |     const ENotFound: u64 = 1;
87 | 
88 |     #[test, expected_failure(abort_code = ENotFound)]
89 |     fun test_will_abort_and_pass() { abort ENotFound }
90 | 
91 |     #[test, expected_failure(abort_code = other_module::ENotFound)]
92 |     fun test_will_abort_and_pass() { other_module::will_abort() }
93 | 
94 |     // FAIL: Will not pass since we are expecting the constant from the wrong module.
95 |     #[test, expected_failure(abort_code = ENotFound)]
96 |     fun test_will_abort_and_pass() { other_module::will_abort() }
97 | }
98 | ```
99 | 
100 | ### 2. `#[expected_failure(arithmetic_error, location = <location>)]`
101 | 
102 | This specifies that the test is expected to fail with an arithmetic error (e.g., integer overflow,
103 | division by zero, etc.) at the specified location. The `<location>` must be a valid path to a module
104 | location, e.g., `Self`, or `my_package::my_module`.
105 | 
106 | ```move
107 | module pkg_addr::other_module {
108 |     public fun will_arith_error() { 1/0; }
109 | }
110 | 
111 | module pkg_addr::my_module {
112 |     use pkg_addr::other_module;
113 |     
114 |     #[test, expected_failure(arithmetic_error, location = Self)]
115 |     fun test_will_arith_error_and_pass1() { 1/0; }
116 | 
117 |     #[test, expected_failure(arithmetic_error, location = pkg_addr::other_module)]
118 |     fun test_will_arith_error_and_pass2() { other_module::will_arith_error() }
119 | 
120 |     // FAIL: Will fail since the location we expect it the fail at is different from where
121 |     // the test actually failed.
122 |     #[test, expected_failure(arithmetic_error, location = Self)]
123 |     fun test_will_arith_error_and_fail() { other_module::will_arith_error() }
124 | }
125 | ```
126 | 
127 | ### 3. `#[expected_failure(out_of_gas, location = <location>)]`
128 | 
129 | This specifies that the test is expected to fail with an out of gas error at the specified location.
130 | The `<location>` must be a valid path to a module location, e.g., `Self`, or
131 | `my_package::my_module`.
132 | 
133 | ```move
134 | module pkg_addr::other_module {
135 |     public fun will_oog() { loop {} }
136 | }
137 | 
138 | module pkg_addr::my_module {
139 |     use pkg_addr::other_module;
140 |     
141 |     #[test, expected_failure(out_of_gas, location = Self)]
142 |     fun test_will_oog_and_pass1() { loop {} }
143 | 
144 |     #[test, expected_failure(arithmetic_error, location = pkg_addr::other_module)]
145 |     fun test_will_oog_and_pass2() { other_module::will_oog() }
146 | 
147 |     // FAIL: Will fail since the location we expect it the fail at is different from where
148 |     // the test actually failed.
149 |     #[test, expected_failure(out_of_gas, location = Self)]
150 |     fun test_will_oog_and_fail() { other_module::will_oog() }
151 | }
152 | ```
153 | 
154 | ### 4. `#[expected_failure(vector_error, minor_status = <u64_opt>, location = <location>)]`
155 | 
156 | This specifies that the test is expected to fail with a vector error at the specified location with
157 | the given `minor_status` (if provided). The `<location>` must be a valid path to a module
158 | location, e.g., `Self`, or `my_package::my_module`. The `<u64_opt>` is an optional parameter that
159 | specifies the minor status of the vector error. If it is not specified, the test will pass if the
160 | test fails with any minor status. If it is specified, the test will only pass if the test fails with
161 | a vector error with the specified minor status.
162 | 
163 | ```move
164 | module pkg_addr::other_module {
165 |     public fun vector_borrow_empty() {
166 |         &vector<u64>[][1];
167 |     }
168 | }
169 | 
170 | module pkg_addr::my_module {
171 |     #[test, expected_failure(vector_error, location = Self)]
172 |     fun vector_abort_same_module() {
173 |         vector::borrow(&vector<u64>[], 1);
174 |     }
175 | 
176 |     #[test, expected_failure(vector_error, location = pkg_addr::other_module)]
177 |     fun vector_abort_same_module() {
178 |         other_module::vector_borrow_empty();
179 |     }
180 | 
181 |     // Can specify minor statues (i.e., vector-specific error codes) to expect.
182 |     #[test, expected_failure(vector_error, minor_status = 1, location = Self)]
183 |     fun native_abort_good_right_code() {
184 |         vector::borrow(&vector<u64>[], 1);
185 |     }
186 | 
187 |     // FAIL: correct error, but wrong location.
188 |     #[test, expected_failure(vector_error, location = pkg_addr::other_module)]
189 |     fun vector_abort_same_module() {
190 |         other_module::vector_borrow_empty();
191 |     }
192 | 
193 |     // FAIL: correct error and location but the minor status differs so this test will fail.
194 |     #[test, expected_failure(vector_error, minor_status = 0, location = Self)]
195 |     fun vector_abort_wrong_minor_code() {
196 |         vector::borrow(&vector<u64>[], 1);
197 |     }
198 | }
199 | ```
200 | 
201 | ### 5. `#[expected_failure]`
202 | 
203 | This will pass if the test aborts with _any_ error code. You should be **_incredibly careful_**
204 | using this to annotate expected tests failures, and always prefer one of the ways described above
205 | instead. Examples of these types of annotations are:
206 | 
207 | ```move
208 | #[test, expected_failure]
209 | fun test_will_abort_and_pass1() { abort 1 }
210 | 
211 | #[test, expected_failure]
212 | fun test_will_arith_error_and_pass2() { 1/0; }
213 | ```
214 | 
215 | ## Test Only Annotations
216 | 
217 | A module and any of its members can be declared as test only. If an item is annotated as
218 | `#[test_only]` the item will only be included in the compiled Move bytecode when compiled in test
219 | mode. Additionally, when compiled outside of test mode, any non-test `use`s of a `#[test_only]`
220 | module will raise an error during compilation.
221 | 
222 | > **Note**: functions that are annotated with `#[test_only]` will only be available to be called
223 | > from test code, but they themselves are not tests and will not be run as tests by the unit testing
224 | > framework.
225 | 
226 | ```move
227 | #[test_only] // test only attributes can be attached to modules
228 | module abc { ... }
229 | 
230 | #[test_only] // test only attributes can be attached to constants
[TRUNCATED]
```

```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Uses and Aliases | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Uses and Aliases
7 | 
8 | The `use` syntax can be used to create aliases to members in other modules. `use` can be used to
9 | create aliases that last either for the entire module, or for a given expression block scope.
10 | 
11 | ## Syntax
12 | 
13 | There are several different syntax cases for `use`. Starting with the most simple, we have the
14 | following for creating aliases to other modules
15 | 
16 | ```move
17 | use <address>::<module name>;
18 | use <address>::<module name> as <module alias name>;
19 | ```
20 | 
21 | For example
22 | 
23 | ```move
24 | use std::vector;
25 | use std::option as o;
26 | ```
27 | 
28 | `use std::vector;` introduces an alias `vector` for `std::vector`. This means that anywhere you
29 | would want to use the module name `std::vector` (assuming this `use` is in scope), you could use
30 | `vector` instead. `use std::vector;` is equivalent to `use std::vector as vector;`
31 | 
32 | Similarly `use std::option as o;` would let you use `o` instead of `std::option`
33 | 
34 | ```move
35 | use std::vector;
36 | use std::option as o;
37 | 
38 | fun new_vec(): vector<o::Option<u8>> {
39 |     let mut v = vector[];
40 |     vector::push_back(&mut v, o::some(0));
41 |     vector::push_back(&mut v, o::none());
42 |     v
43 | }
44 | ```
45 | 
46 | If you want to import a specific module member (such as a function or struct). You can use the
47 | following syntax.
48 | 
49 | ```move
50 | use <address>::<module name>::<module member>;
51 | use <address>::<module name>::<module member> as <member alias>;
52 | ```
53 | 
54 | For example
55 | 
56 | ```move
57 | use std::vector::push_back;
58 | use std::option::some as s;
59 | ```
60 | 
61 | This would let you use the function `std::vector::push_back` without full qualification. Similarly
62 | for `std::option::some` with `s`. Instead you could use `push_back` and `s` respectively. Again,
63 | `use std::vector::push_back;` is equivalent to `use std::vector::push_back as push_back;`
64 | 
65 | ```move
66 | use std::vector::push_back;
67 | use std::option::some as s;
68 | 
69 | fun new_vec(): vector<std::option::Option<u8>> {
70 |     let mut v = vector[];
71 |     vector::push_back(&mut v, s(0));
72 |     vector::push_back(&mut v, std::option::none());
73 |     v
74 | }
75 | ```
76 | 
77 | ### Multiple Aliases
78 | 
79 | If you want to add aliases for multiple module members at once, you can do so with the following
80 | syntax
81 | 
82 | ```move
83 | use <address>::<module name>::{<module member>, <module member> as <member alias> ... };
84 | ```
85 | 
86 | For example
87 | 
88 | ```move
89 | use std::vector::push_back;
90 | use std::option::{some as s, none as n};
91 | 
92 | fun new_vec(): vector<std::option::Option<u8>> {
93 |     let mut v = vector[];
94 |     push_back(&mut v, s(0));
95 |     push_back(&mut v, n());
96 |     v
97 | }
98 | ```
99 | 
100 | ### Self aliases
101 | 
102 | If you need to add an alias to the Module itself in addition to module members, you can do that in a
103 | single `use` using `Self`. `Self` is a member of sorts that refers to the module.
104 | 
105 | ```move
106 | use std::option::{Self, some, none};
107 | ```
108 | 
109 | For clarity, all of the following are equivalent:
110 | 
111 | ```move
112 | use std::option;
113 | use std::option as option;
114 | use std::option::Self;
115 | use std::option::Self as option;
116 | use std::option::{Self};
117 | use std::option::{Self as option};
118 | ```
119 | 
120 | ### Multiple Aliases for the Same Definition
121 | 
122 | If needed, you can have as many aliases for any item as you like
123 | 
124 | ```move
125 | use std::vector::push_back;
126 | use std::option::{Option, some, none};
127 | 
128 | fun new_vec(): vector<Option<u8>> {
129 |     let mut v = vector[];
130 |     push_back(&mut v, some(0));
131 |     push_back(&mut v, none());
132 |     v
133 | }
134 | ```
135 | 
136 | ### Nested imports
137 | 
138 | In Move, you can also import multiple names with the same `use` declaration. This brings all
139 | provided names into scope:
140 | 
141 | ```move
142 | use std::{
143 |     vector::{Self as vec, push_back},
144 |     string::{String, Self as str}
145 | };
146 | 
147 | fun example(s: &mut String) {
148 |     let mut v = vec::empty();
149 |     push_back(&mut v, 0);
150 |     push_back(&mut v, 10);
151 |     str::append_utf8(s, v);
152 | }
153 | ```
154 | 
155 | ## Inside a `module`
156 | 
157 | Inside of a `module` all `use` declarations are usable regardless of the order of declaration.
158 | 
159 | ```move
160 | module a::example;
161 | 
162 | use std::vector;
163 | 
164 | fun new_vec(): vector<Option<u8>> {
165 |     let mut v = vector[];
166 |     vector::push_back(&mut v, 0);
167 |     vector::push_back(&mut v, 10);
168 |     v
169 | }
170 | 
171 | use std::option::{Option, some, none};
172 | ```
173 | 
174 | The aliases declared by `use` in the module usable within that module.
175 | 
176 | Additionally, the aliases introduced cannot conflict with other module members. See
177 | [Uniqueness](#uniqueness) for more details
178 | 
179 | ## Inside an expression
180 | 
181 | You can add `use` declarations to the beginning of any expression block
182 | 
183 | ```move
184 | module a::example;
185 | 
186 | fun new_vec(): vector<Option<u8>> {
187 |     use std::vector::push_back;
188 |     use std::option::{Option, some, none};
189 | 
190 |     let mut v = vector[];
191 |     push_back(&mut v, some(0));
192 |     push_back(&mut v, none());
193 |     v
194 | }
195 | ```
196 | 
197 | As with `let`, the aliases introduced by `use` in an expression block are removed at the end of that
198 | block.
199 | 
200 | ```move
201 | module a::example;
202 | 
203 | fun new_vec(): vector<Option<u8>> {
204 |     let result = {
205 |         use std::vector::push_back;
206 |         use std::option::{Option, some, none};
207 | 
208 |         let mut v = vector[];
209 |         push_back(&mut v, some(0));
210 |         push_back(&mut v, none());
211 |         v
212 |     };
213 |     result
214 | }
215 | ```
216 | 
217 | Attempting to use the alias after the block ends will result in an error
218 | 
219 | ```move
220 | fun new_vec(): vector<Option<u8>> {
221 |     let mut result = {
222 |         use std::vector::push_back;
223 |         use std::option::{Option, some, none};
224 | 
225 |         let mut v = vector[];
226 |         push_back(&mut v, some(0));
227 |         v
228 |     };
229 |     push_back(&mut result, std::option::none());
230 |     // ^^^^^^ ERROR! unbound function 'push_back'
231 |     result
232 | }
233 | ```
234 | 
235 | Any `use` must be the first item in the block. If the `use` comes after any expression or `let`, it
236 | will result in a parsing error
237 | 
238 | ```move
239 | {
240 |     let mut v = vector[];
241 |     use std::vector; // ERROR!
242 | }
243 | ```
244 | 
245 | This allows you to shorten your import blocks in many situations. Note that these imports, as the
246 | previous ones, are all subject to the naming and uniqueness rules described in the following
247 | sections.
248 | 
249 | ## Naming rules
250 | 
251 | Aliases must follow the same rules as other module members. This means that aliases to structs (and
252 | constants) must start with `A` to `Z`
253 | 
254 | ```move
255 | module a::data {
256 |     public struct S {}
257 |     const FLAG: bool = false;
258 |     public fun foo() {}
259 | }
260 | module a::example {
261 |     use a::data::{
262 |         S as s, // ERROR!
263 |         FLAG as fLAG, // ERROR!
264 |         foo as FOO,  // valid
265 |         foo as bar, // valid
266 |     };
267 | }
268 | ```
269 | 
270 | ## Uniqueness
271 | 
272 | Inside a given scope, all aliases introduced by `use` declarations must be unique.
273 | 
274 | For a module, this means aliases introduced by `use` cannot overlap
275 | 
276 | ```move
277 | module a::example;
278 | 
279 | use std::option::{none as foo, some as foo}; // ERROR!
280 | //                                     ^^^ duplicate 'foo'
281 | 
282 | use std::option::none as bar;
283 | 
284 | use std::option::some as bar; // ERROR!
285 | //                       ^^^ duplicate 'bar'
286 | ```
287 | 
288 | And, they cannot overlap with any of the module's other members
289 | 
290 | ```move
291 | module a::data {
292 |     public struct S {}
293 | }
294 | 
295 | module example {
296 |     use a::data::S;
297 | 
298 |     public struct S { value: u64 } // ERROR!
299 |     //            ^ conflicts with alias 'S' above
300 | }
301 | ```
302 | 
303 | Inside of an expression block, they cannot overlap with each other, but they can
304 | [shadow](#shadowing) other aliases or names from an outer scope
305 | 
306 | ## Shadowing
307 | 
308 | `use` aliases inside of an expression block can shadow names (module members or aliases) from the
309 | outer scope. As with shadowing of locals, the shadowing ends at the end of the expression block;
310 | 
311 | ```move
312 | module a::example;
313 | 
314 | public struct WrappedVector { vec: vector<u64> }
315 | 
316 | public fun empty(): WrappedVector {
317 |     WrappedVector { vec: std::vector::empty() }
318 | }
319 | 
320 | public fun push_back(v: &mut WrappedVector, value: u64) {
[TRUNCATED]
```

move-book/reference/variables.md
```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Local Variables and Scope | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Local Variables and Scope
7 | 
8 | Local variables in Move are lexically (statically) scoped. New variables are introduced with the
9 | keyword `let`, which will shadow any previous local with the same name. Locals marked as `mut` are
10 | mutable and can be updated both directly and via a mutable reference.
11 | 
12 | ## Declaring Local Variables
13 | 
14 | ### `let` bindings
15 | 
16 | Move programs use `let` to bind variable names to values:
17 | 
18 | ```move
19 | let x = 1;
20 | let y = x + x;
21 | ```
22 | 
23 | `let` can also be used without binding a value to the local.
24 | 
25 | ```move
26 | let x;
27 | ```
28 | 
29 | The local can then be assigned a value later.
30 | 
31 | ```move
32 | let x;
33 | if (cond) {
34 |   x = 1
35 | } else {
36 |   x = 0
37 | }
38 | ```
39 | 
40 | This can be very helpful when trying to extract a value from a loop when a default value cannot be
41 | provided.
42 | 
43 | ```move
44 | let x;
45 | let mut i = 0;
46 | loop {
47 |     let (res, cond) = foo(i);
48 |     if (!cond) {
49 |         x = res;
50 |         break
51 |     };
52 |     i = i + 1;
53 | }
54 | ```
55 | 
56 | To modify a local variable _after_ it is assigned, or to borrow it mutably `&mut`, it must be
57 | declared as `mut`.
58 | 
59 | ```move
60 | let mut x = 0;
61 | if (cond) x = x + 1;
62 | foo(&mut x);
63 | ```
64 | 
65 | For more details see the section on [assignments](#assignments) below.
66 | 
67 | ### Variables must be assigned before use
68 | 
69 | Move's type system prevents a local variable from being used before it has been assigned.
70 | 
71 | ```move
72 | let x;
73 | // highlight-error
74 | x + x // ERROR! x is used before being assigned
75 | ```
76 | 
77 | ```move
78 | let x;
79 | if (cond) x = 0;
80 | // highlight-error
81 | x + x // ERROR! x does not have a value in all cases
82 | ```
83 | 
84 | ```move
85 | let x;
86 | while (cond) x = 0;
87 | // highlight-error
88 | x + x // ERROR! x does not have a value in all cases
89 | ```
90 | 
91 | ### Valid variable names
92 | 
93 | Variable names can contain underscores `_`, letters `a` to `z`, letters `A` to `Z`, and digits `0`
94 | to `9`. Variable names must start with either an underscore `_` or a letter `a` through `z`. They
95 | _cannot_ start with uppercase letters.
96 | 
97 | ```move
98 | // all valid
99 | let x = e;
100 | let _x = e;
101 | let _A = e;
102 | let x0 = e;
103 | let xA = e;
104 | let foobar_123 = e;
105 | 
106 | // all invalid
107 | // highlight-error-start
108 | let X = e; // ERROR!
109 | let Foo = e; // ERROR!
110 | // highlight-error-end
111 | ```
112 | 
113 | ### Type annotations
114 | 
115 | The type of a local variable can almost always be inferred by Move's type system. However, Move
116 | allows explicit type annotations that can be useful for readability, clarity, or debuggability. The
117 | syntax for adding a type annotation is:
118 | 
119 | ```move
120 | let x: T = e; // "Variable x of type T is initialized to expression e"
121 | ```
122 | 
123 | Some examples of explicit type annotations:
124 | 
125 | ```move
126 | module 0::example;
127 | 
128 | public struct S { f: u64, g: u64 }
129 | 
130 | fun annotated() {
131 |     let u: u8 = 0;
132 |     let b: vector<u8> = b"hello";
133 |     let a: address = @0x0;
134 |     let (x, y): (&u64, &mut u64) = (&0, &mut 1);
135 |     let S { f, g: f2 }: S = S { f: 0, g: 1 };
136 | }
137 | ```
138 | 
139 | Note that the type annotations must always be to the right of the pattern:
140 | 
141 | ```move
142 | // highlight-error-start
143 | // ERROR! should be let (x, y): (&u64, &mut u64) = ...
144 | let (x: &u64, y: &mut u64) = (&0, &mut 1);
145 | // highlight-error-end
146 | ```
147 | 
148 | ### When annotations are necessary
149 | 
150 | In some cases, a local type annotation is required if the type system cannot infer the type. This
151 | commonly occurs when the type argument for a generic type cannot be inferred. For example:
152 | 
153 | ```move
154 | // highlight-error-start
155 | let _v1 = vector[]; // ERROR!
156 | //        ^^^^^^^^ Could not infer this type. Try adding an annotation
157 | // highlight-error-end
158 | let v2: vector<u64> = vector[]; // no error
159 | ```
160 | 
161 | In a rarer case, the type system might not be able to infer a type for divergent code (where all the
162 | following code is unreachable). Both [`return`](./functions#return-expression) and
163 | [`abort`](./abort-and-assert) are expressions and can have any type. A
164 | [`loop`](./control-flow/loops) has type `()` if it has a `break` (or `T` if has a `break e` where
165 | `e: T`), but if there is no break out of the `loop`, it could have any type. If these types cannot
166 | be inferred, a type annotation is required. For example, this code:
167 | 
168 | ```move
169 | let a: u8 = return ();
170 | let b: bool = abort 0;
171 | let c: signer = loop ();
172 | 
173 | // highlight-error-start
174 | let x = return (); // ERROR!
175 | //  ^ Could not infer this type. Try adding an annotation
176 | let y = abort 0; // ERROR!
177 | //  ^ Could not infer this type. Try adding an annotation
178 | let z = loop (); // ERROR!
179 | //  ^ Could not infer this type. Try adding an annotation
180 | // highlight-error-end
181 | ```
182 | 
183 | Adding type annotations to this code will expose other errors about dead code or unused local
184 | variables, but the example is still helpful for understanding this problem.
185 | 
186 | ### Multiple declarations with tuples
187 | 
188 | `let` can introduce more than one local at a time using tuples. The locals declared inside the
189 | parenthesis are initialized to the corresponding values from the tuple.
190 | 
191 | ```move
192 | let () = ();
193 | let (x0, x1) = (0, 1);
194 | let (y0, y1, y2) = (0, 1, 2);
195 | let (z0, z1, z2, z3) = (0, 1, 2, 3);
196 | ```
197 | 
198 | The type of the expression must match the arity of the tuple pattern exactly.
199 | 
200 | ```move
201 | // highlight-error
202 | let (x, y) = (0, 1, 2); // ERROR!
203 | // highlight-error
204 | let (x, y, z, q) = (0, 1, 2); // ERROR!
205 | ```
206 | 
207 | You cannot declare more than one local with the same name in a single `let`.
208 | 
209 | ```move
210 | // highlight-error
211 | let (x, x) = 0; // ERROR!
212 | ```
213 | 
214 | The mutability of the local variables declared can be mixed.
215 | 
216 | ```move
217 | let (mut x, y) = (0, 1);
218 | x = 1;
219 | ```
220 | 
221 | ### Multiple declarations with structs
222 | 
223 | `let` can also introduce more than one local variables at a time when destructuring (or matching
224 | against) a struct. In this form, the `let` creates a set of local variables that are initialized to
225 | the values of the fields from a struct. The syntax looks like this:
226 | 
227 | ```move
228 | public struct T { f1: u64, f2: u64 }
229 | ```
230 | 
231 | ```move
232 | let T { f1: local1, f2: local2 } = T { f1: 1, f2: 2 };
233 | // local1: u64
234 | // local2: u64
235 | ```
236 | 
237 | Similarly for positional structs
238 | 
239 | ```move
240 | public struct P(u64, u64)
241 | ```
242 | 
243 | and
244 | 
245 | ```move
246 | let P (local1, local2) = P ( 1, 2 );
247 | // local1: u64
248 | // local2: u64
249 | ```
250 | 
251 | Here is a more complicated example:
252 | 
253 | ```move
254 | module 0::example;
255 | 
256 | public struct X(u64)
257 | public struct Y { x1: X, x2: X }
258 | 
259 | fun new_x(): X {
260 |     X(1)
261 | }
262 | 
263 | fun example() {
264 |     let Y { x1: X(f), x2 } = Y { x1: new_x(), x2: new_x() };
265 |     assert!(f + x2.0 == 2, 42);
266 | 
267 |     let Y { x1: X(f1), x2: X(f2) } = Y { x1: new_x(), x2: new_x() };
268 |     assert!(f1 + f2 == 2, 42);
269 | 
270 |     // `struct X` without `drop` ability and needs to be destroyed manually
271 |     let X(_) = x2;
272 | }
273 | ```
274 | 
275 | Fields of structs can serve double duty, identifying the field to bind _and_ the name of the
276 | variable. This is sometimes referred to as punning.
277 | 
278 | ```move
279 | let Y { x1, x2 } = e;
280 | ```
281 | 
282 | is equivalent to:
283 | 
284 | ```move
285 | let Y { x1: x1, x2: x2 } = e;
286 | ```
287 | 
288 | As shown with tuples, you cannot declare more than one local with the same name in a single `let`.
289 | 
290 | ```move
291 | // highlight-error
292 | let Y { x1: x, x2: x } = e; // ERROR!
293 | ```
294 | 
295 | And as with tuples, the mutability of the local variables declared can be mixed.
296 | 
[TRUNCATED]
```

1 | # Walrus Glossary
2 | 
3 | To make communication as clear and efficient as possible, we make sure to use a single term for
4 | every Walrus entity/concept and *do not* use any synonyms. The following table lists various
5 | concepts, their canonical name, and how they relate to or differ from other terms.
6 | 
7 | Italicized terms in the description indicate other specific Walrus terms contained in the table.
8 | 
9 | | Approved name                     | Description                                                                                                                                                                                 |
10 | |-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
11 | | storage node (SN)                 | entity storing data for Walrus; holds one or several *shards*                                                                                                                               |
12 | | blob                              | single unstructured data object stored on Walrus                                                                                                                                            |
13 | | permanent blob                    | blob which cannot be deleted by its owner and is guaranteed to be available until at least its expiry epoch (assuming it is valid)                                                          |
14 | | deletable blob                    | blob which can be deleted by its owner at any time to be able to reuse the storage resource                                                                                                 |
15 | | shard                             | (disjoint) subset of erasure-encoded data of all *blobs*; at every point in time, a *shard* is assigned to and stored on a single *SN*                                                      |
16 | | RedStuff                          | our erasure-encoding approach, which uses two different encodings (*primary* and *secondary*) to enable shard recovery; details are available in the [whitepaper](./walrus.pdf)             |
17 | | sliver                            | erasure-encoded data of one *shard* corresponding to a single blob for one of the two encodings; this contains several erasure-encoded symbols of that blob but not the *blob metadata*     |
18 | | sliver pair                       | the combination of a shard’s primary and secondary sliver                                                                                                                                   |
19 | | blob ID                           | cryptographic ID computed from a *blob*’s *slivers*                                                                                                                                         |
20 | | blob metadata                     | metadata of one *blob*; in particular, this contains a hash per *shard* to enable the authentication of *slivers* and recovery symbols                                                      |
21 | | (end) user                        | any entity/person that wants to store or read *blobs* on/from Walrus; can act as a Walrus client itself or use the simple interface exposed by *publishers* and *caches*                    |
22 | | publisher                         | service interacting with Sui and the *SNs* to store *blobs* on Walrus; offers a simple `HTTP POST` endpoint to *end users*                                                                  |
23 | | aggregator                        | service that reconstructs *blobs* by interacting with *SNs* and exposes a simple `HTTP GET` endpoint to *end users*                                                                         |
24 | | cache                             | an *aggregator* with additional caching capabilities                                                                                                                                        |
25 | | (Walrus) client                   | entity interacting directly with the *SNs*; this can be an *aggregator*/*cache*, a *publisher*, or an *end user*                                                                            |
26 | | (blob) reconstruction             | decoding of the primary *slivers* to obtain the blob; includes re-encoding the *blob* and checking the Merkle proofs                                                                        |
27 | | (shard/sliver) recovery           | process of an *SN* recovering a *sliver* or full *shard* by obtaining recovery symbols from other *SNs*                                                                                     |
28 | | storage attestation               | process where *SNs* exchange challenges and responses to demonstrate that they are storing their currently assigned *shards*                                                                |
29 | | certificate of availability (CoA) | a *blob ID* with signatures of *SNs* holding at least \(2f+1\) *shards* in a specific *epoch*                                                                                               |
30 | | point of availability (PoA)       | point in time when a *CoA* is submitted to Sui and the corresponding *blob* is guaranteed to be available until its expiration                                                              |
31 | | inconsistency proof               | set of several recovery symbols with their Merkle proofs such that the decoded *sliver* does not match the corresponding hash; this proves an incorrect/inconsistent encoding by the client |
32 | | inconsistency certificate         | an aggregated signature from 2/3 of *SNs* (weighted by their number of *shards*) that they have seen and stored an *inconsistency proof* for a *blob ID*                                    |
33 | | storage committee                 | the set of *SNs* for a *storage epoch*, including metadata about the *shards* they are responsible for and other metadata                                                                   |
34 | | member                            | an *SN* that is part of a *committee* at some *epoch*                                                                                                                                       |
35 | | storage epoch                     | the epoch for Walrus as distinct to the epoch for Sui                                                                                                                                       |
36 | | availability period               | the period specified in *storage epochs* for which a *blob* is certified to be available on Walrus                                                                                          |
37 | | expiry                            | the end epoch at which a blob is no longer available and can be deleted; the end epoch is always exclusive                                                                                  |
38 | | WAL                               | the native Token of Walrus                                                                                                                                                                  |
39 | | FROST                             | the smallest unit of WAL (similar to MIST for SUI); 1 WAL is equal to 1 billion (1000000000) FROST                                                                                          |
```

walrus-docs/docs/index.md
```
1 | # Walrus
2 | 
3 | Welcome to the developer documentation for Walrus, a decentralized storage and data availability
4 | protocol designed specifically for large binary files, or "blobs". Walrus focuses on providing a
5 | robust but affordable solution for storing unstructured content on decentralized storage nodes
6 | while ensuring high availability and reliability even in the presence of Byzantine faults.
7 | 
8 | ```admonish tip title="Fun fact"
9 | If you are viewing this site at <https://docs.walrus.site>, you are fetching this from
10 | Walrus behind the scenes. See the [Walrus Sites chapter](./walrus-sites/intro.md) for further
11 | details on how this works.
12 | ```
13 | 
14 | ```admonish danger title="Disclaimer about the Walrus Testnet"
15 | The current Testnet release of Walrus and Walrus Sites is a preview intended to showcase
16 | the technology and solicit feedback from builders, users, and storage-node operators.
17 | All transactions are executed on the Sui Testnet and use Testnet WAL and SUI which have no
18 | value. The state of the store **can and will be wiped** at any point and possibly with no warning.
19 | Do not rely on this Testnet for any production purposes, it comes with no availability or
20 | persistence guarantees.
21 | 
22 | Furthermore, encodings and blob IDs may be incompatible with the future Testnet and Mainnet, and
23 | developers will be responsible for migrating any Testnet applications and data to Mainnet. Detailed
24 | migration guides will be provided when Mainnet becomes available.
25 | 
26 | Also see the [Testnet terms of service](../legal/testnet_tos.md) under which this Testnet is made
27 | available.
28 | ```
29 | 
30 | ```admonish danger title="Public access"
31 | **All blobs stored in Walrus are public and discoverable by all.** Therefore you must not use Walrus
32 | to store anything that contains secrets or private data without additional measures to protect
33 | confidentiality.
34 | ```
35 | 
36 | ## Features
37 | 
38 | - **Storage and retrieval:** Walrus supports storage operations to write and read blobs. It also
39 |   allows anyone to prove that a blob has been stored and is available for retrieval at a later
40 |   time.
41 | 
42 | - **Cost efficiency:** By utilizing advanced erasure coding, Walrus maintains storage costs at
43 |   approximately five times the size of the stored blobs, and encoded parts of each blob are stored
44 |   on each storage node. This is significantly more cost-effective than traditional full-replication
45 |   methods and much more robust against failures than protocols that only store each blob on a subset
46 |   of storage nodes.
47 | 
48 | - **Integration with the Sui blockchain:** Walrus leverages [Sui](https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui)
49 |   for coordination, attesting availability, and payments. Storage space is represented as a resource
50 |   on Sui, which can be owned, split, merged, and transferred. Stored blobs are also represented by
51 |   objects on Sui, which means that smart contracts can check whether a blob is available and for how
52 |   long, extend its lifetime or optionally delete it.
53 | 
54 | - **Epochs, tokenomics, and delegated proof of stake** Walrus is operated by a committee of storage
55 |   nodes that evolve between epochs. A native token, WAL (and its subdivision FROST, where 1 WAL is
56 |   equal to 1 billion FROST), is used to delegate stake to storage nodes, and those with high stake
57 |   become part of the epoch committee. The WAL token is also used for payments for storage. At the
58 |   end of each epoch, rewards for selecting storage nodes, storing and serving blobs are distributed
59 |   to storage nodes and whose that stake with them. All these processes are mediated by smart
60 |   contracts on the Sui platform.
61 | 
62 | - **Flexible access:** Users can interact with Walrus through a command-line interface (CLI),
63 |   software development kits (SDKs), and web2 HTTP technologies. Walrus is designed to work well
64 |   with traditional caches and content distribution networks (CDNs), while ensuring all operations
65 |   can also be run using local tools to maximize decentralization.
66 | 
67 | ## Architecture and operations
68 | 
69 | Walrus's architecture ensures that content remains accessible and retrievable even when many
70 | storage nodes are unavailable or malicious. Under the hood it uses modern error correction
71 | techniques based on fast linear fountain codes, augmented to ensure resilience against Byzantine
72 | faults, and a dynamically changing set of storage nodes. The core of Walrus remains simple, and
73 | storage node management and blob certification leverages Sui smart contracts.
74 | 
75 | ## Organization
76 | 
77 | This documentation is split into several parts:
78 | 
79 | 1. *Dev blog* contains announcements and other blog posts.
80 | 1. *Design* describes the objectives, security properties, and architecture of Walrus.
81 | 1. *Usage* provides concrete information for developers. If you want to get started quickly, you can
82 |    jump directly to the [setup chapter](./usage/setup.md).
83 | 1. *Walrus Sites* describes how you can use Walrus and Sui together to build truly decentralized
84 |    websites.
85 | 
86 | Finally, we provide a [glossary](./glossary.md) that explains the terminology used throughout the
87 | documentation.
88 | 
89 | ## Sources
90 | 
91 | This documentation is built using [mdBook](https://rust-lang.github.io/mdBook/) from source files in
92 | <https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/>. Please report or fix any errors you find in this
93 | documentation in that GitHub project.
```

220 | #: docs/index.md:5
221 | msgid ""
222 | "Welcome to the developer documentation for Walrus, a decentralized storage "
223 | "and data availability protocol designed specifically for large binary files, "
224 | "or \"blobs\". Walrus focuses on providing a robust but affordable solution "
225 | "for storing unstructured content on decentralized storage nodes while "
226 | "ensuring high availability and reliability even in the presence of Byzantine "
227 | "faults."
228 | msgstr ""
229 | 
230 | #: docs/index.md:10
231 | msgid ""
232 | "```admonish tip title=\"Fun fact\"\n"
233 | "If you are viewing this site at <https://docs.walrus.site>, you are fetching "
234 | "this from\n"
235 | "Walrus behind the scenes. See the [Walrus Sites "
236 | "chapter](./walrus-sites/intro.md) for further\n"
237 | "details on how this works.\n"
238 | "```"
239 | msgstr ""
240 | 
241 | #: docs/index.md:16 docs/dev-guide/dev-guide.md:19
242 | msgid ""
243 | "```admonish danger title=\"Disclaimer about the Walrus Testnet\"\n"
244 | "The current Testnet release of Walrus and Walrus Sites is a preview intended "
245 | "to showcase\n"
246 | "the technology and solicit feedback from builders, users, and storage-node "
247 | "operators.\n"
248 | "All transactions are executed on the Sui Testnet and use Testnet WAL and SUI "
249 | "which have no\n"
250 | "value. The state of the store **can and will be wiped** at any point and "
251 | "possibly with no warning.\n"
252 | "Do not rely on this Testnet for any production purposes, it comes with no "
253 | "availability or\n"
254 | "persistence guarantees.\n"
255 | "\n"
256 | "Furthermore, encodings and blob IDs may be incompatible with the future "
257 | "Testnet and Mainnet, and\n"
258 | "developers will be responsible for migrating any Testnet applications and "
259 | "data to Mainnet. Detailed\n"
260 | "migration guides will be provided when Mainnet becomes available.\n"

284 | #: docs/index.md:40
285 | msgid ""
286 | "**Storage and retrieval:** Walrus supports storage operations to write and "
287 | "read blobs. It also allows anyone to prove that a blob has been stored and "
288 | "is available for retrieval at a later time."
289 | msgstr ""
290 | 
291 | #: docs/index.md:44
292 | msgid ""
293 | "**Cost efficiency:** By utilizing advanced erasure coding, Walrus maintains "
294 | "storage costs at approximately five times the size of the stored blobs, and "
295 | "encoded parts of each blob are stored on each storage node. This is "
296 | "significantly more cost-effective than traditional full-replication methods "
297 | "and much more robust against failures than protocols that only store each "
298 | "blob on a subset of storage nodes."
299 | msgstr ""
300 | 
301 | #: docs/index.md:50
302 | msgid ""
303 | "**Integration with the Sui blockchain:** Walrus leverages "
304 | "[Sui](https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui) for coordination, attesting "
305 | "availability, and payments. Storage space is represented as a resource on "
306 | "Sui, which can be owned, split, merged, and transferred. Stored blobs are "
307 | "also represented by objects on Sui, which means that smart contracts can "
308 | "check whether a blob is available and for how long, extend its lifetime or "
309 | "optionally delete it."
310 | msgstr ""

221 | msgid ""
222 | "Welcome to the developer documentation for Walrus, a decentralized storage "
223 | "and data availability protocol designed specifically for large binary files, "
224 | "or \"blobs\". Walrus focuses on providing a robust but affordable solution "
225 | "for storing unstructured content on decentralized storage nodes while "
226 | "ensuring high availability and reliability even in the presence of Byzantine "
227 | "faults."

229 | "欢迎使用Walrus开发者文档，Walrus是一个专为大型二进制文件（或称为“blobs”）设计"

231 | "案，用于在去中心化存储节点上存储非结构化内容，同时确保即使在拜占庭故障的情况"
232 | "下也能保持高可用性和可靠性。"

254 | "to showcase\n"
255 | "the technology and solicit feedback from builders, users, and storage-node "
256 | "operators.\n"
257 | "All transactions are executed on the Sui Testnet and use Testnet WAL and SUI "
258 | "which have no\n"
259 | "value. The state of the store **can and will be wiped** at any point and "
260 | "possibly with no warning.\n"
261 | "Do not rely on this Testnet for any production purposes, it comes with no "
262 | "availability or\n"
263 | "persistence guarantees.\n"
264 | "\n"
265 | "Furthermore, encodings and blob IDs may be incompatible with the future "
266 | "Testnet and Mainnet, and\n"
267 | "developers will be responsible for migrating any Testnet applications and "
268 | "data to Mainnet. Detailed\n"
269 | "migration guides will be provided when Mainnet becomes available.\n"
