1 | # Address Type
2 | 
3 | <!--
4 | 
5 | Chapter: Basic Syntax
6 | Goal: Introduce the address type
7 | Notes:
8 |     - a special type
9 |     - named addresses via the Move.toml
10 |     - address literals
11 |     - 0x2 is 0x0000000...02
12 | 
13 | Links:
14 |     - address concept
15 |     - transaction context
16 |     - Move.toml
17 |     - your first move
18 | 
19 |  -->
20 | 
21 | Move uses a special type called [address](./../concepts/address) to represent addresses. It is a
22 | 32-byte value that can represent any address on the blockchain. Addresses can be written in two
23 | forms: hexadecimal addresses prefixed with 0x and named addresses.
24 | 
25 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/address.move anchor=address_literal
26 | 
27 | ```
28 | 
29 | An address literal starts with the `@` symbol followed by a hexadecimal number or an identifier. The
30 | hexadecimal number is interpreted as a 32 byte value. The identifier is looked up in the
31 | [Move.toml](./../concepts/manifest) file and replaced with the corresponding address by the
32 | compiler. If the identifier is not found in the Move.toml file, the compiler will throw an error.
33 | 
34 | ## Conversion
35 | 
36 | Sui Framework offers a set of helper functions to work with addresses. Given that the address type
37 | is a 32 byte value, it can be converted to a `u256` type and vice versa. It can also be converted to
38 | and from a `vector<u8>` type.
39 | 
40 | Example: Convert an address to a `u256` type and back.
41 | 
42 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/address.move anchor=to_u256
43 | 
44 | ```
45 | 
46 | Example: Convert an address to a `vector<u8>` type and back.
47 | 
48 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/address.move anchor=to_bytes
49 | 
50 | ```
51 | 
52 | Example: Convert an address into a string.
53 | 
54 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/address.move anchor=to_string
55 | 
56 | ```
57 | 
58 | ## Further Reading
59 | 
60 | - [Address](./../../reference/primitive-types/address) in the Move Reference.
61 | - [sui::address](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/address) module documentation.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/assert-and-abort.md
```
1 | # Aborting Execution
2 | 
3 | <!-- Consider "aborting execution" -->
4 | 
5 | <!--
6 | 
7 | Chapter: Basic Syntax
8 | Goal: Introduce abort keyword and `assert!` macro.
9 | Notes:
10 |     - previous chapter mentions constants
11 |     - error constants standard ECamelCase
12 |     - `assert!` macro
13 |     - asserts should go before the main logic
14 |     - Move has no catch mechanism
15 |     - abort codes are local to the module
16 |     - there are no error messages emitted
17 |     - error codes should handle all possible scenarios in this module
18 | 
19 | Links:
20 |     - constants (previous section)
21 |  -->
22 | 
23 | A transaction can either succeed or fail. Successful execution applies all changes made to objects
24 | and on-chain data, and the transaction is committed to the blockchain. Alternatively, if a
25 | transaction aborts, changes are not applied. Use the `abort` keyword to abort a transaction and
26 | revert any changes that were made.
27 | 
28 | > It is important to note that there is no catch mechanism in Move. If a transaction aborts, the
29 | > changes made so far are reverted, and the transaction is considered failed.
30 | 
31 | ## Abort
32 | 
33 | The `abort` keyword is used to abort the execution of a transaction. It is used in combination with
34 | an abort code, which is returned to the caller of the transaction. The abort code is an
35 | [integer](./primitive-types) of type `u64`.
36 | 
37 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/assert-and-abort.move anchor=abort
38 | 
39 | ```
40 | 
41 | The code above will, of course, abort with abort code `1`.
42 | 
43 | ## assert!
44 | 
45 | The `assert!` macro is a built-in macro that can be used to assert a condition. If the condition is
46 | false, the transaction will abort with the given abort code. The `assert!` macro is a convenient way
47 | to abort a transaction if a condition is not met. The macro shortens the code otherwise written with
48 | an `if` expression + `abort`. The `code` argument is optional, but has to be a `u64` value or an
49 | `#[error]` (see below for more information).
50 | 
51 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/assert-and-abort.move anchor=assert
52 | 
53 | ```
54 | 
55 | ## Error constants
56 | 
57 | To make error codes more descriptive, it is a good practice to define
58 | [error constants](./constants). Error constants are defined as `const` declarations and are usually
59 | prefixed with `E` followed by a camel case name. Error constants are similar to other constants and
60 | do not have any special handling. However, they are commonly used to improve code readability and
61 | make abort scenarios easier to understand.
62 | 
63 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/assert-and-abort.move anchor=error_const
64 | 
65 | ```
66 | 
67 | ## Error messages
68 | 
69 | Move 2024 introduces a special type of error constant, marked with the `#[error]` attribute. This
70 | attribute allows the error constant to be of type `vector<u8>` and can be used to store an error
71 | message.
72 | 
73 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/assert-and-abort.move anchor=error_attribute
74 | 
75 | ```
76 | 
77 | ## Further Reading
78 | 
79 | - [Abort and Assert](./../../reference/abort-and-assert) in the Move Reference.
80 | - We suggest reading the [Better Error Handling](./../guides/better-error-handling) guide to learn
81 |   about best practices for error handling in Move.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/comments.md
```
1 | # Comments
2 | 
3 | <!--
4 | 
5 | Chapter: Basic Syntax
6 | Goal: Introduce comments.
7 | Notes:
8 |     - doc comments are used in docgen
9 |     - only public members are documented
10 |     - doc comments are placed in between attributes and the definition
11 |     - doc comments are allowed for: modules, structs, functions, constants
12 |     - give an example of how doc comments are translated
13 |  -->
14 | 
15 | Comments are a way to add notes or document your code. They are ignored by the compiler and don't
16 | result in Move bytecode. You can use comments to explain what your code does, add notes to yourself
17 | or other developers, temporarily remove a part of your code, or generate documentation. There are
18 | three types of comments in Move: line comments, block comments, and doc comments.
19 | 
20 | ## Line Comment
21 | 
22 | You can use a double slash `//` to comment out the rest of the line. Everything after `//` will be
23 | ignored by the compiler.
24 | 
25 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/comments-line.move anchor=main
26 | 
27 | ```
28 | 
29 | ## Block Comment
30 | 
31 | Block comments are used to comment out a block of code. They start with `/*` and end with `*/`.
32 | Everything between `/*` and `*/` will be ignored by the compiler. You can use block comments to
33 | comment out a single line or multiple lines. You can even use them to comment out a part of a line.
34 | 
35 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/comments-block.move anchor=main
36 | 
37 | ```
38 | 
39 | This example is a bit extreme, but it shows all the ways that you can use block comments.
40 | 
41 | ## Doc Comment
42 | 
43 | Documentation comments are special comments that are used to generate documentation for your code.
44 | They are similar to block comments but start with three slashes `///` and are placed before the
45 | definition of the item they document.
46 | 
47 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/comments-doc.move anchor=main
48 | 
49 | ```
50 | 
51 | ## Whitespace
52 | 
53 | Unlike some languages, whitespace (spaces, tabs, and newlines) have no impact on the meaning of the
54 | program.
55 | 
56 | <!-- TODO: docgen, which members are in the documentation -->
```

move-book/book/move-basics/constants.md
```
1 | # Constants
2 | 
3 | <!--
4 | 
5 | Chapter: Basic Syntax
6 | Goal: Introduce constants.
7 | Notes:
8 |     - constants are immutable
9 |     - constants are private
10 |     - start with a capital letter always
11 |     - stored in the bytecode (but w/o a name)
12 |     - mention standard for naming constants
13 | 
14 | Links:
15 |     - next section (abort and assert)
16 |     - coding conventions (constants)
17 |     - constants (language reference)
18 | 
19 |  -->
20 | 
21 | Constants are immutable values that are defined at the module level. They often serve as a way to
22 | give names to static values that are used throughout a module. For example, if there's a default
23 | price for a product, you might define a constant for it. Constants are stored in the module's
24 | bytecode, and each time they are used, the value is copied.
25 | 
26 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/constants-shop-price.move anchor=shop_price
27 | 
28 | ```
29 | 
30 | ## Naming Convention
31 | 
32 | Constants must start with a capital letter - this is enforced at the compiler level. For constants
33 | used as a value, the convention is to use all uppercase letters and underscores between words, which
34 | makes constants stand out from other identifiers in the code. An exception is made for
35 | [error constants](./assert-and-abort#error-constants), which are written in ECamelCase.
36 | 
37 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/constants-naming.move anchor=naming
38 | 
39 | ```
40 | 
41 | ## Constants are Immutable
42 | 
43 | Constants can't be changed and assigned new values. As part of the package bytecode, they are
44 | inherently immutable.
45 | 
46 | ```move
47 | module book::immutable_constants;
48 | 
49 | const ITEM_PRICE: u64 = 100;
50 | 
51 | // emits an error
52 | fun change_price() {
53 |     ITEM_PRICE = 200;
54 | }
55 | ```
56 | 
57 | ## Using Config Pattern
58 | 
59 | A common use case for an application is to define a set of constants that are used throughout the
60 | codebase. But due to constants being private to the module, they can't be accessed from other
61 | modules. One way to solve this is to define a "config" module that exports the constants.
62 | 
63 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/constants-config.move anchor=config
64 | 
65 | ```
66 | 
67 | This way other modules can import and read the constants, and the update process is simplified. If
68 | the constants need to be changed, only the config module needs to be updated during the package
69 | upgrade.
70 | 
71 | ## Links
72 | 
73 | - [Constants](./../../reference/constants) in the Move Reference
74 | - [Coding conventions for constants](./../guides/code-quality-checklist#regular-constant-are-all_caps)
```

move-book/book/move-basics/control-flow.md
```
1 | # Control Flow
2 | 
3 | <!--
4 | 
5 | Chapter: Basic Syntax
6 | Goal: Introduce control flow statements.
7 | Notes:
8 |     - if/else is an expression
9 |     - while () {} loop
10 |     - continue and break
11 |     - loop {}
12 |     - infinite loop is possible but will lead to gas exhaustion
13 |     - return keyword
14 |     - if is an expression and as such requires a semicolon (!!!)
15 | 
16 | Links:
17 |     - reference (control flow)
18 |     - coding conventions (control flow)
19 | 
20 |  -->
21 | 
22 | Control flow statements are used to control the flow of execution in a program. They are used to
23 | make decisions, repeat a block of code, or exit a block of code early. Move includes the following
24 | control flow statements (explained in detail below):
25 | 
26 | - [`if` and `if-else`](#conditional-statements) - making decisions on whether to execute a block of
27 |   code
28 | - [`loop` and `while` loops](#repeating-statements-with-loops) - repeating a block of code
29 | - [`break` and `continue` statements](#exiting-a-loop-early) - exiting a loop early
30 | - [`return`](#early-return) statement - exiting a function early
31 | 
32 | ## Conditional Statements
33 | 
34 | The `if` expression is used to make decisions in a program. It evaluates a
35 | [boolean expression](./expression#literals) and executes a block of code if the expression is true.
36 | Paired with `else`, it can execute a different block of code if the expression is false.
37 | 
38 | The syntax for an `if` expression is:
39 | 
40 | ```move
41 | if (<bool_expression>) <expression>;
42 | if (<bool_expression>) <expression> else <expression>;
43 | ```
44 | 
45 | Just like any other expression, `if` requires a semicolon if there are other expressions following
46 | it. The `else` keyword is optional, except when the resulting value is assigned to a variable, as
47 | all branches must return a value to ensure type safety. Let’s examine how an `if` expression works
48 | in Move with the following example:
49 | 
50 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/control-flow.move anchor=if_condition
51 | 
52 | ```
53 | 
54 | Let's see how we can use `if` and `else` to assign a value to a variable:
55 | 
56 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/control-flow.move anchor=if_else
57 | 
58 | ```
59 | 
60 | In this example, the value of the `if` expression is assigned to the variable `y`. If `x` is greater
61 | than 0, `y` is assigned the value 1; otherwise, it is assigned 0. The `else` block is required
62 | because both branches of the `if` expression must return a value of the same type. Omitting the
63 | `else` block would result in a compiler error, as it ensures all possible branches are accounted for
64 | and type safety is maintained.
65 | 
66 | <!-- TODO: add an error -->
67 | 
68 | Conditional expressions are among the most important control flow statements in Move. They evaluate
69 | user-provided input or stored data to make decisions. One key use case is in the
70 | [`assert!` macro](./assert-and-abort), which checks if a condition is true and aborts execution if
71 | it is not. We’ll explore this in detail shortly.
72 | 
73 | ## Repeating Statements with Loops
74 | 
75 | Loops are used to execute a block of code multiple times. Move has two built-in types of loops:
76 | `loop` and `while`. In many cases they can be used interchangeably, but usually `while` is used when
77 | the number of iterations is known in advance, and `loop` is used when the number of iterations is
78 | not known in advance or there are multiple exit points.
79 | 
80 | Loops are useful for working with collections, such as vectors, or for repeating a block of code
81 | until a specific condition is met. However, take care to avoid infinite loops, which can exhaust gas
82 | limits and cause the transaction to abort.
83 | 
84 | ## The `while` Loop
85 | 
86 | The `while` statement executes a block of code repeatedly as long as the associated boolean
87 | expression evaluates to true. Just like we've seen with `if`, the boolean expression is evaluated
88 | before each iteration of the loop. Additionally, like conditional statements, the `while` loop is an
89 | expression and requires a semicolon if there are other expressions following it.
90 | 
91 | The syntax for the `while` loop is:
92 | 
93 | ```move
94 | while (<bool_expression>) { <expressions>; };
95 | ```
96 | 
97 | Here is an example of a `while` loop with a very simple condition:
98 | 
99 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/control-flow.move anchor=while_loop
100 | 
101 | ```
102 | 
103 | ## Infinite `loop`
104 | 
105 | Now let's imagine a scenario where the boolean expression is always `true`. For example, if we
106 | literally passed `true` to the `while` condition. This is similar to how the `loop` statement
107 | functions, except that `while` evaluates a condition.
108 | 
109 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/control-flow.move anchor=infinite_while
110 | 
111 | ```
112 | 
113 | An infinite `while` loop, or a `while` loop with an always `true` condition, is equivalent to a
114 | `loop`. The syntax for creating a `loop` is straightforward:
115 | 
116 | ```move
117 | loop { <expressions>; };
118 | ```
119 | 
120 | Let's rewrite the previous example using `loop` instead of `while`:
121 | 
122 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/control-flow.move anchor=infinite_loop
123 | 
124 | ```
125 | 
126 | Infinite loops are rarely practical in Move, as every operation consumes gas, and an infinite loop
127 | will inevitably lead to gas exhaustion. If you find yourself using a loop, consider whether there
128 | might be a better approach, as many use cases can be handled more efficiently with other control
129 | flow structures. That said, `loop` might be useful when combined with `break` and `continue`
130 | statements to create controlled and flexible looping behavior.
131 | 
132 | ## Exiting a Loop Early
133 | 
134 | As we already mentioned, infinite loops are rather useless on their own. And that's where we
135 | introduce the `break` and `continue` statements. They are used to exit a loop early, and to skip the
136 | rest of the current iteration, respectively.
137 | 
138 | Syntax for the `break` statement is (without a semicolon):
139 | 
140 | ```move
141 | break
142 | ```
143 | 
144 | The `break` statement is used to stop the execution of a loop and exit it early. It is often used in
145 | combination with a conditional statement to exit the loop when a certain condition is met. To
146 | illustrate this point, let's turn the infinite `loop` from the previous example into something that
147 | looks and behaves more like a `while` loop:
148 | 
149 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/control-flow.move anchor=break_loop
150 | 
151 | ```
152 | 
153 | Almost identical to the `while` loop, right? The `break` statement is used to exit the loop when `x`
154 | is 5. If we remove the `break` statement, the loop will run forever, just like in the previous
155 | example.
156 | 
157 | ## Skipping an Iteration
158 | 
159 | The `continue` statement is used to skip the rest of the current iteration and start the next one.
160 | Similarly to `break`, it is used in combination with a conditional statement to skip the rest of an
161 | iteration when a certain condition is met.
162 | 
163 | Syntax for the `continue` statement is (without a semicolon):
164 | 
165 | ```move
166 | continue
167 | ```
168 | 
169 | The example below skips odd numbers and prints only even numbers from 0 to 10:
170 | 
171 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/control-flow.move anchor=continue_loop
172 | 
173 | ```
174 | 
175 | `break` and `continue` statements can be used in both `while` and `loop` loops.
176 | 
177 | ## Early Return
178 | 
179 | The `return` statement is used to exit a [function](./function) early and return a value. It is
180 | often used in combination with a conditional statement to exit the function when a certain condition
181 | is met. The syntax for the `return` statement is:
182 | 
183 | ```move
184 | return <expression>
185 | ```
186 | 
187 | Here is an example of a function that returns a value when a certain condition is met:
188 | 
189 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/control-flow.move anchor=return_statement
190 | 
191 | ```
192 | 
193 | Unlike in many other languages, the `return` statement is not required for the last expression in a
194 | function. The last expression in a function block is automatically returned. However, the `return`
195 | statement is useful when we want to exit a function early if a certain condition is met.
196 | 
197 | ## Further Reading
198 | 
199 | - [Control Flow](./../../reference/control-flow) chapter in the Move Reference.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/copy-ability.md
```
1 | # Abilities: Copy
2 | 
3 | In Move, the _copy_ ability on a type indicates that the instance or the value of the type can be
4 | copied, or duplicated. While this behavior is provided by default when working with numbers or other
5 | primitive types, it is not the default for custom types. Move is designed to express digital assets
6 | and resources, and controlling the ability to duplicate resources is a key principle of the resource
7 | model. However, the Move type system allows you to add the _copy_ ability to custom types:
8 | 
9 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/copy-ability.move anchor=copyable
10 | 
11 | ```
12 | 
13 | In the example above, we define a custom type `Copyable` with the _copy_ ability. This means that
14 | instances of `Copyable` can be copied, both implicitly and explicitly.
15 | 
16 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/copy-ability.move anchor=copyable_test
17 | 
18 | ```
19 | 
20 | In the example above, `a` is copied to `b` implicitly, and then explicitly copied to `c` using the
21 | dereference operator. If `Copyable` did not have the _copy_ ability, the code would not compile, and
22 | the Move compiler would raise an error.
23 | 
24 | > Note: In Move, destructuring with empty brackets is often used to consume unused variables,
25 | > especially for types without the drop ability. This prevents compiler errors from values going out
26 | > of scope without explicit use. Also, Move requires the type name in destructuring (e.g.,
27 | > `Copyable` in `let Copyable {} = a;`) because it enforces strict typing and ownership rules.
28 | 
29 | ## Copying and Drop
30 | 
31 | The `copy` ability is closely related to the [`drop` ability](./drop-ability). If a type has the
32 | _copy_ ability, it is very likely that it should have `drop` too. This is because the _drop_ ability
33 | is required to clean up resources when the instance is no longer needed. If a type only has _copy_,
34 | managing its instances gets more complicated, as the instances must be explicitly used or consumed.
35 | 
36 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/copy-ability.move anchor=copy_drop
37 | 
38 | ```
39 | 
40 | All of the primitive types in Move behave as if they have the _copy_ and _drop_ abilities. This
41 | means that they can be copied and dropped, and the Move compiler will handle the memory management
42 | for them.
43 | 
44 | ## Types with the `copy` Ability
45 | 
46 | All native types in Move have the `copy` ability. This includes:
47 | 
48 | - [bool](./../move-basics/primitive-types#booleans)
49 | - [unsigned integers](./../move-basics/primitive-types#integer-types)
50 | - [vector](./../move-basics/vector)
51 | - [address](./../move-basics/address)
52 | 
53 | All of the types defined in the standard library have the `copy` ability as well. This includes:
54 | 
55 | - [Option](./../move-basics/option)
56 | - [String](./../move-basics/string)
57 | - [TypeName](./../move-basics/type-reflection)
58 | 
59 | ## Further Reading
60 | 
61 | - [Type Abilities](./../../reference/abilities) in the Move Reference.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/drop-ability.md
```
1 | # Abilities: Drop
2 | 
3 | <!-- TODO: reiterate, given that we introduce abilities one by one -->
4 | 
5 | <!-- TODO:
6 | 
7 | - introduce abilities first
8 | - mention them all
9 | - then do one by one
10 | 
11 | consistency: we / I / you ?
12 | who is we? I am alone, there's no one else here
13 | 
14 | 
15 | -->
16 | 
17 | <!--
18 | 
19 | // Shall we only talk about `drop` ?
20 | // So that we don't explain scopes and `copy` / `move` semantics just yet?
21 | 
22 | Chapter: Basic Syntax
23 | Goal: Introduce Copy and Drop abilities of Move. Follows the `struct` section
24 | Notes:
25 |     - compare them to primitive types introduces before;
26 |     - what is an ability without drop
27 |     - drop is not necessary for unpacking
28 |     - make a joke about a bacteria pattern in the code
29 |     - mention that a struct with only `drop` ability is called a Witness
30 |     - mention that a struct without abilities is called a Hot Potato
31 |     - mention that there are two more abilities which are covered in a later chapter
32 | 
33 | Links:
34 |     - language reference (abilities)
35 |     - authorization patterns (or witness)
36 |     - hot potato pattern
37 |     - key and store abilities (later chapter)
38 | 
39 |  -->
40 | 
41 | The `drop` ability - the simplest of them - allows the instance of a struct to be _ignored_ or
42 | _discarded_. In many programming languages this behavior is considered default. However, in Move, a
43 | struct without the `drop` ability is not allowed to be ignored. This is a safety feature of the Move
44 | language, which ensures that all assets are properly handled. An attempt to ignore a struct without
45 | the `drop` ability will result in a compilation error.
46 | 
47 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/drop-ability.move anchor=main
48 | 
49 | ```
50 | 
51 | The `drop` ability is often used on custom collection types to eliminate the need for special
52 | handling of the collection when it is no longer needed. For example, a `vector` type has the `drop`
53 | ability, which allows the vector to be ignored when it is no longer needed. However, the biggest
54 | feature of Move's type system is the ability to not have `drop`. This ensures that the assets are
55 | properly handled and not ignored.
56 | 
57 | A struct with a single `drop` ability is called a _Witness_. We explain the concept of a _Witness_
58 | in the [Witness and Abstract Implementation](./../programmability/witness-pattern) section.
59 | 
60 | ## Types with the `drop` Ability
61 | 
62 | All native types in Move have the `drop` ability. This includes:
63 | 
64 | - [`bool`](./../move-basics/primitive-types#booleans)
65 | - [unsigned integers](./../move-basics/primitive-types#integer-types)
66 | - [`vector<T>`](./../move-basics/vector) when `T` has `drop`
67 | - [`address`](./../move-basics/address)
68 | 
69 | All of the types defined in the standard library have the `drop` ability as well. This includes:
70 | 
71 | - [`Option<T>`](./../move-basics/option) when `T` has `drop`
72 | - [`String`](./../move-basics/string)
73 | - [`TypeName`](./../move-basics/type-reflection)
74 | 
75 | ## Further Reading
76 | 
77 | - [Type Abilities](./../../reference/abilities) in the Move Reference.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/enum-and-match.md
```
1 | # Enums and Match
2 | 
3 | An enum is a user-defined data structure that, unlike a [struct](./struct), can represent multiple
4 | variants. Each variant can contain primitive types, structs, or other enums. However, recursive enum
5 | definitions — similar to recursive struct definitions — are not allowed.
6 | 
7 | ## Definition
8 | 
9 | An enum is defined using the `enum` keyword, followed by optional abilities and a block of variant
10 | definitions. Each variant has a tag name and may optionally include either positional values or
11 | named fields. Enum must have at least one variant. The structure of each variant is not flexible,
12 | and the total number of variants can be relatively large - up to 100.
13 | 
14 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/enum-and-match.move anchor=definition
15 | 
16 | ```
17 | 
18 | In the code sample above we defined a public `Segment` enum, which has the `drop` and `copy`
19 | abilities, and 3 variants:
20 | 
21 | - `Empty`, which has no fields.
22 | - `String`, which contains a single positional field of type `String`.
23 | - `Special`, which uses named fields: `content` of type `vector<u8>` and `encoding` of type `u8`.
24 | 
25 | ## Instantiating
26 | 
27 | Enums are _internal_ to the module in which they are defined. This means an enum can only be
28 | constructed, read, and unpacked within the same module.
29 | 
30 | [Similar to structs](./struct#create-and-use-an-instance), enums are instantiated by specifying the
31 | type, the variant, and the values for any fields defined in that variant.
32 | 
33 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/enum-and-match.move anchor=constructors
34 | 
35 | ```
36 | 
37 | Depending on the use case, you may want to provide public constructors, or instantiate enums
38 | internally as a part of application logic.
39 | 
40 | ## Using in Type Definitions
41 | 
42 | The biggest benefit of using enums is the ability to represent varying data structures under a
43 | single type. To demonstrate this, let’s define a struct that contains a vector of `Segment` values:
44 | 
45 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/enum-and-match.move anchor=struct
46 | 
47 | ```
48 | 
49 | All variants of the Segment enum share the same type – `Segment` – which allows us to create a
50 | homogeneous vector containing instances of different variants. This kind of flexibility is not
51 | achievable with structs, as each struct defines a single, fixed shape.
52 | 
53 | ## Pattern Matching
54 | 
55 | Unlike structs, enums require special handling when it comes to accessing the inner value or
56 | checking the variant. We simply cannot read the inner fields of an enum using the `.` (dot) syntax,
57 | because we need to make sure that the value we are trying to access is the right one. For that Move
58 | offers _pattern matching_ syntax.
59 | 
60 | > This chapter doesn't intend to cover all the features of pattern matching in Move. Refer to the
61 | > [Pattern Matching](./../../reference/control-flow/pattern-matching) section in the Move Reference.
62 | 
63 | Pattern matching allows conditioning the logic based on the _pattern_ of the value. It is performed
64 | using the `match` expression, followed by the matched value in parenthesis and the block of _match
65 | arms_, defining the pattern and expression to be performed if the pattern is right.
66 | 
67 | Let's extend our example by adding a set of `is_variant`-like functions, so external packages can
68 | check the variant. Starting with `is_empty`.
69 | 
70 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/enum-and-match.move anchor=is_empty
71 | 
72 | ```
73 | 
74 | The `match` keyword begins the expression, and `s` is the value being tested. Each match arm checks
75 | for a specific variant of the `Segment` enum. If `s` matches `Segment::Empty`, the function returns
76 | `true`; otherwise, it returns `false`.
77 | 
78 | For variants with fields, we need to bind the inner structure to local variables (even if we don’t
79 | use them, marking unused values with `_` to avoid compiler warnings).
80 | 
81 | ### Trick #1 - _any_ Condition
82 | 
83 | The Move compiler infers the type of the value used in a `match` expression and ensures that the
84 | _match arms_ are exhaustive – that is, all possible variants or values must be covered.
85 | 
86 | However, in some cases, such as matching on a primitive value or a collection like a vector, it's
87 | not feasible to list every possible case. For these situations, match supports a wildcard pattern
88 | (`_`), which acts as a default arm. This arm is executed when no other patterns match.
89 | 
90 | We can demonstrate this by simplifying our `is_empty` function and replacing the non-`Empty`
91 | variants with a wildcard:
92 | 
93 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/enum-and-match.move anchor=is_empty_2
94 | public fun is_empty(s: &Segment): bool {
95 | 
96 | ```
97 | 
98 | Similarly, we can use the same approach to define `is_special` and `is_string`:
99 | 
100 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/enum-and-match.move anchor=accessors
101 | 
102 | ```
103 | 
104 | ### Trick #2 - `try_into` Helpers
105 | 
106 | With the addition of `is_variant` functions, we enabled external modules to check which variant an
107 | enum instance represents. However, this is often not enough – external code still cannot access the
108 | inner value of a variant due to enums being internal to their module.
109 | 
110 | A common pattern for addressing this is to define `try_into` functions. These functions match on the
111 | value and return an `Option` containing the inner contents if the `match` succeeds.
112 | 
113 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/enum-and-match.move anchor=try_into_inner_string
114 | 
115 | ```
116 | 
117 | This pattern safely exposes internal data in a controlled way, avoiding abort.
118 | 
119 | ### Trick #3 - Matching on Primitive Values
120 | 
121 | The `match` expression in Move can be used with values of any type – enums, structs, or primitives.
122 | To demonstrate this, let’s implement a `to_string` function that creates a new `String` from a
123 | `Segment`. In the case of the `Special` variant, we will match on the `encoding` field to determine
124 | how to decode the content.
125 | 
126 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/enum-and-match.move anchor=to_string
127 | 
128 | ```
129 | 
130 | This function demonstrates two key things:
131 | 
132 | - Nested `match` expressions can be used for deeper logic branching.
133 | - Wildcards are essential for covering all possible values in primitive types like `u8`.
134 | 
135 | ## The Final Test
136 | 
137 | Now we can finalize the test we started before using the features we have added. Let's create a
138 | scenario where we build enums into a vector.
139 | 
140 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/enum-and-match-2.move anchor=enum_test
141 | 
142 | ```
143 | 
144 | This test demonstrates the full enum workflow: instantiating different variants, using public
145 | accessors, and performing logic with pattern matching. That should be enough to get you started!
146 | 
147 | To learn more about enums and pattern matching, refer to the resources listed in the
148 | [further reading](#further-reading) section.
149 | 
150 | ## Summary
151 | 
152 | - Enums are user-defined types that can represent multiple variants under a single type.
153 | - Each variant can contain different types of data (primitives, structs, or other enums).
154 | - Enums are internal to their defining module and require pattern matching for access.
155 | - Pattern matching is done using the `match` expression, which:
156 |   - Works with enums, structs, and primitive values;
157 |   - Must handle all possible cases (be exhaustive);
158 |   - Supports the `_` wildcard pattern for remaining cases;
159 |   - Can return values and be used in expressions;
160 | - Common patterns for enums include `is_variant` checks and `try_into` helper functions.
161 | 
162 | ## Further Reading
163 | 
164 | - [Enums](./../../reference/enums) in the Move Reference
165 | - [Pattern Matching](/reference/control-flow/pattern-matching) in the Move Reference
```

```
1 | # Expression
2 | 
3 | In programming languages, an expression is a unit of code that returns a value. In Move, almost
4 | everything is an expression, with the sole exception of the `let` statement, which is a declaration.
5 | In this section, we cover the types of expressions and introduce the concept of scope.
6 | 
7 | > Expressions are sequenced with semicolons `;`. If there's "no expression" after the semicolon, the
8 | > compiler will insert a `unit ()`, which represents an empty expression.
9 | 
10 | ## Literals
11 | 
12 | In the [Primitive types](./primitive-types) section, we introduced the basic types of Move. And to
13 | illustrate them, we used literals. A literal is a notation for representing a fixed value in source
14 | code. Literals can be used to initialize variables or directly pass fixed values as arguments to
15 | functions. Move has the following literals:
16 | 
17 | - Boolean values: `true` and `false`
18 | - Integer values: `0`, `1`, `123123`
19 | - Hexadecimal values: Numbers prefixed with 0x to represent integers, such as `0x0`, `0x1`, `0x123`
20 | - Byte vector values: Prefixed with `b`, such as `b"bytes_vector"`
21 | - Byte values: Hexadecimal literals prefixed with `x`, such as `x"0A"`
22 | 
23 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/expression.move anchor=literals
24 | 
25 | ```
26 | 
27 | ## Operators
28 | 
29 | Arithmetic, logical, and bitwise operators are used to perform operations on values. Since these
30 | operations produce values, they are considered expressions.
31 | 
32 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/expression.move anchor=operators
33 | 
34 | ```
35 | 
36 | ## Blocks
37 | 
38 | A block is a sequence of statements and expressions enclosed in curly braces `{}`. It returns the
39 | value of the last expression in the block (note that this final expression must not have an ending
40 | semicolon). A block is an expression, so it can be used anywhere an expression is expected.
41 | 
42 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/expression.move anchor=block
43 | 
44 | ```
45 | 
46 | ## Function Calls
47 | 
48 | We go into detail about functions in the [Functions](./function) section. However, we have already
49 | used function calls in previous sections, so it's worth mentioning them here. A function call is an
50 | expression that calls a function and returns the value of the last expression in the function body,
51 | provided the last expression does not have a terminating semi-colon.
52 | 
53 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/expression.move anchor=fun_call
54 | 
55 | ```
56 | 
57 | ## Control Flow Expressions
58 | 
59 | Control flow expressions are used to control the flow of the program. They are also expressions, so
60 | they return a value. We cover control flow expressions in the [Control Flow](./control-flow)
61 | section. Here's a very brief overview:
62 | 
63 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/expression.move anchor=control_flow
64 | 
65 | ```
```
