1 | # Functions
2 | 
3 | Functions are the building blocks of Move programs. They are called from
4 | [user transactions](./../concepts/what-is-a-transaction) and from other functions and group
5 | executable code into reusable units. Functions can take arguments and return a value. They are
6 | declared with the `fun` keyword at the module level. Just like any other module member, by default
7 | they're private and can only be accessed from within the module.
8 | 
9 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/function.move anchor=math
10 | 
11 | ```
12 | 
13 | In this example, we define a function `add` that takes two arguments of type `u64` and returns their
14 | sum. The `test_add` function, located in the same module, is a test function that calls `add`. The
15 | test uses the `assert!` macro to compare the result of `add` with the expected value. If the
16 | condition inside `assert!` evaluates to false, the execution is aborted automatically.
17 | 
18 | ## Function declaration
19 | 
20 | > In Move, functions are typically named using the `snake_case` convention. This means function
21 | > names should be all lowercase, with words separated by underscores. Examples include
22 | > `do_something`, `add`, `get_balance`, `is_authorized`, and so on.
23 | 
24 | A function is declared with the `fun` keyword followed by the function name (a valid Move
25 | identifier), a list of arguments in parentheses, and a return type. The function body is a block of
26 | code that contains a sequence of statements and expressions. The last expression the function body
27 | is the return value of the function.
28 | 
29 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/function.move anchor=return_nothing
30 | 
31 | ```
32 | 
33 | ## Accessing functions
34 | 
35 | Just like other module members, functions can be imported and accessed using a path. The path
36 | consists of the module path and the function name, separated by ::. For example, if you have a
37 | function named `add` in the `math` module within the `book` package, its full path would be
38 | `book::math::add`. If the module has already been imported, you can access it directly as
39 | `math::add` as in the following example:
40 | 
41 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/function_use.move anchor=use_math
42 | 
43 | ```
44 | 
45 | ## Multiple return values
46 | 
47 | Move functions can return multiple values, which is particularly useful when you need to return more
48 | than one piece of data from a function. The return type is specified as a tuple of types, and the
49 | return value is provided as a tuple of expressions:
50 | 
51 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/function.move anchor=tuple_return
52 | 
53 | ```
54 | 
55 | The result of a function call with a tuple return has to be unpacked into variables via the
56 | `let (tuple)` syntax:
57 | 
58 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/function.move anchor=tuple_return_imm
59 | 
60 | ```
61 | 
62 | If any of the declared values need to be declared as mutable, the `mut` keyword is placed before the
63 | variable name:
64 | 
65 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/function.move anchor=tuple_return_mut
66 | 
67 | ```
68 | 
69 | If some of the arguments are not used, they can be ignored with the `_` symbol:
70 | 
71 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/function.move anchor=tuple_return_ignore
72 | 
73 | ```
74 | 
75 | ## Further Reading
76 | 
77 | - [Functions](./../../reference/functions) in the Move Reference.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/generics.md
```
1 | # Generics
2 | 
3 | Generics are a way to define a type or function that can work with any type. This is useful when you
4 | want to write a function which can be used with different types, or when you want to define a type
5 | that can hold any other type. Generics are the foundation of many advanced features in Move
6 | including collections, abstract implementations, and more.
7 | 
8 | ## In the Standard Library
9 | 
10 | In this chapter we already mentioned the [vector](./vector) type, which is a generic type that can
11 | hold any other type. Another example of a generic type in the standard library is the
12 | [Option](./option) type, which is used to represent a value that may or may not be present.
13 | 
14 | ## Generic Syntax
15 | 
16 | To define a generic type or function, a type signature needs to have a list of generic parameters
17 | enclosed in angle brackets (`<` and `>`). The generic parameters are separated by commas.
18 | 
19 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/generics.move anchor=container
20 | 
21 | ```
22 | 
23 | In the example above, `Container` is a generic type with a single type parameter `T`, the `value`
24 | field of the container stores the `T`. The `new` function is a generic function with a single type
25 | parameter `T`, and it returns a `Container` with the given value. Generic types must be initialized
26 | with a concrete type, and generic functions must be called with a concrete type, although in some
27 | cases the Move compiler can infer the correct type.
28 | 
29 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/generics.move anchor=test_container
30 | 
31 | ```
32 | 
33 | In the test function `test_container`, we demonstrate three equivalent ways to create a new
34 | `Container` with a `u8` value. Because numeric constants have ambiguous types, we must specify the
35 | type of the number literal somewhere (in the type of the container, the parameter to `new`, or the
36 | number literal itself); once we specify one of these the compiler can infer the others.
37 | 
38 | ## Multiple Type Parameters
39 | 
40 | You can define a type or function with multiple type parameters. The type parameters are separated
41 | by commas.
42 | 
43 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/generics.move anchor=pair
44 | 
45 | ```
46 | 
47 | In the example above, `Pair` is a generic type with two type parameters `T` and `U`, and the
48 | `new_pair` function is a generic function with two type parameters `T` and `U`. The function returns
49 | a `Pair` with the given values. The order of the type parameters is important, and should match the
50 | order of the type parameters in the type signature.
51 | 
52 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/generics.move anchor=test_pair
53 | 
54 | ```
55 | 
56 | If we added another instance where we swapped type parameters in the `new_pair` function, and tried
57 | to compare two types, we'd see that the type signatures are different, and cannot be compared.
58 | 
59 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/generics.move anchor=test_pair_swap
60 | 
61 | ```
62 | 
63 | Since the types for `pair1` and `pair2` are different, the comparison `pair1 == pair2` will not
64 | compile.
65 | 
66 | ## Why Generics?
67 | 
68 | In the examples above we focused on instantiating generic types and calling generic functions to
69 | create instances of these types. However, the real power of generics lies in their ability to define
70 | shared behavior for the base, generic type, and then use it independently of the concrete types.
71 | This is especially useful when working with collections, abstract implementations, and other
72 | advanced features in Move.
73 | 
74 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/generics.move anchor=user
75 | 
76 | ```
77 | 
78 | In the example above, `User` is a generic type with a single type parameter `T`, with shared fields
79 | `name`, `age`, and the generic `metadata` field, which can store any type. No matter what `metadata`
80 | is, all instances of `User` will contain the same fields and methods.
81 | 
82 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/generics.move anchor=update_user
83 | 
84 | ```
85 | 
86 | ## Phantom Type Parameters
87 | 
88 | In some cases, you may want to define a generic type with a type parameter that is not used in the
89 | fields or methods of the type. This is called a _phantom type parameter_. Phantom type parameters
90 | are useful when you want to define a type that can hold any other type, but you want to enforce some
91 | constraints on the type parameter.
92 | 
93 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/generics.move anchor=phantom
94 | 
95 | ```
96 | 
97 | The `Coin` type here does not contain any fields or methods that use the type parameter `T`. It is
98 | used to differentiate between different types of coins, and to enforce some constraints on the type
99 | parameter `T`.
100 | 
101 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/generics.move anchor=test_phantom
102 | 
103 | ```
104 | 
105 | In the example above, we demonstrate how to create two different instances of `Coin` with different
106 | phantom type parameters `USD` and `EUR`. The type parameter `T` is not used in the fields or methods
107 | of the `Coin` type, but it is used to differentiate between different types of coins. This helps
108 | ensure that the `USD` and `EUR` coins are not mistakenly mixed up.
109 | 
110 | ## Constraints on Type Parameters
111 | 
112 | Type parameters can be constrained to have certain abilities. This is useful when you need the inner
113 | type to allow certain behaviors, such as _copy_ or _drop_. The syntax for constraining a type
114 | parameter is `T: <ability> + <ability>`.
115 | 
116 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/generics.move anchor=constraints
117 | 
118 | ```
119 | 
120 | The Move Compiler will enforce that the type parameter `T` has the specified abilities. If the type
121 | parameter does not have the specified abilities, the code will not compile.
122 | 
123 | <!-- TODO: failure case -->
124 | 
125 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/generics.move anchor=test_constraints
126 | 
127 | ```
128 | 
129 | ## Further Reading
130 | 
131 | - [Generics](./../../reference/generics) in the Move Reference.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/importing-modules.md
```
1 | # Importing Modules
2 | 
3 | <!--
4 |     TODO: create a better example for:
5 |         1. Importing a module in general
6 |         2. Importing a member
7 |         3. Importing multiple members
8 |         4. Grouping imports
9 |         5. Self keyword for groups
10 | -->
11 | 
12 | <!--
13 | 
14 | Goals:
15 |     - Show the import syntax
16 |     - Local dependencies
17 |     - External dependencies
18 |     - Importing modules from other packages
19 | 
20 |  -->
21 | 
22 | Move achieves high modularity and code reuse by allowing module imports. Modules within the same
23 | package can import each other, and a new package can depend on already existing packages and use
24 | their modules too. This section will cover the basics of importing modules and how to use them in
25 | your own code.
26 | 
27 | ## Importing a Module
28 | 
29 | Modules defined in the same package can import each other. The `use` keyword is followed by the
30 | module path, which consists of the package address (or alias) and the module name separated by `::`.
31 | 
32 | ```move title="File: sources/module_one.move" file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/importing-modules.move anchor=module_one
33 | 
34 | ```
35 | 
36 | Another module defined in the same package can import the first module using the `use` keyword.
37 | 
38 | ```move title="File: sources/module_two.move" file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/importing-modules-two.move anchor=module_two
39 | 
40 | ```
41 | 
42 | > Note: Any item (struct, function, constant, etc.) that you want to import from another module must
43 | > be marked with the `public` (or `public(package)` - see [visibility modifiers](./visibility))
44 | > keyword to make it accessible outside its defining module. For example, the `Character` struct and
45 | > the `new` function in `module_one` are marked public so they can be used in `module_two`.
46 | 
47 | ## Importing Members
48 | 
49 | You can also import specific members from a module. This is useful when you only need a single
50 | function or a single type from a module. The syntax is the same as for importing a module, but you
51 | add the member name after the module path.
52 | 
53 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/importing-modules-members.move anchor=members
54 | 
55 | ```
56 | 
57 | ## Grouping Imports
58 | 
59 | Imports can be grouped into a single `use` statement using curly braces `{}`. This allows for
60 | cleaner and more organized code when importing multiple members from the same module or package.
61 | 
62 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/importing-modules-grouped.move anchor=grouped
63 | 
64 | ```
65 | 
66 | Importing function names is less common in Move, since the function names can overlap and cause
67 | confusion. A recommended practice is to import the entire module and use the module path to access
68 | the function. Types have unique names and should be imported individually.
69 | 
70 | To import members and the module itself in the group import, you can use the `Self` keyword. The
71 | `Self` keyword refers to the module itself and can be used to import the module and its members.
72 | 
73 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/importing-modules-self.move anchor=self
74 | 
75 | ```
76 | 
77 | ## Resolving Name Conflicts
78 | 
79 | When importing multiple members from different modules, it is possible to have name conflicts. For
80 | example, if you import two modules that both have a function with the same name, you will need to
81 | use the module path to access the function. It is also possible to have modules with the same name
82 | in different packages. To resolve the conflict and avoid ambiguity, Move offers the `as` keyword to
83 | rename the imported member.
84 | 
85 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/importing-modules-conflict-resolution.move anchor=conflict
86 | 
87 | ```
88 | 
89 | ## Adding an External Dependency
90 | 
91 | Move packages can depend on other packages; the dependencies are listed in the
92 | [Package Manifest](./../concepts/manifest) file called `Move.toml`.
93 | 
94 | Package dependencies are defined in the [Package Manifest](./../concepts/manifest) as follows:
95 | 
96 | ```ini title="Move.toml"
97 | [dependencies]
98 | Example = { git = "https://github.com/Example/example.git", subdir = "path/to/package", rev = "v1.2.3" }
99 | Local = { local = "../my_other_package" }
100 | ```
101 | 
102 | The `dependencies` section contains an entry for each package dependency. The key of the entry is
103 | the name of the package (`Example` or `Local` in the example), and the value is either a git import
104 | table or a local path. The git import contains the URL of the package, the subdirectory where the
105 | package is located, and the revision of the package. The local path is a relative path to the qa
106 | package directory.
107 | 
108 | If you add a dependency, all of its dependencies also become available to your package.
109 | 
110 | If a dependency is added to the `Move.toml` file, the compiler will automatically fetch (and later
111 | refetch) the dependencies when building the package.
112 | 
113 | > Starting with version 1.45 of the sui CLI, the system packages are automatically included as
114 | > dependencies for all packages if they are not present in `Move.toml`. Therefore, `MoveStdlib`,
115 | > `Sui`, `System`, `Bridge`, and `Deepbook` are all available without an explicit import.
116 | 
117 | ## Importing a Module from Another Package
118 | 
119 | Normally, packages define their addresses in the `[addresses]` section. You can use aliases instead
120 | of full addresses. For example, instead of using `0x2::coin` to reference the Sui `coin` module, you
121 | can use `sui::coin`. The `sui` alias is defined in the Sui Framework package's manifest. Similarly,
122 | the `std` alias is defined in the Standard Library package and can be used instead of `0x1` to
123 | access standard library modules.
124 | 
125 | To import a module from another package, use the `use` keyword followed by the module path. The
126 | module path consists of the package address (or alias) and the module name, separated by `::`.
127 | 
128 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/importing-modules-external.move anchor=external
129 | 
130 | ```
131 | 
132 | > Note: Module address names come from the `[addresses]` section of the manifest file (`Move.toml`),
133 | > not the names used in the `[dependencies]` section.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/index.md
```
1 | # Move Basics
2 | 
3 | This chapter is all about the basic syntax of the Move language. It covers the basics of the
4 | language, such as types, modules, functions, and control flow. It focuses on the language without a
5 | storage model or a blockchain, and explains the essential concepts of the language. To learn
6 | features specific to Sui, such as storage functions and abilities, refer to the
7 | [Using Objects](./../storage/) chapter, however, it is recommended to start with this chapter first.
8 | 
9 | <!-- TODO: cross link with Reference -->
```

move-book/book/move-basics/module.md
```
1 | # Module
2 | 
3 | <!--
4 | 
5 | Chapter: Base Syntax
6 | Goal: Introduce module keyword.
7 | Notes:
8 |     - modules are the base unit of code organization
9 |     - module members are private by default
10 |     - types internal to the module have special access rules
11 |     - only module can pack and unpack its types
12 | 
13 |  -->
14 | 
15 | A module is the base unit of code organization in Move. Modules are used to group and isolate code,
16 | and all members of the module are private to the module by default. In this section you will learn
17 | how to define a module, declare its members, and access it from other modules.
18 | 
19 | ## Module Declaration
20 | 
21 | Modules are declared using the `module` keyword followed by the package address, module name,
22 | semicolon, and the module body. The module name should be in `snake_case` - all lowercase letters
23 | with underscores between words. Modules names must be unique in the package.
24 | 
25 | Usually, a single file in the `sources/` folder contains a single module. The file name should match
26 | the module name - for example, a `donut_shop` module should be stored in the `donut_shop.move` file.
27 | You can read more about coding conventions in the
28 | [Coding Conventions](./../guides/code-quality-checklist) section.
29 | 
30 | > If you need to declare more than one module in a file, you must use [Module Block](#module-block)
31 | > syntax.
32 | 
33 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/module-label.move anchor=module
34 | 
35 | ```
36 | 
37 | Structs, functions, constants and imports all part of the module:
38 | 
39 | - [Structs](./struct)
40 | - [Functions](./function)
41 | - [Constants](./constants)
42 | - [Imports](./importing-modules)
43 | - [Struct Methods](./struct-methods)
44 | 
45 | ## Address and Named Address
46 | 
47 | The module address can be specified as both: an address _literal_ (does not require the `@` prefix)
48 | or a named address specified in the [Package Manifest](./../concepts/manifest). In the example
49 | below, both are identical because there's a `book = "0x0"` record in the `[addresses]` section of
50 | the `Move.toml`.
51 | 
52 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/module.move anchor=address_literal
53 | 
54 | ```
55 | 
56 | Addresses section in the Move.toml:
57 | 
58 | ```toml
59 | # Move.toml
60 | [addresses]
61 | book = "0x0"
62 | ```
63 | 
64 | ## Module Members
65 | 
66 | Module members are declared inside the module body. To illustrate that, let's define a simple module
67 | with a struct, a function and a constant:
68 | 
69 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/module-members.move anchor=members
70 | 
71 | ```
72 | 
73 | ## Module Block
74 | 
75 | The pre-2024 edition of Move required the body of the module to be a _module block_ - the contents
76 | of the module needed to be surrounded by curly braces `{}`. The main reason to use block syntax and
77 | not _label_ syntax is if you need to define more than one module in a file. However, using module
78 | blocks is not recommended practice.
79 | 
80 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/module.move anchor=members
81 | 
82 | ```
83 | 
84 | ## Further Reading
85 | 
86 | - [Modules](./../../reference/modules) in the Move Reference.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/option.md
```
1 | # Option
2 | 
3 | `Option` is a type that represents an optional value which may or may not exist. The concept of
4 | `Option` in Move is borrowed from Rust, and it is a very useful primitive in Move. `Option` is
5 | defined in the [Standard Library](./standard-library), and is defined as follows:
6 | 
7 | ```move
8 | module std::option;
9 | 
10 | /// Abstraction of a value that may or may not be present.
11 | public struct Option<Element> has copy, drop, store {
12 |     vec: vector<Element>
13 | }
14 | ```
15 | 
16 | _See [full documentation for std::option][option-stdlib] module._
17 | 
18 | > The 'std::option' module is implicitly imported in every module, so you don't need to add an
19 | > explicit import.
20 | 
21 | The `Option` type is a generic type with an `Element` type parameter. It contains a single field,
22 | `vec`, which is a `vector` of `Element`. The vector can have a length of 0 or 1, representing the
23 | absence or presence of a value, respectively.
24 | 
25 | > Note: You might be surprised that `Option` is a `struct` containing a `vector` instead of an
26 | > [enum][enum-reference]. This is for historical reasons: `Option` was added to Move before it had
27 | > support for enums.
28 | 
29 | The `Option` type has two variants: `Some` and `None`. The `Some` variant contains a value, while
30 | the `None` variant represents the absence of a value. The `Option` type is used to represent the
31 | absence of a value in a type-safe way, avoiding the need for empty or `undefined` values.
32 | 
33 | ## In Practice
34 | 
35 | To showcase why the `Option` type is necessary, let's look at an example. Consider an application
36 | which takes a user input and stores it in a variable. Some fields are required, and some are
37 | optional. For example, a user's middle name is optional. While we could use an empty string to
38 | represent the absence of a middle name, it would require extra checks to differentiate between an
39 | empty string and a missing middle name. Instead, we can use the `Option` type to represent the
40 | middle name.
41 | 
42 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/option.move anchor=registry
43 | 
44 | ```
45 | 
46 | In the previous example, the `middle_name` field is of type `Option<String>`. This means that the
47 | `middle_name` field can either contain a String value, wrapped in Some, or be explicitly empty,
48 | represented by None. Using the `Option` type makes the optional nature of the field clear, avoiding
49 | ambiguity and the need for extra checks to differentiate between an empty string and a missing
50 | middle name.
51 | 
52 | ## Creating and Using Option values
53 | 
54 | The `Option` type, along with the `std::option` module, is implicitly imported in Move. This means
55 | you can use the `Option` type directly without needing a `use` statement.
56 | 
57 | To create a value of the `Option` type, you can use the `option::some` or `option::none` methods.
58 | `Option` values also support several operations (borrowing will be discussed in the
59 | [references](references#references-1) chapter):
60 | 
61 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/option.move anchor=usage
62 | 
63 | ```
64 | 
65 | ## Further Reading
66 | 
67 | - [std::option][option-stdlib] in the standard library
68 | 
69 | [enum-reference]: ./../../reference/enums
70 | [option-stdlib]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/option
```

move-book/book/move-basics/ownership-and-scope.md
```
1 | # Ownership and Scope
2 | 
3 | Every variable in Move has a scope and an owner. The scope is the range of code where the variable
4 | is valid, and the owner is the scope that this variable belongs to. Once the owner scope ends, the
5 | variable is dropped. This is a fundamental concept in Move, and it is important to understand how it
6 | works.
7 | 
8 | <!--
9 | 
10 | - Borrow Checker
11 | - Mention Rust's borrow checker
12 | - Borrowing / References intro
13 | 
14 | -->
15 | 
16 | ## Ownership
17 | 
18 | A variable defined in a function scope is owned by this scope. The runtime goes through the function
19 | scope and executes every expression and statement. After the function scope ends, the variables
20 | defined in it are dropped or deallocated.
21 | 
22 | ```move
23 | module book::ownership;
24 | 
25 | public fun owner() {
26 |     let a = 1; // a is owned by the `owner` function
27 | } // a is dropped here
28 | 
29 | public fun other() {
30 |     let b = 2; // b is owned by the `other` function
31 | } // b is dropped here
32 | 
33 | #[test]
34 | fun test_owner() {
35 |     owner();
36 |     other();
37 |     // a & b are not valid here
38 | }
39 | ```
40 | 
41 | In the example above, the variable `a` is owned by the `owner` function, and the variable `b` is
42 | owned by the `other` function. When each of these functions are called, the variables are defined,
43 | and when the function ends, the variables are discarded.
44 | 
45 | ## Returning a Value
46 | 
47 | If we changed the `owner` function to return the variable `a`, then the ownership of `a` would be
48 | transferred to the caller of the function.
49 | 
50 | ```move
51 | module book::ownership;
52 | 
53 | public fun owner(): u8 {
54 |     let a = 1; // a defined here
55 |     a // scope ends, a is returned
56 | }
57 | 
58 | #[test]
59 | fun test_owner() {
60 |     let a = owner();
61 |     // a is valid here
62 | } // a is dropped here
63 | ```
64 | 
65 | ## Passing by Value
66 | 
67 | Additionally, if we passed the variable `a` to another function, the ownership of `a` would be
68 | transferred to this function. When performing this operation, we _move_ the value from one scope to
69 | another. This is also called _move semantics_.
70 | 
71 | ```move
72 | module book::ownership;
73 | 
74 | public fun owner(): u8 {
75 |     let a = 10;
76 |     a
77 | } // a is returned
78 | 
79 | public fun take_ownership(v: u8) {
80 |     // v is owned by `take_ownership`
81 | } // v is dropped here
82 | 
83 | #[test]
84 | fun test_owner() {
85 |     let a = owner();
86 |     // `u8` is copyable, pass `move a` when calling the function to force the transfer of its ownership
87 |     take_ownership(move a);
88 |     // a is not valid here
89 | }
90 | ```
91 | 
92 | ## Scopes with Blocks
93 | 
94 | Each function has a main scope, and it can also have sub-scopes via the use of blocks. A block is a
95 | sequence of statements and expressions, and it has its own scope. Variables defined in a block are
96 | owned by this block, and when the block ends, the variables are dropped.
97 | 
98 | ```move
99 | module book::ownership;
100 | 
101 | public fun owner() {
102 |     let a = 1; // a is owned by the `owner` function's scope
103 |     {
104 |         let b = 2; // the block that declares b owns it
105 |         {
106 |             let c = 3; // the block that declares c owns it
107 |         }; // c is dropped here
108 |     }; // b is dropped here
109 |     // a = b; // error: b is not valid here
110 |     // a = c; // error: c is not valid here
111 | } // a is dropped here
112 | ```
113 | 
114 | However, if we return a value from a block, the ownership of the variable is transferred to the
115 | caller of the block.
116 | 
117 | ```move
118 | module book::ownership;
119 | 
120 | public fun owner(): u8 {
121 |     let a = 1; // a is owned by the `owner` function's scope
122 |     let b = {
123 |         let c = 2; // the block that declares c owns it
124 |         c // c is returned from the block and transferred to b
125 |     };
126 |     a + b // both a and b are valid here
127 | }
128 | ```
129 | 
130 | ## Copyable Types
131 | 
132 | Some types in Move are _copyable_, which means that they can be copied without transferring
133 | ownership. This is useful for types that are small and cheap to copy, such as integers and booleans.
134 | The Move compiler will automatically copy these types when they are passed to or returned from a
135 | function, or when they're _moved_ to another scope and then accessed in their original scope.
136 | 
137 | ## Further Reading
138 | 
139 | - [Local Variables and Scopes](./../../reference/variables) in the Move Reference.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/primitive-types.md
```
1 | # Primitive Types
2 | 
3 | <!-- TODO: Shall we split this into two pages? Maybe give an overview and focus more on specifics? -->
4 | 
5 | For simple values, Move has a number of built-in primitive types. They're the foundation for all
6 | other types. The primitive types are:
7 | 
8 | - [Booleans](#booleans)
9 | - [Unsigned Integers](#integer-types)
10 | - [Addresses](./address) - covered in the next section
11 | 
12 | Before we get to the primitive types, let's first take a look at how to declare and assign variables
13 | in Move.
14 | 
15 | ## Variables and Assignment
16 | 
17 | Variables are declared using the `let` keyword. They are immutable by default, but can be made
18 | mutable by adding the `mut` keyword:
19 | 
20 | ```
21 | let <variable_name>[: <type>]  = <expression>;
22 | let mut <variable_name>[: <type>] = <expression>;
23 | ```
24 | 
25 | Where:
26 | 
27 | - `<variable_name>` - the name of the variable
28 | - `<type>` - the type of the variable, optional
29 | - `<expression>` - the value to be assigned to the variable
30 | 
31 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/primitive-types.move anchor=variables_and_assignment
32 | 
33 | ```
34 | 
35 | A mutable variable can be reassigned using the `=` operator.
36 | 
37 | ```move
38 | y = 43;
39 | ```
40 | 
41 | Variables can also be shadowed by re-declaring them.
42 | 
43 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/primitive-types.move anchor=shadowing
44 | 
45 | ```
46 | 
47 | ## Booleans
48 | 
49 | The `bool` type represents a boolean value - yes or no, true or false. It has two possible values:
50 | `true` and `false`, which are keywords in Move. For booleans, the compiler can always infer the type
51 | from the value, so there is no need to explicitly specify it.
52 | 
53 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/primitive-types.move anchor=boolean
54 | 
55 | ```
56 | 
57 | Booleans are often used to store flags and to control the flow of the program. Please refer to the
58 | [Control Flow](./control-flow) section for more information.
59 | 
60 | ## Integer Types
61 | 
62 | Move supports unsigned integers of various sizes, from 8-bit to 256-bit. The integer types are:
63 | 
64 | - `u8` - 8-bit
65 | - `u16` - 16-bit
66 | - `u32` - 32-bit
67 | - `u64` - 64-bit
68 | - `u128` - 128-bit
69 | - `u256` - 256-bit
70 | 
71 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/primitive-types.move anchor=integers
72 | 
73 | ```
74 | 
75 | While boolean literals like `true` and `false` are clearly booleans, an integer literal like `42`
76 | could be any of the integer types. In most of the cases, the compiler will infer the type from the
77 | value, usually defaulting to `u64`. However, sometimes the compiler is unable to infer the type and
78 | will require an explicit type annotation. It can either be provided during assignment or by using a
79 | type suffix.
80 | 
81 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/primitive-types.move anchor=integer_explicit_type
82 | 
83 | ```
84 | 
85 | ### Operations
86 | 
87 | Move supports the standard arithmetic operations for integers: addition, subtraction,
88 | multiplication, division, and modulus (remainder). The syntax for these operations is:
89 | 
90 | | Syntax | Operation           | Aborts If                                |
91 | | ------ | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
92 | | +      | addition            | Result is too large for the integer type |
93 | | -      | subtraction         | Result is less than zero                 |
94 | | \*     | multiplication      | Result is too large for the integer type |
95 | | %      | modulus (remainder) | The divisor is 0                         |
96 | | /      | truncating division | The divisor is 0                         |
97 | 
98 | > For more operations, including bitwise operations, please refer to the
99 | > [Move Reference](./../../reference/primitive-types/integers#bitwise).
100 | 
101 | The types of the operands _must match_, or the compiler will raise an error. The result of the
102 | operation will be of the same type as the operands. To perform operations on different types, the
103 | operands need to be cast to the same type.
104 | 
105 | <!-- TODO: add examples + parentheses for arithmetic operations -->
106 | <!-- TODO: add bitwise operators -->
107 | 
108 | ### Casting with `as`
109 | 
110 | Move supports explicit casting between integer types. The syntax is as follows:
111 | 
112 | ```move
113 | <expression> as <type>
114 | ```
115 | 
116 | Note that parentheses around the expression may be required to prevent ambiguity:
117 | 
118 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/primitive-types.move anchor=cast_as
119 | 
120 | ```
121 | 
122 | A more complex example, preventing overflow:
123 | 
124 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/primitive-types.move anchor=overflow
125 | 
126 | ```
127 | 
128 | ### Overflow
129 | 
130 | Move does not support overflow / underflow; an operation that results in a value outside the range
131 | of the type will raise a runtime error. This is a safety feature to prevent unexpected behavior.
132 | 
133 | ```move
134 | let x = 255u8;
135 | let y = 1u8;
136 | 
137 | // This will raise an error
138 | let z = x + y;
139 | ```
140 | 
141 | ## Further Reading
142 | 
143 | - [Bool](./../../reference/primitive-types/bool) in the Move Reference.
144 | - [Integer](./../../reference/primitive-types/integers) in the Move Reference.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/references.md
```
1 | # References
2 | 
3 | <!--
4 | 
5 | Chapter: Basic Syntax
6 | Goal: Show what the borrow checker is and how it works.
7 | Notes:
8 |     - give the metro pass example
9 |     - show why passing by reference is useful
10 |     - mention that reference comparison is faster
11 |     - references can be both mutable and immutable
12 |     - immutable access to shared objects is faster
13 |     - implicit copy
14 |     - moving the value
15 |     - unpacking a reference (mutable and immutable)
16 | 
17 |  -->
18 | 
19 | In the [Ownership and Scope](./ownership-and-scope) section, we explained that when a value is
20 | passed to a function, it is _moved_ to the function's scope. This means that the function becomes
21 | the owner of the value, and the original scope (owner) can no longer use it. This is an important
22 | concept in Move, as it ensures that the value is not used in multiple places at the same time.
23 | However, there are use cases when we want to pass a value to a function but retain ownership. This
24 | is where references come into play.
25 | 
26 | To illustrate this, let's consider a simple example - an application for a metro (subway) pass. We
27 | will look at 4 different scenarios where a card can be:
28 | 
29 | 1. Purchased at a kiosk for a fixed price
30 | 2. Shown to an inspector to prove that the passenger has a valid pass
31 | 3. Used at the turnstile to enter the metro, and purchase a ride
32 | 4. Recycled after it's empty
33 | 
34 | ## Layout
35 | 
36 | The initial layout of the metro pass application is simple. We define the `Card` type and the `USES`
37 | [constant](./constants) that represents the number of rides on a single card. We also add
38 | [error constants](./assert-and-abort#error-constants) for the case when the card is empty and when the card is not empty.
39 | 
40 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/references.move anchor=header_new
41 | module book::metro_pass;
42 | 
43 | 
44 | ```
45 | 
46 | <!-- In [the previous section](./ownership-and-scope) we explained the ownership and scope in Move. We showed how the value is *moved* to a new scope, and how it changes the owner. In this section, we will explain how to *borrow* a reference to a value to avoid moving it, and how Move's *borrow checker* ensures that the references are used correctly. -->
47 | 
48 | ## References
49 | 
50 | References are a way to _show_ a value to a function without giving up ownership. In our case, when
51 | we show the Card to the inspector, we don't want to give up ownership of it, and we don't allow the
52 | inspector to use up any of our rides. We just want to allow the _reading_ of the value of our Card
53 | and to prove its ownership.
54 | 
55 | To do so, in the function signature, we use the `&` symbol to indicate that we are passing a
56 | _reference_ to the value, not the value itself.
57 | 
58 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/references.move anchor=immutable
59 | 
60 | ```
61 | 
62 | Because the function does not take ownership of the Card, it can _read_ its data but cannot _write_
63 | to it, meaning it cannot modify the number of rides. Additionally, the function signature ensures
64 | that it cannot be called without a Card instance. This is an important property that allows the
65 | [Capability Pattern](./../programmability/capability), which we will cover in the next chapters.
66 | 
67 | Creating a reference to a value is often referred to as "borrowing" the value. For example, the
68 | method to get a reference to the value wrapped by an `Option` is called `borrow`.
69 | 
70 | ## Mutable Reference
71 | 
72 | In some cases, we want to allow the function to modify the Card. For example, when using the Card at
73 | a turnstile, we need to deduct a ride. To achieve this, we use the `&mut` keyword in the function
74 | signature.
75 | 
76 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/references.move anchor=mutable
77 | 
78 | ```
79 | 
80 | As you can see in the function body, the `&mut` reference allows mutating the value, and the
81 | function can spend rides.
82 | 
83 | ## Passing by Value
84 | 
85 | Lastly, let's illustrate what happens when we pass the value itself to the function. In this case,
86 | the function takes the ownership of the value, making it inaccessible in the original scope. The
87 | owner of the Card can recycle it and thereby relinquish ownership to the function.
88 | 
89 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/references.move anchor=move
90 | 
91 | ```
92 | 
93 | In the `recycle` function, the Card is passed by value, transferring ownership to the function. This
94 | allows it to be unpacked and destroyed.
95 | 
96 | > Note: In Move, `_` is a wildcard pattern used in destructuring to ignore a field while still
97 | > consuming the value. Destructuring must match all fields in a struct type. If a struct has fields,
98 | > you must list all of them explicitly or use `_` to ignore unwanted fields.
99 | 
100 | ## Full Example
101 | 
102 | To illustrate the full flow of the application, let's put all the pieces together in a test.
103 | 
104 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/references.move anchor=move_2024
105 | 
106 | ```
107 | 
108 | ## Further Reading
109 | 
110 | - [References](/reference/primitive-types/references) in the Move
111 |   Reference.
112 | 
113 | <!-- ## Dereference and Copy -->
114 | 
115 | <!-- TODO: defer and copy, *& -->
116 | 
117 | <!-- ## Notes -->
118 | 
119 | <!--
120 |     Move 2024 is great but it's better to show the example with explicit &t and &mut t
121 |     ...and then say that the example could be rewritten with the new syntax
122 | 
123 | 
124 | -->
125 | 
126 | <!-- ## Move 2024
127 | 
128 | Here's the test from this page written with the Move 2024 syntax:
129 | 
130 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/references.move anchor=move_2024
131 | ```
132 | -->
```

move-book/book/move-basics/standard-library.md
```
1 | # Standard Library
2 | 
3 | <!-- The Move standard library provides a set of modules  -->
4 | 
5 | The Move Standard Library provides functionality for native types and operations. It is a standard
6 | collection of modules that do not interact with storage, but provide basic tools for working with
7 | and manipulating data. It is the only dependency of the
8 | [Sui Framework](./../programmability/sui-framework), and is imported together with it.
9 | 
10 | ## Most Common Modules
11 | 
12 | In this book we go into detail about most of the modules in the Standard Library, however, it is
13 | also helpful to give an overview of the features, so that you can get a sense of what is available
14 | and which module implements it.
15 | 
16 | <!-- Custom CSS addition in the theme/custom.css  -->
17 | <div class="modules-table">
18 | 
19 | | Module                                                                           | Description                                                                | Chapter                              |
20 | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
21 | | [std::string](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/string)               | Provides basic string operations                                           | [String](./string)                   |
22 | | [std::ascii](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/ascii)                 | Provides basic ASCII operations                                            | -                                    |
23 | | [std::option](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/option)               | Implements `Option<T>`                                                     | [Option](./option)                   |
24 | | [std::vector](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/vector)               | Native operations on the vector type                                       | [Vector](./vector)                   |
25 | | [std::bcs](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/bcs)                     | Contains the `bcs::to_bytes()` function                                    | [BCS](./../programmability/bcs)      |
26 | | [std::address](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/address)             | Contains a single `address::length` function                               | [Address](./address)                 |
27 | | [std::type_name](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/type_name)         | Allows runtime _type reflection_                                           | [Type Reflection](./type-reflection) |
28 | | [std::hash](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/hash)                   | Hashing functions: `sha2_256` and `sha3_256`                               | -                                    |
29 | | [std::debug](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/debug)                 | Contains debugging functions, which are available in only in **test** mode | -                                    |
30 | | [std::bit_vector](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/bit_vector)       | Provides operations on bit vectors                                         | -                                    |
31 | | [std::fixed_point32](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/fixed_point32) | Provides the `FixedPoint32` type                                           | -                                    |
32 | 
33 | </div>
34 | 
35 | ## Integer Modules
36 | 
37 | The Move Standard Library provides a set of functions associated with integer types. These functions
38 | are split into multiple modules, each associated with a specific integer type. The modules should
39 | not be imported directly, as their functions are available on every integer value.
40 | 
41 | > All of the modules provide the same set of functions. Namely, `max`, `diff`,
42 | > `divide_and_round_up`, `sqrt` and `pow`.
43 | 
44 | <!-- Custom CSS addition in the theme/custom.css  -->
45 | <div class="modules-table">
46 | 
47 | | Module                                                         | Description                   |
48 | | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
49 | | [std::u8](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/u8)     | Functions for the `u8` type   |
50 | | [std::u16](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/u16)   | Functions for the `u16` type  |
51 | | [std::u32](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/u32)   | Functions for the `u32` type  |
52 | | [std::u64](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/u64)   | Functions for the `u64` type  |
53 | | [std::u128](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/u128) | Functions for the `u128` type |
54 | | [std::u256](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/u256) | Functions for the `u256` type |
55 | 
56 | </div>
57 | 
58 | ## Exported Addresses
59 | 
60 | The Standard Library exports a single named address - `std = 0x1`. Note the alias `std` is defined
61 | here.
62 | 
63 | ```toml
64 | [addresses]
65 | std = "0x1"
66 | ```
67 | 
68 | ## Implicit Imports
69 | 
70 | Some modules are imported implicitly and are available in the module without the explicit `use`
71 | import. For the Standard Library, these modules and types include:
72 | 
73 | - std::vector
74 | - std::option
75 | - std::option::Option
76 | 
77 | ## Importing std without Sui Framework
78 | 
79 | The Move Standard Library can be imported to the package directly. However, `std` alone is not
80 | enough to build a meaningful application, as it does not provide any storage capabilities and can't
81 | interact with the on-chain state.
82 | 
83 | ```toml
84 | MoveStdlib = { git = "https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui.git", subdir = "crates/sui-framework/packages/move-stdlib", rev = "framework/mainnet" }
85 | ```
86 | 
87 | ## Source Code
88 | 
89 | The source code of the Move Standard Library is available in the
90 | [Sui repository](https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/tree/main/crates/sui-framework/packages/move-stdlib/sources).
```

move-book/book/move-basics/string.md
```
1 | # String
2 | 
3 | While Move does not have a built-in type to represent strings, it does have two standard
4 | implementations for strings in the [Standard Library](./standard-library). The `std::string` module
5 | defines a `String` type and methods for UTF-8 encoded strings, and the second module, `std::ascii`,
6 | provides an ASCII `String` type and its methods.
7 | 
8 | > The Sui execution environment automatically converts bytevector into `String` in transaction
9 | > inputs. As a result, in many cases, constructing a String directly within the
10 | > [Transaction Block](./../concepts/what-is-a-transaction) is unnecessary.
11 | 
12 | <!--
13 | 
14 | ## Bytestring Literal
15 | 
16 | TODO:
17 | 
18 | - reference vector
19 | - reference literals - [Expression](./expression#literals)
20 | 
21 | -->
22 | 
23 | ## Strings are bytes
24 | 
25 | No matter which type of string you use, it is important to know that strings are just bytes. The
26 | wrappers provided by the `string` and `ascii` modules are just that: wrappers. They do provide
27 | safety checks and methods to work with strings, but at the end of the day, they are just vectors of
28 | bytes.
29 | 
30 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/string.move anchor=custom
31 | 
32 | ```
33 | 
34 | ## Working with UTF-8 Strings
35 | 
36 | While there are two types of strings (`string` and `ascii`) in the standard library, the `string`
37 | module should be considered the default. It has native implementations of many common operations,
38 | leveraging low-level, optimized runtime code for superior performance. In contrast, the `ascii`
39 | module is fully implemented in Move, relying on higher-level abstractions and making it less
40 | suitable for performance-critical tasks.
41 | 
42 | ### Definition
43 | 
44 | The `String` type in the `std::string` module is defined as follows:
45 | 
46 | ```move
47 | module std::string;
48 | 
49 | /// A `String` holds a sequence of bytes which is guaranteed to be in utf8 format.
50 | public struct String has copy, drop, store {
51 |     bytes: vector<u8>,
52 | }
53 | ```
54 | 
55 | _See [full documentation for std::string][string-stdlib] module._
56 | 
57 | ### Creating a String
58 | 
59 | To create a new UTF-8 `String` instance, you can use the `string::utf8` method. The
60 | [Standard Library](./standard-library) provides an alias `.to_string()` on the `vector<u8>` for
61 | convenience.
62 | 
63 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/string.move anchor=utf8
64 | 
65 | ```
66 | 
67 | ### Common Operations
68 | 
69 | UTF8 String provides a number of methods to work with strings. The most common operations on strings
70 | are: concatenation, slicing, and getting the length. Additionally, for custom string operations, the
71 | `bytes()` method can be used to get the underlying byte vector.
72 | 
73 | ```move
74 | let mut str = b"Hello,".to_string();
75 | let another = b" World!".to_string();
76 | 
77 | // append(String) adds the content to the end of the string
78 | str.append(another);
79 | 
80 | // `sub_string(start, end)` copies a slice of the string
81 | str.sub_string(0, 5); // "Hello"
82 | 
83 | // `length()` returns the number of bytes in the string
84 | str.length(); // 12 (bytes)
85 | 
86 | // methods can also be chained! Get a length of a substring
87 | str.sub_string(0, 5).length(); // 5 (bytes)
88 | 
89 | // whether the string is empty
90 | str.is_empty(); // false
91 | 
92 | // get the underlying byte vector for custom operations
93 | let bytes: &vector<u8> = str.bytes();
94 | ```
95 | 
96 | ### Safe UTF-8 Operations
97 | 
98 | The default `utf8` method may abort if the bytes passed into it are not valid UTF-8. If you are not
99 | sure that the bytes you are passing are valid, you should use the `try_utf8` method instead. It
100 | returns an `Option<String>`, which contains no value if the bytes are not valid UTF-8, and a string
101 | otherwise.
102 | 
103 | > Hint: Functions with names starting with `try_*` typically return an `Option`. If the operation
104 | > succeeds, the result is wrapped in `Some`. If it fails, the function returns `None`. This naming
105 | > convention, commonly used in Move, is inspired by Rust.
106 | 
107 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/string.move anchor=safe_utf8
108 | 
109 | ```
110 | 
111 | ### UTF-8 Limitations
112 | 
113 | The `string` module does not provide a way to access individual characters in a string. This is
114 | because UTF-8 is a variable-length encoding, and the length of a character can be anywhere from 1 to
115 | 4 bytes. Similarly, the `length()` method returns the number of bytes in the string, not the number
116 | of characters.
117 | 
118 | However, methods like `sub_string` and `insert` validate character boundaries and abort if the
119 | specified index falls within the middle of a character.
120 | 
121 | ## ASCII Strings
122 | 
123 | This section is coming soon!
124 | 
125 | ## Further Reading
126 | 
127 | - [std::string][string-stdlib] module documentation.
128 | - [std::ascii][ascii-stdlib] module documentation.
129 | 
130 | [enum-reference]: /reference/enums.html
131 | [string-stdlib]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/string
132 | [ascii-stdlib]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/ascii
```

move-book/book/move-basics/struct-methods.md
```
1 | # Struct Methods
2 | 
3 | Move Compiler supports _receiver syntax_ `e.f()`, which allows defining methods which can be called
4 | on instances of a struct. The term "receiver" specifically refers to the instance that receives the
5 | method call. This is like the method syntax in other programming languages. It is a convenient way
6 | to define functions that operate on the fields of a struct, providing direct access to the struct's
7 | fields and creating cleaner, more intuitive code than passing the struct as a parameter.
8 | 
9 | ## Method syntax
10 | 
11 | If the first argument of a function is a struct internal to the module that defines the function,
12 | then the function can be called using the `.` operator. However, if the type of the first argument
13 | is defined in another module, then method won't be associated with the struct by default. In this
14 | case, the `.` operator syntax is not available, and the function must be called using standard
15 | function call syntax.
16 | 
17 | When a module is imported, its methods are automatically associated with the struct.
18 | 
19 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/struct-methods.move anchor=hero
20 | 
21 | ```
22 | 
23 | ## Method Aliases
24 | 
25 | Method aliases help avoid name conflicts when modules define multiple structs and their methods.
26 | They can also provide more descriptive method names for structs.
27 | 
28 | Here's the syntax:
29 | 
30 | ```move
31 | // for local method association
32 | use fun function_path as Type.method_name;
33 | 
34 | // exported alias
35 | public use fun function_path as Type.method_name;
36 | ```
37 | 
38 | > Public aliases are only allowed for structs defined in the same module. For structs defined in
39 | > other modules, aliases can still be created but cannot be made public.
40 | 
41 | In the example below, we changed the `hero` module and added another type - `Villain`. Both `Hero`
42 | and `Villain` have similar field names and methods. To avoid name conflicts, we prefixed methods
43 | with `hero_` and `villain_` respectively. However, using aliases allows these methods to be called
44 | on struct instances without the prefix:
45 | 
46 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/struct-methods-2.move anchor=hero_and_villain
47 | 
48 | ```
49 | 
50 | In the test function, the `health` method is called directly on the `Hero` and `Villain` instances
51 | without the prefix, as the compiler automatically associates the methods with their respective
52 | structs.
53 | 
54 | > Note: In the test function, `hero.health()` is calling the aliased method, not directly accessing
55 | > the private `health` field. While the `Hero` and `Villain` structs are public, their fields remain
56 | > private to the module. The method call `hero.health()` uses the public alias defined by
57 | > `public use fun hero_health as Hero.health`, which provides controlled access to the private
58 | > field.
59 | 
60 | <!-- ## Aliasing an external module's method
61 | 
62 | It is also possible to associate a function defined in another module with a struct from the current
63 | module. Following the same approach, we can create an alias for the method defined in another
64 | module. Let's use the `bcs::to_bytes` method from the [Standard Library](./standard-library) and
65 | associate it with the `Hero` struct. It will allow serializing the `Hero` struct to a vector of
66 | bytes.
67 | 
68 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/struct-methods-3.move anchor=hero_to_bytes
69 | ``` -->
70 | 
71 | ## Further Reading
72 | 
73 | - [Method Syntax](./../../reference/method-syntax) in the Move Reference.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/struct.md
```
1 | # Custom Types with Struct
2 | 
3 | Move's type system shines when it comes to defining custom types. User defined types can be custom
4 | tailored to the specific needs of the application, not only on the data level, but also in its
5 | behavior. In this section we introduce the struct definition and how to use it.
6 | 
7 | ## Struct
8 | 
9 | To define a custom type, you can use the `struct` keyword followed by the name of the type. After
10 | the name, you can define the fields of the struct. Each field is defined with the
11 | `field_name: field_type` syntax. Field definitions must be separated by commas. The fields can be of
12 | any type, including other structs.
13 | 
14 | > Move does not support recursive structs, meaning a struct cannot contain itself as a field.
15 | 
16 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/struct.move anchor=def
17 | 
18 | ```
19 | 
20 | In the example above, we define a `Record` struct with five fields. The `title` field is of type
21 | `String`, the `artist` field is of type `Artist`, the `year` field is of type `u16`, the `is_debut`
22 | field is of type `bool`, and the `edition` field is of type `Option<u16>`. The `edition` field is of
23 | type `Option<u16>` to represent that the edition is optional.
24 | 
25 | Structs are private by default, meaning they cannot be imported and used outside of the module they
26 | are defined in. Their fields are also private and can't be accessed from outside the module. See
27 | [visibility](./visibility) for more information on different visibility modifiers.
28 | 
29 | > Fields of a struct are private and can only be accessed by the module defining the struct. Reading
30 | > and writing the fields of a struct in other modules is only possible if the module defining the
31 | > struct provides public functions to access the fields.
32 | 
33 | ## Create and use an instance
34 | 
35 | We described the _definition_ of a struct. Now let's see how to initialize a struct and use it. A
36 | struct can be initialized using the `struct_name { field1: value1, field2: value2, ... }` syntax.
37 | The fields can be initialized in any order, and all of the required fields must be set.
38 | 
39 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/struct.move anchor=pack
40 | 
41 | ```
42 | 
43 | In the example above, we create an instance of the `Artist` struct and set the `name` field to a
44 | string "The Beatles".
45 | 
46 | To access the fields of a struct, you can use the `.` operator followed by the field name.
47 | 
48 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/struct.move anchor=access
49 | 
50 | ```
51 | 
52 | Only the module defining the struct can access its fields (both mutably and immutably). So the above
53 | code should be in the same module as the `Artist` struct.
54 | 
55 | <!-- ## Accessing Fields
56 | 
57 | Struct fields are private and can be accessed only by the module defining the struct. To access the fields of a struct, you can use the `.` operator followed by the field name.
58 | 
59 | ```move
60 | # anchor: access file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/struct.move anchor=access
61 | ```
62 | -->
63 | 
64 | ## Unpacking a struct
65 | 
66 | Structs are non-discardable by default, meaning that the initialized struct value must be used,
67 | either by storing it or unpacking it. Unpacking a struct means deconstructing it into its fields.
68 | This is done using the `let` keyword followed by the struct name and the field names.
69 | 
70 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/struct.move anchor=unpack
71 | 
72 | ```
73 | 
74 | In the example above we unpack the `Artist` struct and create a new variable `name` with the value
75 | of the `name` field. Because the variable is not used, the compiler will raise a warning. To
76 | suppress the warning, you can use the underscore `_` to indicate that the variable is intentionally
77 | unused.
78 | 
79 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/struct.move anchor=unpack_ignore
80 | 
81 | ```
82 | 
83 | ## Further Reading
84 | 
85 | - [Structs](./../../reference/structs) in the Move Reference.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/testing.md
```
1 | # Testing
2 | 
3 | Testing is a crucial aspect of software development, especially in blockchain applications where
4 | security and correctness are paramount. In this section, we will cover the fundamentals of testing
5 | in Move, including how to write and organize tests effectively.
6 | 
7 | ## The `#[test]` Attribute
8 | 
9 | Tests in Move are functions marked with the `#[test]` attribute. This attribute tells the compiler
10 | that the function is a test function and should be run when tests are executed. Test functions are
11 | regular functions, but they must take no arguments and have no return value. They are excluded from
12 | the bytecode and are never published.
13 | 
14 | ```move
15 | module book::testing;
16 | 
17 | // The test attribute is placed before the `fun` keyword (can be both above or
18 | // right before the `fun` keyword, as in `#[test] fun my_test() { ... }`)
19 | // The name of the test in this case would be `book::testing::simple_test`.
20 | #[test]
21 | fun simple_test() {
22 |     let sum = 2 + 2;
23 |     assert!(sum == 4);
24 | }
25 | 
26 | // The name of this test would be `book::testing::more_advanced_test`.
27 | #[test] fun more_advanced_test() {
28 |     let sum = 2 + 2 + 2;
29 |     assert!(sum == 4);
30 | }
31 | ```
32 | 
33 | ## Running Tests
34 | 
35 | To run tests, you can use the `sui move test` command. This command will first build the package in
36 | _test mode_ and then run all tests found in the package. In test mode, modules from both `sources/`
37 | and `tests/` directories are processed and their tests executed.
38 | 
39 | ```bash
40 | $ sui move test
41 | > UPDATING GIT DEPENDENCY https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui.git
42 | > INCLUDING DEPENDENCY Bridge
43 | > INCLUDING DEPENDENCY DeepBook
44 | > INCLUDING DEPENDENCY SuiSystem
45 | > INCLUDING DEPENDENCY Sui
46 | > INCLUDING DEPENDENCY MoveStdlib
47 | > BUILDING book
48 | > Running Move unit tests
49 | > ...
50 | ```
51 | 
52 | <!-- TODO: fill output -->
53 | 
54 | ## Test Fail Cases with `#[expected_failure]`
55 | 
56 | Tests for fail cases can be marked with `#[expected_failure]`. This attribute, when added to a
57 | `#[test]` function, tells the compiler that the test is expected to fail. This is useful when you
58 | want to test that a function fails when a certain condition is met.
59 | 
60 | > Note: This attribute can only be added to a `#[test]` function.
61 | 
62 | The attribute can take an argument specifying the expected abort code that should be returned if the
63 | test fails. If the test returns an abort code different from the one specified in the argument, it
64 | will fail. Likewise, if execution does not result in an abort, the test will also fail.
65 | 
66 | ```move
67 | module book::testing_failure;
68 | 
69 | const EInvalidArgument: u64 = 1;
70 | 
71 | #[test]
72 | #[expected_failure(abort_code = 0)]
73 | fun test_fail() {
74 |     abort 0 // aborts with 0
75 | }
76 | 
77 | // attributes can be grouped together
78 | #[test, expected_failure(abort_code = EInvalidArgument)]
79 | fun test_fail_1() {
80 |     abort 1 // aborts with 1
81 | }
82 | ```
83 | 
84 | The `abort_code` argument can use constants defined in the tests module as well as imported from
85 | other modules. This is the only case where constants can be used and "accessed" in other modules.
86 | 
87 | ## Utilities with `#[test_only]`
88 | 
89 | In some cases, it is helpful to give the test environment access to some internal functions or
90 | features. This simplifies the testing process and allows for more thorough testing. However, it is
91 | important to remember that these functions should not be included in the final package. This is
92 | where the `#[test_only]` attribute comes in handy.
93 | 
94 | ```move
95 | module book::testing;
96 | 
97 | // Public function which uses the `secret` function.
98 | public fun multiply_by_secret(x: u64): u64 {
99 |     x * secret()
100 | }
101 | 
102 | /// Private function which is not available to the public.
103 | fun secret(): u64 { 100 }
104 | 
105 | #[test_only]
106 | /// This function is only available for testing purposes in tests and other
107 | /// test-only functions. Mind the visibility - for `#[test_only]` it is
108 | /// common to use `public` visibility.
109 | public fun secret_for_testing(): u64 {
110 |     secret()
111 | }
112 | 
113 | #[test]
114 | // In the test environment we have access to the `secret_for_testing` function.
115 | fun test_multiply_by_secret() {
116 |     let expected = secret_for_testing() * 2;
117 |     assert!(multiply_by_secret(2) == expected);
118 | }
119 | ```
120 | 
121 | Functions marked with the `#[test_only]` will be available to the test environment, and to the other
122 | modules if their visibility is set to `public`.
123 | 
124 | ## Further Reading
125 | 
126 | - [Unit Testing](/reference/unit-testing) in the Move Reference.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/type-reflection.md
```
1 | # Type Reflection
2 | 
3 | In programming languages, _reflection_ is the ability of a program to examine and modify its own
4 | structure and behavior. Move has a limited form of reflection that allows you to inspect the type of
5 | a value at runtime. This is useful when you need to store type information in a homogeneous
6 | collection, or when you need to check if a type belongs to a package.
7 | 
8 | Type reflection is implemented in the [Standard Library](./standard-library) module
9 | [`std::type_name`][type-name-stdlib]. Expressed very roughly, it gives a single function `get<T>()`
10 | which returns the name of the type `T`.
11 | 
12 | ## In practice
13 | 
14 | The module is straightforward, and operations allowed on the result are limited to getting a string
15 | representation and extracting the module and address of the type.
16 | 
17 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/type-reflection.move anchor=main
18 | 
19 | ```
20 | 
21 | ## Further Reading
22 | 
23 | - [std::type_name][type-name-stdlib] module documentation.
24 | 
25 | [type-name-stdlib]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/type_name
```

move-book/book/move-basics/vector.md
```
1 | # Vector
2 | 
3 | Vectors are a native way to store collections of elements in Move. They are similar to arrays in
4 | other programming languages, but with a few differences. In this section, we introduce the `vector`
5 | type and its operations.
6 | 
7 | ## Vector syntax
8 | 
9 | The `vector` type is written using the `vector` keyword followed by the type of the elements in
10 | angle brackets. The type of the elements can be any valid Move type, including other vectors.
11 | 
12 | Move has a vector literal syntax that allows you to create vectors using the `vector` keyword
13 | followed by square brackets containing the elements (or no elements for an empty vector).
14 | 
15 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/vector.move anchor=literal
16 | 
17 | ```
18 | 
19 | The `vector` type is a built-in type in Move, and does not need to be imported from a module.
20 | Vector operations are defined in the `std::vector` module, which is implicitly imported
21 | and can be used directly without explicit `use` import.
22 | 
23 | ## Vector operations
24 | 
25 | The standard library provides methods to manipulate vectors. The following are some of the most
26 | commonly used operations:
27 | 
28 | - `push_back`: Adds an element to the end of the vector.
29 | - `pop_back`: Removes the last element from the vector.
30 | - `length`: Returns the number of elements in the vector.
31 | - `is_empty`: Returns true if the vector is empty.
32 | - `remove`: Removes an element at a given index.
33 | 
34 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/vector.move anchor=methods
35 | 
36 | ```
37 | 
38 | ## Destroying a Vector of non-droppable types
39 | 
40 | A vector of non-droppable types cannot be discarded. If you define a vector of types without the
41 | `drop` ability, the vector value cannot be ignored. If the vector is empty, the compiler requires an
42 | explicit call to the `destroy_empty` function.
43 | 
44 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/move-basics/vector.move anchor=no_drop
45 | 
46 | ```
47 | 
48 | The `destroy_empty` function will fail at runtime if you call it on a non-empty vector.
49 | 
50 | ## Further Reading
51 | 
52 | - [Vector](./../../reference/primitive-types/vector) in the Move Reference.
53 | - [std::vector](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/std/vector) module documentation.
```

move-book/book/move-basics/visibility.md
```
1 | # Visibility Modifiers
2 | 
3 | Every module member has a visibility. By default, all module members are _private_ - meaning they
4 | are only accessible within the module they are defined in. However, you can add a visibility
5 | modifier to make a module member _public_ - visible outside the module, or _public(package)_ -
6 | visible in the modules within the same package, or _entry_ - can be called from a transaction but
7 | can't be called from other modules.
8 | 
9 | ## Internal Visibility
10 | 
11 | A function or a struct defined in a module which has no visibility modifier is _private_ to the
12 | module. It can't be called from other modules.
13 | 
14 | ```move
15 | module book::internal_visibility;
16 | 
17 | // This function can be called from other functions in the same module
18 | fun internal() { /* ... */ }
19 | 
20 | // Same module -> can call internal()
21 | fun call_internal() {
22 |     internal();
23 | }
24 | ```
25 | 
26 | The following code will not compile:
27 | 
28 | <!-- TODO: add failure flag to example -->
29 | 
30 | ```move
31 | module book::try_calling_internal;
32 | 
33 | use book::internal_visibility;
34 | 
35 | // Different module -> can't call internal()
36 | fun try_calling_internal() {
37 |     internal_visibility::internal();
38 | }
39 | ```
40 | 
41 | Note that just because a struct field is not visible from Move does not mean that its value is kept
42 | confidential &mdash; it is always possible to read the contents of an on-chain object from outside
43 | of Move. You should never store unencrypted secrets inside of objects.
44 | 
45 | ## Public Visibility
46 | 
47 | A struct or a function can be made _public_ by adding the `public` keyword before the `fun` or
48 | `struct` keyword.
49 | 
50 | ```move
51 | module book::public_visibility;
52 | 
53 | // This function can be called from other modules
54 | public fun public_fun() { /* ... */ }
55 | ```
56 | 
57 | A public function can be imported and called from other modules. The following code will compile:
58 | 
59 | ```move
60 | module book::try_calling_public;
61 | 
62 | use book::public_visibility;
63 | 
64 | // Different module -> can call public_fun()
65 | fun try_calling_public() {
66 |     public_visibility::public_fun();
67 | }
68 | ```
69 | 
70 | Unlike some languages, struct fields cannot be made public.
71 | 
72 | ## Package Visibility
73 | 
74 | A function with _package_ visibility can be called from any module within the same package, but not
75 | from modules in other packages. In other words, it is _internal_ to the package.
76 | 
77 | ```move
78 | module book::package_visibility;
79 | 
80 | public(package) fun package_only() { /* ... */ }
81 | ```
82 | 
83 | A package function can be called from any module within the same package:
84 | 
85 | ```move
86 | module book::try_calling_package;
87 | 
88 | use book::package_visibility;
89 | 
90 | // Same package `book` -> can call package_only()
91 | fun try_calling_package() {
92 |     package_visibility::package_only();
93 | }
94 | ```
95 | 
96 | ## Native Functions
97 | 
98 | Some functions in the [framework](./../programmability/sui-framework) and
99 | [standard library](./standard-library) are marked with the `native` modifier. These functions are
100 | natively provided by the Move VM and do not have a body in Move source code. To learn more about the
101 | native modifier, refer to the
102 | [Move Reference](./../../reference/functions?highlight=native#native-functions).
103 | 
104 | ```move
105 | module std::type_name;
106 | 
107 | public native fun get<T>(): TypeName;
108 | ```
109 | 
110 | This is an example from `std::type_name`, learn more about this module in the
111 | [reflection chapter](./type-reflection).
112 | 
113 | ## Further Reading
114 | 
115 | - [Visibility](./../../reference/functions#visibility) in the Move Reference.
```
