move-book/book/programmability/bcs.md
```
1 | # Binary Canonical Serialization
2 | 
3 | Binary Canonical Serialization (BCS) is a binary encoding format for structured data. It was
4 | originally designed in Diem, and became the standard serialization format for Move. BCS is simple,
5 | efficient, deterministic, and easy to implement in any programming language.
6 | 
7 | > The full format specification is available in the
8 | > [BCS repository](https://github.com/zefchain/bcs).
9 | 
10 | ## Format
11 | 
12 | BCS is a binary format that supports unsigned integers up to 256 bits, options, booleans, unit
13 | (empty value), fixed and variable-length sequences, and maps. The format is designed to be
14 | deterministic, meaning that the same data will always be serialized to the same bytes.
15 | 
16 | > "BCS is not a self-describing format. As such, in order to deserialize a message, one must know
17 | > the message type and layout ahead of time" from the [README](https://github.com/zefchain/bcs)
18 | 
19 | Integers are stored in little-endian format, and variable-length integers are encoded using a
20 | variable-length encoding scheme. Sequences are prefixed with their length as ULEB128, enumerations
21 | are stored as the index of the variant followed by the data, and maps are stored as an ordered
22 | sequence of key-value pairs.
23 | 
24 | Structs are treated as a sequence of fields, and the fields are serialized in the order they are
25 | defined in the struct. The fields are serialized using the same rules as the top-level data.
26 | 
27 | ## Using BCS
28 | 
29 | The [Sui Framework](./sui-framework) includes the sui::bcs module for encoding and decoding data.
30 | Encoding functions are native to the VM, and decoding functions are implemented in Move.
31 | 
32 | ## Encoding
33 | 
34 | To encode data, use the `bcs::to_bytes` function, which converts data references into byte vectors.
35 | This function supports encoding any types, including structs.
36 | 
37 | ```move
38 | module std::bcs;
39 | 
40 | public native fun to_bytes<T>(t: &T): vector<u8>;
41 | ```
42 | 
43 | The following example shows how to encode a struct using BCS. The `to_bytes` function can take any
44 | value and encode it as a vector of bytes.
45 | 
46 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/bcs.move anchor=encode
47 | 
48 | ```
49 | 
50 | ### Encoding a Struct
51 | 
52 | Structs encode similarly to simple types. Here is how to encode a struct using BCS:
53 | 
54 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/bcs.move anchor=encode_struct
55 | 
56 | ```
57 | 
58 | ## Decoding
59 | 
60 | Because BCS does not self-describe and Move is statically typed, decoding requires prior knowledge
61 | of the data type. The `sui::bcs` module provides various functions to assist with this process.
62 | 
63 | ### Wrapper API
64 | 
65 | BCS is implemented as a wrapper in Move. The decoder takes the bytes by value, and then allows the
66 | caller to _peel off_ the data by calling different decoding functions, prefixed with `peel_*`. The
67 | data is split off the bytes, and the remainder bytes are kept in the wrapper until the
68 | `into_remainder_bytes` function is called.
69 | 
70 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/bcs.move anchor=decode
71 | 
72 | ```
73 | 
74 | There is a common practice to use multiple variables in a single `let` statement during decoding. It
75 | makes code a little bit more readable and helps to avoid unnecessary copying of the data.
76 | 
77 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/bcs.move anchor=chain_decode
78 | 
79 | ```
80 | 
81 | ### Decoding Vectors
82 | 
83 | While most of the primitive types have a dedicated decoding function, vectors need special handling,
84 | which depends on the type of the elements. For vectors, first you need to decode the length of the
85 | vector, and then decode each element in a loop.
86 | 
87 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/bcs.move anchor=decode_vector
88 | 
89 | ```
90 | 
91 | For most common scenarios, `bcs` module provides a basic set of functions for decoding vectors:
92 | 
93 | - `peel_vec_address(): vector<address>`
94 | - `peel_vec_bool(): vector<bool>`
95 | - `peel_vec_u8(): vector<u8>`
96 | - `peel_vec_u64(): vector<u64>`
97 | - `peel_vec_u128(): vector<u128>`
98 | - `peel_vec_vec_u8(): vector<vector<u8>>` - vector of byte vectors
99 | 
100 | ### Decoding Option
101 | 
102 | <!--
103 | > Coincidentally, Option, being a vector in Move, overlaps with the representation of an enum with a
104 | > single variant in BCS, and makes Option in Rust fully compatible with the one in Move.
105 | -->
106 | 
107 | [Option](./../move-basics/option) is represented as a vector of either 0 or 1 element. To read an
108 | option, you would treat it like a vector and check its length (first byte - either 1 or 0).
109 | 
110 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/bcs.move anchor=decode_option
111 | 
112 | ```
113 | 
114 | > If you need to decode an option of a custom type, use the method in the code snippet above.
115 | 
116 | The most common scenarios, `bcs` module provides a basic set of functions for decoding Option's:
117 | 
118 | - `peel_option_address(): Option<address>`
119 | - `peel_option_bool(): Option<bool>`
120 | - `peel_option_u8(): Option<u8>`
121 | - `peel_option_u64(): Option<u64>`
122 | - `peel_option_u128(): Option<u128>`
123 | 
124 | ### Decoding Structs
125 | 
126 | Structs are decoded field by field, and there is no standard function to automatically decode bytes
127 | into a Move struct, and it would have been a violation of the Move's type system. Instead, you need
128 | to decode each field manually.
129 | 
130 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/bcs.move anchor=decode_struct
131 | 
132 | ```
133 | 
134 | ## Summary
135 | 
136 | Binary Canonical Serialization is an efficient binary format for structured data, ensuring
137 | consistent serialization across platforms. The Sui Framework provides comprehensive tools for
138 | working with BCS, allowing extensive functionality through built-in functions.
```

move-book/book/programmability/capability.md
```
1 | # Pattern: Capability
2 | 
3 | In programming, a _capability_ is a token that gives the owner the right to perform a specific
4 | action. It is a pattern that is used to control access to resources and operations. A simple example
5 | of a capability is a key to a door. If you have the key, you can open the door. If you don't have
6 | the key, you can't open the door. A more practical example is an Admin Capability which allows the
7 | owner to perform administrative operations, which regular users cannot.
8 | 
9 | ## Capability is an Object
10 | 
11 | In the [Sui Object Model](./../object/), capabilities are represented as objects. An owner of an
12 | object can pass this object to a function to prove that they have the right to perform a specific
13 | action. Due to strict typing, the function taking a capability as an argument can only be called
14 | with the correct capability.
15 | 
16 | > There's a convention to name capabilities with the `Cap` suffix, for example, `AdminCap` or
17 | > `KioskOwnerCap`.
18 | 
19 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/capability.move anchor=main
20 | 
21 | ```
22 | 
23 | ## Using `init` for Admin Capability
24 | 
25 | A very common practice is to create a single `AdminCap` object on package publish. This way, the
26 | application can have a setup phase where the admin account prepares the state of the application.
27 | 
28 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/capability-2.move anchor=admin_cap
29 | 
30 | ```
31 | 
32 | ## Address Check vs Capability
33 | 
34 | Utilizing objects as capabilities is a relatively new concept in blockchain programming. And in
35 | other smart-contract languages, authorization is often performed by checking the address of the
36 | sender. This pattern is still viable on Sui, however, overall recommendation is to use capabilities
37 | for better security, discoverability, and code organization.
38 | 
39 | Let's look at how the `new` function that creates a user would look like if it was using the address
40 | check:
41 | 
42 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/capability-3.move anchor=with_address
43 | 
44 | ```
45 | 
46 | And now, let's see how the same function would look like with the capability:
47 | 
48 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/capability-4.move anchor=with_capability
49 | 
50 | ```
51 | 
52 | Using capabilities has several advantages over the address check:
53 | 
54 | - Migration of admin rights is easier with capabilities due to them being objects. In case of
55 |   address, if the admin address changes, all the functions that check the address need to be
56 |   updated - hence, require a package upgrade.
57 | - Function signatures are more descriptive with capabilities. It is clear that the `new` function
58 |   requires the `AdminCap` to be passed as an argument. And this function can't be called without it.
59 | - Object Capabilities don't require extra checks in the function body, and hence, decrease the
60 |   chance of a developer mistake.
61 | - An owned Capability also serves in discovery. The owner of the AdminCap can see the object in
62 |   their account (via a Wallet or Explorer), and know that they have the admin rights. This is less
63 |   transparent with the address check.
64 | 
65 | However, the address approach has its own advantages. For example, if an address is multisig, and
66 | transaction building gets more complex, it might be easier to check the address. Also, if there's a
67 | central object of the application that is used in every function, it can store the admin address,
68 | and this would simplify migration. The central object approach is also valuable for revocable
69 | capabilities, where the admin can revoke the capability from the user.
```

move-book/book/programmability/collections.md
```
1 | # Collections
2 | 
3 | Collection types are a fundamental part of any programming language. They are used to store a
4 | collection of data, such as a list of items. The `vector` type has already been covered in the
5 | [vector section](./../move-basics/vector), and in this chapter we will cover the vector-based
6 | collection types offered by the [Sui Framework](./sui-framework).
7 | 
8 | ## Vector
9 | 
10 | While we have previously covered the `vector` type in the [vector section](./../move-basics/vector),
11 | it is worth going over it again in a new context. This time we will cover the usage of the `vector`
12 | type in objects and how it can be used in an application.
13 | 
14 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/collections.move anchor=vector
15 | 
16 | ```
17 | 
18 | ## VecSet
19 | 
20 | `VecSet` is a collection type that stores a set of unique items. It is similar to a `vector`, but it
21 | does not allow duplicate items. This property makes it useful for storing a collection of unique
22 | items, such as a list of IDs or addresses.
23 | 
24 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/collections-2.move anchor=vec_set
25 | 
26 | ```
27 | 
28 | VecSet will fail on attempt to insert an item that already exists in the set.
29 | 
30 | ## VecMap
31 | 
32 | `VecMap` is a collection type that stores a map of key-value pairs. It is similar to a `VecSet`, but
33 | it allows you to associate a value with each item in the set. This makes it useful for storing a
34 | collection of key-value pairs, such as a list of addresses and their balances, or a list of user IDs
35 | and their associated data.
36 | 
37 | Keys in a `VecMap` are unique, and each key can only be associated with a single value. If you try
38 | to insert a key-value pair with a key that already exists in the map, the old value will be replaced
39 | with the new value.
40 | 
41 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/collections-3.move anchor=vec_map
42 | 
43 | ```
44 | 
45 | ## Limitations
46 | 
47 | Standard collection types are a great way to store typed data with guaranteed safety and
48 | consistency. However, they are limited by the type of data they can store - the type system won't
49 | allow you to store a wrong type in a collection; and they're limited in size - by the object size
50 | limit. They will work for relatively small-sized sets and lists, but for larger collections you may
51 | need to use a different approach.
52 | 
53 | Another limitations on collection types is inability to compare them. Because the order of insertion
54 | is not guaranteed, an attempt to compare a `VecSet` to another `VecSet` may not yield the expected
55 | results.
56 | 
57 | > This behavior is caught by the linter and will emit a warning: _Comparing collections of type
58 | > 'sui::vec_set::VecSet' may yield unexpected result_
59 | 
60 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/collections-4.move anchor=vec_set_comparison
61 | 
62 | ```
63 | 
64 | In the example above, the comparison will fail because the order of insertion is not guaranteed, and
65 | the two `VecSet` instances may have different orders of elements. And the comparison will fail even
66 | if the two `VecSet` instances contain the same elements.
67 | 
68 | ## Summary
69 | 
70 | - Vector is a native type that allows storing a list of items.
71 | - VecSet is built on top of vector and allows storing sets of unique items.
72 | - VecMap is used to store key-value pairs in a map-like structure.
73 | - Vector-based collections are strictly typed and limited by the object size limit and are best
74 |   suited for small-sized sets and lists.
75 | 
76 | ## Next Steps
77 | 
78 | In the next section we will cover the [Wrapper Type Pattern](./wrapper-type-pattern) - a design
79 | pattern often used with collection types to extend or restrict their behavior.
```

move-book/book/programmability/display.md
```
1 | # Object Display
2 | 
3 | Objects on Sui are explicit in their structure and behavior and can be displayed in an
4 | understandable way. However, to support richer metadata for clients, there's a standard and
5 | efficient way of "describing" them to the client - the `Display` object defined in the
6 | [Sui Framework](./sui-framework).
7 | 
8 | ## Background
9 | 
10 | Historically, there were different attempts to agree on a standard structure of an object so it can
11 | be displayed in a user interface. One of the approaches was to define certain fields in the object
12 | struct which, when present, would be used in the UI. This approach was not flexible enough and
13 | required developers to define the same fields in every object, and sometimes the fields did not make
14 | sense for the object.
15 | 
16 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/display.move anchor=background
17 | 
18 | ```
19 | 
20 | If any of the fields contained static data, it would be duplicated in every object. And, since Move
21 | does not have interfaces, it is not possible to know if an object has a specific field without
22 | "manually" checking the object's type, which makes the client fetching more complex.
23 | 
24 | ## Object Display
25 | 
26 | To address these issues, Sui introduces a standard way of describing an object for display. Instead
27 | of defining fields in the object struct, the display metadata is stored in a separate object, which
28 | is associated with the type. This way, the display metadata is not duplicated, and it is easy to
29 | extend and maintain.
30 | 
31 | Another important feature of Sui Display is the ability to define templates and use object fields in
32 | those templates. Not only it allows for a more flexible display, but it also frees the developer
33 | from the need to define the same fields with the same names and types in every object.
34 | 
35 | > The Object Display is natively supported by the
36 | > [Sui Full Node](https://docs.sui.io/guides/operator/sui-full-node), and the client can fetch the
37 | > display metadata for any object if the object type has a Display associated with it.
38 | 
39 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/display.move anchor=hero
40 | 
41 | ```
42 | 
43 | ## Creator Privilege
44 | 
45 | While the objects can be owned by accounts and may be a subject to
46 | [True Ownership](./../object/ownership#account-owner-or-single-owner), the Display can be owned by
47 | the creator of the object. This way, the creator can update the display metadata and apply the
48 | changes globally without the need to update every object. The creator can also transfer Display to
49 | another account or even build an application around the object with custom functionality to manage
50 | the metadata.
51 | 
52 | ## Standard Fields
53 | 
54 | The fields that are supported most widely are:
55 | 
56 | - `name` - A name for the object. The name is displayed when users view the object.
57 | - `description` - A description for the object. The description is displayed when users view the
58 |   object.
59 | - `link` - A link to the object to use in an application.
60 | - `image_url` - A URL or a blob with the image for the object.
61 | - `thumbnail_url` - A URL to a smaller image to use in wallets, explorers, and other products as a
62 |   preview.
63 | - `project_url` - A link to a website associated with the object or creator.
64 | - `creator` - A string that indicates the object creator.
65 | 
66 | > Please, refer to the [Sui Documentation](https://docs.sui.io/standards/display) for the most
67 | > up-to-date list of supported fields.
68 | 
69 | While there's a standard set of fields, the Display object does not enforce them. The developer can
70 | define any fields they need, and the client can use them as they see fit. Some applications may
71 | require additional fields, and omit other, and the Display is flexible enough to support them.
72 | 
73 | ## Working with Display
74 | 
75 | The `Display` object is defined in the `sui::display` module. It is a generic struct that takes a
76 | phantom type as a parameter. The phantom type is used to associate the `Display` object with the
77 | type it describes. The `fields` of the `Display` object are a `VecMap` of key-value pairs, where the
78 | key is the field name and the value is the field value. The `version` field is used to version the
79 | display metadata, and is updated on the `update_display` call.
80 | 
81 | ```move
82 | module sui::display;
83 | 
84 | public struct Display<phantom T: key> has key, store {
85 |     id: UID,
86 |     /// Contains fields for display. Currently supported
87 |     /// fields are: name, link, image and description.
88 |     fields: VecMap<String, String>,
89 |     /// Version that can only be updated manually by the Publisher.
90 |     version: u16
91 | }
92 | ```
93 | 
94 | The [Publisher](./publisher) object is required to a new Display, since it serves as the proof of
95 | ownership of type.
96 | 
97 | ## Template Syntax
98 | 
99 | Currently, Display supports simple string interpolation and can use struct fields (and paths) in its
100 | templates. The syntax is trivial - `{path}` is replaced with the value of the field at the path. The
101 | path is a dot-separated list of field names, starting from the root object in case of nested fields.
102 | 
103 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/display.move anchor=nested
104 | 
105 | ```
106 | 
107 | The Display for the type `LittlePony` above could be defined as follows:
108 | 
109 | ```json
110 | {
111 |   "name": "Just a pony",
112 |   "image_url": "{image_url}",
113 |   "description": "{metadata.description}"
114 | }
115 | ```
116 | 
117 | ## Multiple Display Objects
118 | 
119 | There's no restriction to how many `Display<T>` objects can be created for a specific `T`. However,
120 | the most recently updated `Display<T>` will be used by the full node.
121 | 
122 | ## Further Reading
123 | 
124 | - [Sui Object Display](https://docs.sui.io/standards/display) is Sui Documentation
125 | - [Publisher](./publisher) - the representation of the creator
```

move-book/book/programmability/dynamic-collections.md
```
1 | # Dynamic Collections
2 | 
3 | [Sui Framework](./sui-framework) offers a variety of collection types that build on the
4 | [dynamic fields](./dynamic-fields) and [dynamic object fields](./dynamic-object-fields) concepts.
5 | These collections are designed to be a safer and more understandable way to store and manage dynamic
6 | fields and objects.
7 | 
8 | For each collection type we will specify the primitive they use, and the specific features they
9 | offer.
10 | 
11 | > Unlike dynamic (object) fields which operate on UID, collection types have their own type and
12 | > allow calling [associated functions](./../move-basics/struct-methods).
13 | 
14 | ## Common Concepts
15 | 
16 | All of the collection types share the same set of methods, which are:
17 | 
18 | - `add` - adds a field to the collection
19 | - `remove` - removes a field from the collection
20 | - `borrow` - borrows a field from the collection
21 | - `borrow_mut` - borrows a mutable reference to a field from the collection
22 | - `contains` - checks if a field exists in the collection
23 | - `length` - returns the number of fields in the collection
24 | - `is_empty` - checks if the `length` is 0
25 | 
26 | All collection types support index syntax for `borrow` and `borrow_mut` methods. If you see square
27 | brackets in the examples, they are translated into `borrow` and `borrow_mut` calls.
28 | 
29 | ```move
30 | let hat: &Hat = &bag[b"key"];
31 | let hat_mut: &mut Hat = &mut bag[b"key"];
32 | 
33 | // is equivalent to
34 | let hat: &Hat = bag.borrow(b"key");
35 | let hat_mut: &mut Hat = bag.borrow_mut(b"key");
36 | ```
37 | 
38 | In the examples we won't focus on these functions, but rather on the differences between the
39 | collection types.
40 | 
41 | ## Bag
42 | 
43 | Bag, as the name suggests, acts as a "bag" of heterogeneous values. It is a simple, non-generic type
44 | that can store any data. Bag will never allow orphaned fields, as it tracks the number of fields and
45 | can't be destroyed if it's not empty.
46 | 
47 | ```move
48 | module sui::bag;
49 | 
50 | public struct Bag has key, store {
51 |     /// the ID of this bag
52 |     id: UID,
53 |     /// the number of key-value pairs in the bag
54 |     size: u64,
55 | }
56 | ```
57 | 
58 | _See [full documentation for sui::bag][bag-framework] module._
59 | 
60 | Due to Bag storing any types, the extra methods it offers is:
61 | 
62 | - `contains_with_type` - checks if a field exists with a specific type
63 | 
64 | Used as a struct field:
65 | 
66 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-collections.move anchor=bag_struct
67 | 
68 | ```
69 | 
70 | Using the Bag:
71 | 
72 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-collections.move anchor=bag_usage
73 | 
74 | ```
75 | 
76 | ## ObjectBag
77 | 
78 | Defined in the `sui::object_bag` module. Identical to [Bag](#bag), but uses
79 | [dynamic object fields](./dynamic-object-fields) internally. Can only store objects as values.
80 | 
81 | _See [full documentation for sui::object_bag][object-bag-framework] module._
82 | 
83 | ## Table
84 | 
85 | Table is a typed dynamic collection that has a fixed type for keys and values. It is defined in the
86 | `sui::table` module.
87 | 
88 | ```move
89 | module sui::table;
90 | 
91 | public struct Table<phantom K: copy + drop + store, phantom V: store> has key, store {
92 |     /// the ID of this table
93 |     id: UID,
94 |     /// the number of key-value pairs in the table
95 |     size: u64,
96 | }
97 | ```
98 | 
99 | _See [full documentation for sui::table][table-framework] module._
100 | 
101 | Used as a struct field:
102 | 
103 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-collections.move anchor=table_struct
104 | 
105 | ```
106 | 
107 | Using the Table:
108 | 
109 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-collections.move anchor=table_usage
110 | 
111 | ```
112 | 
113 | ## ObjectTable
114 | 
115 | Defined in the `sui::object_table` module. Identical to [Table](#table), but uses
116 | [dynamic object fields](./dynamic-object-fields) internally. Can only store objects as values.
117 | 
118 | _See [full documentation for sui::object_table][object-table-framework] module._
119 | 
120 | ## LinkedTable
121 | 
122 | It is defined in the `sui::linked_table` module, similar to [Table](#table) but the values are linked together,
123 | allowing for ordered insertion and removal.
124 | 
125 | ```move
126 | module sui::linked_table;
127 | 
128 | public struct LinkedTable<K: copy + drop + store, phantom V: store> has key, store {
129 |     /// the ID of this table
130 |     id: UID,
131 |     /// the number of key-value pairs in the table
132 |     size: u64,
133 |     /// the front of the table, i.e. the key of the first entry
134 |     head: Option<K>,
135 |     /// the back of the table, i.e. the key of the last entry
136 |     tail: Option<K>,
137 | }
138 | ```
139 | 
140 | _See [full documentation for sui::linked_table][linked-table-framework] module._
141 | 
142 | Since the values stored in LinkedTable are linked together, it has unique methods for adding and deleting.
143 | 
144 | - `push_front` - inserts a key-value pair at the front of the table
145 | - `push_back` - inserts a key-value pair at the back of the table
146 | - `remove` - removes a key-value pair by key and returns the value
147 | - `pop_front` - removes the front of the table, returns the key and value
148 | - `pop_back` - removes the back of the table, returns the key and value
149 | 
150 | Used as a struct field:
151 | 
152 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-collections.move anchor=linked_table_struct
153 | 
154 | ```
155 | 
156 | Using the LinkedTable:
157 | 
158 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-collections.move anchor=linked_table_usage
159 | 
160 | ```
161 | 
162 | ## Summary
163 | 
164 | - [Bag](#bag) - a simple collection that can store any type of data.
165 | - [ObjectBag](#objectbag) - a collection that can store only objects.
166 | - [Table](#table) - a typed dynamic collection that has a fixed type for keys and values.
167 | - [ObjectTable](#objecttable) - same as Table, but can only store objects.
168 | - [LinkedTable](#linkedtable) - similar to Table but the values are linked together.
169 | 
170 | ## Further Reading
171 | 
172 | - [sui::table][table-framework] module documentation.
173 | - [sui::object_table][object-table-framework] module documentation.
174 | - [sui::linked_table][linked-table-framework] module documentation.
175 | - [sui::bag][bag-framework] module documentation.
176 | - [sui::object_bag][object-bag-framework] module documentation.
177 | 
178 | [table-framework]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/table
179 | [object-table-framework]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/object_table
180 | [linked-table-framework]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/linked_table
181 | [bag-framework]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/bag
182 | [object-bag-framework]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/object_bag
183 | 
184 | <!-- TODO! -->
185 | 
186 | <!-- ## Choosing a Collection Type
187 | 
188 | Depending on the needs of your project, you may choose to -->
```

move-book/book/programmability/dynamic-fields.md
```
1 | # Dynamic Fields
2 | 
3 | Sui Object model allows objects to be attached to other objects as _dynamic fields_. The behavior is
4 | similar to how a `Map` works in other programming languages. However, unlike a `Map` which in Move
5 | would be strictly typed (we have covered it in the [Collections](./collections) section), dynamic
6 | fields allow attaching objects of any type. A similar approach from the world of frontend
7 | development would be a JavaScript Object type which allows storing any type of data dynamically.
8 | 
9 | > There's no limit to the number of dynamic fields that can be attached to an object. Thus, dynamic
10 | > fields can be used to store large amounts of data that don't fit into the object limit size.
11 | 
12 | Dynamic Fields allow for a wide range of applications, from splitting data into smaller parts to
13 | avoid [object size limit](./../guides/building-against-limits) to attaching objects as a part of
14 | application logic.
15 | 
16 | ## Definition
17 | 
18 | Dynamic Fields are defined in the `sui::dynamic_field` module of the
19 | [Sui Framework](./sui-framework). They are attached to object's `UID` via a _name_, and can be
20 | accessed using that name. There can be only one field with a given name attached to an object.
21 | 
22 | ```move
23 | module sui::dynamic_field;
24 | 
25 | /// Internal object used for storing the field and value
26 | public struct Field<Name: copy + drop + store, Value: store> has key {
27 |     /// Determined by the hash of the object ID, the field name
28 |     /// value and it's type, i.e. hash(parent.id || name || Name)
29 |     id: UID,
30 |     /// The value for the name of this field
31 |     name: Name,
32 |     /// The value bound to this field
33 |     value: Value,
34 | }
35 | ```
36 | 
37 | As the definition shows, dynamic fields are stored in an internal `Field` object, which has the
38 | `UID` generated in a deterministic way based on the object ID, the field name, and the field type.
39 | The `Field` object contains the field name and the value bound to it. The constraints on the `Name`
40 | and `Value` type parameters define the abilities that the key and value must have.
41 | 
42 | ## Usage
43 | 
44 | The methods available for dynamic fields are straightforward: a field can be added with `add`,
45 | removed with `remove`, and read with `borrow` and `borrow_mut`. Additionally, the `exists_` method
46 | can be used to check if a field exists (for stricter checks with type, there is an
47 | `exists_with_type` method).
48 | 
49 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-fields.move anchor=usage
50 | 
51 | ```
52 | 
53 | In the example above, we define a `Character` object and two different types of accessories that
54 | could never be put together in a vector. However, dynamic fields allow us to store them together in
55 | a single object. Both objects are attached to the `Character` via a `vector<u8>` (bytestring
56 | literal), and can be accessed using their respective names.
57 | 
58 | As you can see, when we attached the accessories to the Character, we passed them _by value_. In
59 | other words, both values were moved to a new scope, and their ownership was transferred to the
60 | `Character` object. If we changed the ownership of `Character` object, the accessories would have
61 | been moved with it.
62 | 
63 | And the last important property of dynamic fields we should highlight is that they are _accessed
64 | through their parent_. This means that the `Hat` and `Mustache` objects are not directly accessible
65 | and follow the same rules as the parent object.
66 | 
67 | ## Foreign Types as Dynamic Fields
68 | 
69 | Dynamic fields allow objects to carry data of any type, including those defined in other modules.
70 | This is possible due to their generic nature and relatively weak constraints on the type parameters.
71 | Let's illustrate this by attaching a few different values to a `Character` object.
72 | 
73 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-fields.move anchor=foreign_types
74 | 
75 | ```
76 | 
77 | In this example we showed how different types can be used for both _name_ and the _value_ of a
78 | dynamic field. The `String` is attached via a `vector<u8>` name, the `u64` is attached via a `u32`
79 | name, and the `bool` is attached via a `bool` name. Anything is possible with dynamic fields!
80 | 
81 | ## Orphaned Dynamic Fields
82 | 
83 | > To prevent orphaned dynamic fields, please, use [Dynamic Collection Types](./dynamic-collections)
84 | > such as `Bag` as they track the dynamic fields and won't allow unpacking if there are attached
85 | > fields.
86 | 
87 | The `object::delete()` function, which is used to delete a UID, does not track the dynamic fields,
88 | and cannot prevent dynamic fields from becoming orphaned. Once the parent UID is deleted, the
89 | dynamic fields are not automatically deleted, and they become orphaned. This means that the dynamic
90 | fields are still stored in the blockchain, but they will never become accessible again.
91 | 
92 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-fields.move anchor=orphan_fields
93 | 
94 | ```
95 | 
96 | Orphaned objects are not a subject to storage rebate, and the storage fees will remain unclaimed.
97 | One way to avoid orphaned dynamic fields during unpacking of an object is to return the `UID` and
98 | store it somewhere temporarily until the dynamic fields are removed and handled properly.
99 | 
100 | ## Custom Type as a Field Name
101 | 
102 | In the examples above, we used primitive types as field names since they have the required set of
103 | abilities. But dynamic fields get even more interesting when we use custom types as field names.
104 | This allows for a more structured way of storing data, and also allows for protecting the field
105 | names from being accessed by other modules.
106 | 
107 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-fields.move anchor=custom_type
108 | 
109 | ```
110 | 
111 | Two field names that we defined above are `AccessoryKey` and `MetadataKey`. The `AccessoryKey` has a
112 | `String` field in it, hence it can be used multiple times with different `name` values. The
113 | `MetadataKey` is an empty key, and can be attached only once.
114 | 
115 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-fields.move anchor=custom_type_usage
116 | 
117 | ```
118 | 
119 | As you can see, custom types do work as field names but as long as they can be _constructed_ by the
120 | module, in other words - if they are _internal_ to the module and defined in it. This limitation on
121 | struct packing can open up new ways in the design of the application.
122 | 
123 | This approach is used in the Object Capability<!--[]](./object-capability)--> pattern, where an
124 | application can authorize a foreign object to perform operations in it while not exposing the
125 | capabilities to other modules.
126 | 
127 | ## Exposing UID
128 | 
129 | <div class="warning">
130 | 
131 | Mutable access to `UID` is a security risk. Exposing `UID` of your type as a mutable reference can
132 | lead to unwanted modifications or removal of the object's dynamic fields. Additionally, it affects
133 | the Transfer to Object<!--[](./../storage/transfer-to-object)--> and
134 | [Dynamic Object Fields](./dynamic-object-fields). Make sure to understand the implications before
135 | exposing the `UID` as a mutable reference.
136 | 
137 | </div>
138 | 
139 | Because dynamic fields are attached to `UID`s, their usage in other modules depends on whether the
140 | `UID` can be accessed. By default struct visibility protects the `id` field and won't let other
141 | modules access it directly. However, if there's a public accessor method that returns a reference to
142 | `UID`, dynamic fields can be read in other modules.
143 | 
144 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-fields.move anchor=exposed_uid
145 | 
146 | ```
147 | 
148 | In the example above, we show how to expose the `UID` of a `Character` object. This solution may
149 | work for some applications, however, it is important to remember that exposed `UID` allows reading
150 | _any_ dynamic field attached to the object.
151 | 
152 | If you need to expose the `UID` only within the package, use a restrictive visibility, like
153 | `public(package)`, or even better - use more specific accessor methods that would allow only reading
154 | specific fields.
155 | 
156 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-fields.move anchor=exposed_uid_measures
157 | 
158 | ```
159 | 
160 | ## Dynamic Fields vs Fields
161 | 
162 | Dynamic Fields are more expensive than regular fields, as they require additional storage and costs
163 | for accessing them. Their flexibility comes at a price, and it is important to understand the
164 | implications when making a decision between using dynamic fields and regular fields.
165 | 
166 | ## Limits
167 | 
168 | Dynamic Fields are not subject to the [object size limit](./../guides/building-against-limits), and
169 | can be used to store large amounts of data. However, they are still subject to the
170 | [dynamic fields created limit](./../guides/building-against-limits), which is set to 1000 fields per
171 | transaction.
172 | 
173 | ## Applications
174 | 
175 | Dynamic Fields can play a crucial role in applications of any complexity. They open up a variety of
176 | different use cases, from storing heterogeneous data to attaching objects as part of the application
177 | logic. They allow for certain [upgradeability practices](./../guides/upgradeability-practices) based
178 | on the ability to define them _later_ and change the type of the field.
179 | 
180 | ## Next Steps
181 | 
182 | In the next section we will cover [Dynamic Object Fields](./dynamic-object-fields) and explain how
183 | they differ from dynamic fields, and what are the implications of using them.
```

move-book/book/programmability/dynamic-object-fields.md
```
1 | # Dynamic Object Fields
2 | 
3 | > This section expands on the [Dynamic Fields](./dynamic-fields). Please, read it first to
4 | > understand the basics of dynamic fields.
5 | 
6 | Another variation of dynamic fields is _dynamic object fields_, which have certain differences from
7 | regular dynamic fields. In this section, we will cover the specifics of dynamic object fields and
8 | explain how they differ from regular dynamic fields.
9 | 
10 | > General recommendation is to avoid using dynamic object fields in favor of (just) dynamic fields,
11 | > especially if there's no need for direct discovery through the ID. The extra costs of dynamic
12 | > object fields may not be justified by the benefits they provide.
13 | 
14 | ## Definition
15 | 
16 | Dynamic Object Fields are defined in the `sui::dynamic_object_fields` module in the
17 | [Sui Framework](./sui-framework). They are similar to dynamic fields in many ways, but unlike them,
18 | dynamic object fields have an extra constraint on the `Value` type. The `Value` must have a
19 | combination of `key` and `store`, not just `store` as in the case of dynamic fields.
20 | 
21 | They're less explicit in their framework definition, as the concept itself is more abstract:
22 | 
23 | ```move
24 | module sui::dynamic_object_field;
25 | 
26 | /// Internal object used for storing the field and the name associated with the
27 | /// value. The separate type is necessary to prevent key collision with direct
28 | /// usage of dynamic_field
29 | public struct Wrapper<Name> has copy, drop, store {
30 |     name: Name,
31 | }
32 | ```
33 | 
34 | Unlike `Field` type in the [Dynamic Fields](./dynamic-fields#definition) section, the `Wrapper` type
35 | only stores the name of the field. The value is the object itself, and is _not wrapped_.
36 | 
37 | The constraints on the `Value` type become visible in the methods available for dynamic object
38 | fields. Here's the signature for the `add` function:
39 | 
40 | ```move
41 | /// Adds a dynamic object field to the object `object: &mut UID` at field
42 | /// specified by `name: Name`. Aborts with `EFieldAlreadyExists` if the object
43 | /// already has that field with that name.
44 | public fun add<Name: copy + drop + store, Value: key + store>(
45 |     // we use &mut UID in several spots for access control
46 |     object: &mut UID,
47 |     name: Name,
48 |     value: Value,
49 | ) { /* implementation omitted */ }
50 | ```
51 | 
52 | The rest of the methods which are identical to the ones in the
53 | [Dynamic Fields](./dynamic-fields#usage) section have the same constraints on the `Value` type.
54 | Let's list them for reference:
55 | 
56 | - `add` - adds a dynamic object field to the object
57 | - `remove` - removes a dynamic object field from the object
58 | - `borrow` - borrows a dynamic object field from the object
59 | - `borrow_mut` - borrows a mutable reference to a dynamic object field from the object
60 | - `exists_` - checks if a dynamic object field exists
61 | - `exists_with_type` - checks if a dynamic object field exists with a specific type
62 | 
63 | Additionally, there is an `id` method which returns the `ID` of the `Value` object without
64 | specifying its type.
65 | 
66 | ## Usage & Differences with Dynamic Fields
67 | 
68 | The main difference between dynamic fields and dynamic object fields is that the latter allows
69 | storing _only objects_ as values. This means that you can't store primitive types like `u64` or
70 | `bool`. It may be considered a limitation, if not for the fact that dynamic object fields are _not
71 | wrapped_ into a separate object.
72 | 
73 | > The relaxed requirement for wrapping keeps the object available for off-chain discovery via its
74 | > ID. However, this property may not be outstanding if wrapped object indexing is implemented,
75 | > making the dynamic object fields a redundant feature.
76 | 
77 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/dynamic-object-fields.move anchor=usage
78 | 
79 | ```
80 | 
81 | ## Pricing Differences
82 | 
83 | Dynamic Object Fields come a little more expensive than dynamic fields. Because of their internal
84 | structure, they require 2 objects: the Wrapper for Name and the Value. Because of this, the cost of
85 | adding and accessing object fields (loading 2 objects compared to 1 for dynamic fields) is higher.
86 | 
87 | ## Next Steps
88 | 
89 | Both dynamic field and dynamic object fields are powerful features which allow for innovative
90 | solutions in applications. However, they are relatively low-level and require careful handling to
91 | avoid orphaned fields. In the next section, we will introduce a higher-level abstraction -
92 | [Dynamic Collections](./dynamic-collections) - which can help with managing dynamic fields and
93 | objects more effectively.
```

move-book/book/programmability/epoch-and-time.md
```
1 | # Epoch and Time
2 | 
3 | Sui has two ways of accessing the current time: `Epoch` and `Time`. The former represents
4 | operational periods in the system and changed roughly every 24 hours. The latter represents the
5 | current time in milliseconds since the Unix Epoch. Both can be accessed freely in the program.
6 | 
7 | ## Epoch
8 | 
9 | Epochs are used to separate the system into operational periods. During an epoch the validator set
10 | is fixed, however, at the epoch boundary, the validator set can be changed. Epochs play a crucial
11 | role in the consensus algorithm and are used to determine the current validator set. They are also
12 | used as measurement in the staking mechanism.
13 | 
14 | Epoch can be read from the [transaction context](./transaction-context):
15 | 
16 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/epoch-and-time.move anchor=epoch
17 | 
18 | ```
19 | 
20 | It is also possible to get the unix timestamp of the epoch start:
21 | 
22 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/epoch-and-time.move anchor=epoch_start
23 | 
24 | ```
25 | 
26 | Normally, epochs are used in staking and system operations, however, in custom scenarios they can be
27 | used to emulate 24h periods. They are critical if an application relies on the staking logic or
28 | needs to know the current validator set.
29 | 
30 | ## Time
31 | 
32 | For a more precise time measurement, Sui provides the `Clock` object. It is a system object that is
33 | updated during checkpoints by the system, which stores the current time in milliseconds since the
34 | Unix Epoch. The `Clock` object is defined in the `sui::clock` module and has a reserved address
35 | `0x6`.
36 | 
37 | Clock is a shared object, but a transaction attempting to access it mutably will fail. This
38 | limitation allows parallel access to the `Clock` object, which is important for maintaining
39 | performance.
40 | 
41 | ```move
42 | module sui::clock;
43 | 
44 | /// Singleton shared object that exposes time to Move calls.  This
45 | /// object is found at address 0x6, and can only be read (accessed
46 | /// via an immutable reference) by entry functions.
47 | ///
48 | /// Entry Functions that attempt to accept `Clock` by mutable
49 | /// reference or value will fail to verify, and honest validators
50 | /// will not sign or execute transactions that use `Clock` as an
51 | /// input parameter, unless it is passed by immutable reference.
52 | public struct Clock has key {
53 |     id: UID,
54 |     /// The clock's timestamp, which is set automatically by a
55 |     /// system transaction every time consensus commits a
56 |     /// schedule, or by `sui::clock::increment_for_testing` during
57 |     /// testing.
58 |     timestamp_ms: u64,
59 | }
60 | ```
61 | 
62 | There is only one public function available in the `Clock` module - `timestamp_ms`. It returns the
63 | current time in milliseconds since the Unix Epoch.
64 | 
65 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/epoch-and-time.move anchor=clock
66 | 
67 | ```
68 | 
69 | ## Testing
70 | 
71 | The `Clock` module provides a number of methods for use in testing.
72 | 
73 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/epoch-and-time.move anchor=test
74 | 
75 | ```
```

move-book/book/programmability/events.md
```
1 | # Events
2 | 
3 | Events are a way to notify off-chain listeners about on-chain events. They are used to emit
4 | additional information about the transaction that is not stored - and, hence, can't be accessed -
5 | on-chain. Events are emitted by the `sui::event` module located in the
6 | [Sui Framework](./sui-framework).
7 | 
8 | > Any custom type with the [copy](./../move-basics/copy-ability) and
9 | > [drop](./../move-basics/drop-ability) abilities can be emitted as an event. Sui Verifier requires
10 | > the type to be internal to the module.
11 | 
12 | ```move
13 | module sui::event;
14 | 
15 | /// Emit a custom Move event, sending the data off-chain.
16 | ///
17 | /// Used for creating custom indexes and tracking on-chain
18 | /// activity in a way that suits a specific application the most.
19 | ///
20 | /// The type `T` is the main way to index the event, and can contain
21 | /// phantom parameters, eg `emit(MyEvent<phantom T>)`.
22 | public native fun emit<T: copy + drop>(event: T);
23 | ```
24 | 
25 | ## Emitting Events
26 | 
27 | Events are emitted using the `emit` function in the `sui::event` module. The function takes a single
28 | argument - the event to be emitted. The event data is passed by value,
29 | 
30 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/events.move anchor=emit
31 | 
32 | ```
33 | 
34 | The Sui Verifier requires the type passed to the `emit` function to be _internal to the module_. So
35 | emitting a type from another module will result in a compilation error. Primitive types, although
36 | they match the _copy_ and _drop_ requirement, are not allowed to be emitted as events.
37 | 
38 | ## Event Structure
39 | 
40 | Events are a part of the transaction result and are stored in the _transaction effects_. As such,
41 | they natively have the `sender` field which is the address who sent the transaction. So adding a
42 | "sender" field to the event is not necessary. Similarly, event metadata contains the timestamp. But
43 | it is important to note that the timestamp is relative to the node and may vary a little from node
44 | to node.
45 | 
46 | <!-- ## Reliability -->
```

move-book/book/programmability/fast-path.md
```
1 | # Fast Path
2 | 
3 | Due to the object model and the data organization model of Sui, some operations can be performed in
4 | a more efficient and parallelized way. This is called the **fast path**. Transaction that touches
5 | shared state requires consensus because it can be accessed by multiple parties at the same time.
6 | However, if the transaction only touches the private state (owned objects), there is no need for
7 | consensus. This is the fast path.
8 | 
9 | We have a favorite example for this: a coffee machine and a coffee cup. The coffee machine placed in
10 | the office is a shared resource - everyone can use it, but there can be only one user at a time. The
11 | coffee cup, on the other hand, is a private resource - it belongs to a specific person, and only
12 | that person can use it. To make coffee, one needs to use the coffee machine and wait if there's
13 | someone else using it. However, once the coffee is made and poured into the cup, the person can take
14 | the cup and drink the coffee without waiting for anyone else.
15 | 
16 | The same principle applies to Sui. If a transaction only touches the private state (the cup with
17 | coffee), it can be executed without consensus. If it touches the shared state (the coffee machine),
18 | it requires consensus. This is the fast path.
19 | 
20 | ## Frozen objects
21 | 
22 | Consensus is only required for mutating the shared state. If the object is immutable, it is treated
23 | as a "constant" and can be accessed in parallel. Frozen objects can be used to share unchangeable
24 | data between multiple parties without requiring consensus.
25 | 
26 | ## In Practice
27 | 
28 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/fast-path.move anchor=main
29 | 
30 | ```
31 | 
32 | ## Special Case: Clock
33 | 
34 | The `Clock` object with the reserved address `0x6` is a special case of a shared object which cannot
35 | be passed by a mutable reference in a regular transaction. An attempt to do so will not succeed, and
36 | the transaction will be rejected. Because of this limitation, the `Clock` object can only be
37 | accessed immutably, which allows executing transactions in parallel without consensus.
38 | 
39 | <!-- Add more on why and how -->
```

move-book/book/programmability/hot-potato-pattern.md
```
1 | # Pattern: Hot Potato
2 | 
3 | A case in the abilities system - a struct without any abilities - is called _hot potato_. It cannot
4 | be stored (not as [an object](./../storage/key-ability) nor as
5 | [a field in another struct](./../storage/store-ability)), it cannot be
6 | [copied](./../move-basics/copy-ability) or [discarded](./../move-basics/drop-ability). Hence, once
7 | constructed, it must be gracefully [unpacked by its module](./../move-basics/struct), or the
8 | transaction will abort due to unused value without drop.
9 | 
10 | > If you're familiar with languages that support _callbacks_, you can think of a hot potato as an
11 | > obligation to call a callback function. If you don't call it, the transaction will abort.
12 | 
13 | The name comes from the children's game where a ball is passed quickly between players, and none of
14 | the players want to be the last one holding it when the music stops, or they are out of the game.
15 | This is the best illustration of the pattern - the instance of a hot-potato struct is passed between
16 | calls, and none of the modules can keep it.
17 | 
18 | ## Defining a Hot Potato
19 | 
20 | A hot potato can be any struct with no abilities. For example, the following struct is a hot potato:
21 | 
22 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/hot-potato-pattern.move anchor=definition
23 | 
24 | ```
25 | 
26 | Because the `Request` has no abilities and cannot be stored or ignored, the module must provide a
27 | function to unpack it. For example:
28 | 
29 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/hot-potato-pattern.move anchor=new_request
30 | 
31 | ```
32 | 
33 | ## Example Usage
34 | 
35 | In the following example, the `Promise` hot potato is used to ensure that the borrowed value, when
36 | taken from the container, is returned back to it. The `Promise` struct contains the ID of the
37 | borrowed object, and the ID of the container, ensuring that the borrowed value was not swapped for
38 | another and is returned to the correct container.
39 | 
40 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/hot-potato-pattern.move anchor=container_borrow
41 | 
42 | ```
43 | 
44 | ## Applications
45 | 
46 | Below we list some of the common use cases for the hot potato pattern.
47 | 
48 | ### Borrowing
49 | 
50 | As shown in the [example above](#example-usage), the hot potato is very effective for borrowing with
51 | a guarantee that the borrowed value is returned to the correct container. While the example focuses
52 | on a value stored inside an `Option`, the same pattern can be applied to any other storage type, say
53 | a [dynamic field](./dynamic-fields).
54 | 
55 | ### Flash Loans
56 | 
57 | Canonical example of the hot potato pattern is flash loans. A flash loan is a loan that is borrowed
58 | and repaid in the same transaction. The borrowed funds are used to perform some operations, and the
59 | repaid funds are returned to the lender. The hot potato pattern ensures that the borrowed funds are
60 | returned to the lender.
61 | 
62 | An example usage of this pattern may look like this:
63 | 
64 | ```move
65 | // Borrow the funds from the lender.
66 | let (asset_a, potato) = lender.borrow(amount);
67 | 
68 | // Perform some operations with the borrowed funds.
69 | let asset_b = dex.trade(loan);
70 | let proceeds = another_contract::do_something(asset_b);
71 | 
72 | // Keep the commission and return the rest to the lender.
73 | let pay_back = proceeds.split(amount, ctx);
74 | lender.repay(pay_back, potato);
75 | transfer::public_transfer(proceeds, ctx.sender());
76 | ```
77 | 
78 | ### Variable-path Execution
79 | 
80 | The hot potato pattern can be used to introduce variation in the execution path. For example, if
81 | there is a module which allows purchasing a `Phone` for some "Bonus Points" or for USD, the hot
82 | potato can be used to decouple the purchase from the payment. The approach is very similar to how
83 | some shops work - you take the item from the shelf, and then you go to the cashier to pay for it.
84 | 
85 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/hot-potato-pattern.move anchor=phone_shop
86 | 
87 | ```
88 | 
89 | This decoupling technique allows separating the purchase logic from the payment logic, making the
90 | code more modular and easier to maintain. The `Ticket` could be split into its own module, providing
91 | a basic interface for the payment, and the shop implementation could be extended to support other
92 | goods without changing the payment logic.
93 | 
94 | ### Compositional Patterns
95 | 
96 | Hot potato can be used to link together different modules in a compositional way. Its module may
97 | define ways to interact with the hot potato, for example, stamp it with a type signature, or to
98 | extract some information from it. This way, the hot potato can be passed between different modules,
99 | and even different packages within the same transaction.
100 | 
101 | <!-- TODO: add [Request Pattern](./request-pattern) -->
102 | 
103 | The most important compositional pattern is the Request Pattern, which we will cover in the next
104 | section.
105 | 
106 | ### Usage in the Sui Framework
107 | 
108 | The pattern is used in various forms in the Sui Framework. Here are some examples:
109 | 
110 | - [sui::borrow][borrow-framework] - uses hot potato to ensure that the borrowed value is returned to
111 |   the correct container.
112 | - [sui::transfer_policy][transfer-policy-framework] - defines a `TransferRequest` - a hot potato
113 |   which can only be consumed if all conditions are met.
114 | - [sui::token][token-framework] - in the Closed Loop Token system, an `ActionRequest` carries the
115 |   information about the performed action and collects approvals similarly to `TransferRequest`.
116 | 
117 | [borrow-framework]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui-framework/borrow
118 | [transfer-policy-framework]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui-framework/transfer_policy
119 | [token-framework]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui-framework/token
120 | 
121 | ## Summary
122 | 
123 | - A hot potato is a struct without abilities, it must come with a way to create and destroy it.
124 | - Hot potatoes are used to ensure that some action is taken before the transaction ends, similar to
125 |   a callback.
126 | - Most common use cases for hot potato are borrowing, flash loans, variable-path execution, and
127 |   compositional patterns.
```

move-book/book/programmability/module-initializer.md
```
1 | # Module Initializer
2 | 
3 | A common use case in many applications is to run certain code just once when the package is
4 | published. Imagine a simple store module that needs to create the main Store object upon its
5 | publication. In Sui, this is achieved by defining an `init` function within the module. This
6 | function will automatically be called when the module is published.
7 | 
8 | > All of the modules' `init` functions are called during the publishing process. Currently, this
9 | > behavior is limited to the publish command and does not extend to package upgrades.
10 | >
11 | > <!-- [package upgrades]() -->
12 | 
13 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/module-initializer.move anchor=main
14 | 
15 | ```
16 | 
17 | In the same package, another module can have its own `init` function, encapsulating distinct logic.
18 | 
19 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/module-initializer-2.move anchor=other
20 | 
21 | ```
22 | 
23 | ## `init` Features
24 | 
25 | The function is called on publish, if it is present in the module and follows the rules:
26 | 
27 | - The function has to be named `init`, be private and have no return values.
28 | - Takes one or two arguments: [One Time Witness](./one-time-witness) (optional) and
29 |   [TxContext](./transaction-context). With `TxContext` always being the last argument.
30 | 
31 | ```move
32 | fun init(ctx: &mut TxContext) { /* ... */}
33 | fun init(otw: OTW, ctx: &mut TxContext) { /* ... */ }
34 | ```
35 | 
36 | TxContext can also be passed as immutable reference: `&TxContext`. However, practically speaking, it
37 | should always be `&mut TxContext` since the `init` function can't access the on-chain state and to
38 | create new objects it requires the mutable reference to the context.
39 | 
40 | ```move
41 | fun init(ctx: &TxContext) { /* ... */}
42 | fun init(otw: OTW, ctx: &TxContext) { /* ... */ }
43 | ```
44 | 
45 | ## Trust and Security
46 | 
47 | While `init` function can be used to create sensitive objects once, it is important to know that the
48 | same object (e.g. `StoreOwnerCap` from the first example) can still be created in another function.
49 | Especially given that new functions can be added to the module during an upgrade. So the `init`
50 | function is a good place to set up the initial state of the module, but it is not a security measure
51 | on its own.
52 | 
53 | There are ways to guarantee that the object was created only once, such as the
54 | [One Time Witness](./one-time-witness). And there are ways to limit or disable the upgrade of the
55 | module, which we will cover in the Package Upgrades chapter.
56 | 
57 | ## Next Steps
58 | 
59 | As follows from the definition, the `init` function is guaranteed to be called only once when the
60 | module is published. So it is a good place to put the code that initializes module's objects and
61 | sets up the environment and configuration.
62 | 
63 | For example, if there's a [Capability](./capability) which is required for certain actions, it
64 | should be created in the `init` function. In the next chapter we will talk about the `Capability`
65 | pattern in more detail.
```

move-book/book/programmability/one-time-witness.md
```
1 | # One Time Witness
2 | 
3 | While regular [Witness](./witness-pattern) is a great way to statically prove the ownership of a
4 | type, there are cases where we need to ensure that a Witness is instantiated only once. And this is
5 | the purpose of the One Time Witness (OTW).
6 | 
7 | <!--
8 | Notes to self:
9 |   - background first or definition first - which one is better?
10 |   - why would someone read this section?
11 |   - if we removed the OTW from docs, then we should give definition first.
12 | -->
13 | 
14 | ## Definition
15 | 
16 | The OTW is a special type of Witness that can be used only once. It cannot be manually created and
17 | it is guaranteed to be unique per module. Sui Adapter treats a type as an OTW if it follows these
18 | rules:
19 | 
20 | 1. Has only `drop` ability.
21 | 2. Has no fields.
22 | 3. Is not a generic type.
23 | 4. Named after the module with all uppercase letters.
24 | 
25 | Here is an example of an OTW:
26 | 
27 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/one-time-witness.move anchor=definition
28 | 
29 | ```
30 | 
31 | The OTW cannot be constructed manually, and any code attempting to do so will result in a
32 | compilation error. The OTW can be received as the first argument in the
33 | [module initializer](./module-initializer). And because the `init` function is called only once per
34 | module, the OTW is guaranteed to be instantiated only once.
35 | 
36 | ## Enforcing the OTW
37 | 
38 | To check if a type is an OTW, `sui::types` module of the [Sui Framework](./sui-framework) offers a
39 | special function `is_one_time_witness` that can be used to check if the type is an OTW.
40 | 
41 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/one-time-witness.move anchor=usage
42 | 
43 | ```
44 | 
45 | <!-- ## Background
46 | 
47 | Before we get to actual definition of the OTW, let's consider a simple example. We want to build a generic implementation of a Coin type, which can be initialized with a witness. A instance of a witness `T` is used to create a new `TreasuryCap<T>` which is then used to mint a new `Coin<T>`.
48 | 
49 | ```move
50 | module book::simple_coin {
51 | 
52 |     /// Controls the supply of the Coin.
53 |     public struct TreasuryCap<phantom T> has key, store {
54 |         id: UID,
55 |         total_supply: u64,
56 |     }
57 | 
58 |     /// The Coin type where the `T` is a witness.
59 |     public struct Coin<phantom T> has key, store {
60 |         id: UID,
61 |         value: u64,
62 |     }
63 | 
64 |     /// Create a new TreasuryCap with a witness.
65 |     /// Vulnerable: we can create multiple TreasuryCap<T> with the same witness.
66 |     public fun new<T: drop>(_: T, ctx: &mut TxContext): TreasuryCap<T> {
67 |         TreasuryCap { id: object::new(ctx), total_supply: 0 }
68 |     }
69 | 
70 |     /// We use a regular witness to authorize the minting.
71 |     public fun mint<T>(
72 |         treasury: &mut TreasuryCap<T>,
73 |         value: u64,
74 |         ctx: &mut TxContext
75 |     ) {
76 |         treasury.total_supply = treasury.total_supply + value;
77 |         Coin { id: object::new(ctx), value }
78 |     }
79 | }
80 | ```
81 | 
82 | A dishonest developer would be able to create multiple `TreasuryCap`s with the same witness, and mint more `Coin`s than expected. Here is an example of such a malicious module:
83 | 
84 | ```move
85 | module book::simple_coin_cheater {
86 |     /// The Coin witness.
87 |     public struct Move has drop {}
88 | 
89 |     /// Initialize the TreasuryCap with the Move witness.
90 |     /// ...and do it twice! >_<
91 |     fun init(ctx: &mut TxContext) {
92 |         let treasury_cap = book::simple_coin::new(Move {}, ctx);
93 |         let secret_treasury = book::simple_coin::new(Move {}, ctx);
94 | 
95 |         transfer::public_transfer(treasury_cap, ctx.sender())
96 |         transfer::public_transfer(secret_treasury, ctx.sender())
97 |     }
98 | }
99 | 
100 | ```
101 | 
102 | The example above has no protection against issuing multiple `TreasuryCap`s with the same witness, and in real-world application, this creates a problem of trust. If it was a human decision to support a Coin based on this implementation, they would have to make sure that:
103 | 
104 | - there is only one `TreasuryCap` for a given `T`.
105 | - the module cannot be upgraded to issue more `TreasuryCap`s.
106 | - the module code does not contain any backdoors to issue more `TreasuryCap`s.
107 | 
108 | However, it is not possible to check any of these conditions inside the Move code. And to prevent the need for trust, Sui introduces the OTW pattern.
109 | 
110 | ## Solving the Coin Problem
111 | 
112 | To solve the case of multiple `TreasuryCap`s, we can use the OTW pattern. By defining the `COIN_OTW` type as an OTW, we can ensure that the `COIN_OTW` is used only once. The `COIN_OTW` is then used to create a new `TreasuryCap` and mint a new `Coin`.
113 | 
114 | ```move
115 | 
116 | With
117 | 
118 | ```move
119 | module book::coin_otw {
120 | 
121 |     /// The OTW for the `book::coin_otw` module.
122 |     struct COIN_OTW has drop {}
123 | 
124 |     /// Receive the instance of `COIN_OTW` as the first argument.
125 |     fun init(otw: COIN_OTW, ctx: &mut TxContext) {
126 |         let treasury_cap = book::simple_coin::new(COIN_OTW {}, ctx);
127 |         transfer::public_transfer(treasury_cap, ctx.sender())
128 |     }
129 | }
130 | ```
131 | 
132 | 
133 |  -->
134 | 
135 | <!-- ## Case Study: Coin
136 | 
137 | TODO: add a story behind TreasuryCap and Coin
138 | 
139 | -->
140 | 
141 | ## Summary
142 | 
143 | The OTW pattern is a great way to ensure that a type is used only once. Most of the developers
144 | should understand how to define and receive the OTW, while the OTW checks and enforcement is mostly
145 | needed in libraries and frameworks. For example, the `sui::coin` module requires an OTW in the
146 | `coin::create_currency` method, therefore enforcing that the `coin::TreasuryCap` is created only
147 | once.
148 | 
149 | OTW is a powerful tool that lays the foundation for the [Publisher](./publisher) object, which we
150 | will cover in the next section.
151 | 
152 | <!--
153 | 
154 | ## Questions
155 | - What other ways could be used to prevent multiple `TreasuryCap`s?
156 | - Are there any other ways to use the OTW?
157 | 
158 |  -->
```

move-book/book/programmability/publisher.md
```
1 | # Publisher Authority
2 | 
3 | In application design and development, it is often needed to prove publisher authority. This is
4 | especially important in the context of digital assets, where the publisher may enable or disable
5 | certain features for their assets. The Publisher Object is an object, defined in the
6 | [Sui Framework](./sui-framework), that allows the publisher to prove their _authority over a type_.
7 | 
8 | ## Definition
9 | 
10 | The Publisher object is defined in the `sui::package` module of the Sui Framework. It is a very
11 | simple, non-generic object that can be initialized once per module (and multiple times per package)
12 | and is used to prove the authority of the publisher over a type. To claim a Publisher object, the
13 | publisher must present a [One Time Witness](./one-time-witness) to the `package::claim` function.
14 | 
15 | ```move
16 | module sui::package;
17 | 
18 | public struct Publisher has key, store {
19 |     id: UID,
20 |     package: String,
21 |     module_name: String,
22 | }
23 | ```
24 | 
25 | > If you're not familiar with the One Time Witness, you can read more about it
26 | > [here](./one-time-witness).
27 | 
28 | Here's a simple example of claiming a `Publisher` object in a module:
29 | 
30 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/publisher.move anchor=publisher
31 | 
32 | ```
33 | 
34 | ## Usage
35 | 
36 | The Publisher object has two functions associated with it which are used to prove the publisher's
37 | authority over a type:
38 | 
39 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/publisher.move anchor=use_publisher
40 | 
41 | ```
42 | 
43 | ## Publisher as Admin Role
44 | 
45 | For small applications or simple use cases, the Publisher object can be used as an admin
46 | [capability](./capability). While in the broader context, the Publisher object has control over
47 | system configurations, it can also be used to manage the application's state.
48 | 
49 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/publisher.move anchor=publisher_as_admin
50 | 
51 | ```
52 | 
53 | However, Publisher misses some native properties of [Capabilities](./capability), such as type
54 | safety and expressiveness. The signature for the `admin_action` is not very explicit, can be called
55 | by anyone else. And due to `Publisher` object being standard, there now is a risk of unauthorized
56 | access if the `from_module` check is not performed. So it's important to be cautious when using the
57 | `Publisher` object as an admin role.
58 | 
59 | ## Role on Sui
60 | 
61 | Publisher is required for certain features on Sui. [Object Display](./display) can be created only
62 | by the Publisher, and TransferPolicy - an important component of the Kiosk system - also requires
63 | the Publisher object to prove ownership of the type.
64 | 
65 | ## Next Steps
66 | 
67 | In the next chapter we will cover the first feature that requires the Publisher object - Object
68 | Display - a way to describe objects for clients, and standardize metadata. A must-have for
69 | user-friendly applications.
```

1 | # Sui Framework
2 | 
3 | Sui Framework is a default dependency set in the [Package Manifest](./../concepts/manifest). It
4 | depends on the [Standard Library](./../move-basics/standard-library) and provides Sui-specific
5 | features, including the interaction with the storage, and Sui-specific native types and modules.
6 | 
7 | _For convenience, we grouped the modules in the Sui Framework into multiple categories. But they're
8 | still part of the same framework._
9 | 
10 | ## Core
11 | 
12 | <!-- Custom CSS addition in the theme/custom.css  -->
13 | <div class="modules-table">
14 | 
15 | | Module                                                                                         | Description                                                             | Chapter                                          |
16 | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
17 | | [sui::address](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/address)                           | Adds conversion methods to the [address type](./../move-basics/address) | [Address](./../move-basics/address)              |
18 | | [sui::transfer](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/transfer)                         | Implements the storage operations for Objects                           | [It starts with an Object](./../object)          |
19 | | [sui::tx_context](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/tx_context)                     | Contains the `TxContext` struct and methods to read it                  | [Transaction Context](./transaction-context)     |
20 | | [sui::object](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/object)                             | Defines the `UID` and `ID` type, required for creating objects          | [It starts with an Object](./../object)          |
21 | | [sui::clock](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/clock)                               | Defines the `Clock` type and its methods                                | [Epoch and Time](./epoch-and-time)               |
22 | | [sui::dynamic_field](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/dynamic_field)               | Implements methods to add, use and remove dynamic fields                | [Dynamic Fields](./dynamic-fields)               |
23 | | [sui::dynamic_object_field](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/dynamic_object_field) | Implements methods to add, use and remove dynamic object fields         | [Dynamic Object Fields](./dynamic-object-fields) |
24 | | [sui::event](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/event)                               | Allows emitting events for off-chain listeners                          | [Events](./events)                               |
25 | | [sui::package](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/package)                           | Defines the `Publisher` type and package upgrade methods                | [Publisher](./publisher), Package Upgrades       |
26 | | [sui::display](https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/display)                           | Implements the `Display` object and ways to create and update it        | [Display](./display)                             |
27 | 
28 | </div>
29 | 
30 | ## Collections
31 | 
32 | <div class="modules-table">
33 | 
34 | | Module                                                                         | Description                                                       | Chapter                                      |
35 | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |

move-book/book/programmability/transaction-context.md
```
1 | # Transaction Context
2 | 
3 | Every transaction has the execution context. The context is a set of predefined variables that are
4 | available to the program during execution. For example, every transaction has a sender address, and
5 | the transaction context contains a variable that holds the sender address.
6 | 
7 | The transaction context is available to the program through the `TxContext` struct. The struct is
8 | defined in the [`sui::tx_context`][tx-context-framework] module and contains the following fields:
9 | 
10 | [tx-context-framework]: https://docs.sui.io/references/framework/sui/tx_context
11 | 
12 | ```move
13 | module sui::tx_context;
14 | 
15 | /// Information about the transaction currently being executed.
16 | /// This cannot be constructed by a transaction--it is a privileged object created by
17 | /// the VM and passed in to the entrypoint of the transaction as `&mut TxContext`.
18 | public struct TxContext has drop {
19 |     /// The address of the user that signed the current transaction
20 |     sender: address,
21 |     /// Hash of the current transaction
22 |     tx_hash: vector<u8>,
23 |     /// The current epoch number
24 |     epoch: u64,
25 |     /// Timestamp that the epoch started at
26 |     epoch_timestamp_ms: u64,
27 |     /// Counter recording the number of fresh id's created while executing
28 |     /// this transaction. Always 0 at the start of a transaction
29 |     ids_created: u64
30 | }
31 | ```
32 | 
33 | Transaction context cannot be constructed manually or directly modified. It is created by the system
34 | and passed to the function as a reference in a transaction. Any function called in a
35 | [Transaction](./../concepts/what-is-a-transaction) has access to the context and can pass it into
36 | the nested calls.
37 | 
38 | > `TxContext` has to be the last argument in the function signature.
39 | 
40 | ## Reading the Transaction Context
41 | 
42 | With only exception of the `ids_created`, all of the fields in the `TxContext` have getters. The
43 | getters are defined in the `sui::tx_context` module and are available to the program. The getters
44 | don't require `&mut` because they don't modify the context.
45 | 
46 | ```move file=packages/samples/sources/programmability/transaction-context.move anchor=reading
47 | 
48 | ```
49 | 
50 | ## Mutability
51 | 
52 | The `TxContext` is required to create new objects (or just `UID`s) in the system. New UIDs are
53 | derived from the transaction digest, and for the digest to be unique, there needs to be a changing
54 | parameter. Sui uses the `ids_created` field for that. Every time a new UID is created, the
55 | `ids_created` field is incremented by one. This way, the digest is always unique.
56 | 
57 | Internally, it is represented as the `derive_id` function:
58 | 
59 | ```move
60 | native fun derive_id(tx_hash: vector<u8>, ids_created: u64): address;
61 | ```
62 | 
63 | ## Generating Unique Addresses
64 | 
65 | The underlying `derive_id` function can also be utilized in your program to generate unique
66 | addresses. The function itself is not exposed, but a wrapper function `fresh_object_address` is
67 | available in the `sui::tx_context` module. It may be useful if you need to generate a unique
68 | identifier in your program.
69 | 
70 | ```move
71 | module sui::tx_context;
72 | 
73 | /// Create an `address` that has not been used. As it is an object address, it will never
74 | /// occur as the address for a user.
75 | /// In other words, the generated address is a globally unique object ID.
76 | public fun fresh_object_address(ctx: &mut TxContext): address {
77 |     let ids_created = ctx.ids_created;
78 |     let id = derive_id(*&ctx.tx_hash, ids_created);
79 |     ctx.ids_created = ids_created + 1;
80 |     id
81 | }
82 | ```
```

move-book/book/programmability/witness-pattern.md
```
1 | # Pattern: Witness
2 | 
3 | Witness is a pattern of proving an existence by constructing a proof. In the context of programming,
4 | witness is a way to prove a certain property of a system by providing a value that can only be
5 | constructed if the property holds.
6 | 
7 | ## Witness in Move
8 | 
9 | In the [Struct](./../move-basics/struct) section we have shown that a struct can only be created -
10 | or _packed_ - by the module defining it. Hence, in Move, a module proves ownership of the type by
11 | constructing it. This is one of the most important patterns in Move, and it is widely used for
12 | generic type instantiation and authorization.
13 | 
14 | Practically speaking, for the witness to be used, there has to be a function that expects a witness
15 | as an argument. In the example below it is the `new` function that expects a witness of the `T` type
16 | to create a `Instance<T>` instance.
17 | 
18 | > It is often the case that the witness struct is not stored, and for that the function may require
19 | > the [Drop](./../move-basics/drop-ability) ability for the type.
20 | 
21 | ```move
22 | module book::witness;
23 | 
24 | /// A struct that requires a witness to be created.
25 | public struct Instance<T> { t: T }
26 | 
27 | /// Create a new instance of `Instance<T>` with the provided T.
28 | public fun new<T>(witness: T): Instance<T> {
29 |     Instance { t: witness }
30 | }
31 | ```
32 | 
33 | The only way to construct an `Instance<T>` is to call the `new` function with an instance of the
34 | type `T`. This is a basic example of the witness pattern in Move. A module providing a witness often
35 | has a matching implementation, like the module `book::witness_source` below:
36 | 
37 | ```move
38 | module book::witness_source;
39 | 
40 | use book::witness::{Self, Instance};
41 | 
42 | /// A struct used as a witness.
43 | public struct W {}
44 | 
45 | /// Create a new instance of `Instance<W>`.
46 | public fun new_instance(): Instance<W> {
47 |     witness::new(W {})
48 | }
49 | ```
50 | 
51 | The instance of the struct `W` is passed into the `new_instance` function to create an
52 | `Instance<W>`, thereby proving that the module `book::witness_source` owns the type `W`.
53 | 
54 | ## Instantiating a Generic Type
55 | 
56 | Witness allows generic types to be instantiated with a concrete type. This is useful for inheriting
57 | associated behaviors from the type with an option to extend them, if the module provides the ability
58 | to do so.
59 | 
60 | ```move
61 | module sui::balance;
