```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Tuples and Unit | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Tuples and Unit
7 | 
8 | Move does not fully support tuples as one might expect coming from another language with them as a
9 | [first-class value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-class_citizen). However, in order to support
10 | multiple return values, Move has tuple-like expressions. These expressions do not result in a
11 | concrete value at runtime (there are no tuples in the bytecode), and as a result they are very
12 | limited:
13 | 
14 | - They can only appear in expressions (usually in the return position for a function).
15 | - They cannot be bound to local variables.
16 | - They cannot be bound to local variables.
17 | - They cannot be stored in structs.
18 | - Tuple types cannot be used to instantiate generics.
19 | 
20 | Similarly, [unit `()`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_type) is a type created by the Move source
21 | language in order to be expression based. The unit value `()` does not result in any runtime value.
22 | We can consider unit`()` to be an empty tuple, and any restrictions that apply to tuples also apply
23 | to unit.
24 | 
25 | It might feel weird to have tuples in the language at all given these restrictions. But one of the
26 | most common use cases for tuples in other languages is for functions to allow functions to return
27 | multiple values. Some languages work around this by forcing the users to write structs that contain
28 | the multiple return values. However in Move, you cannot put references inside of
29 | [structs](./../structs). This required Move to support multiple return values. These multiple return
30 | values are all pushed on the stack at the bytecode level. At the source level, these multiple return
31 | values are represented using tuples.
32 | 
33 | ## Literals
34 | 
35 | Tuples are created by a comma separated list of expressions inside of parentheses.
36 | 
37 | | Syntax          | Type                                                                         | Description                                                  |
38 | | --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
39 | | `()`            | `(): ()`                                                                     | Unit, the empty tuple, or the tuple of arity 0               |
40 | | `(e1, ..., en)` | `(e1, ..., en): (T1, ..., Tn)` where `e_i: Ti` s.t. `0 < i <= n` and `n > 0` | A `n`-tuple, a tuple of arity `n`, a tuple with `n` elements |
41 | 
42 | Note that `(e)` does not have type `(e): (t)`, in other words there is no tuple with one element. If
43 | there is only a single element inside of the parentheses, the parentheses are only used for
44 | disambiguation and do not carry any other special meaning.
45 | 
46 | Sometimes, tuples with two elements are called "pairs" and tuples with three elements are called
47 | "triples."
48 | 
49 | ### Examples
50 | 
51 | ```move
52 | module 0::example;
53 | 
54 | // all 3 of these functions are equivalent
55 | 
56 | // when no return type is provided, it is assumed to be `()`
57 | fun returns_unit_1() { }
58 | 
59 | // there is an implicit () value in empty expression blocks
60 | fun returns_unit_2(): () { }
61 | 
62 | // explicit version of `returns_unit_1` and `returns_unit_2`
63 | fun returns_unit_3(): () { () }
64 | 
65 | 
66 | fun returns_3_values(): (u64, bool, address) {
67 |     (0, false, @0x42)
68 | }
69 | fun returns_4_values(x: &u64): (&u64, u8, u128, vector<u8>) {
70 |     (x, 0, 1, b"foobar")
71 | }
72 | ```
73 | 
74 | ## Operations
75 | 
76 | The only operation that can be done on tuples currently is destructuring.
77 | 
78 | ### Destructuring
79 | 
80 | For tuples of any size, they can be destructured in either a `let` binding or in an assignment.
81 | 
82 | For example:
83 | 
84 | ```move
85 | module 0x42::example;
86 | 
87 | // all 3 of these functions are equivalent
88 | fun returns_unit() {}
89 | fun returns_2_values(): (bool, bool) { (true, false) }
90 | fun returns_4_values(x: &u64): (&u64, u8, u128, vector<u8>) { (x, 0, 1, b"foobar") }
91 | 
92 | fun examples(cond: bool) {
93 |     let () = ();
94 |     let (mut x, mut y): (u8, u64) = (0, 1);
95 |     let (mut a, mut b, mut c, mut d) = (@0x0, 0, false, b"");
96 | 
97 |     () = ();
98 |     (x, y) = if (cond) (1, 2) else (3, 4);
99 |     (a, b, c, d) = (@0x1, 1, true, b"1");
100 | }
101 | 
102 | fun examples_with_function_calls() {
103 |     let () = returns_unit();
104 |     let (mut x, mut y): (bool, bool) = returns_2_values();
105 |     let (mut a, mut b, mut c, mut d) = returns_4_values(&0);
106 | 
107 |     () = returns_unit();
108 |     (x, y) = returns_2_values();
109 |     (a, b, c, d) = returns_4_values(&1);
110 | }
111 | ```
112 | 
113 | For more details, see [Move Variables](./../variables).
114 | 
115 | ## Subtyping
116 | 
117 | Along with references, tuples are the only types that have
118 | [subtyping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtyping) in Move. Tuples have subtyping only in the
119 | sense that subtype with references (in a covariant way).
120 | 
121 | For example:
122 | 
123 | ```move
124 | let x: &u64 = &0;
125 | let y: &mut u64 = &mut 1;
126 | 
127 | // (&u64, &mut u64) is a subtype of (&u64, &u64)
128 | // since &mut u64 is a subtype of &u64
129 | let (a, b): (&u64, &u64) = (x, y);
130 | 
131 | // (&mut u64, &mut u64) is a subtype of (&u64, &u64)
132 | // since &mut u64 is a subtype of &u64
133 | let (c, d): (&u64, &u64) = (y, y);
134 | 
135 | // highlight-error-start
136 | // ERROR! (&u64, &mut u64) is NOT a subtype of (&mut u64, &mut u64)
137 | // since &u64 is NOT a subtype of &mut u64
138 | let (e, f): (&mut u64, &mut u64) = (x, y);
139 | // highlight-error-end
140 | ```
141 | 
142 | ## Ownership
143 | 
144 | As mentioned above, tuple values don't really exist at runtime. And currently they cannot be stored
145 | into local variables because of this (but it is likely that this feature will come at some point in
146 | the future). As such, tuples can only be moved currently, as copying them would require putting them
147 | into a local variable first.
```

move-book/reference/primitive-types/vector.md
```
1 | ---
2 | title: 'Vector | Reference'
3 | description: ''
4 | ---
5 | 
6 | # Vector
7 | 
8 | `vector<T>` is the only primitive collection type provided by Move. A `vector<T>` is a homogeneous
9 | collection of `T`'s that can grow or shrink by pushing/popping values off the "end".
10 | 
11 | A `vector<T>` can be instantiated with any type `T`. For example, `vector<u64>`, `vector<address>`,
12 | `vector<0x42::my_module::MyData>`, and `vector<vector<u8>>` are all valid vector types.
13 | 
14 | ## Literals
15 | 
16 | ### General `vector` Literals
17 | 
18 | Vectors of any type can be created with `vector` literals.
19 | 
20 | | Syntax                | Type                                                                          | Description                                |
21 | | --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
22 | | `vector[]`            | `vector[]: vector<T>` where `T` is any single, non-reference type             | An empty vector                            |
23 | | `vector[e1, ..., en]` | `vector[e1, ..., en]: vector<T>` where `e_i: T` s.t. `0 < i <= n` and `n > 0` | A vector with `n` elements (of length `n`) |
24 | 
25 | In these cases, the type of the `vector` is inferred, either from the element type or from the
26 | vector's usage. If the type cannot be inferred, or simply for added clarity, the type can be
27 | specified explicitly:
28 | 
29 | ```move
30 | vector<T>[]: vector<T>
31 | vector<T>[e1, ..., en]: vector<T>
32 | ```
33 | 
34 | #### Example Vector Literals
35 | 
36 | ```move
37 | (vector[]: vector<bool>);
38 | (vector[0u8, 1u8, 2u8]: vector<u8>);
39 | (vector<u128>[]: vector<u128>);
40 | (vector<address>[@0x42, @0x100]: vector<address>);
41 | ```
42 | 
43 | ### `vector<u8>` literals
44 | 
45 | A common use-case for vectors in Move is to represent "byte arrays", which are represented with
46 | `vector<u8>`. These values are often used for cryptographic purposes, such as a public key or a hash
47 | result. These values are so common that specific syntax is provided to make the values more
48 | readable, as opposed to having to use `vector[]` where each individual `u8` value is specified in
49 | numeric form.
50 | 
51 | There are currently two supported types of `vector<u8>` literals, _byte strings_ and _hex strings_.
52 | 
53 | #### Byte Strings
54 | 
55 | Byte strings are quoted string literals prefixed by a `b`, e.g. `b"Hello!\n"`.
56 | 
57 | These are ASCII encoded strings that allow for escape sequences. Currently, the supported escape
58 | sequences are:
59 | 
60 | | Escape Sequence | Description                                    |
61 | | --------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
62 | | `\n`            | New line (or Line feed)                        |
63 | | `\r`            | Carriage return                                |
64 | | `\t`            | Tab                                            |
65 | | `\\`            | Backslash                                      |
66 | | `\0`            | Null                                           |
67 | | `\"`            | Quote                                          |
68 | | `\xHH`          | Hex escape, inserts the hex byte sequence `HH` |
69 | 
70 | #### Hex Strings
71 | 
72 | Hex strings are quoted string literals prefixed by a `x`, e.g. `x"48656C6C6F210A"`.
73 | 
74 | Each byte pair, ranging from `00` to `FF`, is interpreted as hex encoded `u8` value. So each byte
75 | pair corresponds to a single entry in the resulting `vector<u8>`.
76 | 
77 | #### Example String Literals
78 | 
79 | ```move
80 | fun byte_and_hex_strings() {
81 |     assert!(b"" == x"", 0);
82 |     assert!(b"Hello!\n" == x"48656C6C6F210A", 1);
83 |     assert!(b"\x48\x65\x6C\x6C\x6F\x21\x0A" == x"48656C6C6F210A", 2);
84 |     assert!(
85 |         b"\"Hello\tworld!\"\n \r \\Null=\0" ==
86 |             x"2248656C6C6F09776F726C6421220A200D205C4E756C6C3D00",
87 |         3
88 |     );
89 | }
90 | ```
91 | 
92 | ## Operations
93 | 
94 | `vector` supports the following operations via the `std::vector` module in the Move standard
95 | library:
96 | 
97 | | Function                                                   | Description                                                                                                                                                     | Aborts?                        |
98 | | ---------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
99 | | `vector::empty<T>(): vector<T>`                            | Create an empty vector that can store values of type `T`                                                                                                        | Never                          |
100 | | `vector::singleton<T>(t: T): vector<T>`                    | Create a vector of size 1 containing `t`                                                                                                                        | Never                          |
101 | | `vector::push_back<T>(v: &mut vector<T>, t: T)`            | Add `t` to the end of `v`                                                                                                                                       | Never                          |
102 | | `vector::pop_back<T>(v: &mut vector<T>): T`                | Remove and return the last element in `v`                                                                                                                       | If `v` is empty                |
103 | | `vector::borrow<T>(v: &vector<T>, i: u64): &T`             | Return an immutable reference to the `T` at index `i`                                                                                                           | If `i` is not in bounds        |
104 | | `vector::borrow_mut<T>(v: &mut vector<T>, i: u64): &mut T` | Return a mutable reference to the `T` at index `i`                                                                                                              | If `i` is not in bounds        |
105 | | `vector::destroy_empty<T>(v: vector<T>)`                   | Delete `v`                                                                                                                                                      | If `v` is not empty            |
106 | | `vector::append<T>(v1: &mut vector<T>, v2: vector<T>)`     | Add the elements in `v2` to the end of `v1`                                                                                                                     | Never                          |
107 | | `vector::contains<T>(v: &vector<T>, e: &T): bool`          | Return true if `e` is in the vector `v`. Otherwise, returns false                                                                                               | Never                          |
108 | | `vector::swap<T>(v: &mut vector<T>, i: u64, j: u64)`       | Swaps the elements at the `i`th and `j`th indices in the vector `v`                                                                                             | If `i` or `j` is out of bounds |
109 | | `vector::reverse<T>(v: &mut vector<T>)`                    | Reverses the order of the elements in the vector `v` in place                                                                                                   | Never                          |
110 | | `vector::index_of<T>(v: &vector<T>, e: &T): (bool, u64)`   | Return `(true, i)` if `e` is in the vector `v` at index `i`. Otherwise, returns `(false, 0)`                                                                    | Never                          |
111 | | `vector::remove<T>(v: &mut vector<T>, i: u64): T`          | Remove the `i`th element of the vector `v`, shifting all subsequent elements. This is O(n) and preserves ordering of elements in the vector                     | If `i` is out of bounds        |
112 | | `vector::swap_remove<T>(v: &mut vector<T>, i: u64): T`     | Swap the `i`th element of the vector `v` with the last element and then pop the element, This is O(1), but does not preserve ordering of elements in the vector | If `i` is out of bounds        |
113 | 
114 | <!-- TODO we should just link out to generated stdlib docs? Maybe?  -->
115 | 
116 | More operations may be added over time.
117 | 
118 | ## Example
119 | 
120 | ```move
121 | use std::vector;
122 | 
123 | let mut v = vector::empty<u64>();
124 | vector::push_back(&mut v, 5);
125 | vector::push_back(&mut v, 6);
126 | 
127 | assert!(*vector::borrow(&v, 0) == 5, 42);
128 | assert!(*vector::borrow(&v, 1) == 6, 42);
129 | assert!(vector::pop_back(&mut v) == 6, 42);
130 | assert!(vector::pop_back(&mut v) == 5, 42);
131 | ```
132 | 
133 | ## Destroying and copying `vector`s
134 | 
135 | Some behaviors of `vector<T>` depend on the abilities of the element type, `T`. For example, vectors
136 | containing elements that do not have `drop` cannot be implicitly discarded like `v` in the example
137 | above--they must be explicitly destroyed with `vector::destroy_empty`.
138 | 
139 | Note that `vector::destroy_empty` will abort at runtime unless `vec` contains zero elements:
140 | 
141 | ```move
142 | fun destroy_any_vector<T>(vec: vector<T>) {
143 |     vector::destroy_empty(vec) // deleting this line will cause a compiler error
144 | }
145 | ```
146 | 
147 | But no error would occur for dropping a vector that contains elements with `drop`:
148 | 
149 | ```move
150 | fun destroy_droppable_vector<T: drop>(vec: vector<T>) {
151 |     // valid!
152 |     // nothing needs to be done explicitly to destroy the vector
153 | }
154 | ```
155 | 
156 | Similarly, vectors cannot be copied unless the element type has `copy`. In other words, a
157 | `vector<T>` has `copy` if and only if `T` has `copy`. Note that it will be implicitly copied if
158 | needed:
159 | 
160 | ```move
161 | let x = vector[10];
162 | let y = x; // implicit copy
163 | let z = x;
164 | (y, z)
165 | ```
166 | 
167 | Keep in mind, copies of large vectors can be expensive. If this is a concern, annotating the
168 | `intended` usage can prevent accidental copies. For example,
169 | 
170 | ```move
171 | let x = vector[10];
172 | let y = move x;
173 | let z = x; // ERROR! x has been moved
174 | (y, z)
175 | ```
176 | 
177 | For more details see the sections on [type abilities](./../abilities) and [generics](./../generics).
178 | 
179 | ## Ownership
180 | 
181 | As mentioned [above](#destroying-and-copying-vectors), `vector` values can be copied only if the
182 | elements can be copied. In that case, the copy can be done via a
183 | [`copy`](./../variables#move-and-copy) or a
184 | [dereference `*`](./references#reading-and-writing-through-references).
```

walrus-docs/docs/blog/01_announcing_walrus.md
```
1 | # Announcing Walrus: A Decentralized Storage and Data Availability Protocol
2 | 
3 | Walrus is an innovative decentralized storage network for blockchain apps and autonomous agents. The
4 | Walrus storage system is being released today as a developer preview for Sui builders in order to
5 | gather feedback. We expect a broad rollout to other web3 communities very soon!
6 | 
7 | Leveraging innovations in erasure coding, Walrus enables fast and robust encoding of unstructured
8 | data blobs into smaller slivers distributed and stored over a network of storage nodes. A subset of
9 | slivers can be used to rapidly reconstruct the original blob, even when up to two-thirds of the
10 | slivers are missing. This is possible while keeping the replication factor down to a minimal 4x-5x,
11 | similar to existing cloud-based services, but with the additional benefits of decentralization and
12 | resilience to more widespread faults.
13 | 
14 | ## The Replication Challenge
15 | 
16 | Sui is the most advanced blockchain system in relation to storage on validators, with innovations
17 | such as a [storage fund](https://docs.sui.io/concepts/tokenomics/storage-fund) that future-proofs
18 | the cost of storing data on-chain. Nevertheless, Sui still requires complete data replication among
19 | all validators, resulting in a replication factor of 100x or more in today’s Sui Mainnet. While this
20 | is necessary for replicated computing and smart contracts acting on the state of the blockchain, it
21 | is inefficient for simply storing unstructured data blobs, such as music, video, blockchain history,
22 | etc.
23 | 
24 | ## Introducing Walrus: Efficient and Robust Decentralized Storage
25 | 
26 | To tackle the challenge of high replication costs, Mysten Labs has developed Walrus, a decentralized
27 | storage network offering exceptional data availability and robustness with a minimal replication
28 | factor of 4x-5x. Walrus provides two key benefits:
29 | 
30 | 1. **Cost-Effective Blob Storage:** Walrus allows for the uploading of gigabytes of data at a time
31 |    with minimal cost, making it an ideal solution for storing large volumes of data. Walrus can do
32 |    this because the data blob is transmitted only once over the network, and storage nodes only
33 |    spend a fraction of resources compared to the blob size. As a result, the more storage nodes the
34 |    system has, the fewer resources each storage node uses per blob.
35 | 
36 | 1. **High Availability and Robustness:** Data stored on Walrus enjoys enhanced reliability and
37 |    availability under fault conditions. Data recovery is still possible even if two-thirds of the
38 |    storage nodes crash or come under adversarial control. Further, availability may be certified
39 |    efficiently without downloading the full blob.
40 | 
41 | Decentralized storage can take multiple forms in modern ecosystems. For instance, it offers better
42 | guarantees for digital assets traded as NFTs. Unlike current designs that store data off-chain,
43 | decentralized storage ensures users own the actual resource, not just metadata, mitigating risks of
44 | data being taken down or misrepresented.
45 | 
46 | Additionally, decentralized storage is not only useful for storing data such as pictures or files
47 | with high availability; it can also double as a low-cost data availability layer for rollups. Here,
48 | sequencers can upload transactions on Walrus, and the rollup executor only needs to temporarily
49 | reconstruct them for execution.
50 | 
51 | We also believe Walrus will accompany existing disaster recovery strategies for millions of
52 | enterprise companies. Not only is Walrus low-cost, it also provides unmatched layers of data
53 | availability, integrity, transparency, and resilience that centralized solutions by design cannot
54 | offer.
55 | 
56 | Walrus is powered by the Sui Network and scales horizontally to hundreds or thousands of networked
57 | decentralized storage nodes. This should enable Walrus to offer Exabytes of storage at costs
58 | competitive with current centralized offerings, given the higher assurance and decentralization.
59 | 
60 | ## The Future of Walrus
61 | 
62 | By releasing this developer preview we hope to share some of the design decisions with the
63 | decentralized app developer community and gather feedback on the approach and the APIs for storing,
64 | retrieving, and certifying blobs. In this developer preview, all storage nodes are operated by
65 | Mysten Labs to help us understand use cases, fix bugs, and improve the performance of the software.
66 | 
67 | Future updates to Walrus will allow for dynamically changing the set of decentralized storage nodes,
68 | as well as changing the mapping of what slivers are managed by each storage node. The available
69 | operations and tools will also be expanded to cover more storage-related use cases. Many of these
70 | functions will be designed with the feedback we gather in mind.
71 | 
72 | Stay tuned for more updates on how Walrus will revolutionize data storage in the web3 ecosystem.
73 | 
74 | ## What can developers build?
75 | 
76 | As part of this developer preview, we provide a binary client (currently macOS, ubuntu) that can be
77 | operated from the [command line interface](https://docs.walrus.site/usage/client-cli.html), a [JSON
78 | API](https://docs.walrus.site/usage/json-api.html), and an [HTTP
79 | API](https://docs.walrus.site/usage/web-api.html). We also offer the community an aggregator and
80 | publisher service and a Devnet deployment of 10 storage nodes operated by Mysten Labs.
81 | 
82 | We hope developers will experiment with building applications that leverage the Walrus Decentralized
83 | Store in a variety of ways. As examples, we hope to see the community build:
84 | 
85 | - **Storage of media for NFT or dapps:** Walrus can directly store and serve media such as images,
86 |   sounds, sprites, videos, other game assets, etc. This is publicly available media that can be
87 |   accessed using HTTP requests at caches to create multimedia dapps.
88 | 
89 | - **AI-related use cases:** Walrus can store clean data sets of training data, datasets with a known
90 |   and verified provenance, model weights, and proofs of correct training for AI models. Or it may be
91 |   used to store and ensure the availability and authenticity of an AI model output.
92 | 
93 | - **Storage of long term archival of blockchain history:** Walrus can be used as a lower-cost
94 |   decentralized store to store blockchain history. For Sui, this can include sequences of
95 |   checkpoints with all associated transaction and effects content, as well as historic snapshots of
96 |   the blockchain state, code, or binaries.
97 | 
98 | - **Support availability for L2s:** Walrus enables parties to certify the availability of blobs, as
99 |   required by L2s that need data to be stored and attested as available to all. This may also
100 |   include the availability of extra audit data such as validity proofs, zero-knowledge proofs of
101 |   correct execution, or large fraud proofs.
102 | 
103 | - **Support a full decentralized web experience:** Walrus can host full decentralized web
104 |   experiences including all resources (such as js, css, html, and media). These can provide content
105 |   but also host the UX of dapps, enabling fully decentralized front- and back-ends on chain. It
106 |   brings the full "web" back into "web3".
107 | 
108 | - **Support subscription models for media:** Creators can store encrypted media on Walrus and only
109 |   provide access via decryption keys to parties that have paid a subscription fee or have paid for
110 |   content. (Note that Walrus provides the storage; encryption and decryption must be done off
111 |   Walrus).
112 | 
113 | We are excited to see what else the web3 developer community can imagine!
114 | 
115 | ## Getting Started
116 | 
117 | For this developer preview the public Walrus Devnet is openly available to all developers. Developer
118 | documentation is available at <https://docs.walrus.site>.
119 | 
120 | SUI Testnet token is the main currency for interacting with Walrus. Developers pay for Walrus Devnet
121 | storage using SUI Testnet tokens which can be acquired at the [Sui Testnet Discord
122 | faucet](https://discord.com/channels/916379725201563759/1037811694564560966).
123 | 
124 | ## One more thing …
125 | 
126 | The [Walrus Sites website](https://walrus.site), the [Walrus docs](https://docs.walrus.site), and
127 | [this very blog](https://blog.walrus.site) are hosted on Walrus. To learn more about Walrus Sites
128 | and how you can deploy your own, [click here](https://docs.walrus.site/walrus-sites/intro.html).
```

walrus-docs/docs/blog/02_devnet_update.md
```
1 | # Devnet Update
2 | 
3 | Published on: 2024-08-12
4 | 
5 | We have redeployed the Walrus Devnet to incorporate various improvements to the Walrus storage nodes
6 | and clients. In this process, all blobs stored on Walrus were wiped. Note that this may happen again
7 | on Devnet and Testnet, but obviously *not on the future Mainnet*.
8 | 
9 | ## Migration and Re-deployment of Walrus Sites
10 | 
11 | You can obtain the latest version of the `walrus` binary and the new configuration as described in
12 | the [setup chapter](../usage/setup.md).
13 | 
14 | If you had deployed any Walrus Sites, the site object on Sui and any SuiNS name are still valid.
15 | However, you need to re-store all blobs on Walrus. You can achieve this by running the site-builder
16 | tool (from the `walrus-sites` directory) as follows:
17 | 
18 | ```sh
19 | ./target/release/site-builder --config site-builder/assets/builder-example.yaml update --force \
20 |     <path to the site> <site object ID>
21 | ```
22 | 
23 | ## Changes
24 | 
25 | Besides many improvements to the storage nodes, the new version of Walrus includes the following
26 | user-facing changes:
27 | 
28 | - Improved coin management: The client now better selects coins for gas and storage fees. Users no
29 |   longer require multiple coins in their wallet.
30 | - Improved connection management: The client now limits the number of parallel connections to
31 |   improve performance for users with low network bandwidth storing large blobs.
32 | - OpenAPI specification: Walrus storage nodes, aggregators, and publishers expose their API
33 |   specifications at the path `/v1/api`.
34 | - System info in JSON: The `info` command is now also available in JSON mode.
35 | - Client version: The `walrus` CLI now has a `--version` option.
36 | - Support for the empty blob: The empty blob is now supported by Walrus.
37 | - Default configuration-file paths: The client now looks for configuration files in
38 |   `~/.config/walrus` in addition to `~/.walrus` and recognizes the extension `.yml` in addition to
39 |   `.yaml`.
40 | - Home directory in paths: Paths specified in configuration files now expand the `~` symbol at the
41 |   beginning to the user's home directory.
42 | - More robust store and status check: The `store` and `blob-status` commands are now more robust
43 |   against Sui full nodes that aggressively prune past events and against load-balancers that send
44 |   transactions to different full nodes.
45 | - Fix CLI parsing: The `walrus` CLI now properly handles hyphens in blob IDs.
46 | 
47 | This update also increases the number of shards to 1000, which is more representative of the
48 | expected value in Testnet and Mainnet.
```

walrus-docs/docs/blog/03_whitepaper.md
```
1 | # Announcing the Official Walrus Whitepaper
2 | 
3 | In June, Mysten Labs announced Walrus, a new decentralized secure blob store design, and introduced
4 | a developer preview that currently stores over [12TiB](https://capacity.walrus.site/) of data.
5 | [Breaking the Ice](https://info.breakingtheice.sui.io/) gathered over 200 developers to build apps
6 | leveraging decentralized storage.
7 | 
8 | It is time to unveil the next stage of the project: Walrus will become an independent decentralized
9 | network with its own utility token, WAL, that will play a key role in the operation and governance
10 | of the network. Walrus will be operated by storage nodes through a delegated proof-of-stake
11 | mechanism using the WAL token. An independent Walrus foundation will encourage the advancement and
12 | adoption of Walrus, and support its community of users and developers.
13 | 
14 | Today, we published the Walrus [whitepaper](../walrus.pdf) (also on
15 | [GitHub](https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/blob/main/docs/walrus.pdf)) that offers
16 | additional details, including:
17 | 
18 | - The encoding scheme and Read / Write operations Walrus uses to ensure both security and efficient
19 |   scaling to 100s and 1000s of storage nodes, including interactions with the Sui blockchain which
20 |   serves as a coordination layer for Walrus’ operations.
21 | - The reconfiguration of storage nodes across epochs, and how the protocol ensures available blobs
22 |   on Walrus remain available over long periods of time.
23 | - The tokenomics of Walrus based on the WAL token, including how staking and staking rewards are
24 |   structured, how pricing and payments for storage are handled and distributed in each epoch, and
25 |   the governance of key system parameters.
26 | - Forward-looking design options, such as a cheap mechanism to challenge and audit storage nodes,
27 |   options for ensuring reads with a higher service quality, possibly against a payment, and designs
28 |   that empower light nodes to meaningfully contribute to the protocol’s robustness, serve reads, and
29 |   be rewarded.
30 | 
31 | The whitepaper focuses on the steady-state design aspects of Walrus. Further details about the
32 | project, such as timelines, opportunities for community participation, how to join the network as a
33 | storage node, and plans around light nodes, will be shared in subsequent posts.
34 | 
35 | To be part of this journey:
36 | 
37 | - Follow us on [Twitter](https://x.com/WalrusProtocol)
38 | - Join our [Discord](https://discord.com/invite/walrusprotocol)
39 | - [Build apps](../index.md) on Walrus
40 | - [Publish a Walrus Site](../walrus-sites/intro.md) and share it
```

walrus-docs/docs/blog/04_testnet_update.md
```
1 | # Announcing Testnet
2 | 
3 | Published on: 2024-10-17
4 | 
5 | Today, a community of operators launches the first public Walrus Testnet.
6 | This is an important milestone in validating the operation of Walrus as a decentralized blob store,
7 | by operating it on a set of independent storage nodes, that change over time through a delegated
8 | proof of stake mechanism. The Testnet also brings functionality updates relating to governance,
9 | epochs, and blob deletion.
10 | 
11 | ## Blob deletion
12 | 
13 | The most important user-facing new feature is optional blob deletion. The uploader of a blob can
14 | optionally indicate a blob is "deletable". This information is stored in the Sui blob metadata
15 | object, and is also included in the event denoting when the blob is certified. Subsequently, the
16 | owner of the Sui blob metadata object can "delete" it. As a result storage for the remaining
17 | period is reclaimed and can be used by subsequent blob storage operations.
18 | 
19 | Blob deletion allows more fine-grained storage cost management: smart contracts that wrap blob
20 | metadata objects can define logic that stores blobs and delete them to minimize costs, and reclaim
21 | storage space before Walrus epochs end.
22 | 
23 | However, blob deletion is not an effective privacy mechanism in itself: copies of the blob may exist
24 | outside Walrus storage nodes on caches and end-user stores or devices. Furthermore, if the identical
25 | blob is stored by multiple Walrus users, the blob will still be available on Walrus until no copy
26 | exists. Thus deleting your own copy of a blob cannot guarantee that it is deleted from Walrus as a
27 | whole.
28 | 
29 | - Find out how to
30 |   [upload and delete deletable blobs](../usage/client-cli.md#reclaiming-space-via-deletable-blobs)
31 |   through the CLI.
32 | - Find out more about how [delete operations work](../dev-guide/dev-operations.md#delete).
33 | 
34 | ## Epochs
35 | 
36 | Walrus Testnet enables multiple epochs. Initially, the epoch duration is set to a single day to
37 | ensure the logic of epoch change is thoroughly tested. At Mainnet, epochs will likely be multiple
38 | weeks long.
39 | 
40 | The progress of epochs makes the expiry epoch of blobs meaningful, and blobs will become unavailable
41 | after their expiry epoch. The store command may be used to extend the expiry epoch of a blob that is
42 | still available. This operation is efficient and only affects payments and metadata, and does not
43 | re-upload blob contents.
44 | 
45 | - Find out the [current epoch](../usage/client-cli.md#walrus-system-information) through the CLI.
46 | - Find out how to store a blob for
47 |   [multiple epochs](../usage/client-cli.md#storing-querying-status-and-reading-blobs).
48 | 
49 | ## The WAL token and the Testnet WAL faucet
50 | 
51 | Payments for blob storage and extending blob expiry are denominated in Testnet WAL, a
52 | Walrus token issued on the Sui Testnet. Testnet WAL has no value, and an unlimited supply; so no
53 | need to covet or hoard it, it's just for testing purposes and only issued on Sui Testnet.
54 | 
55 | WAL also has a smaller unit called FROST, similar to MIST for SUI. 1 WAL is equal to 1 billion
56 | (1000000000) FROST.
57 | 
58 | To make Testnet WAL available to all who want to experiment with the Walrus Testnet we provide a
59 | utility and smart contract to convert Testnet SUI (which also has no value) into Testnet WAL using
60 | a one-to-one exchange rate. This is chosen arbitrarily, and generally one should not read too much
61 | into the actual WAL denominated costs of storage on Testnet. They have been chosen arbitrarily.
62 | 
63 | Find out how to [request Testnet WAL tokens](../usage/setup.md#testnet-wal-faucet) through the CLI.
64 | 
65 | ## Decentralization through staking & unstaking
66 | 
67 | The WAL token may also be used to stake with storage operators. Staked WAL can be unstaked and
68 | re-staked with other operators or used to purchase storage.
69 | 
70 | Each epoch storage nodes are selected and allocated storage shards according to their delegated
71 | stake. At the end of each epoch payments for storing blobs for the epoch are distributed to storage
72 | nodes and those that delegate stake to them. Furthermore, important network parameters (such as
73 | total available storage and storage price) are set by the selected storage operators each epoch
74 | according to their stake weight.
75 | 
76 | A staking web dApp is provided to experiment with this functionality. Community members have also
77 | created explorers that can be used to view storage nodes when considering who to stake with. Staking
78 | ensures that the ultimate governance of Walrus, directly in terms of storage nodes, and indirectly
79 | in terms of parameters and software they chose, rests with WAL Token holders.
80 | 
81 | Under the hood and over the next months we will be testing many aspects of epoch changes and
82 | storage node committee changes: better shard allocation mechanisms upon changes or storage node
83 | stake; efficient ways to sync state between storage nodes; as well as better ways for storage nodes
84 | to follow Sui event streams.
85 | 
86 | - Explore the [Walrus staking dApp](https://stake.walrus.site).
87 | - Look at recent activity on the [Walrus Explorer](https://walruscan.com/testnet/home).
88 | 
89 | ## New Move contracts & documentation
90 | 
91 | As part of the Testnet release of Walrus, the documentation and Move Smart contracts have been
92 | updated, and can be found in the [`walrus-docs`
93 | repository](https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs).
94 | 
95 | ## New Walrus Sites features
96 | 
97 | With the move to Walrus Testnet, Walrus Sites have also been updated! The new features in this
98 | update greatly increase the flexibility, speed, and security of Walrus Sites. Developers can now
99 | specify client-side routing rules, and add custom HTTP headers to the portals' responses for their
100 | site, expanding the possibilities for what Walrus Sites can do.
101 | 
102 | Migrate now to take advantage of these new features! The old Walrus Sites, based on Walrus Devnet,
103 | will still be available for a short time. However, Devnet will be wiped soon (as described below),
104 | so it is recommended to migrate as soon as possible.
105 | 
106 | ## Discontinuation of Walrus Devnet
107 | 
108 | The previous Walrus Devnet instance is now deprecated and **will be shut down after 2024-10-31**.
109 | All data stored on Walrus Devnet (including Walrus Sites) will no longer be accessible at that
110 | point. You need to re-upload all data to Walrus Testnet if you want it to remain accessible. Walrus
111 | Sites also need to be migrated.
```

walrus-docs/docs/blog/05_testnet_redeployment.md
```
1 | # Announcing Testnet v2
2 | 
3 | Published on: 2025-01-16
4 | 
5 | We are today redeploying the Walrus Testnet to incorporate various improvements, including some
6 | backwards-incompatible changes. Make sure to get the latest binary and configuration as described
7 | in the [setup section](../usage/setup.md).
8 | 
9 | Note that all blob data on the previous Testnet instance has been wiped. All blobs need to be
10 | re-uploaded to the new Testnet instance, including Walrus Sites. In addition, there is a new version
11 | of the WAL token, so your previous WAL tokens will not work anymore. To use the Testnet v2, you
12 | need to obtain new WAL tokens.
13 | 
14 | In the following sections, we describe the notable changes and the actions required for existing
15 | Walrus Sites.
16 | 
17 | ## Epoch duration
18 | 
19 | The epoch duration has been increased from one day to two days to emphasize that this duration is
20 | different from Sui epochs (at Mainnet, epochs will likely be multiple weeks long). In addition, the
21 | maximum number of epochs a blob can be stored for has been reduced from 200 to 183 (corresponding
22 | to one year).
23 | 
24 | The `walrus store` command now also supports the `--epochs max` flag, which will store
25 | the blob for the maximum number of epochs. Note that the `--epochs` flag is now mandatory.
26 | 
27 | ## New features
28 | 
29 | Besides many improvements to the contracts and the storage-node service, the latest Walrus release
30 | also brings several user-facing improvements.
31 | 
32 | - The `walrus store` command now supports storing multiple files at once. This is faster and more
33 |   cost-effective compared to storing each file separately as transactions can be batched through
34 |   [PTBs](https://docs.sui.io/concepts/transactions/prog-txn-blocks). Notably, this is compatible
35 |   with glob patterns offered by many shells, so you can for example run a command like `walrus store
36 |   *.png --epochs 100` to store all PNG files in the current directory.
37 | - The `walrus` CLI now supports creating, funding, and extending *shared blobs* using the `walrus
38 |   share`, `walrus store --share`, and `walrus fund-shared-blob` commands. Shared blobs are an
39 |   example of collectively managed and funded blobs. See the [shared blobs
40 |   section](../usage/client-cli.md#shared-blobs) for more details.
41 | 
42 | ## New WAL token
43 | 
44 | Along with the redeployment of Walrus, we have also deployed a fresh WAL contract. This
45 | means that you cannot use any WAL token from the previous Testnet instance with the new Testnet
46 | instance. You need to request new WAL tokens through the [Testnet WAL
47 | faucet](../usage/setup.md#testnet-wal-faucet).
48 | 
49 | ## Backwards-incompatible changes
50 | 
51 | One reason for a full redeployment is to allow us to make some changes that are
52 | backwards-incompatible. Many of those are related to the contracts and thus less visible to users.
53 | There are, however, some changes that may affect you.
54 | 
55 | ### Configuration files
56 | 
57 | The format of the configuration files for storage nodes and clients has been changed. Make sure to
58 | use the latest version of the configuration files, see the [configuration
59 | section](../usage/setup.md#configuration).
60 | 
61 | ### CLI options
62 | 
63 | Several CLI options of the `walrus` CLI have been changed. Notably, all "short" variants of options
64 | (e.g., `-e` instead of `--epochs`) have been removed to prevent future confusion with new options.
65 | Additionally, the `--epochs` flag is now mandatory for the `walrus store` command (this also affects
66 | the [JSON API](../usage/json-api.md)).
67 | 
68 | Please refer to the CLI help (`walrus --help`, or `walrus <command> --help`) for further details.
69 | 
70 | ### HTTP APIs
71 | 
72 | The paths, request, and response formats of the HTTP APIs have changed for the storage nodes, and
73 | also the aggregator and publisher. Please refer to the section on the [HTTP
74 | API](../usage/web-api.md) for further details.
75 | 
76 | ## Effects on and actions required for existing Walrus Sites
77 | 
78 | The Walrus Sites contracts have not changed, which means that all corresponding objects on Sui are
79 | still valid. However, the resources now point to blob IDs that do not yet exist on the new Testnet.
80 | The easiest way to fix existing sites is to simply update them with the `--force` flag:
81 | 
82 | ```sh
83 | site-builder update --epochs <number of epochs> --force <path to site> <existing site object>
84 | ```
85 | 
86 | ## New Move contracts & documentation
87 | 
88 | As part of the new Testnet release of Walrus, the Move smart contracts have been updated; the
89 | deployed version can be found in the [`walrus-docs`
90 | repository](https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/tree/main/contracts).
```

walrus-docs/docs/design/architecture.md
```
1 | # Basic architecture and security assumptions
2 | 
3 | The key actors in the Walrus architecture are the following:
4 | 
5 | - **Users** through **clients** want to store and read **blobs** identified by their **blob ID**.
6 | 
7 |   These actors are ready to pay for service
8 |   when it comes to writes and non-best-effort reads. Users also want to prove
9 |   the **availability** of a blob to third parties without the cost of sending or receiving the full
10 |   blob.
11 | 
12 |   Users might be malicious in various ways: they might not want to pay for services, prove the
13 |   availability of unavailable blobs, modify/delete blobs without authorization, try to
14 |   exhaust resources of storage nodes, and so on.
15 | 
16 | - **Storage nodes** hold one or many **shards** within a **storage epoch**.
17 | 
18 |   Each blob is erasure-encoded into many **slivers**. Slivers from each stored blob become part
19 |   of all shards. A shard at any storage epoch is associated with a storage node that actually stores
20 |   all slivers of the shard and is ready to serve them.
21 | 
22 |   A Sui smart contract controls the assignment of shards to storage nodes within
23 |   **storage epochs**, and Walrus assumes that more than 2/3 of the
24 |   shards are managed by correct storage nodes within each storage epoch. This means that Walrus must
25 |   tolerate up to 1/3 of the shards managed by Byzantine storage nodes (approximately 1/3 of the
26 |   storage nodes being Byzantine) within each storage epoch and across storage epochs.
27 | 
28 | - All clients and storage nodes operate a blockchain client (specifically on Sui), and mediate
29 |   payments, resources (space), mapping of shards to storage nodes, and metadata through blockchain
30 |   smart contracts. Users interact with the blockchain to acquire storage resources and upload
31 |   certificates for stored blobs. Storage nodes listen to the blockchain events to coordinate
32 |   their operations.
33 | 
34 | Walrus supports any additional number of optional infrastructure actors that can operate in a
35 | permissionless way:
36 | 
37 | - **Aggregators** are clients that reconstruct blobs from slivers and make them available to users
38 |   over traditional web2 technologies (such as HTTP). They are optional in that end users may
39 |   reconstruct blobs directly or run a local aggregator to perform Walrus reads over web2
40 |   technologies locally.
41 | 
42 | - **Caches** are aggregators with additional caching functionality to decrease latency and reduce
43 |   load on storage nodes. Such cache infrastructures may also act as CDNs, split the cost of blob
44 |   reconstruction over many requests, be better connected, and so on. A client can always verify that
45 |   reads from such infrastructures are correct.
46 | 
47 | - **Publishers** are clients that help end users store a blob using web2 technologies,
48 |   using less bandwidth and custom logic.
49 | 
50 |   In effect, they receive the blob to be published over traditional web2 protocols (like HTTP) and
51 |   run the Walrus store protocol on the end user's behalf. This includes encoding the blob into
52 |   slivers, distributing the slivers to storage nodes, collecting storage-node signatures and
53 |   aggregating them into a certificate, as well as all other on-chain actions.
54 | 
55 |   They are optional in that a user can directly interact with Sui and
56 |   the storage nodes to store blobs. An end user can always verify that a publisher
57 |   performed their duties correctly by checking that an event associated with the
58 |   **[point of availability](./properties.md)** for the blob exists on chain
59 |   and then either performing a read to see if Walrus returns the blob or encoding the blob
60 |   and comparing the result to the blob ID in the certificate.
61 | 
62 | Aggregators, publishers, and end users are not considered trusted components of the system, and they
63 | might deviate from the protocol arbitrarily. However, some of the security properties of Walrus only
64 | hold for honest end users that use honest intermediaries (caches and publishers). Walrus provides a
65 | means for end users to audit the correct operation of both caches and publishers.
```

walrus-docs/docs/design/encoding.md
```
1 | # Encoding, overheads, and verification
2 | 
3 | The following list summarizes the basic encoding and cryptographic techniques used in Walrus:
4 | 
5 | - An [erasure code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erasure_code) encode algorithm takes a blob,
6 |   splits it into a number \(k\) of symbols, and encodes it into \(n>k\) symbols in such a way that a
7 |   subset of these \(n\) symbols can be used to reconstruct the blob.
8 | 
9 | - Walrus uses a highly efficient erasure code and selects \(k\) such that a third of symbols can be
10 |   used to reconstruct the blob by the decode algorithm.
11 | 
12 | - The encoding is *systematic*, meaning that some storage nodes hold part of the original blob,
13 |   allowing for fast random-access reads.
14 | 
15 | - All encoding and decoding operations are deterministic, and encoders have no discretion about it.
16 | 
17 | - For each blob, multiple symbols are combined into a **sliver**, which is then assigned to a shard.
18 | 
19 | - Storage nodes manage one or more shards, and corresponding slivers of each blob are distributed
20 |   to all the storage shards.
21 | 
22 | The detailed encoding setup results in an expansion of the blob size by a factor of \(4.5 \sim 5\).
23 | This is independent of the number of shards and the number of storage nodes.
24 | 
25 | ---
26 | 
27 | Each blob is also associated with some metadata including a **blob ID** to allow verification:
28 | 
29 | - The blob ID is computed as an authenticator of the set of all shard data and metadata (byte size,
30 |   encoding, blob hash).
31 | 
32 |   Walrus hashes a sliver representation in each of the shards and adds the resulting hashes into a
33 |   Merkle tree. Then the root of the Merkle tree is the blob hash used to derive the blob ID that
34 |   identifies the blob in the system.
35 | 
36 | - Each storage node can use the blob ID to check if some shard data belongs to a blob using the
37 |   authenticated structure corresponding to the blob hash (Merkle tree). A successful check means
38 |   that the data is indeed as intended by the writer of the blob.
39 | 
40 | - As the writer of a blob might have incorrectly encoded a blob (by mistake or on purpose), any
41 |   party that reconstructs a blob ID from shard slivers must check that it encodes to the correct
42 |   blob ID. The same is necessary when accepting any blob claiming to be a specific blob ID.
43 | 
44 |   This process involves re-encoding the blob using the erasure code, and deriving the blob ID again
45 |   to check that the blob matches. This prevents a malformed blob (incorrectly erasure coded) from
46 |   ever being read as a valid blob at any correct recipient.
47 | 
48 | - A set of slivers equal to the reconstruction threshold belonging to a blob ID that are either
49 |   inconsistent or lead to the reconstruction of a different ID represent an incorrect encoding. This
50 |   happens only if the user that encoded the blob was faulty or malicious and encoded it incorrectly.
51 | 
52 |   Walrus can extract one symbol per sliver to form an inconsistency proof. Storage nodes can delete
53 |   slivers belonging to inconsistently encoded blobs, and upon request return either the
54 |   inconsistency proof or an inconsistency certificate posted on chain.
```

walrus-docs/docs/design/future.md
```
1 | # Future discussion
2 | 
3 | In this document, we left out details of the following features:
4 | 
5 | - **Shard transfer and recovery upon storage epoch change:** The encoding scheme used in Walrus has
6 |   been designed to allow for highly efficient recovery in case of shard failures. A storage node
7 |   attempting to recover slivers only needs to get data of the same magnitude as the missing data to
8 |   reconstruct them.
9 | - **Details of light clients that can be used to sample availability:** Individual clients may
10 |   sample the certified blobs from Sui metadata and sample the availability of some slivers that
11 |   they store. On-chain bounties may be used to retrieve these slivers for missing blobs.
```

walrus-docs/docs/design/objectives_use_cases.md
```
1 | # Objectives and use cases
2 | 
3 | Walrus supports operations to store and read blobs, and to prove and verify their availability.
4 | It ensures content survives storage nodes suffering Byzantine faults and remains available and
5 | retrievable. It provides APIs to access the stored content over a CLI, SDKs and over web2 HTTP
6 | technologies, and supports content delivery infrastructures like caches and content distribution
7 | networks (CDNs).
8 | 
9 | Under the hood, storage cost is a small fixed multiple of the size of blobs (around 5x). Advanced
10 | erasure coding keeps the cost low, in contrast to the full replication of data traditional to
11 | blockchains, such as the >100x multiple for data stored in Sui objects. As a result, storage of much
12 | bigger resources (up to several GiB) is possible on Walrus at substantially lower cost than on Sui
13 | or other blockchains. Because encoded blobs are stored on all storage nodes, Walrus also provides
14 | superior robustness than designs with a small amount of replicas storing the full blob.
15 | 
16 | Walrus uses the Sui chain for coordination and payments. Available storage is represented as Sui
17 | objects that can be acquired, owned, split, merged, and transferred. Storage space can be tied to
18 | a stored blob for a period of time, with the resulting Sui object used to prove
19 | availability on chain in smart contracts, or off chain using light clients.
20 | 
21 | The [next chapter](./overview.md) discusses the above operations relating to storage,
22 | retrieval, and availability in detail.
23 | 
24 | In the future, we plan to include in Walrus some minimal governance to allow storage nodes to
25 | change between storage epochs. Walrus is also compatible with periodic payments for continued
26 | storage. We also plan to implement storage attestation based on challenges to get confidence
27 | that blobs are stored or at least available. Walrus also allows light nodes that store small parts
28 | of blobs to get rewards for proving availability and assisting recovery. We will cover these
29 | topics in later documents. We also provide details of the encoding scheme in a separate document.
30 | 
31 | ## Non-objectives
32 | 
33 | There are a few things that Walrus explicitly is not:
34 | 
35 | - Walrus does not reimplement a CDN that might be geo-replicated or have less than tens of
36 |   milliseconds of latency. Instead, it ensures that traditional CDNs are usable and compatible with
37 |   Walrus caches.
38 | 
39 | - Walrus does not re-implement a full smart contracts platform with consensus or execution. It
40 |   relies on Sui smart contracts when necessary, to manage Walrus resources and processes including
41 |   payments, storage epochs, and so on.
42 | 
43 | - Walrus supports storage of any blob, including encrypted blobs. However, Walrus itself is not the
44 |   distributed key management infrastructure that manages and distributed encryption or decryption
45 |   keys to support a full private storage eco-system. It can, however, provide the storage layer for
46 |   such infrastructures.
47 | 
48 | ## Use cases
49 | 
50 | App builders may use Walrus in conjunction with any L1 or L2 blockchains to build experiences that
51 | require large amounts of data to be stored in a decentralized manner and possibly certified as
52 | available:
53 | 
54 | - **Storage of media for NFT or dApps:** Walrus can directly store and serve media such as images,
55 |   sounds, sprites, videos, other game assets, and so on. This is publicly available media that is
56 |   accessed using HTTP requests at caches to create multimedia dApps.
57 | 
58 | - **AI related use cases:** Walrus can store clean data sets of training data, datasets with a
59 |   known and verified provenance, models, weights and proofs of correct training for AI models.
60 |   It can also store and ensure the availability of an AI model output.
61 | 
62 | - **Storage of long term archival of blockchain history:** Walrus can act as a lower-cost
63 |   decentralized store to store blockchain history. For Sui, this can include sequences of
64 |   checkpoints with all associated transaction and effects content, as well as historic snapshots
65 |   of the blockchain state, code, or binaries.
66 | 
67 | - **Support availability for L2s:** Walrus allows parties to certify the availability of blobs, as
68 |   required by L2s that need data to be stored and be attested as available to all. This may also
69 |   include availability of extra audit data such as validity proofs, zero knowledge proofs of
70 |   correct execution or large fraud proofs.
71 | 
72 | - **Support a fully decentralized web experience:** Walrus can host fully decentralized web
73 |   experiences, including all resources (such as js, css, html, media). These can not only
74 |   provide content, but also host the UX of dApps to enable applications with fully decentralized
75 |   front end and back ends on chain. Walrus puts the full "web" into web3.
76 | 
77 | - **Support subscription models for media:** Creators can store encrypted media on Walrus and only
78 |   provide access via decryption keys to parties that have paid a subscription fee or have paid for
79 |   content. Walrus provides the storage, encryption and decryption needs to happen off
80 |   the system.
```

walrus-docs/docs/design/operations-off-chain.md
```
1 | # Off-chain operations
2 | 
3 | While Walrus operations happen off Sui, they might interact with the blockchain flows defining the
4 | resource life cycle.
5 | 
6 | ## Write paths
7 | 
8 | ![Write paths of Walrus](../assets/WriteFlow.png)
9 | 
10 | Systems overview of writes, illustrated in the previous image:
11 | 
12 | - A user acquires a storage resource of appropriate size and duration on chain, either by directly
13 |   buying it on the Walrus system object or a secondary market. A user can split, merge, and
14 |   transfer owned storage resources.
15 | 
16 | - When users want to store a blob, they first erasure code it and compute the
17 |   blob ID. Then they can perform the following steps themselves, or use a publisher to perform steps
18 |   on their behalf.
19 | 
20 | - The user goes on chain (Sui) and updates a storage resource to register the blob ID with the
21 |   desired size and lifetime. This emits an event, received by storage nodes. After the
22 |   user receives they then continue the upload.
23 | 
24 | - The user sends the blob metadata to all storage nodes and each of the blob slivers to the storage
25 |   node that currently manages the corresponding shard.
26 | 
27 | - A storage node managing a shard receives a sliver and checks it against the blob ID.
28 |   It also checks that there is a blob resource with the blob ID that is authorized to store
29 |   a blob. If correct, the storage node then signs a statement that it holds the sliver for blob ID
30 |   (and metadata) and returns it to the user.
31 | 
32 | - The user puts together the signatures returned from storage nodes into an availability certificate
33 |   and submits it to the chain. When the certificate is verified on chain, an availability event for
34 |   the blob ID is emitted, and all other storage nodes seek to download any missing shards for the
35 |   blob ID. This event emitted by Sui is the [point of availability (PoA)](./properties.md) for the
36 |   blob ID.
37 | 
38 | - After the PoA, and without user involvement, storage nodes sync and recover any missing metadata
39 |   and slivers.
40 | 
41 | The user waits for 2/3 of shard signatures to return to create the certificate of
42 | availability. The rate of the code is below 1/3, allowing for reconstruction even if only 1/3 of
43 | shards return the sliver for a read. Because at most 1/3 of the storage nodes can fail, this ensures
44 | reconstruction if a reader requests slivers from all storage nodes. The full process can
45 | be mediated by a publisher that receives a blob and drives the process to completion.
46 | 
47 | ## Refresh availability
48 | 
49 | Because no content data is required to refresh the duration of storage, refresh is conducted fully
50 | on chain within the protocol. To request an extension to the availability of a blob, a user provides
51 | an appropriate storage resource. Upon success this emits an event that storage nodes receive to
52 | extend the time for which each sliver is stored.
53 | 
54 | ## Inconsistent resource flow
55 | 
56 | When a correct storage node tries to reconstruct a sliver for a blob past [PoA](./properties.md),
57 | this may fail if the encoding of the blob was incorrect. In this case, the storage node can instead
58 | extract an inconsistency proof for the blob ID. It then uses the proof to create an inconsistency
59 | certificate and upload it on chain.
60 | 
61 | The flow is as follows:
62 | 
63 | - A storage node fails to reconstruct a sliver, and instead computes an inconsistency proof.
64 | 
65 | - The storage node sends the blob ID and inconsistency proof to all storage nodes of the Walrus
66 |   epoch. The storage nodes verify the proof and sign it.
67 | 
68 | - The storage node who found the inconsistency aggregates the signatures into an inconsistency
69 |   certificate and sends it to the Walrus smart contract, which verifies it and emits an inconsistent
70 |   resource event.
71 | 
72 | - Upon receiving an inconsistent resource event, correct storage nodes delete sliver data for the
73 |   blob ID and record in the metadata to return `None` for the blob ID for the
74 |   [availability period](./properties.md). No storage attestation challenges are issued for this
75 |   blob ID.
76 | 
77 | ```admonish tip title="Reading inconsistent blobs"
78 | A blob ID that is inconsistent always resolves to `None` upon reading because
79 | the read process re-encodes the received blob to check that the blob ID is correctly derived from a
80 | consistent encoding. This means that an inconsistency proof reveals only a true fact to storage
81 | nodes (that do not otherwise run decoding), and does not change the output of read in any case.
82 | 
83 | However, partial reads leveraging the systematic nature of the encoding might successfully return
84 | partial reads for inconsistently encoded files. Thus, if consistency and availability of reads is
85 | important, dApps should do full reads rather than partial reads.
86 | ```
87 | 
88 | ## Read paths
89 | 
90 | A user can read stored blobs either directly or through an aggregator/cache. The operations are the
91 | same for direct user access, for aggregators, and caches in case of cache misses. In practice, most
92 | reads happen through caches for blobs that are hot and do not result in requests to storage nodes.
93 | 
94 | - The reader gets the metadata for the blob ID from any storage node, and authenticates it using
95 |   the blob ID.
96 | 
97 | - The reader then sends a request to the storage nodes for the shards corresponding to the blob ID
98 |   and waits for \(f+1\) to respond. Sufficient requests are sent in parallel to ensure low latency
99 |   for reads.
100 | 
101 | - The reader authenticates the slivers returned with the blob ID, reconstructs the blob, and decides
102 |   whether the contents are a valid blob or inconsistent.
103 | 
104 | - Optionally, for a cache, the result is cached and can be served without reconstruction until it is
105 |   evicted from the cache. Requests for the blob to the cache return the blob contents, or a proof
106 |   that the blob is inconsistently encoded.
107 | 
108 | ## Challenge mechanism for storage attestation
109 | 
110 | During an epoch, a correct storage node challenges all shards to provide symbols for blob slivers
111 | past PoA:
112 | 
113 | - The list of available blobs for the epoch is determined by the sequence of Sui events up
114 |   to the past epoch. Inconsistent blobs are not challenged, and a record proving this status
115 |   can be returned instead.
116 | 
117 | - A challenge sequence is determined by providing a seed to the challenged shard. The sequence is
118 |   then computed based both on the seed **and** the content of each challenged blob ID. This creates
119 |   a sequential read dependency.
120 | 
121 | - The response to the challenge provides the sequence of shard contents for the blob IDs in a
122 |   timely manner.
123 | 
124 | - The challenger node uses thresholds to determine whether the challenge was passed, and reports
125 |   the result on chain.
126 | 
127 | - The challenge/response communication is authenticated.
128 | 
129 | Challenges provide some reassurance that the storage node can actually recover shard data in a
130 | probabilistic manner, avoiding storage nodes getting payment without any evidence they might
131 | retrieve shard data. The sequential nature of the challenge and some reasonable timeout also ensures
132 | that the process is timely.
```

walrus-docs/docs/design/operations-sui.md
```
1 | # Operations on Sui
2 | 
3 | Walrus uses Sui smart contracts to coordinate storage operations as resources that have a lifetime,
4 | and payments. Smart contracts also facilitate governance to determine the storage nodes holding each
5 | storage shard. The following content outlines these operations and refers to them as part of the
6 | read/write paths.
7 | 
8 | Metadata is the only blob element ever exposed to Sui or its validators, as the content
9 | of blobs is always stored off chain on Walrus storage nodes and caches. The storage nodes or caches
10 | do not have to overlap with any Sui infrastructure components (such as validators), and the storage
11 | epochs can be of different lengths and not have the same start/end times as Sui epochs.
12 | 
13 | ## Storage resource life cycle on Sui
14 | 
15 | A number of Sui smart contracts hold the metadata of the Walrus system and all its entities.
16 | 
17 | - A **Walrus system object** holds the committee of storage nodes for the current storage epoch. The
18 |   system object also holds the total available space on Walrus and the price per unit of storage (1
19 |   KiB).
20 | 
21 |   These values are determined by 2/3 agreement between the storage nodes for the storage
22 |   epoch. Users can pay to purchase storage space for some time duration. These space resources can
23 |   be split, merged, and transferred. Later, they can be used to place a blob ID into Walrus.
24 | 
25 | - The **storage fund** holds funds for storing blobs over one or multiple storage epochs. When
26 |   purchasing storage space from the system object, users pay into the storage fund separated over
27 |   multiple storage epochs. Payments are made each epoch to storage nodes according to performance
28 |   (details follow).
29 | 
30 | - A user acquires some storage through the contracts or transfer and can assign to it a blob ID,
31 |   signifying they want to store this blob ID into it. This emits a Move **resource event** that
32 |   storage nodes listen for to expect and authorize off-chain storage operations.
33 | 
34 | - Eventually a user holds an off-chain **availability certificate** from storage nodes for a blob
35 |   ID. The user **uploads the certificate on chain** to signal that the blob ID is available for an
36 |   availability period. The certificate is checked against the latest Walrus committee,
37 |   and an **availability event** is emitted for the blob ID if correct. This is the point of
38 |   availability for the blob.
39 | 
40 | - At a later time, a certified blob's storage can be **extended** by adding a storage object to it
41 |   with a longer expiry period. This facility can be used by smart contracts to extend the
42 |   availability of blobs stored in perpetuity as long as funds exist to continue providing storage.
43 | 
44 | - In case a blob ID is not correctly encoded, an **inconsistency proof certificate** can be uploaded
45 |   on chain at a later time. This action emits an **inconsistent blob event**, signaling that the
46 |   blob ID read results always return `None`. This indicates that its slivers can be deleted by
47 |   storage nodes, except for an indicator to return `None`.
48 | 
49 | Users writing to Walrus, need to perform Sui transactions to acquire storage and certify blobs.
50 | Users creating or consuming proofs for attestations of blob availability read the chain
51 | only to prove or verify emission of events. Nodes read
52 | the blockchain to get committee metadata only once per epoch, and then request slivers directly
53 | from storage nodes by blob ID to perform reads on Walrus resources.
54 | 
55 | ## Governance operations on Sui
56 | 
57 | Each Walrus storage epoch is represented by the Walrus system object that contains a storage
58 | committee and various metadata or storage nodes, like the mapping between shards and storage nodes,
59 | available space, and current costs.
60 | 
61 | Users can go to the system object for the period and **buy some storage** amount for one or more
62 | storage epochs. At each storage epoch there is a price for storage, and the payment provided becomes
63 | part of a **storage fund** for all the storage epochs that span the storage bought. There is a
64 | maximum number of storage epochs in the future for which storage can be bought (approximately 2
65 | years). Storage is a resource that can be split, merged, and transferred.
66 | 
67 | At the end of the storage epoch, part of the funds in the **storage fund need to be allocated to
68 | storage nodes**. The idea here is for storage nodes to perform light audits of each other,
69 | and suggest which nodes are to be paid based on the performance of these audits.
```

walrus-docs/docs/design/properties.md
```
1 | # Walrus assurance and security properties
2 | 
3 | The properties below hold true subject to the assumption that for all storage epochs 2/3 of shards
4 | are operated by storage nodes that faithfully and correctly follow the Walrus protocol.
5 | 
6 | As described [before](./encoding.md), each blob is encoded into slivers using an erasure code and a
7 | blob ID is cryptographically derived. For a given blob ID there is a **point of availability (PoA)**
8 | and an **availability period**, observable through an event on the Sui chain.
9 | 
10 | The following properties relate to the PoA:
11 | 
12 | - After the PoA, for a blob ID, any correct user that performs a read within the availability period
13 |   will eventually terminate and get a value \(V\) which is either the blob contents \(F\) or `None`.
14 | - After the PoA, if two correct users perform a read and get \(V\) and \(V'\), respectively, then
15 |   \(V = V'\).
16 | - A correct user with an appropriate storage resource can always perform store for a blob \(F\) with
17 |   a blob ID and advance the protocol until the PoA.
18 | - A read after the PoA for a blob \(F\) stored by a correct user, will result in \(F\).
19 | 
20 | Some assurance properties ensure the correct internal processes of Walrus storage nodes.
21 | For the purposes of defining these, an **inconsistency proof** proves that a blob ID was
22 | stored by a user that incorrectly encoded a blob.
23 | 
24 | - After the PoA and for a blob ID stored by a correct user, a storage node is always able to recover
25 |   the correct slivers for its shards for this blob ID.
26 | - After the PoA, if a correct storage node cannot recover a sliver, it can produce an inconsistency
27 |   proof for the blob ID.
28 | - If a blob ID is stored by a correct user, an inconsistently proof cannot be derived for it.
29 | - A read by a correct user for a blob ID for which an inconsistency proof may exist returns `None`.
30 | 
31 | Note that there is no delete operation and a blob ID past the PoA will be available for the full
32 | availability period.
33 | 
34 | ```admonish tip title="Rule of thumb"
35 | Before the PoA it is the responsibility of a client to ensure the availability of a blob and its
36 | upload to Walrus. After the PoA it is the responsibility of Walrus as a system to maintain the
37 | availability of the blob as part of its operation for the full availability period remaining.
38 | Emission of the event corresponding to the PoA for a blob ID attests its availability.
39 | ```
```
