walrus-docs/docs/dev-guide/components.md
```
1 | # Components
2 | 
3 | From a developer perspective, some Walrus components are objects and smart contracts on
4 | Sui, and some components are Walrus-specific binaries and services. As a rule, Sui is used to
5 | manage blob and storage node metadata, while Walrus-specific services are used to store and
6 | read blob contents, which can be very large.
7 | 
8 | Walrus defines a number of objects and smart contracts on Sui:
9 | 
10 | - A shared *system object* records and manages the current committee of storage nodes.
11 | - *Storage resources* represent empty storage space that may be used to store blobs.
12 | - *Blob resources* represent blobs being registered and certified as stored.
13 | - Changes to these objects emit *Walrus-related events*.
14 | 
15 | The Walrus system object ID can be found in the Walrus `client_config.yaml` file (see
16 | [Configuration](../usage/setup.md#configuration)). You may use any Sui explorer to look at its
17 | content, as well as explore the content of blob objects. There is more information about these in
18 | the [quick reference to the Walrus Sui structures](sui-struct.md).
19 | 
20 | Walrus is also composed of a number of Walrus-specific services and binaries:
21 | 
22 | - A client (binary) can be executed locally and provides a
23 |   [Command Line Interface (CLI)](../usage/client-cli.md), a [JSON API](../usage/json-api.md)
24 |   and an [HTTP API](../usage/web-api.md) to perform Walrus operations.
25 | - Aggregator services allow reading blobs via HTTP requests.
26 | - Publisher services are used to store blobs to Walrus.
27 | - A set of storage nodes store encoded blobs. These nodes form the decentralized
28 |   storage infrastructure of Walrus.
29 | 
30 | Aggregators, publishers, and other services use the client APIs to interact with Walrus. End users
31 | of services using Walrus interact with the store via custom services, aggregators, or publishers
32 | that expose HTTP APIs to avoid the need to run locally a binary client.
```

walrus-docs/docs/dev-guide/dev-guide.md
```
1 | # Developer guide
2 | 
3 | This guide introduces all the concepts needed to build applications that use Walrus as a storage
4 | or availability layer. The [overview](../design/overview.md) provides more background and explains
5 | in more detail how Walrus operates internally.
6 | 
7 | This developer guide describes the following:
8 | 
9 | - [Components](components.md) of Walrus of interest to developers that wish to use it for
10 |   storage or availability.
11 | - [Operations](dev-operations.md) supported through client binaries, APIs, or Sui operations.
12 | - [The Sui structures](sui-struct.md) Walrus uses to store metadata, and how they can be read
13 |   from Sui smart contracts, or through the Sui SDK.
14 | 
15 | Refer again to the [glossary](../glossary.md) of terms as a reference.
16 | 
17 | ```admonish danger title="Disclaimer about the Walrus Testnet"
18 | The current Testnet release of Walrus and Walrus Sites is a preview intended to showcase
19 | the technology and solicit feedback from builders, users, and storage-node operators.
20 | All transactions are executed on the Sui Testnet and use Testnet WAL and SUI which have no
21 | value. The state of the store **can and will be wiped** at any point and possibly with no warning.
22 | Do not rely on this Testnet for any production purposes, it comes with no availability or
23 | persistence guarantees.
24 | 
25 | Furthermore, encodings and blob IDs may be incompatible with the future Testnet and Mainnet, and
26 | developers will be responsible for migrating any Testnet applications and data to Mainnet. Detailed
27 | migration guides will be provided when Mainnet becomes available.
28 | 
29 | Also see the [Testnet terms of service](../legal/testnet_tos.md) under which this Testnet is made
30 | available.
31 | ```
```

walrus-docs/docs/dev-guide/dev-operations.md
```
1 | # Operations
2 | 
3 | ## Blob encoding and blob ID
4 | 
5 | Walrus stores blobs across storage nodes in an [encoded form](../design/encoding.md), and refers
6 | to blobs by their *blob ID*. The blob ID is deterministically derived from the content of a blob
7 | and the Walrus configuration. The blob ID of two files with the same content will be the same.
8 | 
9 | You can derive the blob ID of a file locally using the command: `walrus blob-id <file path>`.
10 | 
11 | ## Store
12 | 
13 | Walrus may be used to **store a blob**, via the native client APIs or a publisher.
14 | 
15 | ```admonish danger title="Public access"
16 | **All blobs stored in Walrus are public and discoverable by all.** Therefore you must not use Walrus
17 | to store anything that contains secrets or private data without additional measures to protect
18 | confidentiality.
19 | ```
20 | 
21 | Under the hood a number of operations happen both on Sui as well as on storage nodes:
22 | 
23 | - The client or publisher encodes the blob and derives a *blob ID* that identifies the blob. This
24 |   is a `u256` often encoded as a URL-safe base64 string.
25 | - A transaction is executed on Sui to purchase some storage from the system object, and then to
26 |   *register the blob ID* occupying this storage. Client APIs return the *Sui blob object ID*. The
27 |   transactions use SUI to purchase storage and pay for gas.
28 | - Encoded slivers of the blob are distributed to all storage nodes. They each sign a receipt.
29 | - Signed receipts are aggregated and submitted to the Sui blob object to *certify the blob*.
30 |   Certifying a blob emits a Sui event with the blob ID and the period of availability.
31 | 
32 | A blob is considered available on Walrus once the corresponding Sui blob object has been
33 | certified in the final step. The steps involved in a store operation can be executed by the binary
34 | client, or a publisher that accepts and publishes blobs via HTTP.
35 | 
36 | Walrus currently allows the storage of blobs up to a maximum size that may be determined
37 | through the [`walrus info`](../usage/client-cli.md#walrus-system-information) CLI command. The
38 | maximum blob size is currently 13.3&nbsp;GiB. You may store larger blobs by splitting them into
39 | smaller chunks.
40 | 
41 | Blobs are stored for a certain number of *epochs*, as specified at the time they were stored. Walrus
42 | storage nodes ensure that within these epochs a read succeeds. The current Testnet uses a short
43 | epoch duration of two days for testing purposes, but Mainnet epochs are planned to be multiple
44 | weeks.
45 | 
46 | ## Read
47 | 
48 | Walrus can also be used to **read a blob** after it is stored by providing its blob ID.
49 | A read is executed by performing the following steps:
50 | 
51 | - The system object on Sui is read to determine the Walrus storage node committee.
52 | - A number of storage nodes are queried for blob metadata and the slivers they store.
53 | - The blob is reconstructed from the recovered slivers and checked against the blob ID.
54 | 
55 | The steps involved in the read operation are performed by the binary client, or the aggregator
56 | service that exposes an HTTP interface to read blobs. Reads are extremely resilient and will succeed
57 | in recovering the blob in all cases even if up to one-third of storage nodes are unavailable. In
58 | most cases, after synchronization is complete, blob can be read even if two-thirds of storage nodes
59 | are down.
60 | 
61 | ## Certify Availability
62 | 
63 | Walrus can be used to **certify the availability of a blob** using Sui. Checking that this happened
64 | may currently be done in 3 different ways:
65 | 
66 | - A Sui SDK read can be
67 |   used to authenticate the certified blob event emitted when the blob ID was certified on Sui. The
68 |   client `walrus blob-status` command may be used to identify the event ID that needs to be checked.
69 | - A Sui SDK read may be
70 |   used to authenticate the Sui blob object corresponding to the blob ID, and check it is certified,
71 |   before the expiry epoch, and not deletable.
72 | - A Sui smart contract can read the blob object on Sui (or a reference to it) to check
73 |   it is certified, before the expiry epoch, and not deletable.
74 | 
75 | The underlying protocol of the
76 | [Sui light client](https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/tree/main/crates/sui-light-client)
77 | returns digitally signed evidence for emitted events
78 | or objects, and can be used by off-line or non-interactive applications as a proof of availability
79 | for the blob ID for a certain number of epochs.
80 | 
81 | Once a blob is certified, Walrus will ensure that sufficient slivers will always be
82 | available on storage nodes to recover it within the specified epochs.
83 | 
84 | ## Delete
85 | 
86 | Stored blobs can be optionally set as deletable by the user that creates them. This metadata is
87 | stored in the Sui blob object, and whether a blob is deletable or not is included in certified blob
88 | events. A deletable blob may be deleted by the owner of the blob object, to reclaim and re-use
89 | the storage resource associated with it.
90 | 
91 | If no other copies of the blob exist in Walrus, deleting a blob will eventually make it
92 | unrecoverable using read commands. However, if other copies of the blob exist on Walrus, a delete
93 | command will reclaim storage space for the user that invoked it, but will not make the blob
94 | unavailable until all other copies have been deleted or expire.
```

walrus-docs/docs/dev-guide/sui-struct.md
```
1 | # Sui Structures
2 | 
3 | This section is optional and enables advanced use cases.
4 | 
5 | You can interact with Walrus purely through the client CLI, and JSON or HTTP APIs provided, without
6 | querying or executing transactions on Sui directly. However, Walrus uses Sui to manage its metadata
7 | and smart contract developers can read information about the Walrus system, as well as stored blobs,
8 | on Sui.
9 | 
10 | The Move code of the Walrus Testnet contracts is available at
11 | <https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/blob/main/contracts>. An example package using
12 | the Walrus contracts is available at
13 | <https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/blob/main/examples/move>.
14 | 
15 | The following sections provide further insights into the contract and an overview of how you may use
16 | Walrus objects in your own Sui smart contracts.
17 | 
18 | ```admonish danger title="A word of caution"
19 | Walrus Mainnet will use new Move packages with `struct` layouts and function signatures that may not
20 | be compatible with this package. Move code that builds against this package will need to be rewritten.
21 | ```
22 | 
23 | ## Blob and storage objects
24 | 
25 | Walrus blobs are represented as Sui objects of type `Blob`. A blob is first registered, indicating
26 | that the storage nodes should expect slivers from a Blob ID to be stored. Then a blob is certified,
27 | indicating that a sufficient number of slivers have been stored to guarantee the blob's
28 | availability. When a blob is certified, its `certified_epoch` field contains the epoch in which it
29 | was certified.
30 | 
31 | A `Blob` object is always associated with a `Storage` object, reserving enough space for
32 | a long enough period for the blob's storage. A certified blob is available for the period the
33 | underlying storage resource guarantees storage.
34 | 
35 | Concretely, `Blob` and `Storage` objects have the following fields, which can be read through the
36 | Sui SDKs:
37 | 
38 | ```move
39 | 
40 | /// The blob structure represents a blob that has been registered to with some storage,
41 | /// and then may eventually be certified as being available in the system.
42 | public struct Blob has key, store {
43 |     id: UID,
44 |     registered_epoch: u32,
45 |     blob_id: u256,
46 |     size: u64,
47 |     encoding_type: u8,
48 |     // Stores the epoch first certified.
49 |     certified_epoch: option::Option<u32>,
50 |     storage: Storage,
51 |     // Marks if this blob can be deleted.
52 |     deletable: bool,
53 | }
54 | 
55 | /// Reservation for storage for a given period, which is inclusive start, exclusive end.
56 | public struct Storage has key, store {
57 |     id: UID,
58 |     start_epoch: u32,
59 |     end_epoch: u32,
60 |     storage_size: u64,
61 | }
62 | ```
63 | 
64 | All fields of `Blob` and `Storage` objects can be read using the expected functions:
65 | 
66 | ```move
67 | // Blob functions
68 | public fun blob_id(b: &Blob): u256;
69 | public fun size(b: &Blob): u64;
70 | public fun erasure_code_type(b: &Blob): u8;
71 | public fun registered_epoch(self: &Blob): u32;
72 | public fun certified_epoch(b: &Blob): &Option<u32>;
73 | public fun storage(b: &Blob): &Storage;
74 | ...
75 | 
76 | // Storage functions
77 | public fun start_epoch(self: &Storage): u32;
78 | public fun end_epoch(self: &Storage): u32;
79 | public fun storage_size(self: &Storage): u64;
80 | ...
81 | ```
82 | 
83 | ## Events
84 | 
85 | When a blob is first registered, a `BlobRegistered` event is emitted that informs storage nodes
86 | that they should expect slivers associated with its Blob ID. Eventually when the blob is
87 | certified, a `BlobCertified` is emitted containing information about the blob ID and the epoch
88 | after which the blob will be deleted. Before that epoch the blob is guaranteed to be available.
89 | 
90 | ```move
91 | /// Signals that a blob with metadata has been registered.
92 | public struct BlobRegistered has copy, drop {
93 |     epoch: u32,
94 |     blob_id: u256,
95 |     size: u64,
96 |     encoding_type: u8,
97 |     end_epoch: u32,
98 |     deletable: bool,
99 |     // The object id of the related `Blob` object
100 |     object_id: ID,
101 | }
102 | 
103 | /// Signals that a blob is certified.
104 | public struct BlobCertified has copy, drop {
105 |     epoch: u32,
106 |     blob_id: u256,
107 |     end_epoch: u32,
108 |     deletable: bool,
109 |     // The object id of the related `Blob` object
110 |     object_id: ID,
111 |     // Marks if this is an extension for explorers, etc.
112 |     is_extension: bool,
113 | }
114 | ```
115 | 
116 | The `BlobCertified` event with `deletable` set to false and an `end_epoch` in the future indicates
117 | that the blob will be available until this epoch. A light client proof that this event was emitted
118 | for a blob ID constitutes a proof of availability for the data with this blob ID.
119 | 
120 | When a deletable blob is deleted, a `BlobDeleted` event is emitted:
121 | 
122 | ```move
123 | /// Signals that a blob has been deleted.
124 | public struct BlobDeleted has copy, drop {
125 |     epoch: u32,
126 |     blob_id: u256,
127 |     end_epoch: u32,
128 |     // The object ID of the related `Blob` object.
129 |     object_id: ID,
130 |     // If the blob object was previously certified.
131 |     was_certified: bool,
132 | }
133 | ```
134 | 
135 | The `InvalidBlobID` event is emitted when storage nodes detect an incorrectly encoded blob.
136 | Anyone attempting a read on such a blob is guaranteed to also detect it as invalid.
137 | 
138 | ```move
139 | /// Signals that a BlobID is invalid.
140 | public struct InvalidBlobID has copy, drop {
141 |     epoch: u32, // The epoch in which the blob ID is first registered as invalid
142 |     blob_id: u256,
143 | }
144 | ```
145 | 
146 | System level events such as `EpochChangeStart` and `EpochChangeDone` indicate transitions
147 | between epochs. And associated events such as `ShardsReceived`, `EpochParametersSelected`,
148 | and `ShardRecoveryStart` indicate storage node level events related to epoch transitions,
149 | shard migrations and epoch parameters.
150 | 
151 | ## System and staking information
152 | 
153 | The Walrus system object contains metadata about the available and used storage, as well as the
154 | price of storage per KiB of storage in FROST. The committee
155 | structure within the system object can be used to read the current epoch number, as well as
156 | information about the committee.
157 | 
158 | ```move
159 | public struct SystemStateInnerV1 has key, store {
160 |     id: UID,
161 |     /// The current committee, with the current epoch.
162 |     committee: BlsCommittee,
163 |     // Some accounting
164 |     total_capacity_size: u64,
165 |     used_capacity_size: u64,
166 |     /// The price per unit size of storage.
167 |     storage_price_per_unit_size: u64,
168 |     /// The write price per unit size.
169 |     write_price_per_unit_size: u64,
170 |     /// Accounting ring buffer for future epochs.
171 |     future_accounting: FutureAccountingRingBuffer,
172 |     /// Event blob certification state
173 |     event_blob_certification_state: EventBlobCertificationState,
174 | }
175 | 
176 | /// This represents a BLS signing committee for a given epoch.
177 | public struct BlsCommittee has store, copy, drop {
178 |     /// A vector of committee members
179 |     members: vector<BlsCommitteeMember>,
180 |     /// The total number of shards held by the committee
181 |     n_shards: u16,
182 |     /// The epoch in which the committee is active.
183 |     epoch: u32,
184 | }
185 | 
186 | public struct BlsCommitteeMember has store, copy, drop {
187 |     public_key: Element<G1>,
188 |     weight: u16,
189 |     node_id: ID,
190 | }
191 | 
192 | ```
193 | 
194 | <!-- TODO (#146): say more about staking contracts. -->
```

walrus-docs/docs/usage/client-cli.md
```
1 | # Using the Walrus client
2 | 
3 | The `walrus` binary can be used to interact with Walrus as a client. See the [setup
4 | chapter](./setup.md) for prerequisites, installation, and configuration.
5 | 
6 | Detailed usage information is available through
7 | 
8 | ```sh
9 | walrus --help
10 | ```
11 | 
12 | Each sub-command of `walrus` can also be called with `--help` to print its specific arguments and
13 | their meaning.
14 | 
15 | ## Walrus system information
16 | 
17 | Information about the Walrus system is available through the `walrus info` command. It provides an
18 | overview of current system parameters such as the current epoch, the number of storage nodes and
19 | shards in the system, the maximum blob size, and the current cost in (Testnet) WAL for storing
20 | blobs:
21 | 
22 | ```console
23 | $ walrus info
24 | 
25 | Walrus system information
26 | 
27 | Epochs and storage duration
28 | Current epoch: 6
29 | Epoch duration: 2days
30 | Blobs can be stored for at most 183 epochs in the future.
31 | 
32 | Storage nodes
33 | Number of storage nodes: 58
34 | Number of shards: 1000
35 | 
36 | Blob size
37 | Maximum blob size: 13.3 GiB (14,273,391,930 B)
38 | Storage unit: 1.00 MiB
39 | 
40 | Approximate storage prices per epoch
41 | (Conversion rate: 1 WAL = 1,000,000,000 FROST)
42 | Price per encoded storage unit: 100 FROST
43 | Additional price for each write: 2,000 FROST
44 | Price to store metadata: 6,200 FROST
45 | Marginal price per additional 1 MiB (w/o metadata): 500 FROST
46 | 
47 | Total price for example blob sizes
48 | 16.0 MiB unencoded (135 MiB encoded): 13,500 FROST per epoch
49 | 512 MiB unencoded (2.33 GiB encoded): 0.0002 WAL per epoch
50 | 13.3 GiB unencoded (60.5 GiB encoded): 0.0062 WAL per epoch
51 | ```
52 | 
53 | ```admonish tip title="FROST and WAL"
54 | FROST is the smaller unit of WAL, similar to MIST for SUI. The conversion is also the same as for
55 | SUI: `1 WAL = 1 000 000 000 FROST`.
56 | ```
57 | 
58 | Additional information such as encoding parameters and sizes, BFT system information, and
59 | information on the storage nodes in the current and (if already selected) the next committee,
60 | including their node IDs and stake and shard distribution can be viewed with various subcommands,
61 | see `walrus info --help` for details. Note that the previous `--dev` option has been replaced by the
62 | `all` subcommand.
63 | 
64 | The health of storage nodes can be checked with the `walrus health` command. This command takes
65 | different options to select the nodes to check (see `walrus health --help` for details). For
66 | example, `walrus health --committee` checks the status of all current committee members.
67 | 
68 | ## Storing blobs
69 | 
70 | ```admonish danger title="Public access"
71 | **All blobs stored in Walrus are public and discoverable by all.** Therefore you must not use Walrus
72 | to store anything that contains secrets or private data without additional measures to protect
73 | confidentiality.
74 | ```
75 | 
76 | ```admonish warning
77 | It must be ensured that only a single process uses the Sui wallet for write actions (storing or
78 | deleting). When using multiple instances of the client simultaneously, each of them must be pointed
79 | to a different wallet. Note, it is possible to store multiple blobs with a single `walrus store`
80 | command.
81 | ```
82 | 
83 | ```admonish tip title="Obtaining Testnet WAL"
84 | You can exchange Testnet SUI for Testnet WAL by running `walrus get-wal`. See the [setup
85 | page](./setup.md#testnet-wal-faucet) for further details.
86 | ```
87 | 
88 | Storing one or multiple blobs on Walrus can be achieved through the following command:
89 | 
90 | ```sh
91 | walrus store <FILES> --epochs <EPOCHS>
92 | ```
93 | 
94 | The mandatory CLI argument `--epochs <EPOCHS>` indicates the number of epochs the blob should be
95 | stored for. There is an upper limit on the number of epochs a blob can be stored for, which is 183
96 | for the current Testnet deployment (corresponding to one year). In addition to a positive integer,
97 | you can also use `--epochs max` to store the blob for the maximum number of epochs.
98 | 
99 | You can store a single file or multiple files, separated by spaces. Notably, this is compatible
100 | with glob patterns; for example, `walrus store *.png --epochs <EPOCHS>` will store all PNG files
101 | in the current directory.
102 | 
103 | By default, the command will store the blob as a *permanent* blob. See the [section on deletable
104 | blobs](#reclaiming-space-via-deletable-blobs) for more details on deletable blobs. Also, by default
105 | an owned `Blob` object is created. It is possible to wrap this into a shared object, which can be
106 | funded and extended by anyone, see the [shared blobs section](#shared-blobs).
107 | 
108 | When storing a blob, the client performs a number of automatic optimizations, including the
109 | following:
110 | 
111 | - If the blob is already stored as a *permanent blob* on Walrus for a sufficient number of epochs
112 |   the command does not store it again. This behavior can be overwritten with the `--force`
113 |   CLI option, which stores the blob again and creates a fresh blob object on Sui belonging to the
114 |   wallet address.
115 | - If the user's wallet has a storage resource of suitable size and duration, it is (re-)used instead
116 |   of buying a new one.
117 | - If the blob is already certified on Walrus but as a *deletable* blob or not for a sufficient
118 |   number of epochs, the command skips sending encoded blob data to the storage nodes and just
119 |   collects the availability certificate
120 | 
121 | ## Querying blob status
122 | 
123 | The status of a blob can be queried through one of the following commands:
124 | 
125 | ```sh
126 | walrus blob-status --blob-id <BLOB_ID>
127 | walrus blob-status --file <FILE>
128 | ```
129 | 
130 | This returns whether the blob is stored and its availability period. If you specify a file with the
131 | `--file` option,the CLI re-encodes the content of the file and derives the blob ID before checking
132 | the status.
133 | 
134 | When the blob is available, the `blob-status` command also returns the `BlobCertified` Sui event ID,
135 | which consists of a transaction ID and a sequence number in the events emitted by the transaction.
136 | The existence of this event certifies the availability of the blob.
137 | 
138 | ## Reading blobs
139 | 
140 | Reading blobs from Walrus can be achieved through the following command:
141 | 
142 | ```sh
143 | walrus read <some blob ID>
144 | ```
145 | 
146 | By default the blob data is written to the standard output. The `--out <OUT>` CLI option
147 | can be used to specify an output file name. The `--rpc-url <URL>` may be used to specify
148 | a Sui RPC node to use instead of the one set in the wallet configuration or the default one.
149 | 
150 | ## Reclaiming space via deletable blobs
151 | 
152 | By default `walrus store` uploads a permanent blob available until after its expiry
153 | epoch. Not even the uploader may delete it beforehand. However, optionally, the store command
154 | may be invoked with the `--deletable` flag, to indicate the blob may be deleted before its expiry
155 | by the owner of the Sui blob object representing the blob. Deletable blobs are indicated as such
156 | in the Sui events that certify them, and should not be relied upon for availability by others.
157 | 
158 | A deletable blob may be deleted with the command:
159 | 
160 | ```sh
161 | walrus delete --blob-id <BLOB_ID>
162 | ```
163 | 
164 | Optionally the delete command can be invoked by specifying a `--file <PATH>` option, to derive the
165 | blob ID from a file, or `--object-id <SUI_ID>` to delete the blob in the Sui blob object specified.
166 | 
167 | Before deleting a blob, the `walrus delete` command will ask for confirmation unless the `--yes`
168 | option is specified.
169 | 
170 | The `delete` command reclaims the storage object associated with the deleted blob, which is re-used
171 | to store new blobs. The delete operation provides flexibility around managing storage costs and
172 | re-using storage.
173 | 
174 | The delete operation has limited utility for privacy: It only deletes slivers from the current epoch
175 | storage nodes, and subsequent epoch storage nodes, if no other user has uploaded a copy of the same
176 | blob. If another copy of the same blob exists in Walrus, the delete operation will not make the blob
177 | unavailable for download, and `walrus read` invocations will download it. After the deletion is
178 | finished, the CLI checks the updated status of the blob to see if it is still accessible in Walrus
179 | (unless the `--no-status-check` option is specified). However, even if it isn't, copies of the
180 | public blob may be cached or downloaded by users, and these copies are not deleted.
181 | 
182 | ```admonish danger title="Delete reclaims space only"
183 | **All blobs stored in Walrus are public and discoverable by all.** The `delete` command will
184 | not delete slivers if other copies of the blob are stored on Walrus possibly by other users.
185 | It does not delete blobs from caches, slivers from past storage nodes, or copies
186 | that could have been made by users before the blob was deleted.
187 | ```
188 | 
189 | ## Shared blobs
190 | 
191 | *Shared blobs* are shared Sui objects wrapping "standard" `Blob` objects that can be funded and
192 | whose lifetime can be extended by anyone. See the [shared blobs
[TRUNCATED]
```

walrus-docs/docs/usage/examples.md
```
1 | # Examples
2 | 
3 | As inspiration, we provide several simple examples in different programming languages to interact
4 | with Walrus through the various interfaces. They are located at
5 | <https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/tree/main/examples> and described below.
6 | 
7 | In addition, we have built actual applications on top of Walrus. The prime example is [Walrus
8 | Sites](../walrus-sites/intro.md), with code available in the
9 | <https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-sites> repository.
10 | 
11 | And for an example of how to build a static website and store it as a Walrus Site with GitHub
12 | actions, just look at the [CI
13 | workflow](https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/blob/main/.github/workflows/publish.yaml) we use
14 | to publish this very site. There is also a [Walrus-Sites GitHub
15 | Action](https://github.com/zktx-io/walrus-sites-ga) created by the community you can use to very
16 | easily publish your own Walrus Sites using GitHub Actions (note that this is *not* created or
17 | officially supported by the Walrus team at Mysten Labs).
18 | 
19 | See also our list of existing and upcoming [SDKs and other tools](./sdks.md).
20 | 
21 | ## Python
22 | 
23 | The [Python examples](https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/tree/main/examples/python) folder
24 | contains a number of examples:
25 | 
26 | - How to [use the HTTP
27 |   API](https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/blob/main/examples/python/hello_walrus_webapi.py)
28 |   to store and read a blob.
29 | - How to [use the JSON
30 |   API](https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/blob/main/examples/python/hello_walrus_jsonapi.py)
31 |   to store, read, and check the availability of a blob. Checking the certification of a blob
32 |   illustrates reading the Blob Sui object that certifies (see the [Walrus Sui
33 |   reference](../dev-guide/sui-struct.md)).
34 | - How to [track Walrus related
35 |   Events](https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/blob/main/examples/python/track_walrus_events.py).
36 | 
37 | ## JavaScript
38 | 
39 | A [JavaScript example](https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/tree/main/examples/javascript) is
40 | provided showing how to upload and download a blob through a web form using the HTTP API.
41 | 
42 | ## Move
43 | 
44 | For more complex applications, you may want to interact with Walrus on-chain objects. For that
45 | purpose, the currently deployed Walrus contracts are included [in our GitHub
46 | repository](https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/tree/main/contracts).
47 | 
48 | Furthermore, we provide a simple [example
49 | contract](https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/tree/main/examples/move) that imports and uses
50 | the Walrus objects.
```

walrus-docs/docs/usage/interacting.md
```
1 | # Interacting with Walrus
2 | 
3 | We provide 3 ways to interact directly with the Walrus storage system:
4 | 
5 | - Through the Walrus [client command line interface (CLI)](./client-cli.md).
6 | - Through a [JSON API](./json-api.md) of the Walrus CLI.
7 | - Through an [HTTP API](./web-api.md) exposed by a public or local Walrus client daemon.
8 | 
9 | Furthermore, users can [stake and unstake](./stake.md) through the staking dApp or Sui smart
10 | contracts.
```

walrus-docs/docs/usage/json-api.md
```
1 | # JSON mode
2 | 
3 | All Walrus client commands are also available in JSON mode. In this mode, all the command-line flags
4 | of the original CLI command can be specified in JSON format. The JSON mode therefore simplifies
5 | programmatic access to the CLI.
6 | 
7 | For example, to store a blob, run:
8 | 
9 | ```sh
10 | walrus json \
11 |     '{
12 |         "config": "path/to/client_config.yaml",
13 |         "command": {
14 |             "store": {
15 |                 "files": ["README.md", "LICENSE"],
16 |                 "epochs": 100
17 |             }
18 |         }
19 |     }'
20 | ```
21 | 
22 | Or, to read a blob knowing the blob ID:
23 | 
24 | ```sh
25 | walrus json \
26 |     '{
27 |         "config": "path/to/client_config.yaml",
28 |         "command": {
29 |             "read": {
30 |                 "blobId": "4BKcDC0Ih5RJ8R0tFMz3MZVNZV8b2goT6_JiEEwNHQo"
31 |             }
32 |         }
33 |     }'
34 | ```
35 | 
36 | All options, default values, and commands are equal to those of the "standard" CLI mode, except that
37 | they are written in "camelCase" instead of "kebab-case".
38 | 
39 | The `json` command also accepts input from `stdin`.
40 | 
41 | The output of a `json` command will itself be JSON-formatted, again to simplify parsing the results
42 | in a programmatic way. For example, the JSON output can be piped to the `jq` command for parsing and
43 | manually extracting relevant fields.
```

walrus-docs/docs/usage/sdks.md
```
1 | # Software development kits (SDKs) and other tools
2 | 
3 | The Walrus core team is actively working on a Rust SDK and a TypeScript SDK for Walrus. These will
4 | cover interactions with storage nodes directly and be released around the time of the Mainnet
5 | launch.
6 | 
7 | Besides these upcoming official SDKs, there also exist unofficial third-party SDKs for interacting
8 | with the [HTTP API](./web-api.md#http-api-usage) exposed by Walrus aggregators and publishers:
9 | 
10 | - [Walrus Go SDK](https://github.com/namihq/walrus-go) (maintained by the *Nami Cloud* team)
11 | - [Walrus PHP SDK](https://github.com/suicore/walrus-sdk-php) (maintained by the *Suicore* team)
12 | 
13 | Finally, there is [Tusky](https://docs.tusky.io/about/about-tusky), a complete data storage platform
14 | built on Walrus, including encryption, HTTP APIs, sharing capabilities, and more.
15 | Tusky maintains its own [TypeScript SDK](https://github.com/tusky-io/ts-sdk).
```

walrus-docs/docs/usage/setup.md
```
1 | # Setup
2 | 
3 | At this stage of the project, our Walrus code is not yet public. Instead, we provide a pre-compiled
4 | `walrus` client binary for macOS (Intel and Apple CPUs) and Ubuntu, which supports different usage
5 | patterns (see [the next chapter](./interacting.md)). This chapter describes the
6 | [prerequisites](#prerequisites), [installation](#installation), and [configuration](#configuration)
7 | of the Walrus client.
8 | 
9 | ## Prerequisites: Sui wallet and Testnet SUI {#prerequisites}
10 | 
11 | ```admonish tip title="Quick wallet setup"
12 | If you just want to set up a new Sui wallet for Walrus, you can skip this section and use the
13 | `walrus generate-sui-wallet` command after [installing Walrus](#installation). In that case, make
14 | sure to set the `wallet_config` parameter in the [Walrus
15 | configuration](#advanced-configuration-optional) to the newly generated wallet. Also, make sure to
16 | obtain some Testnet SUI tokens from the [Sui Testnet faucet](https://faucet.sui.io/?network=testnet).
17 | ```
18 | 
19 | Interacting with Walrus requires a valid Sui Testnet wallet with some amount of SUI tokens. The
20 | normal way to set this up is via the Sui CLI; see the [installation
21 | instructions](https://docs.sui.io/guides/developer/getting-started/sui-install) in the Sui
22 | documentation.
23 | 
24 | After installing the Sui CLI, you need to set up a Testnet wallet by running `sui client`, which
25 | prompts you to set up a new configuration. Make sure to point it to Sui Testnet, you can use the
26 | full node at `https://fullnode.testnet.sui.io:443` for this. See
27 | [here](https://docs.sui.io/guides/developer/getting-started/connect) for further details.
28 | 
29 | If you already have a Sui wallet configured, you can directly set up the Testnet environment (if you
30 | don't have it yet),
31 | 
32 | ```sh
33 | sui client new-env --alias testnet --rpc https://fullnode.testnet.sui.io:443
34 | ```
35 | 
36 | and switch the active environment to it:
37 | 
38 | ```sh
39 | sui client switch --env testnet
40 | ```
41 | 
42 | After this, you should get something like this (everything besides the `testnet` line is optional):
43 | 
44 | ```terminal
45 | $ sui client envs
46 | ╭──────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┬────────╮
47 | │ alias    │ url                                 │ active │
48 | ├──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┼────────┤
49 | │ devnet   │ https://fullnode.devnet.sui.io:443  │        │
50 | │ localnet │ http://127.0.0.1:9000               │        │
51 | │ testnet  │ https://fullnode.testnet.sui.io:443 │ *      │
52 | │ mainnet  │ https://fullnode.mainnet.sui.io:443 │        │
53 | ╰──────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┴────────╯
54 | ```
55 | 
56 | Finally, make sure you have at least one gas coin with at least 1 SUI. You can obtain one from the
57 | [Sui Testnet faucet](https://faucet.sui.io/?network=testnet) (you can find your address through the
58 | `sui client active-address` command).
59 | 
60 | After some seconds, you should see your new SUI coins:
61 | 
62 | ```terminal
63 | $ sui client gas
64 | ╭─────────────────┬────────────────────┬──────────────────╮
65 | │ gasCoinId       │ mistBalance (MIST) │ suiBalance (SUI) │
66 | ├─────────────────┼────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
67 | │ 0x65dca966dc... │ 1000000000         │ 1.00             │
68 | ╰─────────────────┴────────────────────┴──────────────────╯
69 | ```
70 | 
71 | The system-wide wallet will be used by Walrus if no other path is specified. If you want to use a
72 | different Sui wallet, you can specify this in the [Walrus configuration file](#configuration) or
73 | when [running the CLI](./interacting.md).
74 | 
75 | ## Installation
76 | 
77 | We currently provide the `walrus` client binary for macOS (Intel and Apple CPUs), Ubuntu, and
78 | Windows:
79 | 
80 | | OS      | CPU                   | Architecture                                                                                                                 |
81 | | ------- | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
82 | | Ubuntu  | Intel 64bit           | [`ubuntu-x86_64`](https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/walrus-testnet-latest-ubuntu-x86_64)                 |
83 | | Ubuntu  | Intel 64bit (generic) | [`ubuntu-x86_64-generic`](https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/walrus-testnet-latest-ubuntu-x86_64-generic) |
84 | | MacOS   | Apple Silicon         | [`macos-arm64`](https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/walrus-testnet-latest-macos-arm64)                     |
85 | | MacOS   | Intel 64bit           | [`macos-x86_64`](https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/walrus-testnet-latest-macos-x86_64)                   |
86 | | Windows | Intel 64bit           | [`windows-x86_64.exe`](https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/walrus-testnet-latest-windows-x86_64.exe)       |
87 | 
88 | ```admonish title="Windows"
89 | We now offer a pre-built binary also for Windows. However, most of the remaining instructions assume
90 | a UNIX-based system for the directory structure, commands, etc. If you use Windows, you may need to
91 | adapt most of those.
92 | ```
93 | 
94 | You can download the latest build from our Google Cloud Storage (GCS) bucket (correctly setting the
95 | `$SYSTEM` variable):
96 | 
97 | ```sh
98 | SYSTEM= # set this to your system: ubuntu-x86_64, ubuntu-x86_64-generic, macos-x86_64, macos-arm64, windows-x86_64.exe
99 | curl https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/walrus-testnet-latest-$SYSTEM -o walrus
100 | chmod +x walrus
101 | ```
102 | 
103 | On Ubuntu, you should generally use the `ubuntu-x86_64` version. However, this is incompatible with
104 | old hardware and certain virtualized environments (throwing an "Illegal instruction (core dumped)"
105 | error); in these cases you can use the `ubuntu-x86_64-generic` version.
106 | 
107 | To be able to run it simply as `walrus`, move the binary to any directory included in your `$PATH`
108 | environment variable. Standard locations are `/usr/local/bin/`, `$HOME/bin/`, or
109 | `$HOME/.local/bin/`.
110 | 
111 | ```admonish warn
112 | Previously, this guide recommended placing the binary in `$HOME/.local/bin/`. If you install the
113 | latest binary somewhere else, make sure to clean up old versions. You can find the binary in use by
114 | calling `which walrus` and its version through `walrus -V`.
115 | ```
116 | 
117 | Once this is done, you should be able to simply type `walrus` in your terminal. For example you can
118 | get usage instructions (see [the next chapter](./interacting.md) for further details):
119 | 
120 | ```terminal
121 | $ walrus --help
122 | Walrus client
123 | 
124 | Usage: walrus [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>
125 | 
126 | Commands:
127 | ⋮
128 | ```
129 | 
130 | ```admonish tip
131 | Our latest Testnet Walrus binaries are also available on Walrus itself, namely on
132 | <https://bin.walrus.site>, for example, <https://bin.walrus.site/walrus-testnet-latest-ubuntu-x86_64>.
133 | Note that due to DoS protection, it may not be possible to download the binaries with `curl` or
134 | `wget`.
135 | ```
136 | 
137 | ### Previous versions (optional)
138 | 
139 | In addition to the latest version of the `walrus` binary, the GCS bucket also contains previous
140 | versions. An overview in XML format is available at
141 | <https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/>.
142 | 
143 | ## Configuration
144 | 
145 | The Walrus client needs to know about the Sui objects that store the Walrus system and staking
146 | information, see the [developer guide](../dev-guide/sui-struct.md#system-and-staking-information).
147 | These need to be configured in a file `~/.config/walrus/client_config.yaml`. Additionally, a
148 | `subsidies` object can be specified, which will subsidize storage bought with the client.
149 | Finally, exchange objects are needed to swap SUI for WAL.
150 | 
151 | The current Testnet deployment uses the following objects:
152 | 
153 | ```yaml
154 | system_object: 0x98ebc47370603fe81d9e15491b2f1443d619d1dab720d586e429ed233e1255c1
155 | staking_object: 0x20266a17b4f1a216727f3eef5772f8d486a9e3b5e319af80a5b75809c035561d
156 | exchange_objects:
157 |   - 0x59ab926eb0d94d0d6d6139f11094ea7861914ad2ecffc7411529c60019133997
158 |   - 0x89127f53890840ab6c52fca96b4a5cf853d7de52318d236807ad733f976eef7b
159 |   - 0x9f9b4f113862e8b1a3591d7955fadd7c52ecc07cf24be9e3492ce56eb8087805
160 |   - 0xb60118f86ecb38ec79e74586f1bb184939640911ee1d63a84138d080632ee28a
161 | subsidies_object: 0x4b23c353c35a4dde72fe862399ebe59423933d3c2c0a3f2733b9f74cb3b4933d
162 | ```
163 | 
164 | <!-- markdownlint-disable code-fence-style -->
165 | ~~~admonish tip
166 | The easiest way to obtain the latest configuration is by downloading it from GitHub:
167 | 
168 | ```sh
169 | curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MystenLabs/walrus-docs/refs/heads/main/docs/client_config.yaml \
170 |     -o ~/.config/walrus/client_config.yaml
171 | ```
172 | ~~~
173 | <!-- markdownlint-enable code-fence-style -->
174 | 
175 | ### Custom path (optional) {#config-custom-path}
176 | 
177 | By default, the Walrus client will look for the `client_config.yaml` (or `client_config.yml`)
178 | configuration file in the current directory, `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/walrus/`, `~/.config/walrus/`, or
179 | `~/.walrus/`. However, you can place the file anywhere and name it anything you like; in this case
180 | you need to use the `--config` option when running the `walrus` binary.
181 | 
182 | ### Advanced configuration (optional)
183 | 
184 | The configuration file currently supports the following parameters:
185 | 
186 | ```yaml
187 | # These are the only mandatory fields. These objects are specific for a particular Walrus
188 | # deployment but then do not change over time.
189 | system_object: 0x98ebc47370603fe81d9e15491b2f1443d619d1dab720d586e429ed233e1255c1
190 | staking_object: 0x20266a17b4f1a216727f3eef5772f8d486a9e3b5e319af80a5b75809c035561d
191 | 
192 | # The exchange objects are used to swap SUI for WAL. If multiple ones are defined (as below), a
193 | # random one is chosen for the exchange.
194 | exchange_objects:
195 |   - 0x59ab926eb0d94d0d6d6139f11094ea7861914ad2ecffc7411529c60019133997
196 |   - 0x89127f53890840ab6c52fca96b4a5cf853d7de52318d236807ad733f976eef7b
197 |   - 0x9f9b4f113862e8b1a3591d7955fadd7c52ecc07cf24be9e3492ce56eb8087805
198 |   - 0xb60118f86ecb38ec79e74586f1bb184939640911ee1d63a84138d080632ee28a
199 | 
200 | # The subsidies object allows the client to use the subsidies contract to purchase storage
201 | # which will reduce the cost of obtaining a storage resource and extending blobs and also
202 | # adds subsidies to the rewards of the staking pools.
203 | subsidies_object: 0x4b23c353c35a4dde72fe862399ebe59423933d3c2c0a3f2733b9f74cb3b4933d
204 | 
205 | # You can define a custom path to your Sui wallet configuration here. If this is unset or `null`,
206 | # the wallet is configured from `./sui_config.yaml` (relative to your current working directory), or
207 | # the system-wide wallet at `~/.sui/sui_config/client.yaml` in this order.
208 | wallet_config: null
209 | 
210 | # The following parameters can be used to tune the networking behavior of the client. There is no
[TRUNCATED]
```

walrus-docs/docs/usage/stake.md
```
1 | # Staking
2 | 
3 | In Walrus, anyone can delegate stake to storage nodes and, by doing so, influence, which storage
4 | nodes get selected for the committee in future epochs, and how many shards these nodes will hold.
5 | Shards are assigned to storage nodes every epoch, roughly proportional to the amount of stake
6 | that was delegated to them. By staking with a storage node, users also earn rewards, as they
7 | will receive a share of the storage fees.
8 | 
9 | Since moving shards from one storage node to another requires transferring a lot of data, and
10 | storage nodes potentially need to expand their storage capacity, the selection of the committee
11 | for the next epoch is done ahead of time, in the middle of the previous epoch. This provides
12 | sufficient time to storage-node operators to provision additional resources, if needed.
13 | 
14 | For stake to affect the shard distribution in epoch `e` and become "active", it must be staked
15 | before the committee for this epoch has been selected, meaning that it has to be staked before
16 | the midpoint of epoch `e - 1`. If it is staked after that point in time, it will only influence
17 | the committee selection for epoch `e + 1` and thus only become active, and accrue rewards, in
18 | that epoch.
19 | 
20 | Unstaking has a similar delay: because unstaking funds only has an effect on the committee in
21 | the next committee selection, the stake will remain active until that committee takes over.
22 | This means that, to unstake at the start of epoch `e`, the user needs to "request withdrawal"
23 | before the midpoint of epoch `e - 1`. Otherwise, that is, if the user unstakes after this point,
24 | the stake will remain active, and continue to accrue rewards, throughout epoch `e`, and the
25 | balance and rewards will be available to withdraw at the start of epoch `e + 1`.
26 | 
27 | ## How to stake with the Walrus Staking dApp
28 | 
29 | The Walrus Staking dApp allows users to stake (or unstake) to any of the storage nodes of the
30 | system.
31 | 
32 | To use the dApp, visit <https://stake.walrus.site> and connect your wallet:
33 | 
34 | - Click the `Connect Wallet` button at the top right corner.
35 | - Select the wallet (if the wallet was connected before, this and the next step won't be required).
36 | - Approve the connection.
37 | - (Make sure the selected wallet network is Testnet).
38 | 
39 | ### Exchange Testnet SUI to WAL
40 | 
41 | To be able to stake you will need to have Testnet WAL in your wallet.
42 | You can exchange your Testnet SUI to WAL using the dApp as follows:
43 | 
44 | - Click the `Get WAL` button.
45 | - Select the amount of SUI. This will be exchanged to WAL at a 1:1 rate.
46 | - And click `Exchange`.
47 | - *Follow the instructions in your wallet to approve the transaction.*
48 | 
49 | ### Stake
50 | 
51 | - Find the storage node that you want to stake to.
52 |   - Below the system stats, there is the list of the "Current Committee" of storage nodes.
53 |   - You can select one of the nodes in that list or, if the storage node is not in the current
54 |     committee, you find all the storage nodes at the bottom of the page.
55 | - Once you selected the storage node, click the stake button.
56 | - Select the amount of WAL.
57 | - Click Stake.
58 | - *Follow the instructions in your wallet to approve the transaction.*
59 | 
60 | ### Unstake
61 | 
62 | - Find the `Staked WAL` you want to unstake.
63 |   - Below the "Current Committee" list you will find all your `Staked WAL`.
64 |   - Also you can expand a storage node and find all your stakes with that node.
65 | - Depending on the state of the `Staked WAL` you will be able to unstake or Withdraw your funds.
66 | - Click the `Unstake` or `Withdraw` button.
67 | - Click continue to confirm your action.
68 | - *Follow the instructions in your wallet to approve the transaction.*
```

walrus-docs/docs/usage/troubleshooting.md
```
1 | # Troubleshooting
2 | 
3 | ```admonish tip title="Debug logging"
4 | You can enable debug logging for Walrus by setting the environment variable `RUST_LOG=walrus=debug`.
5 | ```
6 | 
7 | ## Latest binary
8 | 
9 | Before undertaking any other steps, make sure you have the [latest `walrus`
10 | binary](./setup.md#installation). If you have multiple versions in different locations, find the
11 | binary that will actually be used with `which walrus`. For the current Testnet, a binary version of
12 | at 1.9 or later is required.
13 | 
14 | ## Old hardware or incompatible VMs
15 | 
16 | Our standard Ubuntu binary is known to cause problems on certain old hardware and in certain
17 | virtualized environments. If you experience errors like "Illegal instruction (core dumped)",
18 | [install](./setup.md#installation) the `ubuntu-x86_64-generic` version instead, which is compiled
19 | specifically to be compatible with almost all physical and virtual x86-64 CPUs.
20 | 
21 | ## Latest Walrus configuration
22 | 
23 | The Walrus Testnet is wiped periodically and requires updating to the latest binary and
24 | configuration. If you get an error like "could not retrieve enough confirmations to certify the
25 | blob", you are probably using an outdated configuration pointing to an inactive Walrus system. In
26 | this case, update your configuration file with the latest [configuration](./setup.md#configuration)
27 | and make sure the CLI uses the intended configuration.
28 | 
29 | ```admonish tip
30 | The `walrus` client binary prints information about the used configuration when starting execution,
31 | including the path to the Walrus configuration file and the Sui wallet.
32 | ```
33 | 
34 | ## Correct Sui network configuration
35 | 
36 | If you get an error like "the specified Walrus system object does not exist", make sure your wallet
37 | is set up for Sui **Testnet** and you use the latest [configuration](./setup.md#configuration).
```

walrus-docs/docs/usage/web-api.md
```
1 | # Client Daemon mode & HTTP API
2 | 
3 | In addition to the CLI and JSON modes, the Walrus client offers a *daemon mode*. In this mode, it
4 | runs a simple web server offering HTTP interfaces to store and read blobs in an *aggregator* and
5 | *publisher* role respectively. We also offer
6 | [public aggregator and publisher services](#public-services) to try the Walrus HTTP APIs without
7 | the need to run a local client.
8 | 
9 | ## Starting the daemon locally {#local-daemon}
10 | 
11 | You can run a local Walrus daemon through the `walrus` binary. There are three different commands:
12 | 
13 | - `walrus aggregator` starts an "aggregator" that offers an HTTP interface to read blobs from
14 |   Walrus.
15 | - `walrus publisher` starts a "publisher" that offers an HTTP interface to store blobs in Walrus.
16 | - `walrus daemon` offers the combined functionality of an aggregator and publisher on the same
17 |   address and port.
18 | 
19 | The aggregator does not perform any on-chain actions, and only requires specifying the address on
20 | which it listens:
21 | 
22 | ```sh
23 | walrus aggregator --bind-address "127.0.0.1:31415"
24 | ```
25 | 
26 | The publisher and daemon perform on-chain actions and thus require a Sui Testnet wallet with
27 | sufficient SUI and WAL balances. To enable handling many parallel requests without object
28 | conflicts, they create internal sub-wallets since version 1.4.0, which are funded from the main
29 | wallet. These sub-wallets are persisted in a directory specified with the `--sub-wallets-dir`
30 | argument; any existing directory can be used. If it already contains sub-wallets, they will be
31 | reused.
32 | 
33 | By default, 8 sub-wallets are created and funded. This can be changed with the `--n-clients`
34 | argument. For simple local testing, 1 or 2 sub-wallets are usually sufficient.
35 | 
36 | For example, you can run a publisher with a single sub-wallet stored in the Walrus configuration
37 | directory with the following command:
38 | 
39 | ```sh
40 | PUBLISHER_WALLETS_DIR=~/.config/walrus/publisher-wallets
41 | mkdir -p "$PUBLISHER_WALLETS_DIR"
42 | walrus publisher \
43 |   --bind-address "127.0.0.1:31416" \
44 |   --sub-wallets-dir "$PUBLISHER_WALLETS_DIR" \
45 |   --n-clients 1
46 | ```
47 | 
48 | Replace `publisher` by `daemon` to run both an aggregator and publisher on the same address and
49 | port.
50 | 
51 | ```admonish warning
52 | While the aggregator does not perform Sui on-chain actions, and therefore consumes no gas, the
53 | publisher does perform actions on-chain and will consume both SUI and WAL tokens. It is therefore
54 | important to ensure only authorized parties may access it, or other measures to manage gas costs,
55 | especially in a future Mainnet deployment.
56 | ```
57 | 
58 | ### Notes on publisher operation
59 | 
60 | We list here a few important details on how the publisher deals with funds and objects on Sui.
61 | 
62 | #### Number of sub-wallets
63 | 
64 | As mentioned above, the publisher uses sub-wallets to allow storing blobs in parallel. By default,
65 | the publisher uses 8 sub-wallets, meaning it can store 8 blobs at the same time.
66 | 
67 | #### Funds in sub-wallets
68 | 
69 | Each of the sub-wallets requires funds to interact with the chain and purchase storage. For this
70 | reason, a background process checks periodically if the sub-wallets have enough funds. In steady
71 | state, each of the sub-wallets will have a balance of 0.5-1.0 SUI and WAL. The amount and triggers
72 | for coin refills can be configured through CLI arguments.
73 | 
74 | #### Lifecycle of created `Blob` objects
75 | 
76 | Each store operation in Walrus creates a `Blob` object on Sui. This blob object represents the
77 | (partial) ownership over the associated data, and allows certain data management operations (e.g.,
78 | in the case of deletable blobs).
79 | 
80 | When the publisher stores a blob on behalf of a client, the `Blob` object is initially owned by the
81 | sub-wallet that stored the blob. Then, the following cases are possible, depending on the
82 | configuration:
83 | 
84 | - If the client requests to store a blob and specifies the `send_object_to` query parameter (see
85 |   [the relevant section](#store) for examples), then the `Blob` object is transferred to the
86 |   specified address. This is a way for clients to get back the created object for their data.
87 | - If the `send_object_to` query parameter is not specified, two cases are possible:
88 |   - If the publisher was run with the `--keep` flag, then the sub-wallet transfers the
89 |     newly-created blob object to the main wallet, such that all these objects are kept there.
90 |   - If the `--keep` flag was omitted, then the sub-wallet *immediately burns* the `Blob` object.
91 |     Since no one has requested the object, and the availability of the data on Walrus is independent
92 |     of the existence of such object, it is safe to do so. This is to avoid cluttering the sub-wallet
93 |     with many blob objects.
94 | 
95 | ## Using a public aggregator or publisher {#public-services}
96 | 
97 | For some use cases (e.g., a public website), or to just try out the HTTP API, a publicly accessible
98 | aggregator and/or publisher is required. Several entities run such aggregators and publishers, see
99 | the lists of public [aggregators](#public-aggregators) and [publishers](#public-publishers) below.
100 | 
101 | Public publishers limit requests to 10 MiB by default. If you want to upload larger files, you need
102 | to [run your own publisher](#local-daemon) or use the [CLI](./client-cli.md).
103 | 
104 | Also, note that the publisher consumes (Testnet) SUI and WAL on the service side, and a Mainnet
105 | deployment would likely not be able to provide uncontrolled public access to publishing without
106 | requiring some authentication and compensation for the funds used.
107 | 
108 | ### Public aggregators
109 | 
110 | The following is a list of know public aggregators; they are checked periodically, but each of them
111 | may still be temporarily unavailable:
112 | 
113 | - `https://aggregator.walrus-testnet.walrus.space`
114 | - `https://wal-aggregator-testnet.staketab.org`
115 | - `https://walrus-testnet-aggregator.redundex.com`
116 | - `https://walrus-testnet.blockscope.net`
117 | - `https://walrus-testnet-aggregator.nodes.guru`
118 | - `https://walrus-cache-testnet.overclock.run`
119 | - `https://walrus-testnet-aggregator.stakin-nodes.com`
120 | - `https://testnet-aggregator-walrus.kiliglab.io`
121 | - `https://walrus-cache-testnet.latitude-sui.com`
122 | - `https://walrus-testnet-aggregator.nodeinfra.com`
123 | - `https://walrus-testnet-aggregator.stakingdefenseleague.com`
124 | - `https://walrus-aggregator.rubynodes.io`
125 | - `https://walrus-testnet-aggregator.brightlystake.com`
126 | - `https://walrus-testnet-aggregator.nami.cloud`

walrus-docs/docs/operator-guide/aggregator.md
```
1 | # Operating an aggregator
2 | <!-- TODO (#141): Add further details and example cache setup. -->
3 | 
4 | Below is an example of an aggregator node which hosts a HTTP endpoint that can be used
5 | to fetch data from Walrus over the web.
6 | 
7 | The aggregator process is run via the `walrus` client binary in [daemon mode](../usage/web-api.md).
8 | It can be run in many ways, one example being via a systemd service:
9 | 
10 | ```ini
11 | [Unit]
12 | Description=Walrus Aggregator
13 | 
14 | [Service]
15 | User=walrus
16 | Environment=RUST_BACKTRACE=1
17 | Environment=RUST_LOG=info,walrus=debug
18 | ExecStart=/opt/walrus/bin/walrus --config /opt/walrus/config/client_config.yaml aggregator --bind-address 0.0.0.0:9000
19 | Restart=always
20 | 
21 | LimitNOFILE=65536
22 | ```
```

walrus-docs/docs/operator-guide/operator-guide.md
```
1 | # Operator guide
2 | 
3 | This chapter introduces all the concepts needed for operators of the different components that make
4 | up the Walrus system. It is currently a work in progress and will be updated as the platform
5 | matures.
6 | 
7 | Specifically, this guide describes the following:
8 | 
9 | - [Storage node](storage-node.md) contains the most relevant instructions for operators of a Walrus
10 |   storage node.
11 | - [Aggregator](aggregator.md) describes the operation of a Walrus aggregator host.
```

walrus-docs/docs/operator-guide/storage-node.md
```
1 | # Operating a storage node
2 | <!-- TODO (#141): Update and add further details, also on monitoring. -->
3 | 
4 | The binary of the storage node is not yet publicly available. Prior to official network launch the
5 | code will be open-sourced.
6 | 
7 | A basic systemd service running the Storage Node could look like this:
8 | 
9 | ```ini
10 | [Unit]
11 | Description=Walrus Storage Node
12 | 
13 | [Service]
14 | User=walrus
15 | Environment=RUST_BACKTRACE=1
16 | Environment=RUST_LOG=info,walrus=debug
17 | ExecStart=/opt/walrus/bin/walrus-node run --config-path /opt/walrus/config/walrus-node.yaml
18 | Restart=always
19 | 
20 | LimitNOFILE=65536
21 | ```
22 | 
23 | Make sure to adjust any paths and, if desired, the log level.
24 | 
25 | The `walrus-node` binary stores slivers in RocksDB, which means the data will be stored on disk, to
26 | a path configured by the `/opt/walrus/config/walrus-node.yaml` file. The full format with all
27 | mandatory and optional configuration parameters will be made available with the binary.
28 | 
29 | Here are some important config params from a shortened version of the `walrus-node.yaml` config
30 | file:
31 | 
32 | ```yaml
33 | storage_path: /opt/walrus/db
34 | metrics_address: 127.0.0.1:9184
35 | rest_api_address: 0.0.0.0:9185
36 | sui:
37 |   rpc: https://fullnode.testnet.sui.io:443
38 |   system_object: 0xWALRUS_CONTRACT
39 | blob_recovery:
40 |   max_concurrent_blob_syncs: 10
41 |   retry_interval_min_secs: 1
42 |   retry_interval_max_secs: 3600
43 |   metadata_request_timeout_secs: 5
44 |   max_concurrent_metadata_requests: 1
45 |   sliver_request_timeout_secs: 300
46 |   invalidity_sync_timeout_secs: 300
47 | ```
48 | 
49 | For monitoring, you can configure Grafana Agent to fetch metrics from `localhost:9184/metrics`
50 | (or whatever you've configured `metrics_address` to be).
```
