walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/authentication.md
```
1 | # Site data authentication
2 | 
3 | Walrus Sites offer a simple mechanism to authenticate the data that is served from the Walrus
4 | storage on the client side. Thus, Walrus Sites can guarantee (with various degrees of confidence,
5 | depending on the setup) that the site data is authentic and has not been tampered with by a
6 | malicious aggregator.
7 | 
8 | ## Authentication mechanism
9 | 
10 | The Walrus Sites resource object on Sui stores, alongside the resource information, a SHA-256 hash
11 | of the resource's content.
12 | 
13 | When the client requests a resource, the portal will check that the hash of the data received from
14 | the Walrus storage (and the Walrus aggregator in particular) matches the hash stored on Sui.
15 | 
16 | If the hashes do not match, the portal will return the following warning page:
17 | 
18 | ![Hash mismatch warning page](../assets/walrus-sites-hash-mismatch.png)
19 | 
20 | ## Authentication Guarantees
21 | 
22 | Depending on the type of deployment, this technique gives increasing levels of confidence that the
23 | site data is authentic. We list them here in increasing order of assurance.
24 | 
25 | ### Remote server-side portal deployment
26 | 
27 | In this case, the user must fully trust the portal provider to authenticate the data. With a trusted
28 | portal, the authentication mechanism guarantees that the aggregator or cache (from which the blob
29 | has been fetched) did not tamper with the contents of the blob.
30 | 
31 | ### Remote service-worker portal deployment
32 | 
33 | Here, the portal provider is only trusted to provide the correct service worker code to the user.
34 | The user's browser will then perform the fetching and authentication. The guarantees are therefore
35 | the same as with the remote server-side portal, with the addition that the user can inspect the code
36 | returned by the portal provider and verify its integrity (e.g., by comparing it the hash of the
37 | service worker code to one that is known to be correct).
38 | 
39 | ### Local portal deployment
40 | 
41 | Finally, a user can clone the Walrus Sites repository and deploy a portal locally, browsing Walrus
42 | Sites through `localhost`. In this case, the user has full control over the portal code and can
43 | verify its operation. Therefore, they can fully authenticate that the data served by Walrus and
44 | Walrus Sites is what the original developer intended.
```

walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/builder-config.md
```
1 | # Configuring the site builder
2 | 
3 | Configuring the `site-builder` tool is straightforward, but care is required to ensure that
4 | everything works correctly.
5 | 
6 | The `site-builder` tool requires a configuration file to know which package to use on Sui, which
7 | wallet to use, the gas budget, and other operational details. Most of these are abstracted away
8 | through sensible defaults, so you should not need to touch them. Yet, for completeness, we provide
9 | here the details for all the configuration options.
10 | 
11 | ## Minimal configuration
12 | 
13 | The config file is expected to be in one of the [default
14 | locations](../usage/setup.html#config-custom-path), and it is possible to point elsewhere with the
15 | `--config` flag. For your first run, it should be sufficient to call the `site-builder` without
16 | specifying the config explicitly, which is already configured if you followed thoroughly the
17 | [installation steps](./tutorial-install.html#configuration).
18 | 
19 | If, for any reason, you didn't add `walrus` to `$PATH`, make sure to configure a pointer to the
20 | binary, see below.
21 | 
22 | ## Additional options
23 | 
24 | If you want to have more control over the behavior of the site builder, you can customize the
25 | following variables in the config file:
26 | 
27 | - `package`: the object ID of the Walrus Sites package on Sui. This must always be specified in the
28 |   config, and is already appropriately configured in `./sites-config.yaml`.
29 | - `portal`: the name of the portal through which the site will be viewed; this only affects the
30 |   output of the CLI, and nothing else (default: `walrus.site`). All Walrus Sites are accessible
31 |   through any portal independent of this setting.
32 | - `general`: these are general options that can be configured both through the CLI and the config:
33 |   - `rpc_url`: The URL of the Sui RPC node to use. If not set, the `site-builder` will infer it from
34 |     the wallet.
35 |   - `wallet`: Pointer to the Sui wallet to be used. By default, it uses the system-wide wallet (the
36 |     one from `sui client addresses`).
37 |   - `walrus_binary`: Pointer to the `walrus` binary. By default, this is expected to be run from
38 |     `$PATH`.
39 |   - `walrus_config`: The configuration for the `walrus` client binary, see the [relevant
40 |     chapter](../usage/setup.md).
41 |   - `gas_budget`: The maximum amount of gas to be spent for transactions (default: 500M MIST).
42 | 
43 | ```admonish note
44 | From time to time there are package upgrades happening. This will require you to
45 | update the `package` field in the config file.
46 | ```
```

walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/commands.md
```
1 | # Site builder commands
2 | 
3 | We now describe in more detail the commands available through the site builder.
4 | 
5 | ```admonish tip
6 | In general, the `--help` flag is your friend, you can add it to get further details for the whole
7 | CLI (`site-builder --help`) or individual commands (e.g. `site-builder update --help`).
8 | ```
9 | 
10 | ## `publish`
11 | 
12 | The `publish` command, as described in the [previous section](./tutorial-publish.md), publishes a
13 | new site on Sui. The command takes a directory as input and creates a new Walrus Site from the
14 | resources contained within.
15 | 
16 | The `--epochs` flag allows you to specify for how long the site data will be stored on Walrus.
17 | 
18 | ```admonish danger title="Epoch duration on Walrus Testnet"
19 | On Walrus Testnet, the epoch duration is **two days**. Therefore, consider storing your site for a
20 | large number of epochs if you want to make it available for the following months! The maximum
21 | duration is set to 183 epochs (corresponding to one year).
22 | ```
23 | 
24 | If you are just uploading raw files without an `index.html`, you may want to use the
25 | `--list-directory` flag, which will automatically create an index page to browse the files. See for
26 | example <https://bin.blob.store>.
27 | 
28 | The `publish` command will also respect the instructions in the `ws-resources.json` configuration
29 | file. To know more, see the section on [specifying headers and routing](./routing.md).
30 | 
31 | ## `update`
32 | 
33 | This command is the equivalent of `publish`, but for updating an existing site. It takes the same
34 | arguments, with the addition of the Sui object ID of the site to update.
35 | 
36 | ```admonish note
37 | The wallet you are using to call `update` must be the *owner* of the Walrus Site object to be able
38 | to update it.
39 | ```
40 | 
41 | ## `convert`
42 | 
43 | The `convert` command converts an object ID in hex format to the equivalent Base36 format. This
44 | command is useful if you have the Sui object ID of a Walrus Site, and want to know the subdomain
45 | where you can browse it.
46 | 
47 | ## `site-map`
48 | 
49 | The `sitemap` command shows the resources that compose the Walrus Site at the given object ID.
50 | 
51 | ## `list-directory`
52 | 
53 | With `list-directory`, you can obtain the `index.html` file that would be generated by running
54 | `publish` or `update` with the `--list-directory` flag. This is useful to see how the index page
55 | would look like before publishing it—and possibly editing to make it look nicer!
```

walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/intro.md
```
1 | # Introduction to Walrus Sites
2 | 
3 | *Walrus Sites* are "web"-sites that use Sui and Walrus as their underlying technology. They are a
4 | prime example of how Walrus can be used to build new and exciting decentralized applications. Anyone
5 | can build and deploy a Walrus Site and make it accessible to the world! Funnily, this documentation
6 | is itself available as a Walrus Site at <https://docs.walrus.site/walrus-sites/intro.html> (if you
7 | aren't there already).
8 | 
9 | At a high level, here are some of the most exciting features:
10 | 
11 | - Publishing a site does not require managing servers or complex configurations; just provide the
12 |   source files (produced by your favorite web framework), publish them to Walrus Sites using the
13 |   [site-builder tool](./overview.md#the-site-builder), and you are done!
14 | - Sites can be linked to from ordinary Sui objects. This feature enables, for example, creating an
15 |   NFT collection in which *every single NFT* has a *personalized website dedicated to it*.
16 | - Walrus Sites are owned by addresses on Sui and can be exchanged, shared, and updated thanks to
17 |   Sui's flexible programming model. This means, among other things, that Walrus Sites can leverage
18 |   the [SuiNS](https://suins.io/) naming system to have human-readable names. No more messing around
19 |   with DNS!
20 | - Thanks to Walrus's decentralization and extremely high data availability, there is no risk of
21 |   having your site wiped for no reason.
22 | - Since they live on Walrus, these sites cannot have a backend in the traditional sense, and can be
23 |   therefore considered "static" sites. However, the developer can integrate with Sui-compatible
24 |   wallets and harness Sui's programmability to add backend functionality to Walrus Sites!
25 | 
26 | ## Show me
27 | 
28 | To give you a very high-level intuition of how Walrus Sites work, let's look at an example: A simple
29 | NFT collection on Sui that has a frontend dApp to mint the NFTs hosted on Walrus Sites, and in
30 | which *each NFT* has a *specific, personalized Walrus Site*.
31 | 
32 | You can check out the mint page at <https://flatland.walrus.site/>. This site is served to your
33 | browser through the Walrus Site *portal* <https://walrus.site>. While the portal's operation is
34 | explained in a [later section](./portal.md), consider for now that there can be many portals (hosted
35 | by whoever wants to have their own, and even on `localhost`). Further, the only function of the
36 | portal is to retrieve the metadata (from Sui) and the resource files (from Walrus) that constitute
37 | the site.
38 | 
39 | If you have a Sui wallet with some Testnet SUI, you can try and "mint a new Flatlander" from the
40 | site. This creates an NFT from the collection and shows you two links: one to the explorer, and one
41 | to the "Flatlander site". This latter site is a special Walrus Site that exists only for that NFT,
42 | and has special characteristics (the background color, the image, ...) that are based on the
43 | contents of the NFT.
44 | 
45 | The URL to this per-NFT site looks something like this:
46 | `https://2hzpawjycxuiuh36047yocxapc69g8ercrypa7ccsk8ek4iqu6.walrus.site/`. You'll notice that the
47 | domain remains `walrus.site`, but the subdomain is a long and random-looking string. This string is
48 | actually the [Base36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base36) encoding of the object ID of the NFT,
49 | which is
50 | [0x644bc958...](https://suiscan.xyz/testnet/object/0x644bc958052463785c026a13be051d579c8a4d2dc93b1874dce5839d4fb18c5e).
51 | 
52 | In summary:
53 | 
54 | - Walrus Sites are served through a portal; in this case, `https://walrus.site`. There can be many
55 |   portals, and anyone can host one.
56 | - The subdomain on the URL points to a specific object on Sui that allows the browser to fetch and
57 |   render the site resources. This pointer can be
58 |   - a SuiNS name, such as `flatland` in `https://flatland.walrus.site`, or
59 |   - the Base36 encoding of a the Sui object ID, such as `0x644bc958...` in the example above.
60 | 
61 | Curious to know how this magic is possible? Read the [technical overview](./overview.md)! If you
62 | just want to get started trying Walrus Sites out, check the [tutorial](./tutorial.md).
```

walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/linking.md
```
1 | # Linking from and to Walrus Sites
2 | 
3 | ``` admonish warning title="Walrus Sites links are currently unavailable"
4 | This feature is currently unavailable on server-side portals. So if you are browsing a Walrus Site
5 | on <https://walrus.site>, you will not be able to use Walrus Sites links.
6 | 
7 | We are working on enabling this feature. Stay tuned!
8 | ```
9 | 
10 | Links in Walrus Sites work *almost* as you would expect in a regular website. We specify here a few
11 | of the details.
12 | 
13 | ## Linking to resources within the same site
14 | 
15 | Relative and absolute links (`href="/path/to/resource.html"`) work as usual.
16 | 
17 | ## Linking to resources on the web
18 | 
19 | Linking to a resource on the web (`href="https://some.cdn.example.com/stylesheet.css"`) also works
20 | as usual.
21 | 
22 | ## Linking to resources in other Walrus Sites
23 | 
24 | Here is the part that is a bit different. Assume there is some image that you can browse at
25 | `https://gallery.walrus.site/walrus_arctic.webp`, and you want to link it from your own Walrus Site.
26 | 
27 | Recall that, however, `https://walrus.site` is just one of the possibly many portals. I.e., the same
28 | resource is browsable from a local portal (`http://gallery.localhost:8080/walrus_arctic.webp`), or
29 | from any other portal (e.g., `https://gallery.blob.store/walrus_arctic.webp`). Therefore, how
30 | can you link the resource in a *portal-independent way*? This is important for interoperability,
31 | availability, and respecting the user's choice of portal.
32 | 
33 | ### The solution: Walrus Sites links
34 | 
35 | We solve this problem by having the portals interpret special links that are normally invalid on
36 | the web and redirect to the corresponding Walrus Sites resource in the portal itself.
37 | 
38 | Consider the example above, where the resource `/walrus_arctic.webp` is browsed from the Walrus Site
39 | with SuiNS name `gallery`, which points to the object ID `abcd123…` (in Base36 encoding). Then,
40 | the portal-independent link is: `https://gallery.suiobj/walrus_arctic.webp`. To fix the object ID
41 | instead of the SuiNS name, you can use `https://abcd123….suiobj/walrus_arctic.webp`.
42 | 
43 | Another possibility is to directly point to the Walrus *blob ID* of the resource, and have the
44 | browser "sniff" the content type. This works for images, for example, but not for script or
45 | stylesheets. For example to point to the blob ID (e.g., containing an image) `qwer5678…`, use the
46 | URL `https://blobid.walrus/qwer5678…`.
47 | 
48 | With such a link, the portal will extract the blob ID and redirect the request to the aggregator it
49 | is using to fetch blobs.
```

walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/overview.md
```
1 | # Technical Overview
2 | 
3 | In the following sections, we delve deeper in the technical specification of Walrus Sites.
4 | 
5 | ## High-level picture
6 | 
7 | Walrus Sites are enabled by Sui and Walrus. The resources of the Walrus Site (`html`, `css`, `js`,
8 | images, etc.) are stored on Walrus, while the main entry point to it is an object stored on Sui,
9 | which contains the metadata for the site and point to the Walrus blob IDs.
10 | 
11 | ### The Walrus Sites objects on Sui
12 | 
13 | A Walrus `Site` is represented on Sui as a very simple object:
14 | 
15 | ``` move
16 | struct Site has key, store {
17 |     id: UID,
18 |     name: String,
19 | }
20 | ```
21 | 
22 | The resources associated with this site are then added to this object as [dynamic
23 | fields](https://docs.sui.io/concepts/versioning#dynamic-fields) of type `Resource`:
24 | 
25 | ``` move
26 | struct Resource has store, drop {
27 |     path: String,
28 |     // The walrus blob id containing the bytes for this resource
29 |     blob_id: u256,
30 |     ⋮
31 | }
32 | ```
33 | 
34 | Importantly, each resource contains:
35 | 
36 | - the `path` of the resource, for example `/index.html` (all the paths are always represented as
37 |   starting from root `/`);
38 | - the `blob_id`, which is the Walrus blob ID where the resource can be found; and
39 | - additional fields, that will be explained later in the documentation.
40 | 
41 | These `Resource` dynamic fields are keyed with a struct of type `ResourcePath`
42 | 
43 | ``` move
44 | struct ResourcePath has copy, store, drop {
45 |     path: String,
46 | }
47 | ```
48 | 
49 | This struct just holds the string of the path (`/index.html`); having a separate type ensures that
50 | we will not have namespace collisions with other dynamic fields, possibly added by other packages.
51 | 
52 | To see this in action, look at [a Walrus Site in the
53 | explorer](https://suiscan.xyz/testnet/object/0xd20b90149409ba5d005d4a2cd981db9494bc3cdb2f04c47ca1af98dd8f71610a),
54 | and check its dynamic fields.
55 | 
56 | ### The site rendering path
57 | 
58 | Given the Sui object ID of a Walrus Site, it is easy to look up the resources that compose it
59 | by looking at the dynamic fields, and then fetch these resources from Walrus using the blob ID
60 | contained in the `Resource` struct.
61 | 
62 | The only outstanding question is, therefore, how to perform these lookups on the client. A few
63 | approaches are possible:
64 | 
65 | - Having a server that accepts requests for a Sui object ID and possibly a path, and performs this
66 |   resolution on behalf of the client, serving back the resource as a standard HTML Response.
67 | - Using a custom application on the client that has both a web browser and knowledge of how Walrus
68 |   Sites work, and can locally perform this resolution.
69 | - A hybrid approach based on service workers, where a service worker that is able to perform the
70 |   resolution is installed in the browser from a portal.
71 | 
72 | All of these approaches are viable (the first has been used for similar applications in IPFS
73 | gateways, for example), and have trade-offs.
74 | 
75 | Currently, we provide the server-side and the service-worker based approaches.
76 | 
77 | ### Browsing and domain isolation
78 | 
79 | We must ensure that, when browsing multiple sites through a portal, for example the one hosted at
80 | <https://walrus.site>, these sites are isolated. Isolation is necessary for security, and to ensure
81 | that the wallet connection in the browser works as expected.
82 | 
83 | To do so, we give each Walrus Site a specific *subdomain* of the portal's domain. For example, the
84 | Flatland mint dApp is hosted at <https://flatland.walrus.site>, where the subdomain `flatland` is
85 | uniquely associated to the object ID of the Walrus Site through SuiNS.
86 | 
87 | Walrus Sites also work without SuiNS: a site can *always* be browsed by using as subdomain the
88 | Base36 encoding of the Sui object ID of the site. For the Flatland dApp, this URL is:
89 | <https://58gr4pinoayuijgdixud23441t55jd94ugep68fsm72b8mwmq2.walrus.site>.
90 | 
91 | Base36 was chosen for two reasons, forced by the subdomain standards:
92 | 
93 | 1. A subdomain can have at most 63 characters, while a Hex-encoded Sui object ID requires 64.
94 | 1. A subdomain is case *insensitive*, ruling out other popular encodings, e.g., Base64 or Base58.
95 | 
96 | ## Walrus Site portals
97 | 
98 | ### Portal types
99 | 
100 | As mentioned before, we provide two types of portals to browse Walrus Sites:
101 | 
102 | - The server-side portal, which is a server that resolves a Walrus Site, returning it to the
103 |   browser. The server-side portal is hosted at <https://walrus.site>.
104 | - The service-worker portal, which is a service worker that is installed in the browser and
105 |   resolves a Walrus Site. The service-worker portal is no longer hosted at a specific domain, but
106 |   the code is still maintained so that it can be used by anyone.
107 | 
108 | We now show in greater detail how a Walrus Site is rendered in a client's browser using a generic
109 | portal. Depending on the different type of portal, some details may differ, but the general picture
110 | remains unchanged.
111 | 
112 | ### The end-to-end resolution of a Walrus Site
113 | 
114 | The steps below all reference the following figure:
115 | 
116 | ![Walrus Site resolution](../assets/walrus-sites-portal-diagram.svg)
117 | 
118 | - **Site publishing** (step 0): The site developer publishes the Walrus Site using the
119 |   [`site-builder`](#the-site-builder), or making use of a publisher. Assume the developer uses the
120 |   SuiNS name `dapp.sui` to point to the object ID of the created Walrus Site.
121 | - **Browsing starts** (step 1): A client browses `dapp.walrus.site/index.html` in their browser.
122 | - **Site resolution** (steps 2-6): The portal interprets its *origin* `dapp.walrus.site`, and makes
123 |   a SuiNS resolution for `dapp.sui`, obtaining the related object ID. Using the object ID, it then
124 |   fetches the dynamic fields of the object (also checking [redirects](./portal.md)). From the
125 |   dynamic fields, it selects the one for `/index.html`, and extracts its Walrus blob ID and headers
126 |   (see the [advanced section on headers](./routing.md)).
127 | - **Blob fetch** (steps 7-11): Given the blob ID, the portal queries a Walrus aggregator for the
128 |   blob data.
129 | - **Returning the response** (steps 12-13): Now that the portal has the bytes for `/index.html`, and
130 |   its headers, it can craft a response that is then rendered by the
131 |   browser.
132 | 
133 | These steps are executed for all resources the browser may query thereafter (for example, if
134 | `/index.html` points to `assets/cat.png`).
135 | 
136 | ## The site builder
137 | 
138 | To facilitate the creation of Walrus Sites, we provide the "site builder" tool. The site builder
139 | takes care of creating Walrus Sites object on Sui, with the correct structure, and stores the site
140 | resources to Walrus. Refer to the [tutorial](./tutorial.md) for setup and usage instructions.
```

walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/portal.md
```
1 | # The Walrus Sites portal
2 | 
3 | We use the term "portal" to indicate any technology that is used to access and browse Walrus Sites.
4 | As mentioned in the [overview](./overview.md#the-site-rendering-path), we foresee three kinds of
5 | portals:
6 | 
7 | 1. server-side portals;
8 | 1. custom local apps; and
9 | 1. service-worker based portals in the browser.
10 | 
11 | Currently, only a server-side portal is served at <https://walrus.site>.
12 | 
13 | ```admonish note title="Hosting of the service worker"
14 | In the past, the service-worker based portal was hosted at <https://walrus.site> and the
15 | server-portal at <https://blob.store>. This is no longer the case.
16 | 
17 | The service-worker portal is no longer hosted, but you can still run it locally. Its code is
18 | available in the `walrus-sites` repository. For more information, see
19 | [running the portal locally](#running-the-portal-locally).
20 | 
21 | The old domain, `blob.store` is currently an alias for `walrus.site` but will be removed in the
22 | future.
23 | ```
24 | 
25 | ```admonish danger title="Walrus Sites stable branch"
26 | The stable branch of Walrus Sites is `testnet`.
27 | ```
28 | 
29 | ## Configuring the portal
30 | 
31 | There are two main locations where the portal needs to be configured: The `constants.ts` file and
32 | the environment variables.
33 | 
34 | You can find the `constants.ts` file in the `portal/common/lib` directory. It holds key
35 | configuration parameters for the portal. Typically, you won't need to modify these, but if you do,
36 | here are the explanations for each parameter:
37 | 
38 | - `NETWORK`: The Sui network to be used for fetching the Walrus Sites objects. Currently, we
39 |   use Sui `testnet`.
40 | - `AGGREGATOR`: The URL of the [aggregator](../usage/web-api.md) from which the portal will
41 |   fetch the Walrus blobs.
42 | - `SITE_PACKAGE`: The Sui object ID of the Walrus Sites package.
43 | - `MAX_REDIRECT_DEPTH`: The number of [redirects](./redirects.md) the portal will follow
44 |   before stopping.
45 | - `SITE_NAMES`: Hard coded `name: objectID` mappings, to override the SuiNS names. For development
46 |   only. Use this at your own risk, may render some sites with legitimate SuiNS names unusable.
47 | 
48 | Next, the environment variables are set in the `.env.local`. To just run a simple instance of the
49 | portal, you can just use the environment variables specified in the `.env.example` file.
50 | 
51 | ```sh
52 | cp ./portal/server/.env.example ./portal/server/.env.local
53 | ```
54 | 
55 | Likewise, if you want to run the service-worker portal, you can copy the `.env.example` file to
56 | `.env.local` in the `portal/worker` directory.
57 | 
58 | ```sh
59 | cp ./portal/worker/.env.example ./portal/worker/.env.local
60 | ```
61 | 
62 | ## Running the portal locally
63 | 
64 | You can run a portal locally if you want to browse Walrus Sites without accessing
65 | external portals or for development purposes.
66 | 
67 | This requires having the [`pnpm`](https://pnpm.io/) tool installed. To start, clone the
68 | `walrus-sites` repo and enter the `portal` directory.
69 | 
70 | Make sure you are on the stable branch:
71 | 
72 | ``` sh
73 | git checkout testnet
74 | ```
75 | 
76 | ``` sh
77 | cd portal
78 | bun install
79 | # Build the portal you want to use, or both
80 | bun build:server
81 | bun build:worker
82 | 
83 | ```
84 | 
85 | to install the dependencies, and then either one of the following commands:
86 | 
87 | ``` sh
88 | # Serve the server-side portal
89 | bun run server
90 | 
91 | # Serve the service-worker portal
92 | bun run worker
93 | ```
94 | 
95 | to serve one of the portals. Typically, you will find it served at `localhost:3000` (for the server
96 | side portal) or `localhost:8080` for the service worker (but check the output of the serve
97 | command).
```

walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/redirects.md
```
1 | # Redirecting objects to Walrus Sites
2 | 
3 | We have seen in the [overview](./overview.md) how a Walrus Site object on Sui looks like. We will
4 | discuss now how you can create ensure that a *set of arbitrary objects* can all be tied to a
5 | specific, and possibly unique, Walrus Site.
6 | 
7 | ## The goal
8 | 
9 | Consider a collection of NFTs, such as the one published by <https://flatland.walrus.site>. As we
10 | show there, each minted NFT has its own Walrus Site, which can be personalized based on the contents
11 | (e.g., the color) of the NFT itself. How can we achieve this?
12 | 
13 | ## Redirect links
14 | 
15 | The solution is simple: We add a "redirect" in the NFT's
16 | [`Display`](https://docs.sui.io/standards/display#sui-utility-objects) property. Each time an NFT's
17 | object ID is browsed through a portal, the portal will check the `Display` of the NFT and, if it
18 | encounters the `walrus site address` key, it will go fetch the Walrus Site that is at the
19 | corresponding object ID.
20 | 
21 | ### Redirects in Move
22 | 
23 | Practically speaking, when creating the `Display` of the NFT, you can include the key-value pair
24 | that points to the Walrus Site that is to be used.
25 | 
26 | ``` move
27 | ...
28 | const VISUALIZATION_SITE: address = @0x901fb0...;
29 | display.add(b"walrus site address".to_string(), VISUALIZATION_SITE.to_string());
30 | ...
31 | ```
32 | 
33 | ### How to change the site based on the NFT?
34 | 
35 | The code above will only open the specified Walrus Site when browsing the object ID of the NFT. How
36 | do we ensure that the properties of the NFT can be used to personalize the site?
37 | 
38 | This needs to be done in the `VISUALIZATION_SITE`: Since the subdomain is still pointing to the
39 | NFT's object ID, the Walrus Site that is loaded can check its `origin` in JavaScript, and use the
40 | subdomain to determine the NFT, fetch it from chain, and use its internal fields to modify the
41 | displayed site.
42 | 
43 | For an end-to-end example, see the `flatland`
44 | [repo](https://github.com/MystenLabs/example-walrus-sites/tree/main/flatland).
```

walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/restrictions.md
```
1 | # Known restrictions
2 | 
3 | Walrus Sites can be used to deploy almost any form of traditional static web2 website build for
4 | modern browsers. There are, however, a number of restrictions that a developer should keep in mind
5 | when creating or porting a website to Walrus Sites.
6 | 
7 | ## No secret values
8 | 
9 | Walrus Sites are fully publicly accessible, as the metadata is stored on Sui, and the site content
10 | is stored on Walrus. Therefore, developers *must not* store secret values within the sites.
11 | 
12 | We emphasize again that any such backend-specific operations (storing secret values, authentication,
13 | etc.) are achievable by leveraging the integration with the Sui blockchain and a Sui-compatible
14 | wallet.
15 | 
16 | ## There is a maximum redirect depth
17 | 
18 | The number of consecutive redirects a Walrus Site can perform is capped by the
19 | portal (see [Portal configuration](./portal.md)). This measure ensures that loading a Walrus Site
20 | does not result in an infinite loading loop.
21 | 
22 | Different portals can set this limit as they desire. The limit for the portal hosted at
23 | <https://walrus.site> has a maximum redirect depth of 3.
24 | 
25 | ## Service-worker portal limitations
26 | 
27 | The following limitations only apply to portals based on service workers.
28 | 
29 | ``` admonish tip
30 | If you need to support any of the features listed below, you should use a server-side portal.
31 | ```
32 | 
33 | ### Service-worker portals, can't serve sites based on service workers
34 | 
35 | Service-worker portals leverage service workers in the clients' browsers to perform essential
36 | operations:
37 | 
38 | 1. reading the site metadata from Sui;
39 | 1. fetching the page content from Walrus; and
40 | 1. serving the content to the browser.
41 | 
42 | Therefore, a site accessed by a service-worker portal cannot use service workers itself. i.e.
43 | you can't "stack" service workers! Installing a service worker from within a Walrus Site will
44 | result in a dysfunctional site and a poor experience for the user.
45 | 
46 | ### iOS Sui mobile wallets do not work with the service-worker portal
47 | 
48 | ```admonish warning
49 | This limitation **only applies to portal based on service workers**. If you need to access sites
50 | that support this feature, you should use a server-side portal.
51 | ```
52 | 
53 | Service workers cannot be loaded inside an in-app browser on iOS, because of a limitation of the
54 | WebKit engine. As a consequence, Walrus Sites that are accessed through a service worker portal
55 | cannot be used within Sui-compatible wallet apps on iOS. Therefore, Sui wallets cannot currently
56 | be used on a service-worker portal on iOS. Note, however, that *browsing* a Walrus Site is still
57 | possible on iOS through any browser.
58 | 
59 | Given that you decided to use a service-worker portal as your main point of access to your sites,
60 | to provide a seamless experience for iOS users (and other users on browsers that do not support
61 | service workers), it is recommended to redirect to a server-side portal (<https://walrus.site>).
62 | Whenever a user on an iOS wallet browses a Walrus Site, the redirect will automatically take them
63 | to the `<site_name>.walrus.site` server-side portal. This way, the user can still use the wallet.
64 | 
65 | ### Service worker portals do not support progressive web apps (PWAs)
66 | 
67 | ```admonish warning
68 | This limitation **only applies to portal based on service workers**. If you need to access sites
69 | that support this feature, you should use a server-side portal.
70 | ```
71 | 
72 | With the current design, service-worker portals cannot be used to access progressive web apps
73 | (PWAs).
74 | 
75 | Two characteristics of the service-worker portal prevent support for PWAs:
76 | 
77 | - Since the service worker needs to be registered for the page to work, the PWA's manifest file
78 |   cannot be loaded by the browser directly.
79 | - There can only be one service worker registered per origin. Therefore, registering a PWA's service
80 |   worker would remove the Walrus Sites service worker, breaking Walrus Sites' functionality.
81 | 
82 | Note that the server-side portal does not share these limitations. However, for the moment, we
83 | support both technologies: Walrus Sites must be able to load from both a service-worker portal and a
84 | server-side portal, and therefore have to be built with the more restrictive feature set. For more
85 | details, see the [installation requirements for
86 | PWAs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_web_app#Installation_criteria).
```

walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/routing.md
```
1 | # Specifying headers and routing
2 | 
3 | ``` admonish tip title="New with Walrus Sites Testnet version"
4 | The following features have been released with the Walrus Sites Testnet version.
5 | ```
6 | 
7 | In its base configuration, Walrus Sites serves static assets through a portal. However, many modern
8 | web applications require more advanced features, such as custom headers and client-side routing.
9 | 
10 | Therefore, the site-builder can read a `ws-resource.json` configuration file, in which you can
11 | directly specify resource headers and routing rules.
12 | 
13 | ## The `ws-resources.json` file
14 | 
15 | This file is optionally placed in the root of the site directory, and it is *not* uploaded with the
16 | site's resources (in other words, the file is not part of the resulting Walrus Site and is not
17 | served by the portal).
18 | 
19 | If you don't want to use this default location, you can specify the path to the configuration file
20 | with the `--ws-resources` flag when running the `publish` or `update` commands.
21 | 
22 | The file is JSON-formatted, and looks like the following:
23 | 
24 | ``` JSON
25 | {
26 |   "headers": {
27 |     "/index.html": {
28 |       "Content-Type": "text/html; charset=utf-8",
29 |       "Cache-Control": "max-age=3500"
30 |     }
31 |   },
32 |   "routes": {
33 |     "/*": "/index.html",
34 |     "/accounts/*": "/accounts.html",
35 |     "/path/assets/*": "/assets/asset_router.html"
36 |   }
37 | }
38 | ```
39 | 
40 | We now describe in details the two sections of the configuration file, `headers` and `routes`.
41 | 
42 | ## Specifying HTTP response headers
43 | 
44 | The `headers` section allows you to specify custom HTTP response headers for specific resources.
45 | The keys in the `headers` object are the paths of the resources, and the values are lists of
46 | key-value pairs corresponding to the headers that the portal will attach to the response.
47 | 
48 | For example, in the configuration above, the file `index.html` will be served with the
49 | `Content-Type` header set to `text/html; charset=utf-8` and the `Cache-Control` header set to
50 | `max-age=3500`.
51 | 
52 | This mechanism allows you to control various aspects of the resource delivery, such as caching,
53 | encoding, and content types.
54 | 
55 | ```admonish
56 | The resource path is always represented as starting from the root `/`.
57 | ```
58 | 
59 | ### Default headers
60 | 
61 | By default, no headers need to be specified, and the `ws-resources.json` file can be omitted. The
62 | site-builder will automatically try to infer the `Content-Type` header based on the file extension,
63 | and set the `Content-Encoding` to `identity` (no transformation).
64 | 
65 | In case the content type cannot be inferred, the `Content-Type` will be set to
66 | `application/octet-stream`.
67 | 
68 | These defaults will be overridden by any headers specified in the `ws-resources.json` file.
69 | 
70 | ## Specifying client-side routing
71 | 
72 | The `routes` section allows you to specify client-side routing rules for your site. This is useful
73 | when you want to use a single-page application (SPA) framework, such as React or Angular.
74 | 
75 | The configuration in the `routes` object is a mapping from route keys to resource paths.
76 | 
77 | The **`routes` keys** are path patterns in the form `/path/to/some/*`, where the `*` character
78 | represents a wildcard.
79 | 
80 | ```admonish
81 | Currently, the wildcard *can only be specified at the end of the path*.
82 | Therefore, `/path/*` is a valid path, while `/path/*/to` and `*/path/to/*` are not.
83 | ```
84 | 
85 | The **`routes` values** are the resource paths that should be served when the route key is matched.
86 | 
87 | ```admonish danger title="Important"
88 | The paths in the values **must** be valid resource paths, meaning that they must be present among
89 | the site's resources. The Walrus sites contract will **abort** if the user tries to create a route
90 | that points to a non-existing resource.
91 | ```
92 | 
93 | The simple routing algorithm is as follows:
94 | 
95 | - Whenever a resource path *is not found among the sites resources*, the portal tries to match the
96 |   path to the `routes`.
97 | - All matching routes are then *lexicographically ordered*, and the *longest* match is chosen.
98 | - The resource corresponding to this longest match is then served.
99 | 
100 | ```admonish
101 | In other words, the portal will *always* serve a resource if present, and if not present will serve
102 | the resource with the *longest matching prefix* among the routes.
103 | ```
104 | 
105 | Recall the example above:
106 | 
107 | ``` JSON
108 | "routes": {
109 |   "/*": "/index.html",
110 |   "/path/*": "/accounts.html",
111 |   "/path/assets/*": "/assets/asset_router.html"
112 | }
113 | ```
114 | 
115 | The following matchings will occur:
116 | 
117 | - browsing `/any/other/test.html` will serve `/index.html`;
118 | - browsing `/path/test.html` will serve `/accounts.html`, as it is a more specific match than the
119 |   previous one;
120 | - similarly, browsing `/path/assets/test.html` will serve `/assets/asset_router.html`.
121 | 
122 | `/index.html`, `/accounts.html`, and `/assets/asset_router.html` are all existing resources on the
123 | Walrus Sites object on Sui.
```

1 | <!-- markdownlint-disable -->

3 | # Walrus Sites - TERMS of SERVICE
4 | 
5 | Last Updated: June 18, 2024

walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/tutorial-install.md
```
1 | # Installing the site builder
2 | 
3 | This section describes the steps necessary to setup the Walrus Sites' `site-builder` tool and
4 | prepare your environment for development.
5 | 
6 | ## Prerequisites
7 | 
8 | Before you start, make sure you
9 | 
10 | - have a recent version of [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install) installed;
11 | - followed all [Walrus setup instructions](../usage/setup.md).
12 | 
13 | Then, follow these additional setup steps.
14 | 
15 | ## Installation
16 | 
17 | Similar to the `walrus` client CLI tool, we currently provide the `site-builder` client binary for
18 | macOS (Intel and Apple CPUs), Ubuntu, and Windows:
19 | 
20 | | OS      | CPU                   | Architecture |
21 | |---------|-----------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
22 | | Ubuntu  | Intel 64bit           | [`ubuntu-x86_64`](https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/site-builder-testnet-latest-ubuntu-x86_64)                |
23 | | Ubuntu  | Intel 64bit (generic) | [`ubuntu-x86_64-generic`](https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/site-builder-testnet-latest-ubuntu-x86_64-generic)|
24 | | MacOS   | Apple Silicon         | [`macos-arm64`](https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/site-builder-testnet-latest-macos-arm64)                    |
25 | | MacOS   | Intel 64bit           | [`macos-x86_64`](https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/site-builder-testnet-latest-macos-x86_64)                  |
26 | | Windows | Intel 64bit           | [`windows-x86_64.exe`](https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/site-builder-testnet-latest-windows-x86_64.exe)      |
27 | 
28 | ```admonish title="Windows"
29 | We now offer a pre-built binary also for Windows. However, most of the remaining instructions assume
30 | a UNIX-based system for the directory structure, commands, etc. If you use Windows, you may need to
31 | adapt most of those.
32 | ```
33 | 
34 | You can download the latest build from our Google Cloud Storage (GCS) bucket (correctly setting the
35 | `$SYSTEM` variable):
36 | 
37 | ``` sh
38 | SYSTEM= # set this to your system: ubuntu-x86_64, ubuntu-x86_64-generic, macos-x86_64, macos-arm64, windows-x86_64.exe
39 | curl https://storage.googleapis.com/mysten-walrus-binaries/site-builder-testnet-latest-$SYSTEM -o site-builder
40 | chmod +x site-builder
41 | ```
42 | 
43 | To be able to run it simply as `site-builder`, move the binary to any directory included in your
44 | `$PATH` environment variable. Standard locations are `/usr/local/bin/`, `$HOME/bin/`, or
45 | `$HOME/.local/bin/`.
46 | 
47 | ```admonish note
48 | The site builder will look for the default configuration file `sites-config.yaml` in the current
49 | directory, the `$XDG_HOME/walrus/sites-config.yaml` and `$HOME/walrus/sites-config.yaml` directory.
50 | In case you want to use explicitly a different `sites-config.yaml`, use the `--config` flag to
51 | specify the path to the configuration file.
52 | ```
53 | 
54 | Once this is done, you should be able to simply type `site-builder` in your terminal.
55 | 
56 | ```terminal
57 | $ site-builder
58 | Usage: site-builder [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>
59 | 
60 | Commands:
61 |   publish  Publish a new site on Sui
62 |   update   Update an existing site
63 |   convert  Convert an object ID in hex format to the equivalent Base36
64 |                format
65 |   sitemap  Show the pages composing the Walrus site at the given object ID
66 |   help     Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)
67 | 
68 |   ⋮
69 | ```
70 | 
71 | ## Configuration
72 | 
73 | The `site-builder` tool needs a configuration file to work. This file is called `sites-config.yaml`
74 | and looks like this:
75 | 
76 | ```yaml
77 | # module: site
78 | # portal: walrus.site
79 | package: 0xdf9033cac39b7a9b9f76fb6896c9fc5283ba730d6976a2b1d85ad1e6036c3272
80 | # general:
81 | #   rpc_url: https://fullnode.testnet.sui.io:443
82 | #   wallet: /path/to/.sui/sui_config/client.yaml
83 | #   walrus_binary: /path/to/walrus
84 | #   walrus_config: /path/to/devnet_deployment/client_config.yaml
85 | #   gas_budget: 500000000
86 | ```
87 | 
88 | As you can see, the configuration file is quite simple. The only mandatory field is the `package`
89 | field, which represents the Sui object ID of the Walrus Sites smart contract. You can find the
90 | latest version of the package in the [Walrus Sites
91 | repository](https://github.com/MystenLabs/walrus-sites/tree/testnet) on the `testnet` branch.
92 | 
93 | ```admonish danger title="Walrus Sites stable branch"
94 | The stable branch of Walrus Sites is `testnet`.
95 | Make sure that you always pull the latest changes from there.
96 | ```
97 | 
98 | You can define the location of the `sites-config.yaml` file using the `--config` flag when running
99 | the `site-builder` commands like so:
100 | 
101 | ``` sh
102 | site-builder --config /path/to/sites-config.yaml publish <build-directory-of-a-site>
103 | ```
104 | 
105 | However, if are not a fan of repeating the same flags over and over, it's always easier to have the
106 | configuration file in one of the [default locations](./tutorial-install.html#admonition-note).
107 | 
108 | Download the `sites-config.yaml` file from the repository, and place it in one of the aforementioned
109 | default locations. To illustrate, we will use the `~/.config/walrus` directory, like so:
110 | 
111 | ```sh
112 | curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MystenLabs/walrus-sites/refs/heads/testnet/sites-config.yaml -o ~/.config/walrus/sites-config.yaml
113 | ```
114 | 
115 | You are now ready to start working on your Walrus Sites! 🎉
```

walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/tutorial-publish.md
```
1 | # Publishing a Walrus Site
2 | 
3 | Now that everything is installed and configured, you should be able to start publishing your first
4 | Walrus Site!
5 | 
6 | ## Select the source material for the site
7 | 
8 | The `site-builder` works by uploading a directory of files produced by any web framework to Walrus
9 | and adding the relevant metadata to Sui. This directory should have a file called `index.html` in
10 | its root, which will be the entry point to the Walrus Site.
11 | 
12 | There is a very useful [example-Walrus-sites](https://github.com/MystenLabs/example-walrus-sites)
13 | repository that contains multiple kinds of sites that you can use for reference.
14 | 
15 | For simplicity, we will start by publishing the most frugal of the sites, the `walrus-snake` game.
16 | 
17 | First, clone the repository of the examples:
18 | 
19 | ``` sh
20 | git clone https://github.com/MystenLabs/example-walrus-sites.git && cd example-walrus-sites
21 | ```
22 | 
23 | ## Publish the site
24 | 
25 | Since we have placed the `walrus` and `site-builder` binaries and configuration in their default
26 | locations, publishing the `./walrus-snake` site is as simple as calling the publishing command:
27 | 
28 | ``` sh
29 | site-builder publish ./walrus-snake --epochs 100
30 | ```
31 | 
32 | ``` admonish tip
33 | Currently on Walrus Testnet, the duration of an epoch is two days. If you want your site to stay up
34 | longer, specify the number of epochs with the `--epochs` flag (maximum 183 epochs).
35 | ```
36 | 
37 | The end of the output should look like the following:
38 | 
39 | ``` txt
40 | Execution completed
41 | Resource operations performed:
42 |   - created resource /Oi-Regular.ttf with blob ID 76npyqDyGF10-jP_ov-UBHpi-RaRFnxcWgslueGEfr0
43 |   - created resource /file.svg with blob ID w70pYgtLmi--38Jg1sTGaLlZkQtximNMHXjxDQdXKa0
44 |   - created resource /index.html with blob ID LVLk9VSnBrEgQ2HJHAgU3p8IarKypQpfn38aSeUZzzE
45 |   - created resource /walrus.svg with blob ID 866UDjMAy_BB8SsTcgjGEOFp2uAO9BbcVbLh5-_oBNE
46 | The site routes were modified
47 | 
48 | Created new site: test site
49 | New site object ID: 0x407a308190eb82b266be9cc28b888d04c5b2e5a503c7d0ffd3f69681ea83b73a
50 | Browse the resulting site at: https://1lupgq2auevjruy7hs9z7tskqwjp5cc8c5ebhci4v57qyl4piy.walrus.site
51 | ```
52 | 
53 | This output tells you that, for each file in the folder, a new Walrus blob was created, and the
54 | respective blob ID. Further, it prints the object ID of the Walrus Site object on Sui (so you can
55 | have a look in the explorer and use it to set the SuiNS name) and, finally, the URL at which you can
56 | browse the site.
57 | 
58 | Note here that we are implicitly using the default `sites-config.yaml` as the config for the site
59 | builder that we set up previously on the [installation section](./tutorial-install.html). The
60 | configuration file is necessary to ensure that the `site-builder` knows the correct Sui package for
61 | the Walrus Sites logic.
62 | 
63 | More details on the configuration of the `site-builder` can be found under the [advanced
64 | configuration](./builder-config.md) section.
65 | 
66 | ## Update the site
67 | 
68 | Let's say now you want to update the content of the site, for example by changing the title from
69 | "eat all the blobs!" to "Glob all the Blobs!".
70 | 
71 | First, make this edit on in the `./walrus-snake/index.html` file.
72 | 
73 | Then, you can update the existing site by running the `update` command, providing the directory
74 | where to find the updated files (still `./walrus-snake`) and the object ID of the existing site
75 | (`0x407a3081...`):
76 | 
77 | ``` sh
78 | site-builder update --epochs 100 ./walrus-snake 0x407a3081...
79 | ```
80 | 
81 | The output this time should be:
82 | 
83 | ``` txt
84 | Execution completed
85 | Resource operations performed:
86 |   - deleted resource /index.html with blob ID LVLk9VSnBrEgQ2HJHAgU3p8IarKypQpfn38aSeUZzzE
87 |   - created resource /index.html with blob ID pcZaosgEFtmP2d2IV3QdVhnUjajvQzY2ev8d9U_D5VY
88 | The site routes were left unchanged
89 | 
90 | Site object ID: 0x407a308190eb82b266be9cc28b888d04c5b2e5a503c7d0ffd3f69681ea83b73a
91 | Browse the resulting site at: https://1lupgq2auevjruy7hs9z7tskqwjp5cc8c5ebhci4v57qyl4piy.walrus.site
92 | ```
93 | 
94 | Compared to the `publish` action, we can see that now the only actions performed were to delete the
95 | old `index.html`, and update it with the newer one.
96 | 
97 | Browsing to the provided URL should reflect the change. You've updated the site!
98 | 
99 | ```admonish note
100 | The wallet you are using must be the *owner* of the Walrus Site object to be able to update it.
101 | ```
102 | 
103 | ```admonish danger title="Extending the expiration date of an existing site"
104 | To extend the expiration date of a previously-stored site, use the `update` command with the
105 | `--force` flag, and specify the number of additional epochs (from the current epoch) with the
106 | `--epochs` flag.
107 | ```
```

walrus-docs/docs/walrus-sites/tutorial-suins.md
```
1 | # Bonus: Set a SuiNS name
2 | 
3 | Browsing a URL like `https://1lupgq2auevjruy7hs9z7tskqwjp5cc8c5ebhci4v57qyl4piy.walrus.site` is not
4 | particularly nice. Therefore, Walrus Sites allows to use SuiNS names (this is like DNS for Sui) to
5 | assign a human-readable name to a Walrus Site. To do so, you simply have to get a SuiNS name you
6 | like, and point it to the object ID of the Walrus Site (as provided by the `publish` or `update`
7 | commands).
8 | 
9 | Let's do this step by step.
10 | 
11 | ## Get a SuiNS name
12 | 
13 | - Navigate to <https://testnet.suins.io> and buy a domain name with your Testnet wallet. For
14 |   example, `walrusgame` (this specific one is already taken, choose another you like).
15 | 
16 |   ```admonish note
17 |   At the moment, you can only select names that are composed of letters `a-z` and numbers `0-9`, but
18 |   no special characters (e.g., `-`).
19 |   ```
20 | 
21 | ## Map the SuiNS name to the Walrus Site
22 | 
23 | Now, you can set the SuiNS name to point to the address of your Walrus Site. To do so, go to the
24 | ["names you own"](https://testnet.suins.io/account/my-names) section of the SuiNS website, click on
25 | the "three dots" menu icon above the name you want to map, and click "Link To Walrus Site". Paste
26 | in the bar the object ID of the Walrus Site, check that it is correct, and click "Apply".
27 | 
28 | After approving the transaction, we can now browse <https://walrusgame.walrus.site>!
29 | 
30 | ``` admonish warning title="Backwards compatibility"
31 | If you previously linked a SuiNs domain to a Walrus Site, you might recall clicking the "Link To
32 | Wallet Address" button instead of the "Link To Walrus Site" button. These old links remain valid,
33 | but we recommend using the procedure above for all new sites and updates to older sites. The portal
34 | will first check if the domain is linked using the "Link to Walrus Site", and, if that is not set,
35 | it will fall back to checking the "Link to Wallet Address".
36 | ```
```

40 |         if: github.event.action != 'closed'
41 |       - name: Deploy preview
42 |         uses: rossjrw/pr-preview-action@v1.6.0
43 |         with:
44 |           source-dir: build/html
```

15 |     }
16 | 
17 |     object {
18 |       object-fit: cover;
19 |     }
20 |   </style>
21 | </head>
22 | 
23 | <body>
24 |   <script>
25 |     const SUI_NETWORK = "testnet";
26 |     const SUI_VIEW_TX_URL = `https://suiscan.xyz/${SUI_NETWORK}/tx`;
27 |     const SUI_VIEW_OBJECT_URL = `https://suiscan.xyz/${SUI_NETWORK}/object`;
28 | 
29 |     /**
30 |      * Handler for submit events from the HTML form.
31 |      *
32 |      * Stores the blob provided in the form, and disable the default HTML form submission.
33 |      */
34 |     function onSubmit(event) {
35 |       // Ensure that the event does not propagate, so that the browser does not
36 |       // perform a POST with the file.
37 |       event.preventDefault();
38 | 
39 |       // Disable the form while uploading.
40 |       enableForm(false);
41 | 
42 |       // Store and display the blob, then re-enable the form.
43 |       storeBlob().then((storageInfo) => {
44 |         displayUpload(storageInfo.info, storageInfo.media_type);
45 |         alert(null);
46 |         enableForm(true);
47 |       }).catch((error) => {
48 |         console.error(error);
49 |         alert(
50 |           "An error occurred while uploading. Check the browser console and ensure that \
51 |                     the aggregator and publisher URLs are correct."
52 |         );
53 |         enableForm(true);
54 |       });
55 | 
56 |       // Return false to cancel form submission.
57 |       return false;
58 |     }
59 | 
60 |     /**
61 |      * Stores the file from the HTML form on Walrus.
62 |      */
63 |     function storeBlob() {
64 |       const inputFile = document.getElementById("file-input").files[0];
65 |       const numEpochs = document.getElementById("epochs-input").value;
66 |       const basePublisherUrl = document.getElementById("publisher-url-input").value;
67 | 
68 |       // Submit a PUT request with the file's content as the body to the /v1/blobs endpoint.
69 |       let sendTo = document.getElementById("send-to-input").value.trim();
70 |       let sendToParam = sendTo ? `&send_object_to=${sendTo}`: "";
71 |       return fetch(`${basePublisherUrl}/v1/blobs?epochs=${numEpochs}${sendToParam}`, {
72 |         method: "PUT",
73 |         body: inputFile,
74 |       }).then((response) => {
75 |         if (response.status === 200) {
76 |           // Parse successful responses as JSON, and return it along with the
77 |           // mime type from the the file input element.
78 |           return response.json().then((info) => {
79 |             console.log(info);
80 |             return { info: info, media_type: inputFile.type };
81 |           });
82 |         } else {
83 |           throw new Error("Something went wrong when storing the blob!");
84 |         }
85 |       })
86 |     }
87 | 
88 |     /**
89 |      * Display the result of uploading the file to Walrus.
90 |      */
91 |     function displayUpload(storage_info, media_type) {
92 |       // Extract the displayed fields from either of the two successful responses:
93 |       // - newlyCreated for blobs that have been uploaded for the first time,
94 |       //   or whose duration has been extended.
95 |       // - alreadyCertified for blobs that have already been uploaded and certified.
96 |       if ("alreadyCertified" in storage_info) {
97 |         info = {
98 |           status: "Already certified",
99 |           blobId: storage_info.alreadyCertified.blobId,
100 |           endEpoch: storage_info.alreadyCertified.endEpoch,
101 |           suiRefType: "Previous Sui Certified Event",
102 |           suiRef: storage_info.alreadyCertified.event.txDigest,
103 |           suiBaseUrl: SUI_VIEW_TX_URL,
104 |         };
105 |       } else if ("newlyCreated" in storage_info) {
106 |         info = {
107 |           status: "Newly created",
108 |           blobId: storage_info.newlyCreated.blobObject.blobId,
109 |           endEpoch: storage_info.newlyCreated.blobObject.storage.endEpoch,
110 |           suiRefType: "Associated Sui Object",
111 |           suiRef: storage_info.newlyCreated.blobObject.id,
112 |           suiBaseUrl: SUI_VIEW_OBJECT_URL,
113 |         };
114 |       } else {
115 |         throw Error("Unhandled successful response!");
116 |       }
117 | 
118 |       // The URL used to download and view the blob.
119 |       const baseAggregatorUrl = document.getElementById("aggregator-url-input").value;
120 |       const blobUrl = `${baseAggregatorUrl}/v1/blobs/${info.blobId}`;
121 | 
122 |       // The URL for viewing the event or object on chain
123 |       const suiUrl = `${info.suiBaseUrl}/${info.suiRef}`
124 | 
125 |       const isImage = media_type.startsWith("image");
126 |       // Create the HTML entry in the page for the uploaded blob.
127 |       //
128 |       // For the associated icon, we use the `<object/>` HTML element, as it allows specifying
129 |       // the media type. The walrus aggregator returns blobs as `application/octect-stream`,
130 |       // so it's necessary to specify the content type to the browser in the `object` element.
131 |       document.getElementById("uploaded-blobs").insertAdjacentHTML(
132 |         "afterBegin",
133 |         `<article class="row border rounded-2 shadow-sm mb-3">
134 |           <object type="${isImage ? media_type : ''}" data="${isImage ? blobUrl : ''}" class="col-4 ps-0"></object>
135 |           <dl class="blob-info col-8 my-2">
136 |             <dt>Status</dt><dd>${info.status}</dd>
137 | 
138 |             <dt>Blob ID</dt>
139 |             <dd class="text-truncate"><a href="${blobUrl}">${info.blobId}</a></dd>
140 | 
141 |             <dt>${info.suiRefType}</dt>
142 |             <dd class="text-truncate">
143 |               <a href="${suiUrl}" target="_blank">${info.suiRef}</a>
144 |             </dd>
145 |             <dt>Stored until epoch</dt><dd>${info.endEpoch}</dd>
146 |           </dl>
147 |         </article>`
148 |       );
149 |     }
150 | 
151 |     /**
152 |      * Helper function to disable the form while uploading.
153 |      */
154 |     function enableForm(isEnabled) {
155 |       if (isEnabled) {
156 |         // Copy the urls, so that they are not reset.
157 |         const publisherUrl = document.getElementById("publisher-url-input").value;
158 |         const aggregatorUrl = document.getElementById("aggregator-url-input").value;
159 |         // Reset the form
160 |         document.getElementById("upload-form").reset()
161 |         // Revert the URLs to their previous values
162 |         document.getElementById("publisher-url-input").value = publisherUrl;
163 |         document.getElementById("aggregator-url-input").value = aggregatorUrl;
164 |         // Disable the progress indication
165 |         document.getElementById("submit-spinner").style.visibility = "collapse";
166 |         document.getElementById("submit-text").textContent = "Upload";
167 |         // Re-enable the form
168 |         document.querySelector("#upload-form fieldset").removeAttribute("disabled");
169 |       } else {
170 |         document.querySelector("#upload-form fieldset").setAttribute("disabled", "");
171 |         document.getElementById("submit-spinner").style.visibility = "visible";
172 |         document.getElementById("submit-text").textContent = "Uploading ...";
173 |       }
174 |     }
175 | 
176 |     /**
177 |      * Helper to display an error message.
178 |      */
179 |     function alert(message) {
180 |       const alertElement = document.getElementById("alert");
181 |       if (message !== null) {
182 |         alertElement.textContent = message;
183 |       }
184 |       alertElement.style.visibility = message !== null ? "visible" : "hidden";
185 |     }
186 |   </script>
187 |

walrus-docs/examples/python/hello_walrus_jsonapi.py
```
1 | # Example of uploading and downloading a file to / from the Walrus service
2 | # Using the walrus client json input & output facilities.
3 | 
4 | # Std lib imports
5 | import os
6 | import subprocess
7 | import json
8 | import tempfile
9 | import base64
10 | 
11 | import requests
12 | 
13 | from utils import num_to_blob_id, PATH_TO_WALRUS, PATH_TO_WALRUS_CONFIG, FULL_NODE_URL
14 | 
15 | try:
16 |     # Create a 1MiB file of random data
17 |     random_data = os.urandom(1024 * 1024)
18 |     tmp = tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False)
19 |     tmp.write(random_data)
20 |     tmp.close()
21 | 
22 |     # Part 1. Upload the file to the Walrus service
23 |     store_json_command = f"""{{ "config" : "{PATH_TO_WALRUS_CONFIG}",
24 |         "command" : {{ "store" :
25 |         {{ "files" : ["{tmp.name}"], "epochs" : 2  }}}}
26 |     }}"""
27 |     result = subprocess.run(
28 |         [PATH_TO_WALRUS, "json"],
29 |         text=True,
30 |         capture_output=True,
31 |         input=store_json_command,
32 |     )
33 | 
34 |     assert result.returncode == 0
35 | 
36 |     # Parse the response and display key information
37 |     json_result_dict = json_result_dict = json.loads(result.stdout.strip())[0]["blobStoreResult"]
38 |     if "newlyCreated" in json_result_dict:
39 |         blob_id = json_result_dict["newlyCreated"]["blobObject"]["blobId"]
40 |         sui_object_id = json_result_dict["newlyCreated"]["blobObject"]["id"]
41 |     elif "alreadyCertified" in json_result_dict:
42 |         blob_id = json_result_dict["alreadyCertified"]["blobId"]
43 |     else:
44 |         raise ValueError("Unexpected response from Walrus")
45 | 
46 |     print(
47 |         f"Upload Blob ID: {blob_id} Size {len(random_data)} bytes"
48 |     )
49 | 
50 |     if sui_object_id:
51 |         print(f"Certificate in Object ID: {sui_object_id}")
52 | 
53 |     # Part 2. Download the file from the Walrus service
54 |     read_json_command = f"""{{ "config" : "{PATH_TO_WALRUS_CONFIG}",
55 |         "command" : {{ "read" :
56 |         {{ "blobId" : "{blob_id}" }}}}
57 |     }}"""
58 |     result = subprocess.run(
59 |         [PATH_TO_WALRUS, "json"],
60 |         text=True,
61 |         capture_output=True,
62 |         input=read_json_command,
63 |     )
64 | 
65 |     assert result.returncode == 0
66 | 
67 |     # Parse the response and display key information
68 |     json_result_dict = json.loads(result.stdout.strip())
69 |     downloaded_data = base64.b64decode(json_result_dict["blob"])
70 |     assert downloaded_data == random_data
71 | 
72 |     print(
73 |         f"Download Blob ID: {json_result_dict['blobId']} Size {len(downloaded_data)} bytes"
74 |     )
75 | 
76 |     # Part 3. Check the availability of the blob
77 |     if sui_object_id:
78 |         request = {
79 |             "jsonrpc": "2.0",
80 |             "id": 1,
81 |             "method": "sui_getObject",
82 |             "params": [
83 |                 sui_object_id,
84 |                 {
85 |                     "showType": True,
86 |                     "showOwner": False,
87 |                     "showPreviousTransaction": True,
88 |                     "showDisplay": False,
89 |                     "showContent": True,
90 |                     "showBcs": False,
91 |                     "showStorageRebate": False,
92 |                 },
93 |             ],
94 |         }
95 |         response = requests.post(FULL_NODE_URL, json=request)
96 |         object_content = response.json()["result"]["data"]["content"]
97 |         print("Object content:")
98 |         print(json.dumps(object_content, indent=4))
99 | 
100 |         # Check that the blob ID matches the one we uploaded
101 |         blob_id_downloaded = int(object_content["fields"]["blob_id"])
102 |         if num_to_blob_id(blob_id_downloaded) == blob_id:
103 |             print("Blob ID matches certificate!")
104 |         else:
105 |             print("Blob ID does not match")
106 | 
107 | finally:
108 |     os.unlink(tmp.name)
```

walrus-docs/examples/python/hello_walrus_webapi.py
```
1 | # Example of uploading and downloading a file to / from the Walrus service
2 | # using the walrus client web API facilities.
3 | #
4 | # Prerequisites:
5 | #
6 | # Run the Walrus client in daemon mode:
7 | '''
8 | ../CONFIG/bin/walrus --config ../CONFIG/config_dir/client_config.yaml daemon \
9 |     --bind-address 127.0.0.1:8899 \
10 |     --sub-wallets-dir ../CONFIG/wallets \
11 |     --n-clients 1
12 | '''
13 | 
14 | # Std lib imports
15 | import os
16 | import time
17 | 
18 | # External requests HTTP library
19 | import requests
20 | 
21 | ADDRESS = "127.0.0.1:8899"
22 | EPOCHS = "5"
23 | 
24 | 
25 | # Helper functions to upload a blob
26 | def upload_blob(ADDRESS, EPOCHS, data):
27 |     # Upload the data to the Walrus service  using a PUT request
28 |     store_url = f"http://{ADDRESS}/v1/blobs?epochs={EPOCHS}"
29 |     response = requests.put(store_url, data=data)
30 | 
31 |     # Assert the response status code
32 |     assert response.status_code == 200
33 |     blob_id = response.json()["newlyCreated"]["blobObject"]["blobId"]
34 |     return blob_id
35 | 
36 | 
37 | # Helper functions to download a blob
38 | def download_blob(ADDRESS, blob_id):
39 |     # Now read the same resource using the blob-id
40 |     read_url = f"http://{ADDRESS}/v1/blobs/{blob_id}"
41 |     response = requests.get(read_url)
42 | 
43 |     # Assert the response status code
44 |     assert response.status_code == 200
45 |     return response.content
46 | 
47 | 
48 | # Upload a random 1MB string then download it, and check it matches
49 | if __name__ == "__main__":
50 |     # Generate a 1MB blob of random data
51 |     random_data = os.urandom(1024 * 1024)
52 | 
53 |     # Upload the blob to the Walrus service
54 |     start_time = time.time()
55 |     blob_id = upload_blob(ADDRESS, EPOCHS, random_data)
56 |     upload_time = time.time()
57 | 
58 |     # Now download the same blob using the blob-id
59 |     data = download_blob(ADDRESS, blob_id)
60 |     assert data == random_data
61 |     download_time = time.time()
62 | 
63 |     # Print some information about the blob
64 |     print(f"Blob ID: {blob_id}")
65 |     print(f"Size {len(random_data)} bytes")
66 |     print(f"Upload time: {upload_time - start_time:.2f}s")
67 |     print(f"Download time: {download_time - upload_time:.2f}s")

1 | # Track Walrus storage related events on the Sui blockchain
2 | 
3 | import datetime
4 | 
5 | # Std lib imports
6 | import requests
7 | import re
8 | 
9 | from utils import num_to_blob_id, PATH_TO_WALRUS_CONFIG
10 | 
11 | system_object_id = re.findall(
12 |     r"system_object:[ ]*(.*)", open(PATH_TO_WALRUS_CONFIG).read()
13 | )[0]
14 | print(f"System object ID: {system_object_id}")
15 | 
16 | # Query the Walrus system object on Sui
17 | request = {
18 |     "jsonrpc": "2.0",
19 |     "id": 1,
20 |     "method": "sui_getObject",
21 |     "params": [
22 |         system_object_id,
23 |         {
24 |             "showType": True,
25 |             "showOwner": False,
26 |             "showPreviousTransaction": False,
27 |             "showDisplay": False,
28 |             "showContent": False,
29 |             "showBcs": False,
30 |             "showStorageRebate": False,
31 |         },
32 |     ],
33 | }
34 | response = requests.post("https://fullnode.testnet.sui.io:443", json=request)
35 | assert response.status_code == 200
36 | 
37 | system_object_content = response.json()["result"]["data"]
38 | walrus_package = re.findall("(0x[0-9a-f]+)::system", system_object_content["type"])[0]
39 | print(f"Walrus type: {walrus_package}")
40 | 
41 | # Query events for the appropriate Walrus type
42 | request = {
43 |     "jsonrpc": "2.0",
44 |     "id": 1,
45 |     "method": "suix_queryEvents",
46 |     "params": [
47 |         # Query by module type
48 |         {"MoveModule": {"package": walrus_package, "module": "blob"}},
49 |         None,
50 |         # Query the latest 100 events
51 |         100,
52 |         True, # Indicates descending order
53 |     ],
54 | }
55 | response = requests.post("https://fullnode.testnet.sui.io:443", json=request)
56 | assert response.status_code == 200
57 | 
58 | events = response.json()["result"]["data"]
59 | for event in events:
60 |     # Parse the Walrus event
61 |     tx_digest = event["id"]["txDigest"]
62 |     event_type = event["type"][68 + 13 :] # Skip the package & module prefix
63 |     parsed_event = event["parsedJson"]
64 |     blob_id = num_to_blob_id(int(parsed_event["blob_id"]))
65 |     timestamp_ms = int(event["timestampMs"])
66 |     time_date = datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(timestamp_ms / 1000.0)
67 | 
68 |     # For registered blobs get their size in bytes
69 |     if event_type == "BlobRegistered":
70 |         size = f"{parsed_event['size']}B"
71 |     else:
72 |         size = ""
73 | 
74 |     print(f"{time_date} {event_type:<15} {size:>10} {blob_id} Tx:{tx_digest:<48}")

1 | import base64
2 | 
3 | # Configure these paths to match your system
4 | FULL_NODE_URL = "https://fullnode.testnet.sui.io:443"
5 | PATH_TO_WALRUS = "../CONFIG/bin/walrus"
6 | PATH_TO_WALRUS_CONFIG = "../CONFIG/config_dir/client_config.yaml"
7 | 
8 | 
9 | # Convert a numeric (u256) blob_id to a base64 encoded Blob ID
10 | def num_to_blob_id(blob_id_num):
11 |     extracted_bytes = []
12 |     for i in range(32):
13 |         extracted_bytes += [blob_id_num & 0xFF]
14 |         blob_id_num = blob_id_num >> 8
15 |     assert blob_id_num == 0
16 |     blob_id_bytes = bytes(extracted_bytes)
17 |     encoded = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(blob_id_bytes)
18 |     return encoded.decode("ascii").strip("=")
19 | 
20 | 
21 | if __name__ == "__main__":
22 |     # A test case for the num_to_blob_id function
23 |     blob_id_num = (
24 |         46269954626831698189342469164469112511517843773769981308926739591706762839432
25 |     )
26 |     blob_id_base64 = "iIWkkUTzPZx-d1E_A7LqUynnYFD-ztk39_tP8MLdS2Y"
27 |     assert num_to_blob_id(blob_id_num) == blob_id_base64

1 | // Copyright (c) Mysten Labs, Inc.
2 | // SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
3 | 
4 | module book::buffer {
5 |     /// Error returned when the buffer is overflowed.
6 |     const EBufferOverflow: u64 = 0;
7 | 
8 |     /// The Buffer struct represents a growable buffer.
9 |     public struct Buffer {
10 |         data: vector<u8>,
11 |         expected_len: Option<u64>
12 |     }
13 | 
14 |     /// Creates a new empty buffer.
15 |     public fun new(): Buffer {
16 |         Buffer { data: vector[], expected_len: option::none() }
17 |     }
18 | 
19 |     /// Creates a new empty buffer with the specified capacity (in bytes).
20 |     /// If the buffer is overflowed, tx aborts with `EBufferOverflow`.
21 |     public fun alloc(len: u64): Buffer {
22 |         Buffer { data: vector[], expected_len: option::some(len) }
23 |     }
24 | 
25 |     /// Pushes the given data to the end of the buffer.
26 |     public fun push(self: &mut Buffer, data: vector<u8>) {
27 |         if (option::is_some(&self.expected_len)) {
28 |             let max_len = *option::borrow(&self.expected_len);
29 |             let future_len = self.len() + vector::length(&data);
30 |             assert!(future_len <= max_len, EBufferOverflow);
31 |         };
32 | 
33 |         vector::append(&mut self.data, data)
34 |     }
35 | 
36 |     /// Unwraps the buffer and returns the underlying vector.
37 |     public fun unwrap(self: Buffer): vector<u8> {
38 |         let Buffer { data, expected_len: _ } = self;
39 |         data
40 |     }
41 | 
42 |     /// Returns the length of the buffer.
43 |     public fun len(self: &Buffer): u64 {
44 |         vector::length(&self.data)
45 |     }
46 | 
47 |     /// Returns `true` if the buffer is empty.
48 |     public fun is_empty(self: &Buffer): bool {
49 |         vector::is_empty(&self.data)
50 |     }
51 | }

4 | module book::ticket {
5 |     /// A Ticket for an event or a service. Non-transferable by default and
6 |     /// the usage varies based on the application.
7 |     public struct Ticket<T: store + drop> has key {
8 |         id: UID,
9 |         used: bool,
10 |         metadata: T
11 |     }
12 | 
13 |     /// Create a new Ticket with the metadata and the context.
14 |     /// No need for a Witness here!
15 |     public fun new<T: store + drop>(metadata: T, ctx: &mut TxContext): Ticket<T> {
16 |         Ticket {
17 |             id: object::new(ctx),
18 |             used: false,
19 |             metadata
20 |         }
21 |     }
22 | 
23 |     /// Consume the Ticket. Requires a Witness of the metadata type.
24 |     /// May or may not be implemented by the application.
25 |     public fun consume<T: store + drop>(_meta: T, ticket: &mut Ticket<T>) {
26 |         ticket.used = true;
27 |     }
28 | 
29 |     /// Transfer the Ticket to another user. Requires a Witness of the metadata type.
30 |     /// May or may not be implemented by the application.
31 |     public fun transfer<T: store + drop>(_meta: T, ticket: Ticket<T>, to: address) {
32 |         transfer::transfer(ticket, to)
33 |     }
34 | 
35 |     /// Get the metadata of the Ticket.
36 |     public fun metadata<T: store + drop>(ticket: &Ticket<T>): &T {
37 |         &ticket.metadata
38 |     }
39 | 
40 |     /// Check if the Ticket has been used.
41 |     public fun is_used<T: store + drop>(ticket: &Ticket<T>): bool {
42 |         ticket.used
43 |     }
44 | }
